cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - physical and chemical properties of water
cards.a: Dissolved oxygen is low in stagnant ponds, deep wells and nutrient-rich (eutrophic) lakes, where decay uses oxygen faster than it is replaced.
cards.w: Moving, turbulent water mixes with air and stays oxygen-rich. Still water does not.

cards.t: Behaviour of minerals and rocks under deformation conditions
cards.a: Rock strength increases with confining pressure and decreases as temperature rises.
cards.w: Pressure presses cracks shut, so the rock is harder to break. Heat softens the rock so it flows more easily.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Ionic radius is the main control on substitution: ions of similar size (within about 15%) and balanced charge can replace one another in a crystal lattice (Goldschmidt's rules).
cards.w: Think of fitting a similar-sized brick into the same hole.

cards.a: Coalification (peat to lignite to bituminous coal to anthracite) releases methane, carbon dioxide, nitrogen and water as by-products while the coal becomes richer in carbon.
cards.w: The coal loses its volatile parts and keeps the carbon.

cards.a: Most of the methane in a coal seam is held by adsorption on the internal surfaces of coal micropores, not as free gas; lowering the pressure by pumping out water releases it.
cards.w: Gas molecules stick on the organic surface like a film.

cards.a: Fire clay (refractory clay) withstands temperatures of about 1500 C and above because of its high alumina content; fluxes such as iron oxide, lime and alkalis lower this resistance.
cards.w: Alumina melts at a very high temperature, so alumina-rich clay is heat-proof.

cards.a: Scheelite (CaWO4) and many uranium minerals fluoresce under ultraviolet light, so UV lamps are used for night prospecting and sorting of tungsten ore.
cards.w: Scheelite glows bright blue-white under short-wave UV.

cards.a: Gas hydrate is an ice-like water cage around gas molecules. Methane, ethane, CO2 and H2S form structure I; larger propane and isobutane form structure II.
cards.w: Bigger guest molecules need bigger cages.

cards.a: Taconite is a hard, low-grade banded iron formation of the Lake Superior region, made of magnetite (or hematite), iron silicates and chert, which is crushed and pelletised before smelting.
cards.w: Taconite is the American name for low-grade BIF ore.

cards.t: Classification and genesis of mineral deposits
cards.a: Placers form by winnowing (elutriation): running water or waves wash away the light grains and leave heavy, resistant minerals such as gold, cassiterite, ilmenite and monazite behind.
cards.w: Like washing rice: light bits float off, heavy bits stay.

cards.a: Deep-sea manganese nodules are concentric layers of manganese and iron oxides (such as todorokite and birnessite) around a small nucleus, and they carry nickel, copper and cobalt.
cards.w: They grow very slowly, like layers of an onion, around a shark tooth or rock fragment.

cards.a: Chromium, nickel and platinum-group metals are tied to ultramafic rocks, whereas tin and tungsten are tied to granites.
cards.w: Ultramafic magma is rich in Mg, Fe, Cr, Ni. Granite melts concentrate Sn, W, Li.

cards.t: Classification and genesis of mineral deposits
cards.a: Rare-metal (lithium-caesium-tantalum) pegmatites crystallise from melts rich in volatiles (water, fluorine, boron, phosphorus) and incompatible elements such as Li, Cs, Ta and Be.
cards.w: Volatiles make the melt runny, so crystals grow giant.

cards.t: Classification and genesis of mineral deposits
cards.a: The massive ore of volcanogenic massive sulphide (VMS) deposits is dominated by pyrite, with chalcopyrite as the main copper mineral (sphalerite and galena in zinc-lead types).
cards.w: VMS = pyrite-rich sea-floor sulphide mound.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: By the law of superposition, in an undisturbed sequence of sedimentary layers the lowest bed is the oldest and the topmost bed is the youngest.
cards.w: Steno's law: you lay new layers on top of old ones.

cards.a: A map is a scaled, two-dimensional representation of part of the Earth's surface; its scale is the ratio of map distance to ground distance.
cards.w: Scale 1:50,000 means 1 cm on the map is 50,000 cm (0.5 km) on the ground.

cards.a: Volcanic rock permeability varies: vesicular, jointed or rubbly-topped basalt can be a good aquifer, but dense massive lava (basalt or rhyolite) is nearly tight; unweathered igneous and metamorphic rocks are generally tight.
cards.w: Permeability comes from vesicles, joints, rubbly flow tops and lava tubes, not from rock name.

cards.a: A neutron probe measures soil moisture: fast neutrons from a source are slowed and scattered by hydrogen in soil water, and the count of slowed neutrons gives the water content.
cards.w: Hydrogen (in water) is the best neutron slower.

cards.a: The Indo-Gangetic alluvium is India's most productive aquifer system: thick sand-gravel beds, river, canal and rainfall recharge give very high yields and large groundwater resources.
cards.w: Think thick, loose sand-gravel plus big rivers.

cards.a: Evaporation absorbs about 590 calories per gram of water (latent heat of vaporisation near 15 C, about 2.47 MJ/kg) and continues until the air above is saturated.
cards.w: This heat comes from the water and surroundings, which is why evaporation cools.

cards.t: Specific yield, specific retention, porosity, hydraulic conductivity, transmissivity, storage coefficient
cards.a: For equal spheres, cubic packing gives the highest porosity (about 47.6%) and rhombohedral packing the lowest (about 26%).
cards.w: Rhombohedral packing nests spheres into each other's hollows.

cards.t: Specific yield, specific retention, porosity, hydraulic conductivity, transmissivity, storage coefficient
cards.a: A formation is isotropic if its hydraulic conductivity is the same in every direction at a point; it is anisotropic if the value changes with direction (in layered sediments horizontal K exceeds vertical K).
cards.w: Isotropic = same in all directions. Homogeneous = same at all places.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: The Bernoulli equation assumes ideal flow: the fluid is non-viscous (frictionless) and incompressible; groundwater velocity is so low that the velocity head is ignored.
cards.w: Real flow in pores loses energy to friction, so Darcy's law is used instead.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: A contact between an aquifer sand and a thick clay bed acts as an impermeable (barrier) boundary, whereas a river or lake in contact with the aquifer acts as a recharge boundary.
cards.w: Clay blocks water, a river supplies it.

cards.a: In crystalline rocks fractures and weathering are strongest near the surface, with sheet joints running parallel to it, so fracture density, aperture and permeability fall with depth.
cards.w: Overburden load closes fractures at depth.

cards.a: In carbonate rocks, burial compaction, cementation and recrystallisation change porosity and permeability (mostly reducing the primary pores), while later dissolution creates secondary porosity.
cards.w: Diagenesis can close pores; dissolution reopens them.

cards.t: Concepts of drainage basin and groundwater basin
cards.a: A groundwater divide is a crest (ridge) of the water table or potentiometric surface from which groundwater flows away in opposite directions.
cards.w: It is the underground equivalent of a ridge line.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Flow is in steady state when conditions, and so the stored mass of water, do not change with time; if any property such as head or temperature changes with time, the system is unsteady (transient).
cards.w: Steady = nothing changes with time. Transient = something does.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Types of wells and well construction
cards.a: Bored wells are made with hand or rotary augers in soft ground; they are shallow, commonly up to about 30 m deep (limit varies by textbook).
cards.w: Auger = a big screw that bores into soil.

cards.a: In the Standard Penetration Test, the N value is the number of blows of a 63.5 kg hammer needed to drive the split-spoon sampler through the last 300 mm of a 450 mm drive.
cards.w: N tells how dense or stiff a soil is. Engineering-geology item, outside the listed syllabus.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: In seismic refraction surveys, geophones placed on the ground detect waves refracted from layer boundaries; travel-time curves give layer velocities and depth to hard rock.
cards.w: Geophone = ground microphone.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: In neutron-capture (pulsed-neutron) logging, chlorine in saline water has a high thermal-neutron capture cross-section, so a high capture reading points to a saline water-bearing formation.
cards.w: Chlorine absorbs slow neutrons strongly.

cards.a: Sandstone shows a very wide range of water yield: weakly cemented, well-sorted sandstone is an excellent aquifer, but tightly cemented or clay-rich sandstone is almost tight unless fractured.
cards.w: Cement and clay fill the pores.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Well points, vacuum methods and electro-osmosis are used to lower the water table (dewatering) at construction sites; electro-osmosis suits fine-grained silts and clays.
cards.w: Electric current drags water through very fine pores.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - criteria for different uses
cards.a: Contaminated drinking water spreads diarrhoea, cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A and polio; polluted water is the main cause of water-borne disease in India.
cards.w: These diseases pass by the faecal-oral route.

cards.a: During artificial recharge the soil and aquifer material act as a natural filter, removing suspended matter and bacteria as water percolates down.
cards.w: This is called soil-aquifer treatment.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - physical and chemical properties of water
cards.a: Alkalinity of water, caused mainly by bicarbonate, carbonate and hydroxide, is reported in mg/L as equivalent calcium carbonate (CaCO3).
cards.w: Hardness is also reported as CaCO3.

cards.a: India is the world's largest user of groundwater, abstracting roughly a quarter of the global total, mostly for irrigation.
cards.w: Ahead of China and the USA.

cards.a: Munnar, in Idukki district at about 1,500 m, is an example of a plateau (the high-range upland) in the Western Ghats of Kerala.
cards.w: Kerala has highland, midland and lowland zones; Munnar is highland.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: The crystalline basement rocks of Kerala (charnockite, gneiss and khondalite) are Precambrian, mainly Archaean to Proterozoic in age.
cards.w: They are the oldest rocks of the state; sedimentary rocks are only Tertiary and Quaternary.

p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Prelims 2021 (Geology Paper II)
cards.a: The nebular hypothesis (Kant and Laplace) says the Sun and planets formed from one rotating cloud of gas and dust; it is the most widely accepted model.
cards.w: A spinning cloud flattens into a disc. This explains why all planets orbit in the same direction and nearly the same plane.

cards.a: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are terrestrial (rocky, dense) planets; Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are Jovian (large, low-density) planets. The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter.
cards.w: Near the hot young Sun only rock and metal could condense. Farther out, gas and ice could collect, making giant planets.

cards.a: The Earth is about 4.55 billion years old, an age first fixed by Clair Patterson (1956) from lead isotopes in meteorites.
cards.w: Earth's first rocks were destroyed by later melting and recycling. Meteorites formed at the same time and stayed unchanged, so they give the true age.

cards.a: Meteorites are stony, iron or stony-iron; stony chondrites are the most common falls, and iron meteorites show the Widmanstatten pattern.
cards.w: Iron meteorites are pieces of broken asteroid cores, so they hint at what Earth's core is made of. The pattern is an intergrowth of two iron-nickel alloys.

cards.a: Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the solar system, followed by helium and then oxygen.
cards.w: The Sun holds almost all the mass of the solar system and it is mostly hydrogen and helium.

cards.a: The mean density of the Earth is about 5.5 g/cm3, the highest of all planets, while surface rocks average only about 2.7 to 3.0 g/cm3.
cards.w: The gap proves the interior must be much denser than the crust. This was early evidence for a heavy iron core.

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
cards.a: Early Earth melted and differentiated: dense iron and nickel sank to form the core, and lighter silicates rose to form the mantle and crust.
cards.w: Heavy things sink and light things float in a molten body. This sorting is called differentiation (the 'iron catastrophe').

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
cards.a: P waves are compressional, the fastest, and travel through solids, liquids and gases; S waves are shear waves, slower, and travel only through solids.
cards.w: Liquids cannot resist a change of shape (no rigidity), so a shear wave dies in them. P = primary/push, S = secondary/shake.

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
cards.a: Love and Rayleigh waves are surface waves; they are slower than P and S waves but cause the most damage. Love waves are faster than Rayleigh waves.
cards.w: Surface waves keep their energy near the ground and have large amplitude. Rayleigh waves roll the ground like sea waves; Love waves shake it sideways.

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
cards.a: The Mohorovicic discontinuity (Moho) separates crust from mantle; P-wave velocity jumps there to about 8 km/s. It was discovered in 1909 from a Croatian earthquake.
cards.w: Mantle peridotite is denser and stiffer than crustal rock, so waves speed up suddenly on entering it.

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Prelims 2021 (Geology Paper II)
cards.a: The Conrad discontinuity separates the upper granitic continental crust (sial) from the lower basaltic crust (sima).
cards.w: It lies inside the continental crust, above the Moho. It is weak and not found everywhere, and is absent under oceans.

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
cards.a: The Gutenberg discontinuity at about 2,900 km depth separates the mantle from the outer core; P-wave velocity drops sharply and S waves stop.
cards.w: The waves pass from solid rock into liquid iron. Liquid has no rigidity, so S waves vanish and P waves slow down.

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
cards.a: The Lehmann discontinuity at about 5,150 km depth separates the liquid outer core from the solid inner core; Inge Lehmann found it in 1936.
cards.w: She saw weak P waves arriving inside the shadow zone. They had bounced off a solid inner core. Huge pressure keeps the inner core solid.

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
cards.a: The Repetti discontinuity separates upper and lower mantle; most Indian texts place it near 700 km (modern value 660 km), some older texts near 1,000 km.
cards.w: Memory order from top to bottom: Conrad, Moho, Repetti, Gutenberg, Lehmann ('Can My Rabbit Go Low').

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
cards.a: The P-wave shadow zone lies roughly between 105 and 145 degrees from the epicentre; direct S waves are absent beyond about 105 degrees.
cards.w: The liquid outer core bends (refracts) P waves and blocks S waves. The shadow zones are the main proof of a liquid outer core.

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
cards.a: R.D. Oldham of the Geological Survey of India gave the first seismic evidence for the Earth's core in 1906; Gutenberg later fixed its depth.
cards.w: Oldham studied records of the 1897 Assam earthquake and first separated P, S and surface waves. Link: Oldham = 'old' = first to find the core.

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
cards.a: The low velocity zone (LVZ), at roughly 100 to 250 km depth, marks the upper asthenosphere, where seismic waves slow down.
cards.w: The rock here is close to melting and has a tiny amount of melt, so it is weak and plastic. Rigid plates slide over this soft layer.

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
cards.a: The lithosphere is the rigid outer shell made of the crust plus the uppermost mantle, about 100 km thick on average; it is broken into plates.
cards.w: Crust and mantle are divided by composition. Lithosphere and asthenosphere are divided by strength (rigid versus plastic). Plates are lithosphere, not just crust.

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
cards.a: The core is mainly iron with some nickel; flow in the liquid outer core generates the Earth's magnetic field (geodynamo).
cards.w: Moving liquid metal carries electric currents, and currents make a magnetic field. The solid inner core cannot flow, so the outer core does this job.

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Mains 2020 (Geology Paper II)
cards.a: The upper mantle is peridotite (olivine and pyroxene). The 410 km discontinuity is a phase change of olivine to a denser spinel-type structure.
cards.w: Pressure squeezes olivine into a tighter crystal packing without changing its chemistry. At 660 km it changes again to still denser lower-mantle minerals.

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
cards.a: Suess named the Earth's layers by composition: SIAL (silica and aluminium, continental crust), SIMA (silica and magnesium, oceanic and lower crust) and NIFE (nickel and iron, core).
cards.w: Each name is built from the chemical symbols of its main elements: Si+Al, Si+Mg, Ni+Fe.

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
cards.a: The average geothermal gradient in the upper crust is about 25 to 30 degrees C per km of depth.
cards.w: Heat flows out from the hot interior and from radioactive decay in crustal rocks. The gradient is higher at ridges and volcanoes, lower in old shields.

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
cards.a: By weight, the crust's most abundant elements are oxygen, silicon, aluminium and iron, in that order; for the whole Earth, iron is first and oxygen second.
cards.w: The crust is made of silicate minerals (O + Si). The whole Earth includes the huge iron core, so iron moves to the top.

cards.a: Continental crust is thick (average about 35 to 40 km, up to about 70 km under Tibet), granitic and light (2.7 g/cm3); oceanic crust is thin (about 7 km), basaltic and denser (3.0 g/cm3).
cards.w: Light continental crust floats high and cannot sink into the mantle. Dense oceanic crust sits low and is the one that subducts.

cards.a: No oceanic crust is older than about 180 million years (Jurassic), but continental rocks are as old as about 4 billion years.
cards.w: Old ocean floor is destroyed at subduction zones, so it is always young. Continents are too light to subduct, so they keep very old rocks.

cards.a: Oceanic crust has three seismic layers: layer 1 sediments, layer 2 pillow basalts and sheeted dykes, and layer 3 gabbro, resting on mantle peridotite.
cards.w: Magma at a ridge erupts on the sea floor as pillow lava, feeds through dykes, and the rest cools slowly below as gabbro.

p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Prelims 2021 (Geology Paper II)
UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Mains 2020 (Geology Paper II)
cards.a: An ophiolite is a slice of oceanic lithosphere thrust onto land; Indian examples occur along the Indus-Tsangpo suture (Ladakh), the Naga Hills and the Andaman Islands.
cards.w: Ophiolites mark where an old ocean closed. Finding one in a mountain belt means a vanished ocean and a suture (join) between plates.

cards.t: Major tectonic features of the Oceanic and Continental crust
cards.a: A craton is the old, stable interior of a continent; it consists of a shield (exposed Precambrian basement) and a platform (basement under flat sedimentary cover).
cards.w: Cratons have not been folded for a very long time. Peninsular India is a shield area made of several cratons such as Dharwar and Bastar.

cards.t: Major tectonic features of the Oceanic and Continental crust
cards.a: The mid-ocean ridge system is the longest mountain chain on Earth, about 65,000 km long. Slow ridges (Mid-Atlantic) have a central rift valley; fast ridges (East Pacific Rise) are smooth.
cards.w: At slow ridges the crust is cooler and breaks along faults, making a valley. At fast ridges plenty of hot magma keeps the crest swollen and smooth.

cards.t: Major tectonic features of the Oceanic and Continental crust
cards.a: Deep-sea trenches mark subduction zones; the deepest point on Earth is the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench (about 11 km), western Pacific. Guyots are flat-topped seamounts.
cards.w: A trench forms where a plate bends and dives down. Guyots are old volcanic islands planed flat by waves and later sunk; Hess named them.

cards.t: Major tectonic features of the Oceanic and Continental crust
cards.a: Passive (Atlantic-type) continental margins are not plate boundaries and have few earthquakes; active (Pacific-type) margins have trenches, volcanoes and earthquakes. Both coasts of India are passive margins.
cards.w: At a passive margin the continent and the ocean floor belong to the same plate, so nothing grinds. At an active margin the ocean plate subducts.

cards.t: Major tectonic features of the Oceanic and Continental crust
cards.a: A triple junction is a point where three plates meet, as at Afar (Red Sea, Gulf of Aden, East African Rift); a failed rift arm is called an aulacogen.
cards.w: A dome over hot mantle cracks into three arms. Usually two arms open into an ocean and the third stops and fills with sediment.

cards.t: Continental drift - geological and geophysical evidence, mechanics, objections, present status
cards.a: Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912 and published 'The Origin of Continents and Oceans' in 1915; his supercontinent Pangaea was surrounded by the ocean Panthalassa.
cards.w: Pangaea means 'all land' and Panthalassa means 'all sea'. Wegener was a German meteorologist, not a geologist.

cards.t: Continental drift - geological and geophysical evidence, mechanics, objections, present status
cards.a: Pangaea split into Laurasia in the north and Gondwanaland in the south, separated by the Tethys Sea.
cards.w: Gondwanaland held South America, Africa, India, Australia and Antarctica. The Tethys later closed to form the Alps and Himalaya.

cards.t: Continental drift - geological and geophysical evidence, mechanics, objections, present status
cards.a: The jigsaw fit of South America and Africa is best along the continental slope, not the coastline, as Bullard's 1965 computer fit showed.
cards.w: The true edge of a continent is under water, at the slope. Coastlines change with sea level, so they fit poorly.

cards.t: Continental drift - geological and geophysical evidence, mechanics, objections, present status
p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Mains 2020 (Geology Paper II)
cards.a: Fossil evidence for drift: the seed fern Glossopteris on all Gondwana continents, the freshwater reptile Mesosaurus in Brazil and South Africa, and the land reptile Lystrosaurus in Africa, India and Antarctica.
cards.w: These plants and animals could not cross wide salty oceans. So the lands must once have been joined.

cards.t: Continental drift - geological and geophysical evidence, mechanics, objections, present status
cards.a: Permo-Carboniferous glacial deposits (tillites) occur in South America, Africa, India, Australia and Antarctica; in India this is the Talchir boulder bed.
cards.w: Ice cannot form at the equator at sea level. These lands must have been together near the South Pole at that time.

cards.t: Continental drift - geological and geophysical evidence, mechanics, objections, present status
cards.a: Wegener said drift was driven by a pole-fleeing force and tidal force; Harold Jeffreys objected that these forces are far too weak.
cards.w: This lack of a working mechanism was the main reason the theory was rejected for decades. Wegener also wrongly had continents ploughing through ocean floor.

cards.t: Continental drift - geological and geophysical evidence, mechanics, objections, present status
cards.a: Arthur Holmes (around 1930) proposed that thermal convection currents in the mantle carry the continents.
cards.w: Hot mantle rises, spreads sideways and sinks, like boiling soup. This gave drift its first workable engine, later used in sea-floor spreading.

cards.t: Continental drift - geological and geophysical evidence, mechanics, objections, present status
cards.a: F.B. Taylor suggested drift in 1910 to explain mountain belts; Alexander du Toit supported Wegener in 'Our Wandering Continents' (1937).
cards.w: Du Toit, a South African geologist, matched rocks of South Africa and South America in detail. Taylor came before Wegener but had little evidence.

cards.t: Continental drift - geological and geophysical evidence, mechanics, objections, present status
cards.a: Present status: drift is accepted as part of plate tectonics; continents ride passively on lithospheric plates, and motions of a few cm per year are measured directly by GPS.
cards.w: Palaeomagnetism and sea-floor spreading in the 1950s and 1960s revived the idea. The continents do not plough through the sea floor; the whole plate moves.

cards.t: Gravity and magnetic anomalies at Mid-ocean ridges, deep sea trenches, continental shield areas and mountain chains
cards.a: Bouguer gravity anomalies are strongly negative over high mountain chains and positive over deep oceans.
cards.w: Mountains have deep roots of light crust (mass deficit below). Under oceans, dense mantle lies close to the surface (mass excess).

cards.t: Gravity and magnetic anomalies at Mid-ocean ridges, deep sea trenches, continental shield areas and mountain chains
p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Mains 2020 (Geology Paper II)
cards.a: Deep-sea trenches show very large negative free-air gravity anomalies, first measured by Vening Meinesz in a submarine; the adjacent island arc shows a positive anomaly.
cards.w: The trench is a deep hole filled with light water and sediment, held down by the sinking plate. It is not in isostatic balance.

cards.t: Gravity and magnetic anomalies at Mid-ocean ridges, deep sea trenches, continental shield areas and mountain chains
cards.a: Over mid-ocean ridges the free-air gravity anomaly is close to zero, and the Bouguer anomaly is lower over the crest than over the flanks.
cards.w: The ridge stands high because hot, light mantle lies below it. The extra height is balanced by the low density beneath (isostatic compensation).

cards.t: Gravity and magnetic anomalies at Mid-ocean ridges, deep sea trenches, continental shield areas and mountain chains
cards.a: Shield areas once covered by ice sheets (Canada, Fennoscandia) show negative gravity anomalies and are still rising, a process called post-glacial rebound.
cards.w: The ice pushed the crust down. The ice melted fast but the thick mantle flows back slowly, so the land is still rising. This is isostasy in action.

cards.t: Gravity and magnetic anomalies at Mid-ocean ridges, deep sea trenches, continental shield areas and mountain chains
p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Mains 2020 (Geology Paper II)
cards.a: Magnetic anomalies on the ocean floor form linear stripes, parallel to and symmetric about the mid-ocean ridge; Vine and Matthews (and Morley) explained them in 1963.
cards.w: New basalt at the ridge records the field direction of its time. The field reverses and the floor spreads both ways, giving mirror-image stripes.

cards.a: The Curie point is the temperature above which a mineral loses its permanent magnetism; it is about 580 degrees C for magnetite and about 680 degrees C for hematite.
cards.w: Heat shakes the atoms so their tiny magnets cannot stay lined up. Magnetite is the chief magnetic mineral in rocks.

cards.a: Lavas gain thermoremanent magnetism (TRM) on cooling below the Curie point; sediments gain detrital remanent magnetism (DRM) as magnetic grains settle and align.
cards.w: TRM is strong and stable, so basalts are the best recorders. A third type, chemical (CRM), forms when magnetic minerals grow in the rock.

cards.a: Palaeolatitude is found from magnetic inclination I using tan I = 2 tan (latitude); inclination is 0 degrees at the magnetic equator and 90 degrees at the poles.
cards.w: A compass needle free to tilt lies flat at the equator and points straight down at the pole. The frozen tilt in a rock tells where it formed.

cards.a: Apparent polar wander (APW) paths differ from continent to continent, which shows the continents moved, not the pole; Runcorn showed this for Europe and North America in the 1950s.
cards.w: The Earth has only one north magnetic pole at a time. Two different paths can only be merged by moving the continents back together.

cards.a: The present normal polarity chron is the Brunhes; before it came the reversed Matuyama chron. The Brunhes-Matuyama boundary is about 0.78 million years old.
cards.w: Order going back in time: Brunhes (normal), Matuyama (reversed), Gauss (normal), Gilbert (reversed). Hook: 'Big Men Get Going'.

cards.a: Harry Hess proposed sea-floor spreading ('History of Ocean Basins', 1962); Robert Dietz coined the term 'sea-floor spreading' in 1961.
cards.w: New ocean floor forms at ridges, moves away like a conveyor belt and is destroyed at trenches. Hess called his own idea 'geopoetry'.

cards.a: J. Tuzo Wilson introduced the hotspot idea (1963), transform faults (1965) and the Wilson cycle of opening and closing of ocean basins.
cards.w: One name, three big ideas. A transform fault links two offset ridge segments and lets plates slide past each other.

cards.a: Plate tectonics was formulated in 1967-68 by Morgan, McKenzie and Parker, and Le Pichon; the Pacific is the largest plate.
cards.w: It grew out of Hess's seafloor spreading (1962) and Wilson's transform faults (1965).

p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Mains 2020 (Geology Paper II)
cards.a: Plate boundaries are divergent (constructive, e.g. Mid-Atlantic Ridge), convergent (destructive, e.g. Andes) and transform (conservative, e.g. San Andreas Fault).
cards.w: Crust is made at divergent, destroyed at convergent, and neither made nor destroyed at transform boundaries. San Andreas is a right-lateral fault.

cards.a: Convergence is of three kinds: ocean-ocean (Mariana, Japan: island arcs), ocean-continent (Andes: continental volcanic arc) and continent-continent (Himalaya, Alps: fold mountains without active volcanoes).
cards.w: Volcanoes need a sinking ocean plate to release water and melt the mantle. In continent-continent collision nothing subducts deeply, so volcanism stops.

cards.a: The main forces that move plates are slab pull, ridge push and mantle drag; slab pull is the strongest.
cards.w: The cold, dense plate sinking at a trench pulls the rest of the plate behind it. Plates with long subducting edges (Pacific) move fastest.

cards.a: Wilson cycle stages with examples: embryonic (East African Rift), juvenile (Red Sea), mature (Atlantic), declining (Pacific), terminal (Mediterranean) and suture (Himalaya).
cards.w: An ocean is born from a rift, widens, then shrinks by subduction and finally closes in a collision. Each stage has a living example today.

p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Prelims 2021 (Geology Paper II)
cards.a: Black smokers are hydrothermal vents at mid-ocean ridges where hot, metal sulphide-rich water jets into cold sea water.
cards.w: Sea water seeps into hot new crust, picks up metals and returns. On meeting cold water the sulphides fall out as black 'smoke'.

p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Prelims 2021 (Geology Paper II)
cards.a: The world's largest earthquakes are megathrust events on the contact between the subducting and overriding plates; the largest recorded is Chile 1960 (Mw 9.5).
cards.w: This contact is a huge, gently dipping fault surface. A bigger rupture area gives a bigger earthquake, and it often lifts the sea floor to cause tsunamis.

cards.t: Island arcs, Oceanic islands and volcanic arcs
cards.a: The Wadati-Benioff zone is the inclined zone of earthquake foci that follows a subducting slab down to about 700 km depth.
cards.w: The cold sinking plate stays brittle and keeps breaking as it goes down. Plotting the foci draws the shape of the slab.

cards.t: Island arcs, Oceanic islands and volcanic arcs
cards.a: An island arc is a curved chain of volcanic islands on the overriding plate, parallel to a trench and convex towards the ocean; examples are Japan, the Aleutians, the Marianas and the Andaman-Sunda arc.
cards.w: It forms at ocean-ocean convergence. The arc shape comes from a flat slab bending into a sphere, like a dent in a ping-pong ball.

cards.t: Island arcs, Oceanic islands and volcanic arcs
cards.a: Andesite is the typical lava of volcanic arcs above subduction zones; the 'Andesite Line' around the Pacific separates basaltic ocean-floor volcanoes from andesitic marginal ones.
cards.w: Water from the sinking slab melts the mantle wedge, and the magma changes on its way up through the crust. Ridges and ocean islands give basalt instead.

cards.t: Island arcs, Oceanic islands and volcanic arcs
cards.a: From ocean to land, an arc-trench system has: trench, accretionary prism, fore-arc basin, volcanic arc and back-arc basin. The Andaman Sea and the Sea of Japan are back-arc basins.
cards.w: The accretionary prism is sediment scraped off the sinking plate. Behind the arc the crust stretches and may open a small ocean (back-arc).

cards.t: Island arcs, Oceanic islands and volcanic arcs
cards.a: The Hawaiian-Emperor chain is a hotspot track: islands get older towards the northwest, showing the Pacific plate moved northwest over a fixed mantle plume. Morgan proposed mantle plumes in 1971.
cards.w: The plume stays put while the plate slides over it, like paper moved over a candle. The active volcanoes are at the young southeast end.

cards.t: Island arcs, Oceanic islands and volcanic arcs
cards.a: Barren Island in the Andaman Sea is India's only active volcano; nearby Narcondam is dormant. Both belong to the Andaman-Sunda volcanic arc.
cards.w: The Indian plate subducts beneath the Burma plate here. The same arc continues south into the volcanoes of Sumatra and Java.

cards.a: The term 'isostasy' was coined by the American geologist Clarence Dutton in 1889.
cards.w: Isostasy means 'equal standing': the crust floats in balance on the denser, plastic mantle, like wood blocks on water.

cards.a: Airy's model: crustal blocks have the same density but different thickness, so high mountains have deep roots.
cards.w: Like icebergs: the taller the block, the deeper it sinks. Seismic studies confirm thick crust under mountains. Hook: Airy = roots.

cards.a: Pratt's model: crustal blocks have different densities but reach down to one uniform level of compensation; higher blocks are made of lighter rock.
cards.w: Pratt (Archdeacon of Calcutta) analysed Survey of India data: the deflection difference between Kaliana and Kalianpur was about 5 seconds of arc against 15 calculated. Hook: Pratt = density.

cards.a: Orogeny is mountain building in long narrow belts by folding, thrusting, metamorphism and magmatism; epeirogeny is broad, gentle uplift or sinking of large areas without much folding (term by G.K. Gilbert).
cards.w: Oros = mountain, epeiros = mainland. Orogeny acts mostly sideways (compression); epeirogeny acts mostly up and down.

p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Prelims 2021 (Geology Paper II)
cards.a: Major orogenies in time order: Caledonian (Ordovician-Silurian to early Devonian), Hercynian or Variscan (Carboniferous-Permian) and Alpine-Himalayan (Cenozoic).
cards.w: Alphabet hook: C, H, A in time order is 'CHA'. The Himalaya belong to the youngest, the Alpine cycle.

cards.a: The geosyncline idea came from James Hall (1859) and the name from J.D. Dana (1873); it explained mountains as uplifted thick sediment troughs and is now replaced by plate tectonics.
cards.w: It could not explain why the trough was squeezed. Plate collision supplies that sideways force.

cards.a: Circum-Pacific belt releases about 80% of earthquake energy (about 68% of earthquakes by number in some Indian texts); Alpine-Himalayan belt is second (about 15-21%); mid-ocean ridges third.
cards.w: The Pacific is ringed by subduction zones, which store and release the most strain. Ridges give only small, shallow shocks.

cards.a: Earthquakes are classed by focal depth as shallow (0-70 km), intermediate (70-300 km) and deep (300-700 km); deep-focus earthquakes occur only in subduction zones.
cards.w: Normal mantle at that depth is too hot and soft to break. Only a cold sinking slab is brittle enough.

cards.a: Intraplate earthquakes occur far from plate boundaries, on old weak zones; the 1993 Latur (Killari) earthquake in Maharashtra, Mw 6.2, struck the stable Peninsular shield.
cards.w: Plate-edge stress travels into the interior and reactivates ancient faults. Such quakes are rare but deadly because buildings are not designed for them.

cards.a: The elastic rebound theory of earthquakes was given by H.F. Reid after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake.
cards.w: Rocks on both sides of a fault bend slowly like a stick. When they snap and spring back, the stored energy is released as an earthquake.

cards.a: Magnitude (Richter, 1935) measures energy at the source; intensity (Modified Mercalli, I to XII) measures effects at a place. One magnitude unit means 10 times the amplitude and about 32 times the energy.
cards.w: One earthquake has one magnitude but many intensities. Lines joining places of equal intensity are isoseismals.

cards.a: Fault type follows boundary type: shallow normal-fault earthquakes at ridges, strike-slip at transform faults, and thrust earthquakes (shallow to deep) at subduction zones.
cards.w: Plates pull apart at ridges, slide past at transforms and push together at trenches. First-motion studies by Sykes (1967) confirmed this.

cards.a: On an oceanic transform fault, earthquakes occur only on the segment between the two offset ridge crests; the fracture zone beyond is seismically quiet.
cards.w: Only between the ridge crests do the two sides move in opposite directions. Beyond, both sides belong to the same plate and move together.

cards.a: India broke away from Gondwanaland in steps: from Antarctica-Australia about 130 Ma, from Madagascar about 88 Ma, and from the Seychelles about 65 Ma.
cards.w: The 88 Ma event left the columnar rhyolites of St. Mary's Islands (Karnataka coast). The 65 Ma event goes with the Deccan Traps.

cards.a: India drifted north very fast, about 15-20 cm/year, and began colliding with Eurasia about 50 million years ago (Eocene); it still converges at about 5 cm/year.
cards.w: The collision closed the Tethys Sea and slowed India down. The continuing push keeps raising the Himalaya and causes its earthquakes.

cards.a: The Deccan Traps erupted about 66 million years ago, at the Cretaceous-Palaeogene boundary, when India passed over the Reunion hotspot.
cards.w: The plume head gave a huge burst of flood basalt (tholeiite). The hotspot today lies under Reunion Island in the Indian Ocean.

p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Mains 2020 (Geology Paper II)
cards.a: The Chagos-Laccadive Ridge (with Lakshadweep) is the track of the Reunion hotspot; the Ninetyeast Ridge and the Rajmahal Traps are linked to the Kerguelen hotspot.
cards.w: As India moved north, each fixed hotspot drew a line of volcanoes on the moving plate. West side = Reunion, east side = Kerguelen.

p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Prelims 2021 (Geology Paper II)
cards.a: The Indus-Tsangpo Suture Zone (ITSZ) marks the line where the Indian plate joined the Eurasian plate; it contains ophiolites, remnants of the Tethys ocean floor.
cards.w: A suture is the scar where an ocean closed. It runs along the Indus and Tsangpo (upper Brahmaputra) river valleys.

cards.a: Himalayan thrusts from south to north: Himalayan Frontal Thrust (Siwalik over plains), Main Boundary Thrust (Lesser Himalaya over Siwalik) and Main Central Thrust (Greater Himalaya over Lesser Himalaya).
cards.w: Thrusts get younger southwards as deformation moves towards the plains. Hook from the plains upward: F-B-C (Frontal, Boundary, Central).

cards.a: Indian plate boundaries: Himalayan collision zone in the north, Andaman-Sunda subduction zone in the east, Chaman transform fault in the west, and Carlsberg-Central Indian Ridge in the south-west.
cards.w: All three boundary types surround India: convergent (north, east), transform (west, a left-lateral fault in Pakistan-Afghanistan) and divergent (ocean ridge).

cards.a: As of March 2026, India's seismic code in force is IS 1893 (Part 1): 2016, with four zones: II (low), III, IV and V (highest). Zone I was merged into Zone II in 2002.
cards.w: A 2025 revision added a new Zone VI for the Himalayan arc, but BIS withdrew it on 3 March 2026 and restored the 2016 map. Recheck before the exam.

cards.a: Zone V (IS 1893: 2016) covers north-east India, parts of Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand and north Bihar, the Rann of Kutch and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Kerala is in Zone III.
cards.w: Zone V follows the plate boundary (Himalaya, Andaman arc) plus the active Kutch rift. Kerala is on the stable shield, so its hazard is moderate.

cards.a: 1897 Shillong earthquake (M 8.7 in older texts, revised Mw about 8.1) was studied by R.D. Oldham; the 1950 Assam-Tibet earthquake (Mw 8.6) is the largest instrumentally recorded on land.
cards.w: Both struck the north-east, where the plate bends around the eastern Himalayan corner. The 1950 shock came on 15 August, Independence Day.

cards.a: The 1967 Koyna earthquake in Maharashtra is the classic case of reservoir-induced seismicity.
cards.w: Water filled behind the Koyna dam added load and seeped into faults, making them slip. Shocks began only after the reservoir was filled.

cards.a: The Bhuj earthquake of 26 January 2001 (Mw 7.7) occurred in the Kutch rift of Gujarat, an intraplate region placed in Zone V.
cards.w: Kutch is an old rift now being squeezed by the northward push of India. It is far from the plate boundary but very active.

cards.a: The 1819 Kutch earthquake raised a long low ridge called the Allah Bund ('dam of God') across the Rann of Kutch.
cards.w: The fault lifted the ground and blocked a branch of the Indus river like a dam. It is a famous example of land uplift by an earthquake.

cards.a: The Sumatra-Andaman earthquake of 26 December 2004 (Mw 9.1-9.3) was a megathrust event where the Indian plate subducts beneath the Burma plate; it caused the Indian Ocean tsunami.
cards.w: About 1,300 km of the plate contact slipped and lifted the sea floor. The tsunami hit the Andaman-Nicobar Islands, Tamil Nadu and the Kerala coast.

cards.a: The Western Ghats are interpreted as the uplifted edge (great escarpment) of a rifted passive margin, formed after India separated from Madagascar and the Seychelles.
cards.w: When a continent rifts, its edge is lifted and then worn back as a steep west-facing scarp. So the Ghats are not fold mountains.

cards.a: The strongest instrumentally recorded earthquake in Kerala is the Erattupetta (Kottayam-Idukki) earthquake of 12 December 2000, magnitude about 5.
cards.w: Kerala has only mild intraplate shocks along old lineaments. This event is the usual example quoted for Kerala's Zone III status.

cards.a: The planetesimal hypothesis (Chamberlin and Moulton) and the tidal hypothesis (Jeans and Jeffreys) both needed a passing star to pull matter out of the Sun to make the planets.
cards.w: These are 'catastrophic' theories; the nebular theory is 'evolutionary'. They are rejected because such close star encounters are extremely rare.

cards.a: The Earth is an oblate spheroid: the equatorial radius (about 6,378 km) is about 21 km longer than the polar radius (about 6,357 km); the mean radius is 6,371 km.
cards.w: The Earth's spin throws material outward at the equator, so it bulges there and is flattened at the poles.

cards.a: The giant impact hypothesis says the Moon formed from debris thrown out when a Mars-sized body (Theia) struck the early Earth about 4.5 billion years ago.
cards.w: It explains why Moon rocks are so like Earth's mantle and why the Moon has only a very small iron core.

cards.a: Heat flow is highest at mid-ocean ridge crests and falls as the sea floor gets older; it is very low at trenches and high again over the volcanic arc and back-arc basin.
cards.w: Hot mantle rises at ridges; a cold slab sinks at trenches and chills the area. Magma under the arc brings heat back up.

cards.a: Ocean depth increases with the age of the sea floor, roughly with the square root of age; ridge crests lie at about 2.5 km depth and old abyssal plains at 5 to 6 km.
cards.w: As new lithosphere moves away from the ridge it cools, shrinks and gets denser, so it sits lower on the asthenosphere.

cards.a: The seven major plates are the Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian and Antarctic; Nazca, Cocos, Philippine, Arabian, Caribbean, Scotia and Juan de Fuca are smaller plates.
cards.w: Memory hook: the major plates carry the names of continents or of the Pacific Ocean. Any other name in a list is a minor plate.

p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Prelims 2021 (Geology Paper II)
cards.a: Trench (slab) rollback is the retreat of the trench and slab hinge towards the ocean side as the slab sinks steeply; it stretches the overriding plate and opens back-arc basins.
cards.w: An old, heavy slab sinks faster than the plates converge, so the bend (hinge) moves backwards. The upper plate is pulled along and thins.

cards.t: Island arcs, Oceanic islands and volcanic arcs
cards.a: A volcanic arc forms above the place where the subducting slab reaches about 100 to 150 km depth; water driven out of the slab lowers the melting point of the mantle wedge above it.
cards.w: This is 'flux melting': water acts like salt on ice. The slab itself mostly does not melt; the hot mantle above it does.

cards.t: Island arcs, Oceanic islands and volcanic arcs
cards.a: Iceland is an oceanic island sitting on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge above a hotspot, so the spreading ridge is exposed on land there; Yellowstone is a hotspot beneath a continent.
cards.w: Ridge plus plume together make far more lava than a normal ridge, enough to build the island above sea level.

cards.a: Isostasy grew out of Everest's survey of India: between Kalianpur and Kaliana the measured plumb-line deflection (5.24 seconds of arc) was only one-third of the 15.89 seconds Pratt calculated for the Himalaya's pull.
cards.w: The mountains attracted the plumb-bob less than their visible mass should. So there must be a mass deficit (light material) beneath them.

cards.a: In Airy isostasy, root thickness = height x crust density / (mantle density - crust density); with densities 2.7 and 3.3 g/cm3 the root is 4.5 times the height of the mountain.
cards.w: The extra weight of the mountain must equal the weight 'saved' by light root replacing heavy mantle. 2.7 / 0.6 = 4.5.

cards.a: Heiskanen's isostasy model combines the Airy and Pratt ideas; Vening Meinesz's regional model says a strong elastic lithosphere bends and spreads a load over a wide area.
cards.w: Airy and Pratt assume each block floats on its own (local compensation). Real lithosphere is stiff, so it flexes like a plank under a weight.

cards.a: In Kober's geosynclinal theory the rigid forelands are 'kratogen', the mountain belt is 'orogen', and a plateau caught between two marginal ranges is a 'Zwischengebirge' (median mass), such as the Tibetan Plateau.
cards.w: Kober pictured two rigid blocks squeezing a sediment-filled trough between them. The squeezed edges rise as ranges; the middle may stay as a high plateau.

cards.a: An earthquake epicentre is located from the S-P arrival time gap at a minimum of three seismograph stations; a longer gap means a more distant earthquake.
cards.w: Each station gives only a distance, which is a circle on the map. Three circles cross at one point.

cards.a: Himalayan zones from south to north: Sub-Himalaya (Siwalik), Lesser Himalaya, Greater Himalaya, Tethys Himalaya, then the Indus-Tsangpo suture. The South Tibetan Detachment, a normal fault, separates the Greater and Tethys Himalaya.
cards.w: Each zone is a slice of the old Indian margin stacked by thrusts. The detachment on top let the deep Greater Himalayan rocks squeeze out southward.

cards.a: The Himalayan arc ends in two sharp hairpin bends called syntaxes: the western syntaxis at Nanga Parbat and the eastern syntaxis at Namcha Barwa.
cards.w: The two corners of the Indian plate dig into Asia like the corners of a wedge, and the mountain ranges wrap around them.

cards.a: The 1905 Kangra and 1934 Bihar-Nepal earthquakes were great Himalayan thrust events; the unbroken stretch between their rupture zones is called the central seismic gap.
cards.w: A seismic gap is a part of an active fault that has not slipped for a long time. Strain keeps building there, so a great earthquake is expected.

cards.a: The Main Himalayan Thrust is the gently north-dipping plate-contact fault (decollement) into which the Frontal, Boundary and Central thrusts merge at depth; it ruptured in the 2015 Gorkha (Nepal) earthquake, Mw 7.8.
cards.w: India slides under the Himalaya along this one basal fault. The thrusts seen at the surface are branches (splays) rising from it.

cards.a: The Indian and Australian plates are separated by a wide, diffuse zone of deformation in the equatorial Indian Ocean; the Mw 8.6 strike-slip earthquake of April 2012 off Sumatra occurred within it.
cards.w: India is slowed by the Himalayan collision while Australia still moves freely into the Sunda trench, so the old single plate is breaking in between.

cards.t: Major tectonic features of the Oceanic and Continental crust
cards.a: The Indian Ocean ridges form an inverted Y: the Central Indian Ridge, the Southwest Indian Ridge and the Southeast Indian Ridge meet at the Rodrigues Triple Junction.
cards.w: Three plates (African, Indo-Australian, Antarctic) meet there, so three spreading ridges must join at one point.

cards.a: In IS 1893 (Part 1): 2016, Zone II matches MSK intensity VI or less, Zone III VII, Zone IV VIII and Zone V IX or more; the zone factors are 0.10, 0.16, 0.24 and 0.36.
cards.w: MSK is an intensity (shaking effect) scale. The zone factor is the expected peak ground shaking as a fraction of gravity, used in building design.

cards.a: Under the 2002/2016 BIS zoning map, about 59% of India's land is in Zones III to V: roughly 11% in Zone V, 18% in Zone IV and 30% in Zone III; the remaining 41% is Zone II.
cards.w: Hook: nearly three-fifths of India can get moderate to severe shaking. The highest zone is the smallest in area.

cards.t: Gravity and magnetic anomalies at Mid-ocean ridges, deep sea trenches, continental shield areas and mountain chains
cards.a: Old, stable continental shields are close to isostatic balance, so their isostatic and free-air gravity anomalies are small (near zero), unlike trenches and young mountain belts.
cards.w: Shields have been worn flat and left undisturbed for a very long time, so they have had time to settle into floating balance.

cards.a: In Goldich's weathering series, olivine weathers fastest and quartz is the most resistant among the common rock-forming minerals.
cards.w: It follows the same order as Bowen's reaction series. Minerals that crystallise first, at the highest temperature, are the least stable at the cool, wet surface.

cards.a: Exfoliation is the peeling of rock in curved sheets, caused mainly by pressure release (unloading) when the overlying rock is eroded away.
cards.w: Granite formed at depth expands when its load is removed and cracks parallel to the surface. This gives rounded exfoliation domes.

cards.a: Frost wedging breaks rock because water expands by about 9% in volume when it freezes inside cracks.
cards.w: It works best where temperature crosses 0 degrees C again and again, as in high mountains. It makes the angular scree (loose rock debris) below cliffs.

cards.a: Hydrolysis is the main chemical weathering process of silicate minerals; it changes feldspar into clay minerals such as kaolinite.
cards.w: Hydrogen ions in slightly acid water replace the K, Na and Ca of feldspar. The leftover aluminium-silicon part becomes clay.

cards.a: The clay formed depends on leaching: smectite (montmorillonite) with poor drainage, kaolinite with good drainage, and gibbsite (bauxite) with extreme leaching.
cards.w: More water passing through removes more silica and bases. What stays behind becomes richer in alumina step by step.

cards.a: A full soil profile from top to bottom is: O (organic litter), A (topsoil), E (leached layer), B (subsoil of accumulation), C (weathered parent material), R (bedrock).
cards.w: Each horizon (layer) records a different job: adding humus, losing material, gaining material, and slowly breaking the rock.

cards.a: Eluviation is the washing out of clay, iron and humus from the A and E horizons; illuviation is their deposition in the B horizon.
cards.w: Hook: E for Exit (eluviation), I for In (illuviation). So the B horizon is the zone of accumulation.

cards.a: The five soil-forming factors (Jenny, 1941) are climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time; climate is usually the most important.
cards.w: Hook: CLORPT. Given enough time, the same climate makes similar soils even on different rocks.

cards.a: Laterite is a residual product of intense tropical weathering: silica and bases are leached out, and iron and aluminium oxides are left behind.
cards.w: It needs heat, heavy rain, good drainage and alternating wet and dry seasons. That is why it caps the midlands of Kerala.

cards.a: Francis Buchanan named laterite in 1807 from Angadipuram in Malappuram district, Kerala; the name comes from the Latin 'later', meaning brick.
cards.w: The soft rock is cut into blocks that harden in air and are used as bricks. GSI keeps a National Geological Monument at Angadipuram.

cards.a: Black cotton soil (regur) forms mainly on Deccan basalt and is rich in montmorillonite clay, so it swells when wet and cracks deeply when dry.
cards.w: Montmorillonite takes water between its layers and expands. This 'self-ploughing' soil holds moisture well but damages buildings.

cards.a: In the Indo-Gangetic plain, khadar is the newer alluvium of the present flood plains; bhangar is the older alluvium on higher ground, with kankar nodules.
cards.w: Khadar is renewed by floods every year, so it is more fertile. Kankar means lime (calcium carbonate) lumps.

cards.a: Alluvial soil is the most widespread soil group in India, while laterite soil is the most widespread soil in Kerala.
cards.w: The great northern plains and deltas are all river-laid alluvium. Kerala's hot, wet climate turns most midland rock into laterite.

cards.a: Mass wasting is the downslope movement of rock and soil under gravity alone, without a transporting agent such as a river, wind or glacier.
cards.w: Water only adds weight and cuts friction; it does not carry the material. That is the difference from erosion.

cards.a: Varnes (1978) classified slope movements by type of movement (fall, topple, slide, spread, flow) and type of material (rock, debris, earth).
cards.w: Names are made by joining the two parts: rock fall, debris flow, earth slide.

cards.a: Creep is the slowest mass movement; its signs are tilted poles and fences, curved tree trunks and down-bent ends of strata.
cards.w: The soil moves a few millimetres a year, too slow to see. Only its long-term effects on fixed objects show it.

cards.a: Solifluction is the slow downslope flow of water-soaked soil over frozen ground, typical of periglacial (cold, near-glacier) regions.
cards.w: In summer only the top layer thaws. Water cannot drain into the frozen layer below, so the soggy top layer slides.

cards.a: A slump is a rotational slide on a curved, concave-up surface; the slipped block tilts backward and leaves a curved scarp at its head.
cards.w: Compare: a translational slide moves on a flat plane such as a bedding or joint surface, with no back-tilting.

cards.a: Heavy rain triggers landslides mainly by raising pore-water pressure, which lowers the effective stress and shear strength of the slope material.
cards.w: Kerala's monsoon debris flows ('urul pottal') in the Western Ghats work this way, e.g. Pettimudi 2020 and Mundakkai-Chooralmala (Wayanad) 2024.

cards.a: Chemical weathering dominates in hot, humid climates; physical weathering dominates in cold climates and in deserts.
cards.w: Chemical reactions need water and speed up with heat. Where water is frozen or missing, only mechanical breaking is left.

cards.a: Peltier (1950) defined nine morphogenetic regions, each with its own typical landform processes, using mean annual temperature and mean annual rainfall.
cards.w: The nine are glacial, periglacial, boreal, maritime, selva, moderate, savanna, semi-arid and arid. Idea: climate decides which process is boss.

cards.a: Limestone is a weak, valley-forming rock in humid climates but a strong, cliff-forming rock in arid climates.
cards.w: Limestone fails mainly by solution, which needs water. With little rain it resists better than most other rocks.

cards.a: W. M. Davis (1899) said a landscape is a function of structure, process and stage (time); this is the 'geographical cycle' or normal cycle of erosion.
cards.w: Hook: SPS = Structure, Process, Stage. 'Normal' means erosion by running water in a humid temperate climate.

cards.a: Davis's cycle begins with rapid uplift, then a long still-stand, and passes through youth, maturity and old age to end in a peneplain.
cards.w: Peneplain = 'almost a plain'. Residual hills left on it are monadnocks. Relief is greatest in maturity; youth has V-valleys and waterfalls.

cards.a: Walther Penck (1924) held that uplift and erosion act together, and that landform shape depends on the ratio of the rate of uplift to the rate of degradation.
cards.w: Speeding uplift gives convex (waxing) slopes; slowing uplift gives concave (waning) slopes. His final low surface is the 'endrumpf'.

cards.a: L. C. King's pediplanation cycle explains landscapes by parallel retreat of scarps: pediments grow and join into a pediplain dotted with inselbergs.
cards.w: Slopes move back while keeping their angle, instead of wearing down as in Davis's model. King based it on semi-arid southern Africa.

cards.a: Base level (J. W. Powell, 1875) is the lowest level to which a river can erode; sea level is the ultimate base level.
cards.w: Lakes and hard rock bands act as local or temporary base levels for the stretch of river above them.

cards.a: Rejuvenation (by uplift or a fall in base level) produces knickpoints, incised meanders, paired river terraces and valley-in-valley forms.
cards.w: The river gets new energy and cuts down again into its old valley floor. The old floor is left as terraces on both sides.

cards.a: Hack's dynamic equilibrium concept (1960) says landforms keep a steady shape when erosional processes and rock resistance are in balance, whatever the stage.
cards.w: It is a time-independent idea, unlike Davis's stages. Every slope is adjusted to the rock under it and the work done on it.

cards.a: Stream competence is the largest particle size a stream can move; stream capacity is the total load it can carry.
cards.w: Competence depends mainly on velocity, capacity mainly on discharge. Load moves in solution, in suspension and as bed load (rolling and hopping).

cards.a: In a meander, erosion on the outer (concave) bank makes a cut bank, and deposition on the inner (convex) bank makes a point bar.
cards.w: The fastest flow swings to the outside of the bend. The slow water on the inside drops its sand.

cards.a: An oxbow lake forms when a river cuts through the narrow neck of a meander loop and abandons the loop.
cards.w: The straight path is shorter and steeper, so the river takes it. The old loop is sealed off by silt.

cards.a: Natural levees are low ridges along river banks built during overbank floods; the coarsest sediment drops nearest the channel, with backswamps beyond.
cards.w: Flood water slows suddenly as it leaves the channel, so it drops sand and silt at once. Only clay reaches the backswamp.

cards.a: Braided channels form where bed load is high, discharge is highly variable, the slope is steep and the banks are easily eroded.
cards.w: The river cannot carry all its coarse load, so it drops bars and splits around them. Common below glaciers and mountain fronts.

cards.a: An alluvial fan forms where a stream leaves a mountain front and suddenly loses slope and confinement; merged fans form a bajada or piedmont plain.
cards.w: The stream spreads out, slows and drops its load in a cone. The bhabar belt at the Himalayan foot is made of such merged fans.

cards.a: Common delta shapes are arcuate (Nile, Ganga-Brahmaputra), bird-foot (Mississippi) and cuspate (Tiber); delta beds are named topset, foreset and bottomset.
cards.w: Waves and currents smooth a delta into an arc. Where the river is stronger than the sea, long finger-like channels build a bird-foot.

cards.a: Kerala has 44 rivers: 41 flow west and 3 (Kabani, Bhavani and Pambar) flow east to join the Cauvery system.
cards.w: The Western Ghats crest lies close to the coast, so most rivers are short, steep and monsoon-fed. Do not confuse Pambar (east) with Pamba (west).

cards.a: Periyar (244 km) is Kerala's longest river, followed by Bharathapuzha (209 km) and Pamba (176 km).
cards.w: Bharathapuzha drains through the Palghat Gap. Pamba, with other rivers, built the Kuttanad delta in Vembanad lake.

cards.a: Kerala has three physiographic belts parallel to the coast: lowland (below 7.5 m), midland (7.5 to 75 m) and highland (above 75 m).
cards.w: Lowland is coastal sand and backwaters, midland is laterite hills and valleys, highland is the Western Ghats.

cards.a: Anamudi (2695 m) in Kerala is the highest peak in India south of the Himalaya; the Palghat Gap is the main break in the Western Ghats.
cards.w: Anamudi is in Eravikulam, Idukki district. The Palghat Gap is a low pass about 30 km wide linking Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

cards.a: Wind erodes by deflation (lifting loose particles) and abrasion (sand-blasting); deflation leaves blow-outs and a lag of pebbles called desert pavement.
cards.w: Wind can lift only sand, silt and dust. The stones it cannot move stay behind and armour the surface.

cards.a: Ventifacts are stones faceted and polished by wind-blown sand; a three-faced ventifact is called a dreikanter.
cards.w: Sand-blast cuts a flat face on the windward side. When the stone turns or the wind shifts, a new face is cut.

cards.a: Yardangs are streamlined ridges cut parallel to the prevailing wind; zeugen are flat-topped masses with a hard cap rock over soft horizontal layers.
cards.w: Both are made by wind abrasion on rocks of unequal hardness. Mushroom rocks are undercut because most sand travels near the ground.

cards.a: A barchan is a crescent-shaped dune whose horns point downwind; it forms with limited sand supply and wind from one steady direction.
cards.w: The thin edges move faster than the thick middle, so they run ahead as horns. The steep slip face is on the lee (sheltered) side.

cards.a: Seif (longitudinal) dunes run parallel to the wind, transverse dunes lie across it, and parabolic dunes have horns pointing upwind, held by vegetation.
cards.w: A parabolic dune is a barchan turned backward: plants pin the arms while the bare middle blows forward.

cards.a: Loess is unstratified wind-blown silt that can stand in vertical walls; the thickest deposits are in the Loess Plateau of north China.
cards.w: The dust comes from deserts and glacial outwash plains. Angular grains and a little lime cement let it stand in cliffs.

cards.a: A pediment is a gently sloping erosional rock surface at the foot of a desert mountain; the bajada beyond it is depositional, and the playa is the flat basin floor.
cards.w: Order from mountain to basin centre: pediment, bajada, playa. A playa holds a temporary salt lake after rain.

cards.a: An inselberg is an isolated, steep-sided residual hill rising abruptly from a plain; a dome-shaped one is called a bornhardt.
cards.w: Inselberg means 'island mountain'. It is the last remnant left when scarps retreat across massive, poorly jointed rock.

cards.a: Wave erosion makes a notch, then a sea cliff and a wave-cut platform; on headlands the sequence is cave, arch, stack and stump.
cards.w: Waves attack weak joints from both sides of a headland. Caves meet to form an arch, and the roof falls to leave a stack.

cards.a: Longshore drift moves sediment along the shore in a zig-zag, because swash runs up the beach obliquely while backwash returns straight down the slope.
cards.w: It happens when waves reach the shore at an angle. Groynes are built to trap this moving sand.

cards.a: A spit is a sand ridge joined to land at one end; a tombolo joins an island to the mainland; a barrier bar or island encloses a lagoon.
cards.w: All three are built by longshore drift. Hook: tombolo 'ties' the island.

cards.a: D. W. Johnson (1919) classified shorelines as submergence, emergence, neutral and compound; rias and fjords are submergence features.
cards.w: Ria = drowned river valley, fjord = drowned glacial trough. Raised beaches and marine terraces show emergence.

cards.a: Kerala's coast is a barrier-lagoon coast: long sandy barrier beaches enclose backwaters (kayals), the largest being Vembanad.
cards.w: Longshore drift built sand barriers across river mouths and trapped lagoons behind them. Kerala has 34 backwaters.

cards.a: Vembanad is Kerala's largest backwater lake and Sasthamkotta its largest freshwater lake; both, with Ashtamudi, were declared Ramsar sites in 2002.
cards.w: Ramsar site = wetland of international importance. Sasthamkotta (Kollam) has no river feeding it; it is fed by groundwater and rain.

cards.a: Kuttanad, the delta and backwater region at the southern end of Vembanad lake, has rice fields lying below mean sea level and acidic peaty 'kari' soils.
cards.w: The fields are reclaimed lake bed kept dry by bunds (earth walls). It is the lowest-lying land in India.

cards.a: Mudbanks ('chakara') are calm near-shore patches of thick suspended mud that appear along the Kerala coast during the south-west monsoon.
cards.w: The fluid mud damps the waves, so the sea stays calm and fish gather there. They are best known off the Alappuzha coast.

cards.a: Karst develops best in thick, dense, well-jointed soluble rock (limestone or dolomite) with good rainfall and enough relief for groundwater to circulate.
cards.w: Rain with dissolved CO2 is a weak acid that dissolves calcite along joints. The name comes from the Karst (Kras) plateau of Slovenia.

cards.a: Lapies (karren) are grooved, fluted limestone surfaces; in a limestone pavement the blocks are called clints and the widened joints grikes.
cards.w: They are small solution sculptures on bare rock, not closed hollows. So lapies are not a kind of sinkhole.

cards.a: Karst closed depressions in order of increasing size are sinkhole (doline), uvala (merged dolines) and polje (a large flat-floored basin).
cards.w: Hook: D-U-P, small to big. A stream vanishing underground enters by a swallow hole (ponor).

cards.a: Stalactites hang from a cave roof, stalagmites grow up from the floor, and the two join to form a column (pillar).
cards.w: Hook: stalaCtite = Ceiling, stalaGmite = Ground. Both are calcite left when dripping water loses CO2.

cards.a: Glaciers erode by plucking (pulling out blocks) and abrasion (grinding); abrasion leaves striations that show the direction of ice flow, and makes rock flour.
cards.w: Stones frozen in the ice base act like sandpaper. Rock flour is the fine powder that makes glacial streams milky.

cards.a: A cirque is an armchair-shaped hollow at a glacier head; two cirques back to back leave an arete, and three or more leave a horn (pyramidal peak).
cards.w: Cirque walls cut backward into the mountain from several sides. A lake left in an empty cirque is a tarn.

cards.a: Valley glaciers carve U-shaped troughs with truncated spurs and hanging valleys; a glacial trough drowned by the sea is a fjord.
cards.w: The big main glacier cuts deeper than its small tributaries. So tributary valleys are left 'hanging' high on the trough wall, often with waterfalls.

cards.a: A roche moutonnee is a bedrock knob with a smooth, gentle up-ice (stoss) side made by abrasion and a steep, rough down-ice (lee) side made by plucking.
cards.w: Ice presses and grinds as it climbs the knob, then pulls blocks away as it leaves. It is an erosional form.

cards.a: A drumlin is a streamlined hill of till with its steep blunt end facing up-ice and its gentle tail pointing down-ice; swarms give 'basket of eggs' topography.
cards.w: It is a depositional form, and its asymmetry is the opposite of a roche moutonnee. Both show the direction of ice flow.

cards.a: Till is unsorted, unstratified debris dropped directly by ice; moraines made of it are lateral, medial, terminal (end), recessional and ground moraines.
cards.w: Ice carries clay and boulders together and cannot sort them. A medial moraine forms where two lateral moraines join.

cards.a: Eskers are long winding ridges of stratified sand and gravel laid by meltwater streams under the ice; kames are mounds; kettles are hollows left by melted buried ice blocks.
cards.w: These are glacio-fluvial (meltwater) deposits, so they are sorted and layered, unlike till.

cards.a: Dendritic (tree-like) drainage develops on uniform rocks or flat-lying beds where there is no structural control.
cards.w: With nothing to guide them, streams branch at random acute angles like the twigs of a tree. It is the most common pattern.

cards.a: Trellis drainage develops on folded or tilted beds of alternating hard and soft rock: long parallel main streams with short tributaries joining at right angles.
cards.w: Main streams follow the soft beds along strike. Short streams run down the hard ridges to meet them.

cards.a: Rectangular drainage, with right-angled bends in main streams and tributaries alike, indicates control by joints or faults.
cards.w: Water follows the fracture lines because broken rock erodes easily. Two fracture sets at right angles give the pattern.

cards.a: Radial drainage flows outward from a dome or volcano, centripetal drainage flows inward into a basin, and annular drainage forms rings around an eroded dome.
cards.w: Annular (ring-like) streams follow the circular outcrops of soft beds exposed when a dome is worn down.

cards.a: A consequent stream follows the original slope; a subsequent stream follows weak rock belts along strike; an obsequent stream flows opposite to the consequent.
cards.w: A resequent stream flows the same way as the consequent but at a lower, later level. An insequent stream shows no control (dendritic).

cards.a: An antecedent river is older than the uplift it cuts across (Indus, Sutlej, Brahmaputra); a superimposed river was let down from a younger cover onto older structures.
cards.w: Antecedent = 'came before' the mountains and kept its course by cutting gorges. Damodar, Subarnarekha and Chambal are usual superimposed examples.

cards.a: In Strahler's stream ordering (1952), fingertip streams are first order; two streams of equal order u join to make order u+1; unequal orders keep the higher order.
cards.w: It is a simplified form of Horton's (1945) system. Example: 2+2 gives 3, but 3+2 stays 3.

cards.a: Bifurcation ratio is the number of streams of one order divided by the number of the next higher order; it is usually 3 to 5 where structure does not control drainage.
cards.w: Higher values point to strong structural control (folds, faults) or a long narrow basin.

cards.a: Horton's law of stream numbers: the number of streams falls with rising order in an inverse geometric series; mean stream length rises in a direct geometric series.
cards.w: So a plot of log (number of streams) against order is a straight line sloping down. Its slope gives the bifurcation ratio.

cards.a: Drainage density is total stream length divided by basin area (km per sq km); it is high on impermeable rocks, steep slopes and sparsely vegetated land.
cards.w: Where water cannot soak in, more of it runs off and cuts more channels. Low density means permeable ground and good recharge.

cards.a: Horton's form factor is basin area divided by the square of basin length; a low value means an elongated basin with a flatter, longer-lasting flood peak.
cards.w: In a long narrow basin, water from far and near parts reaches the outlet at different times. Related shape indices: circularity ratio (Miller), elongation ratio (Schumm).

cards.a: The hypsometric curve relates area to elevation; Strahler's hypsometric integral is high for youthful, little-eroded basins and low for old, deeply eroded ones.
cards.w: The integral is the share of the original rock mass still left. Above about 0.6 is youthful, below about 0.35 is the old (monadnock) stage.

cards.a: Placers concentrate heavy, hard, chemically stable minerals (gold, cassiterite, diamond, ilmenite, monazite) where current speed drops, such as the inside of meander bends and below confluences.
cards.w: Heavy grains settle first when water slows, while light quartz is carried on. So landform study tells where to dig.

cards.a: The Chavara beach placer in Kollam district, Kerala, is rich in ilmenite, rutile, zircon, monazite and sillimanite.
cards.w: Rivers bring heavy minerals from khondalite and charnockite rocks, and waves sort them on the beach. IREL and KMML mine them.

cards.a: In hard-rock terrain, valley fills, buried pediments, palaeochannels and fracture-controlled straight valleys are good groundwater zones; inselbergs and residual hills are poor.
cards.w: Thick loose or weathered material stores water, and fractures let it move. Bare rock hills only shed water as run-off.

cards.a: Dam sites favour a narrow valley with sound, watertight rock; karst terrain is risky because solution cavities leak water and may collapse.
cards.w: Old landslide scars and buried channels found by landform study are also avoided in dam, tunnel and road alignment.

cards.a: Geomorphic mapping supports flood-plain zoning, landslide hazard zonation and coastal erosion studies, because landforms record where these processes acted before.
cards.w: Levees, backswamps and old channels mark flood-prone land. Old scars and debris fans mark slopes that can fail again.

cards.a: The Survey of India, founded in 1767 and headquartered at Dehradun, is India's national mapping agency and publishes the topographical sheets (toposheets).
cards.w: It is the oldest scientific department of the Government of India and works under the Department of Science and Technology.

cards.a: In the India and Adjacent Countries series, each numbered sheet (for example 58) covers 4 degrees by 4 degrees at a scale of 1:1,000,000.
cards.w: These 'million sheets' are the base of the whole numbering system. Southern Kerala falls in sheet 58.

cards.a: Each 4-degree sheet is divided into 16 degree sheets (1 degree by 1 degree), lettered A to P, at a scale of 1:250,000, for example 58 D.
cards.w: 4 x 4 = 16 squares. Letters run down each column, starting from the north-west corner.

cards.a: Each degree sheet is divided into 16 sheets of 15 minutes by 15 minutes, numbered 1 to 16, at a scale of 1:50,000, for example 58 D/14.
cards.w: Each of these is cut again into four 7.5-minute sheets at 1:25,000, named NW, NE, SW and SE (for example 58 D/14/NE).

cards.a: Open Series Maps, brought in by the National Map Policy 2005, use the WGS-84 datum and UTM projection; older toposheets used the Everest datum and polyconic projection.
cards.w: Open Series Maps are for civilian use; Defence Series Maps are restricted. The National Geospatial Policy 2022 (notified December 2022) replaced the 2005 policy.

cards.a: On a 1:50,000 map 2 cm represents 1 km; on a 1:25,000 map 4 cm represents 1 km; on a 1:250,000 map 1 cm represents 2.5 km.
cards.w: 1:50,000 means 1 cm = 50,000 cm = 500 m. A map that shows more detail of a smaller area (1:25,000) is the 'larger scale' map.

cards.a: Closely spaced contours show a steep slope and widely spaced contours a gentle slope; contour V's point upstream in valleys and downhill on spurs.
cards.w: A contour joins points of equal height. Contours of different height cannot cross; they only merge at a vertical cliff.

cards.a: On Survey of India toposheets contours are brown, water features blue, forests green, cultivated land yellow, and settlements and roads red.
cards.w: Black is used for names, railways and boundaries. Hook: brown earth, blue water, green trees, yellow crops.

cards.a: Spheroidal weathering rounds joint-bounded blocks into concentric onion-like shells by chemical attack along joints; it is common in basalt, dolerite and granite.
cards.w: Corners are attacked from three sides and edges from two, so they wear away fastest. It is chemical, unlike exfoliation, which is due to unloading.

cards.a: ICAR groups Indian soils into eight types: alluvial, black, red and yellow, laterite, arid (desert), saline, peaty (marshy) and forest (mountain) soils.
cards.w: Alluvial soil covers the largest area. Black soil goes with Deccan basalt, red soil with old crystalline rocks, laterite with hot wet uplands.

cards.a: Red soil forms on old crystalline rocks (granite, gneiss) of Peninsular India; its colour comes from finely spread ferric iron oxide, and it looks yellow when hydrated.
cards.w: It is poor in nitrogen, phosphorus and humus. It is common in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and Chhattisgarh.

cards.a: The factor of safety of a slope is the resisting force (shear strength) divided by the driving force (shear stress); the slope fails when it falls below 1.
cards.w: Heavy rain, cutting the toe of the slope, loading its top and earthquake shaking all push the ratio down.

cards.a: The angle of repose is the steepest angle at which loose dry material stays stable; it is about 30 to 35 degrees for dry sand.
cards.w: Coarser and more angular fragments can stand steeper. Scree (talus) slopes below cliffs rest at this angle.

cards.a: Humid regions typically have rounded, soil-covered slopes that are convex above and concave below; arid regions have angular, bare slopes with sharp breaks of slope.
