cards.w: In wet climates creep and chemical weathering smooth the land under a soil cover. In deserts weak weathering and rare flash floods leave bare rock and sharp edges.

cards.a: Most desert drainage is internal (endoreic): ephemeral streams flow only after rare storms and end in closed basins instead of reaching the sea.
cards.w: Rain is too little and evaporation too high for rivers to last. The dry channels are called wadis or arroyos.

cards.a: River capture (stream piracy) happens when a stream cutting headward diverts another; it leaves an elbow of capture, a wind gap and a misfit (underfit) stream.
cards.w: The capturing stream has a steeper slope or weaker rock to cut. The beheaded stream is now too small for its old valley.

cards.a: A graded stream has a smooth, concave-upward long profile with a slope just enough to carry its load (Mackin, 1948).
cards.w: The profile is steep near the source and gentle near the mouth. On average such a river neither cuts down nor builds up its bed.

cards.a: The Western Ghats (Sahyadri) run about 1600 km parallel to the west coast from the Tapi valley to Kanyakumari; they became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012.
cards.w: Their steep western face is a great escarpment. It blocks the monsoon winds, so the Kerala side is very wet and its rivers are short and steep.

cards.a: The Palghat Gap lies between the Nilgiri Hills to the north and the Anamalai Hills to the south; the Bharathapuzha flows west through it.
cards.w: It lets road, rail and dry winds pass between Kerala and Tamil Nadu. Farther south, the smaller Shencottah (Aryankavu) gap is the next break.

cards.a: An erg is a sandy desert (sand sea), a reg is a stony desert plain covered with gravel, and a hamada is a bare rock desert plateau.
cards.w: Deflation (wind removal of fines) explains the last two: wind takes the sand away and leaves gravel or bare rock.

cards.a: Darwin's subsidence theory says that as a volcanic island slowly sinks, a fringing reef grows upward to become a barrier reef and finally an atoll.
cards.w: Corals keep growing up toward sunlight as the island goes down. The Lakshadweep islands are atolls.

cards.a: Limestone dissolves by carbonation: rain water with dissolved carbon dioxide (weak carbonic acid) changes calcium carbonate into soluble calcium bicarbonate.
cards.w: CaCO3 + H2O + CO2 gives Ca(HCO3)2. When the water loses CO2 inside a cave, the reaction reverses and calcite is deposited as dripstone.

cards.a: Terra rossa is the red, clay-rich residual soil left on limestone after the carbonate has dissolved away.
cards.w: The insoluble impurities of limestone (clay and iron oxide) stay behind. The name means 'red earth'.

cards.a: Well-known karst caves of India include the Borra Caves (Andhra Pradesh), Kutumsar Cave (Chhattisgarh) and the long cave systems of Meghalaya.
cards.w: All are in thick limestone belts with good rainfall. Kerala has very little limestone, so karst is not important there.

cards.a: Humid tropical karst shows cone (cockpit) karst and steep-sided tower karst, as in South China, instead of the doline plains of temperate karst.
cards.w: Heavy rain and plant acids dissolve limestone fast. Only steep residual hills are left standing between the wide solution hollows.

cards.a: Snow changes to granular firn (neve) and then to glacier ice by compaction and recrystallisation; the snow line is the lower limit of permanent snow.
cards.w: Air is squeezed out as the snow is buried. A glacier gains mass above the snow line (accumulation zone) and loses it below (ablation zone).

cards.a: Parallel drainage develops on steep uniform slopes; deranged drainage with many lakes and swamps marks recently glaciated ground; barbed drainage suggests river capture or tilting.
cards.w: In barbed drainage the tributaries join pointing upstream, like fish-hook barbs. This shows the main river once flowed the other way.

cards.a: Stream frequency is the number of stream segments per unit area; the constant of channel maintenance is the reciprocal of drainage density, and the length of overland flow is half of that.
cards.w: Example: drainage density 2 km per sq km gives a constant of 0.5 sq km per km and an overland flow length of 0.25 km.

cards.a: Elongation ratio (Schumm) is the diameter of a circle with the same area as the basin divided by basin length; circularity ratio (Miller) is basin area divided by the area of a circle with the same perimeter.
cards.w: Both are 1 for a perfectly circular basin and get smaller as the basin gets longer and narrower.

cards.a: Bauxite and laterite occur as flat cappings on plateau tops (old planation surfaces), so mapping such surfaces guides the search for residual deposits.
cards.w: Residual ore needs long, deep weathering on stable flat ground. Examples: bauxite on the Eastern Ghats plateaus and the 'pat' lands of Chotanagpur.

cards.a: A basin with high drainage density, steep slopes and a nearly circular shape gives quick run-off and a sharp, high flood peak.
cards.w: Water from all parts reaches the outlet fast and at about the same time. So morphometry helps to judge flood risk in basins that have no gauges.

cards.a: One 4-degree sheet contains 16 degree sheets and 16 x 16 = 256 sheets of 1:50,000 scale.
cards.w: Each degree sheet (1:250,000) is cut into 16 sheets of 15 minutes. So 16 degree sheets x 16 = 256.

cards.a: The standard contour interval on metric 1:50,000 Survey of India toposheets is 20 m.
cards.w: Contour interval is the height difference between neighbouring contours. Every fifth contour (each 100 m) is drawn thicker as an index contour.

cards.a: Closed contours with values rising inward show a hill; values falling inward show a depression; a saddle (col) is the low point on a ridge between two hills.
cards.w: Evenly spaced contours mean a uniform slope. In a concave slope the contours are close together at the top and wide apart at the bottom.

cards.a: On a toposheet a bench mark (BM) is a permanent point of precisely levelled height, a spot height is a dot with its height printed beside it, and a small triangle marks a triangulation station.
cards.w: These give exact heights between the contours. Heights are measured above mean sea level.

cards.t: Satellite remote sensing - data products and their interpretation
cards.a: Passive sensors record reflected sunlight or emitted heat; active sensors such as radar and LiDAR send out their own energy and record the return.
cards.w: Active means the sensor carries its own 'torch'. So radar works at night, but an ordinary camera does not.

cards.t: Satellite remote sensing - data products and their interpretation
cards.a: Visible light spans about 0.4-0.7 µm: blue 0.4-0.5, green 0.5-0.6 and red 0.6-0.7 µm; near-infrared begins just beyond red at 0.7 µm.
cards.w: Order of increasing wavelength: blue, green, red, then infrared. 'Infra-red' simply means 'beyond red'.

cards.t: Satellite remote sensing - data products and their interpretation
cards.a: Atmospheric windows are wavelength bands where the atmosphere absorbs very little: mainly 0.3-1.3 µm, 1.5-1.8 µm, 2.0-2.4 µm, 3-5 µm, 8-14 µm and the microwave region.
cards.w: Sensors are built only for these 'open windows'. Outside them, water vapour, carbon dioxide and ozone block the signal.

cards.t: Satellite remote sensing - data products and their interpretation
cards.a: Thermal infrared sensing of the Earth's surface uses the 8-14 µm window; the 3-5 µm window suits very hot targets such as fires and lava.
cards.w: The ground at normal temperature gives out most heat near 10 µm. Hotter things glow at shorter wavelengths.

cards.t: Satellite remote sensing - data products and their interpretation
cards.a: Wien's displacement law: wavelength of peak emission (µm) = 2898 / T (kelvin), giving about 0.5 µm for the Sun and about 9.7 µm for the Earth at 300 K.
cards.w: Hotter body, shorter peak wavelength. This is why sunlight peaks in the visible and Earth's own glow is in thermal infrared.

cards.t: Satellite remote sensing - data products and their interpretation
cards.a: Rayleigh scattering by gas molecules varies as the inverse fourth power of wavelength, so short blue wavelengths are scattered far more than red.
cards.w: This makes the sky blue and causes bluish haze on aerial photos. A yellow (minus-blue) haze filter cuts it.

cards.t: Satellite remote sensing - data products and their interpretation
cards.a: Healthy vegetation absorbs blue and red light (chlorophyll), reflects some green, and reflects very strongly in near-infrared because of the internal cell structure of leaves.
cards.w: Low red plus high near-infrared is the 'fingerprint' of green plants. Stressed plants lose the near-infrared peak.

cards.t: Satellite remote sensing - data products and their interpretation
cards.a: Clear water absorbs almost all near-infrared and shortwave-infrared energy, so water bodies look black on infrared images.
cards.w: This makes the land-water boundary very sharp in infrared bands, which is useful for mapping tanks, rivers and shorelines.

cards.t: Satellite remote sensing - data products and their interpretation
cards.a: Snow and cloud are both bright in visible bands, but in shortwave infrared near 1.6 µm snow turns dark while cloud stays bright.
cards.w: Ice absorbs shortwave infrared strongly; tiny cloud droplets still scatter it. So a 1.6 µm band separates the two.

cards.t: Concepts and principles of aerial photography and photogrammetry
cards.a: A vertical aerial photo has the camera axis within about 3° of vertical; a low oblique does not show the horizon; a high oblique shows the horizon.
cards.w: Memory hook: 'High oblique = Horizon'. Vertical photos are the ones used for mapping and stereo work.

cards.t: Concepts and principles of aerial photography and photogrammetry
cards.a: Scale of a vertical aerial photograph = f / (H - h), where f is focal length, H is flying height above datum and h is ground elevation.
cards.w: Longer lens gives a larger scale; flying higher gives a smaller scale. Keep f and H in the same unit.

cards.t: Concepts and principles of aerial photography and photogrammetry
cards.a: Photo scale is not uniform over hilly ground: hilltops are closer to the camera and appear at a larger scale than valleys.
cards.w: Scale depends on the camera-to-ground distance (H - h). So one photo can have many scales; only flat ground gives one scale.

cards.t: Concepts and principles of aerial photography and photogrammetry
cards.a: An aerial photograph is a central (perspective) projection, whereas a map is an orthographic projection.
cards.w: All rays pass through one point, the lens. So tall or high objects lean outward on a photo, but not on a map.

cards.t: Concepts and principles of aerial photography and photogrammetry
cards.a: For stereoscopic cover, successive aerial photos overlap about 60% along the flight line (forward overlap) and about 20-30% between adjacent strips (side lap).
cards.w: More than 50% forward overlap makes sure every ground point appears on at least two photos, which stereo viewing needs.

cards.t: Concepts and principles of aerial photography and photogrammetry
cards.a: Relief displacement d = r x h / H, where r is radial distance of the image point from the photo centre, h is object height and H is flying height above the object's base.
cards.w: It grows with object height and distance from the centre, and shrinks when the aircraft flies higher.

cards.t: Concepts and principles of aerial photography and photogrammetry
cards.a: Relief displacement is radial from the nadir point: tops of elevated objects shift outward, depressions shift inward, and it is zero at the nadir.
cards.w: An object directly below the camera is seen straight down, so it cannot lean. Objects near photo edges lean the most.

cards.t: Concepts and principles of aerial photography and photogrammetry
cards.a: The principal point is where lines joining opposite fiducial marks cross; the nadir is the point vertically below the camera; the isocentre lies midway between them on a tilted photo.
cards.w: On a truly vertical photo all three points coincide. Tilt displacement is radial from the isocentre.

cards.t: Concepts and principles of aerial photography and photogrammetry
cards.a: Stereoscopic parallax is the apparent shift in an object's position on two overlapping photos caused by the change in camera position; higher points show larger parallax.
cards.w: Hold a finger close and blink each eye: a near object jumps more than a far one. Hilltops are 'nearer' to the camera.

cards.t: Concepts and principles of aerial photography and photogrammetry
cards.a: Object height from parallax: h = H x dP / (Pb + dP), where H is flying height, Pb is the absolute parallax at the base and dP is the parallax difference between top and base.
cards.w: A bigger parallax difference means a taller object. Pb is roughly equal to the photo base (distance between photo centres).

cards.t: Concepts and principles of aerial photography and photogrammetry
cards.a: Pocket (lens) and mirror stereoscopes are used to view stereo pairs in 3D; a parallax bar (stereometer) measures the parallax difference between two points.
cards.w: A mirror stereoscope lets you see the whole overlap at once. The parallax bar turns the 3D view into a height number.

cards.t: Concepts and principles of aerial photography and photogrammetry
cards.a: Vertical exaggeration in a stereo model increases with the base-height ratio (air base divided by flying height).
cards.w: Wider spacing between exposures makes hills look steeper than they are. So slopes and dips seen in stereo look too steep.

cards.t: Concepts and principles of aerial photography and photogrammetry
cards.a: The basic elements of photo and image interpretation are tone (or colour), texture, pattern, shape, size, shadow, site and association.
cards.w: Tone is brightness; texture is the roughness or smoothness of tone. Site and association mean location and neighbouring features.

cards.t: Satellite remote sensing - data products and their interpretation
cards.a: Sensor quality is described by four resolutions: spatial (smallest ground detail), spectral (number and width of bands), radiometric (brightness levels) and temporal (revisit interval).
cards.w: Think where, which colour, how many grey shades, and how often. A sensor cannot be best in all four at once.

cards.t: Satellite remote sensing - data products and their interpretation
cards.a: Radiometric resolution is set by the number of bits: an n-bit sensor records 2^n grey levels, so 8-bit data has 256 levels (0-255).
cards.w: Each extra bit doubles the number of levels. 10-bit gives 1024 and 11-bit gives 2048.

cards.t: Satellite remote sensing - data products and their interpretation
cards.a: Most earth-resource satellites use a near-polar sun-synchronous orbit at about 700-900 km, crossing any place at the same local solar time on every pass.
cards.w: Same local time means the same sun angle and shadows, so images of different dates can be compared fairly.

cards.t: Satellite remote sensing - data products and their interpretation
cards.a: A geostationary satellite orbits above the equator at about 35,786 km with a 24-hour period, so it stays fixed over one spot; used for weather and communication (INSAT).
cards.w: It turns with the Earth, so it watches the same area all the time. Very high altitude means coarse image detail.

cards.t: Satellite remote sensing - data products and their interpretation
cards.a: Whiskbroom (across-track) scanners sweep the ground with an oscillating mirror, as in Landsat MSS and TM; pushbroom (along-track) scanners use a line of CCD detectors, as in SPOT and IRS LISS.
cards.w: Pushbroom has no moving mirror, so each detector looks longer at the ground and gives a cleaner signal.

cards.t: Satellite remote sensing - data products and their interpretation
cards.a: Multispectral sensors record a few broad bands; hyperspectral sensors record hundreds of narrow, contiguous bands that can identify individual minerals.
cards.w: Narrow continuous bands trace the full reflectance curve, so small absorption dips of each mineral become visible.

cards.t: Satellite remote sensing - data products and their interpretation
cards.a: In a standard false colour composite (FCC), near-infrared is shown as red, red as green and green as blue, so healthy vegetation appears red.
cards.w: Plants reflect near-infrared most, and that band is displayed in red. Clear water appears dark blue to black.

cards.t: Satellite remote sensing - data products and their interpretation
cards.a: On thermal infrared images, water bodies appear cooler (darker) than land by day and warmer (brighter) than land at night.
cards.w: Water heats and cools slowly (high thermal inertia). Pre-dawn thermal images are preferred for geology as sun-heating effects are least.

cards.t: Satellite remote sensing - data products and their interpretation
cards.a: Microwave remote sensing works day and night and through cloud; common radar bands in order of increasing wavelength are X (~3 cm), C (~5.6 cm), S (~10 cm) and L (~23 cm).
cards.w: Long waves pass through cloud droplets. Longer wavelengths such as L-band also penetrate vegetation and dry soil more.

cards.t: Satellite remote sensing - data products and their interpretation
cards.a: Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) is a side-looking active sensor that uses the platform's forward motion to imitate a very long antenna, giving fine along-track (azimuth) resolution.
cards.w: A real antenna that long cannot be carried. So SAR adds up many echoes recorded along the flight path.

cards.t: Satellite remote sensing - data products and their interpretation
cards.a: On radar images, smooth surfaces such as calm water look dark (specular reflection), rough surfaces look bright, and buildings act as corner reflectors and look very bright.
cards.w: A smooth surface bounces the beam away from the antenna like a mirror. Moist soil also returns more signal than dry soil.

cards.t: Satellite remote sensing - data products and their interpretation
cards.a: Side-looking radar images of hilly terrain suffer from foreshortening, layover and radar shadow.
cards.w: Radar measures distance, not angle. A hilltop can be nearer to the radar than its base, so the slope looks squeezed or folded over.

cards.t: Satellite remote sensing - data products and their interpretation
cards.a: Radar interferometry (InSAR) uses the phase difference between two radar images to derive elevation models and to measure ground movement of centimetre scale.
cards.w: It is used for land subsidence from groundwater over-pumping, landslide creep and earthquake deformation.

cards.a: Pre-processing corrects an image radiometrically (sensor and atmosphere errors) and geometrically; geometric correction fits the image to map coordinates using ground control points (GCPs).
cards.w: GCPs are points seen clearly on both image and map, like road crossings. This step must come before enhancement or classification.

cards.a: Resampling methods are nearest neighbour, bilinear interpolation (4 pixels) and cubic convolution (16 pixels); only nearest neighbour keeps the original pixel values unchanged.
cards.w: Nearest neighbour just copies the closest pixel, so it is used for classified maps. The others average pixels and look smoother.

cards.a: Contrast stretching (linear stretch, histogram equalisation) spreads the recorded brightness values over the full display range to make an image clearer.
cards.w: Raw data often use only a small part of the 0-255 range and look dull. Stretching does not add new information.

cards.a: Band ratioing (dividing one band by another) reduces brightness differences caused by slope and shadow, and highlights spectral differences between materials.
cards.w: The same rock on sunny and shaded slopes has a different brightness but nearly the same ratio. Hence ratios suit hilly terrain.

cards.a: NDVI = (NIR - Red) / (NIR + Red); it ranges from -1 to +1, with dense healthy vegetation high positive, bare soil near zero and water negative.
cards.w: Plants are bright in near-infrared and dark in red, so the difference is large. Water is darker in near-infrared than in red.

cards.a: Supervised classification uses analyst-chosen training sites (e.g. maximum likelihood classifier); unsupervised classification groups pixels automatically into spectral clusters (e.g. ISODATA, K-means).
cards.w: Supervised: you teach the computer first. Unsupervised: the computer groups first and you name the groups later.

cards.a: Classification accuracy is checked with an error (confusion) matrix against ground truth, giving overall accuracy, producer's and user's accuracy and the kappa coefficient.
cards.w: Kappa tells how much better the map is than a chance result. The diagonal of the matrix holds the correctly classified pixels.

cards.a: Spatial filtering changes a pixel using its neighbours: low-pass filters smooth an image, high-pass filters sharpen edges, and directional filters enhance linear features of a chosen trend.
cards.w: Edges are sudden brightness changes (high spatial frequency). Directional filters are a common aid in lineament mapping.

cards.t: Remote sensing in landform and land use mapping
cards.a: The Anderson (USGS, 1976) land use / land cover scheme is a multi-level classification; its broad Level I classes can be mapped from Landsat-type satellite data.
cards.w: Finer levels need more detailed images. In India, NRSC maps national land use / land cover using Resourcesat AWiFS and LISS-III data.

cards.t: Remote sensing in landform and land use mapping
cards.a: Drainage texture on images reflects permeability: fine, closely spaced drainage develops on impermeable rocks like shale, and coarse drainage on permeable material like sandstone or gravel.
cards.w: Where water cannot soak in, more of it runs off and cuts more channels. This helps in both landform and rock-type mapping.

cards.a: A lineament is a mappable straight or gently curved linear feature of the surface, believed to reflect a subsurface structure such as a fault, fracture or shear zone.
cards.w: The term was introduced by Hobbs (1904) and the widely used definition is by O'Leary and others (1976).

cards.a: Lineaments appear on images as straight stream segments, aligned vegetation or tonal lines and linear scarps; low sun-angle images and radar images enhance them.
cards.w: Long shadows exaggerate small relief. Lineament trends are then summarised in a rose diagram.

cards.a: On stereo photos and images, dip direction is read from dip slopes and the 'rule of V's', and folds are recognised from curved, closing outcrop patterns of marker beds.
cards.w: An outcrop makes a V across a valley that points in the dip direction (for dips steeper than the stream slope). Remember vertical exaggeration makes dips look steeper.

cards.a: In hard-rock terrain, lineaments and especially lineament intersections mark fracture zones that are favourable sites for high-yielding bore wells.
cards.w: Crystalline rock stores water only in cracks and weathered zones. Most of Kerala's midland and highland is such hard rock.

cards.a: Valley fills, buried pediments, deeply weathered pediplains, alluvial plains and palaeochannels are good groundwater prospect zones; inselbergs, structural hills and rocky pediments are poor (run-off zones).
cards.w: Thick loose or weathered material stores water. Bare rock hills shed the rain as run-off.

cards.a: Groundwater potential zones are mapped in GIS by weighted overlay of thematic layers such as geology, geomorphology, lineament density, drainage density, slope, soil, land use and rainfall.
cards.w: High lineament density and gentle slope favour recharge; high drainage density and steep slope favour run-off. Weights are often set by AHP (pairwise comparison).

cards.a: Under the Rajiv Gandhi National Drinking Water Mission, NRSA (now NRSC) prepared groundwater prospects (hydrogeomorphological) maps at 1:50,000 scale from IRS satellite data.
cards.w: These maps guide where to drill wells and where to build recharge structures. They are served through the Bhuvan 'Bhujal' portal.

cards.a: The GRACE twin satellites (launched 2002; follow-on GRACE-FO 2018) measure changes in Earth's gravity, used to estimate changes in groundwater storage over large regions.
cards.w: Losing a big mass of water slightly lowers local gravity. GRACE data showed heavy groundwater depletion in north-west India.

cards.a: In mineral exploration, images are used to map hydrothermal alteration: iron oxides (gossans) show in visible bands, and clay or hydroxyl minerals show an absorption feature near 2.2 µm in shortwave infrared.
cards.w: Altered rock around ore bodies is far larger than the ore itself, so it is an easy target. Landsat TM ratio 5/7 highlights clays and 3/1 highlights iron oxides.

cards.a: ASTER (on NASA's Terra satellite, 1999) has 14 bands including six shortwave-infrared and five thermal bands, making it widely used for mapping alteration minerals and rock types.
cards.w: Several narrow shortwave-infrared bands separate clay, carbonate and mica groups better than the single broad Landsat band.

cards.a: Landsat-1, launched by the USA in 1972 as ERTS-1, was the first earth-resources satellite; Landsat Thematic Mapper data have 30 m resolution and a 16-day repeat cycle.
cards.w: Landsat gives the longest continuous record of the Earth's land surface. Its scene is about 185 km wide.

cards.a: As of 2026, Landsat 8 (launched 2013) and Landsat 9 (launched 2021) are operating, together imaging the Earth every 8 days; Landsat 7 (1999) was decommissioned on 4 June 2025.
cards.w: Two satellites, each on a 16-day cycle and offset from one another, halve the wait to 8 days. NASA plans the next one, Landsat 10, for about 2031.

cards.a: SPOT-1, launched by France (CNES) in 1986, introduced pushbroom scanning and off-nadir pointing for stereo imaging, with 10 m panchromatic and 20 m multispectral data.
cards.w: Its mirror could look sideways, so the same area could be seen from two orbits to get a 3D view.

cards.a: In Europe's Copernicus programme, Sentinel-1 carries a C-band SAR and Sentinel-2 carries a 13-band multispectral imager with 10 m best resolution and 5-day revisit; data are free.
cards.w: Sentinel-1A was launched in 2014 and Sentinel-2A in 2015. The newest radar unit, Sentinel-1D, was launched on 4 November 2025 by Ariane 6.

cards.a: The Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM), flown on Space Shuttle Endeavour in February 2000, used radar interferometry to produce a near-global digital elevation model.
cards.w: It is the most widely used free elevation data (30 m and 90 m grids) for drainage and slope analysis.

cards.a: Aryabhata (1975) was India's first satellite and Bhaskara-I (1979) was India's first experimental remote sensing satellite; both were launched by Soviet rockets.
cards.w: Bhaskara carried TV cameras and a microwave radiometer. It prepared the way for the operational IRS series.

cards.a: IRS-1A, India's first operational remote sensing satellite, was launched on 17 March 1988 by a Soviet Vostok rocket and carried LISS-I (72.5 m) and LISS-II (36.25 m) cameras.
cards.w: LISS means Linear Imaging Self-Scanning sensor, a pushbroom scanner. IRS-1C (1995) later added a 5.8 m panchromatic camera.

cards.a: Resourcesat satellites carry three cameras: LISS-IV (5.8 m), LISS-III (23.5 m) and AWiFS (56 m); Resourcesat-1 was launched in 2003, Resourcesat-2 in 2011 and Resourcesat-2A in 2016.
cards.w: Finer camera, narrower strip: AWiFS covers a very wide swath for crop monitoring; LISS-IV gives village-level detail.

cards.a: Cartosat-1 (2005) carried two 2.5 m panchromatic cameras for along-track stereo mapping; Cartosat-3 (November 2019) gives about 0.25 m panchromatic resolution.
cards.w: 'Carto' stands for cartography (map making). Cartosat-1 stereo pairs were used to build the CartoDEM elevation model of India.

cards.a: RISAT-2 (2009, X-band) was India's first radar imaging satellite; RISAT-1 (2012) was the first indigenous one, with a C-band SAR; EOS-04 (RISAT-1A) followed in February 2022.
cards.w: RISAT means Radar Imaging Satellite. Radar sees through monsoon cloud, so it is used for flood and kharif crop mapping.

cards.a: Oceansat-1 (IRS-P4, 1999) was India's first ocean-observation satellite; Oceansat-2 followed in 2009 and Oceansat-3 (EOS-06) in November 2022; the main sensor is the Ocean Colour Monitor.
cards.w: Ocean colour shows chlorophyll, which marks likely fishing zones. Later Oceansats also carry a scatterometer for sea-surface winds.

cards.a: Chandrayaan-1, India's first Moon mission, was launched on 22 October 2008 by PSLV; its data confirmed water (hydroxyl) molecules on the lunar surface.
cards.w: The finding came from NASA's Moon Mineralogy Mapper carried on board. The orbiter worked until August 2009.

cards.a: Chandrayaan-3 soft-landed near the lunar south pole on 23 August 2023, making India the fourth country to soft-land on the Moon and the first near the south pole.
cards.w: It was launched on 14 July 2023 by LVM3. Chandrayaan-2 (2019) lost its lander, but its orbiter is still working.

cards.a: The Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan) was launched on 5 November 2013 by PSLV-C25 and entered Mars orbit on 24 September 2014, on India's first attempt.
cards.w: India was the first Asian country to reach Mars orbit. Contact with the orbiter was lost in 2022.

cards.a: Aditya-L1, India's first solar observatory in space, was launched on 2 September 2023 and placed in a halo orbit around the Sun-Earth L1 point on 6 January 2024.
cards.w: L1 is about 1.5 million km from Earth towards the Sun. From there the Sun is seen without any eclipse.

cards.a: NISAR, the joint NASA-ISRO radar satellite, was launched on 30 July 2025 by GSLV-F16; it carries L-band (NASA) and S-band (ISRO) SAR and images land and ice every 12 days.
cards.w: It is the first SAR satellite to carry two radar bands. It orbits at about 747 km and was declared operational in November 2025.

cards.a: The National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC) of ISRO, at Hyderabad, receives, processes and distributes satellite data; the Indian Institute of Remote Sensing (IIRS) is at Dehradun.
cards.w: NRSC's ground station is at Shadnagar near Hyderabad. IIRS is the training institute.

cards.a: Bhuvan is ISRO's web geoportal, launched in 2009 and run by NRSC, giving online maps, satellite imagery and thematic layers of India.
cards.w: Bhuvan means 'Earth' in Sanskrit. Satellite data sets themselves are downloaded from NRSC's Bhoonidhi portal.

cards.a: GPS (USA) has a nominal 24 satellites in six orbital planes at about 20,200 km altitude; at least four satellites must be in view for a 3D position fix.
cards.w: Three distances fix the position and the fourth corrects the receiver's clock error. Positions are given on the WGS 84 datum.

cards.a: NavIC (IRNSS), India's regional navigation system, is designed with seven satellites (three geostationary, four inclined geosynchronous) covering India and about 1500 km around it.
cards.w: Run by ISRO. In 2026 it fell to three working satellites (IRNSS-1F's last atomic clock failed in March 2026), fewer than the four needed for a fix; NVS-03 was due for launch in October 2026 - recheck the count before the exam.

cards.t: Geographic Information System (GIS) - principles and applications
cards.a: A GIS is a computer-based system to capture, store, manage, analyse and display geographically referenced data; its components are hardware, software, data, people and methods.
cards.w: What makes it more than a drawing tool is analysis: it can combine map layers to answer 'where' questions.

cards.t: Geographic Information System (GIS) - principles and applications
cards.a: GIS data have two linked parts: spatial data (location and shape of features) and attribute data (descriptive information stored in tables).
cards.w: Example: a well is a point (spatial); its depth, yield and water quality are attributes.

cards.t: Geographic Information System (GIS) - principles and applications
cards.a: The vector data model represents features as points, lines and polygons defined by x,y coordinates, for example wells, streams and watershed boundaries.
cards.w: It suits features with sharp boundaries. It gives neat maps and small file sizes.

cards.t: Geographic Information System (GIS) - principles and applications
cards.a: The raster data model represents space as a grid of cells (pixels), each holding one value; satellite images and digital elevation models are raster data.
cards.w: It suits things that change gradually, like elevation or rainfall. The cell size sets the detail.

cards.t: Geographic Information System (GIS) - principles and applications
cards.a: Raster data have a simple structure and make overlay easy but need more storage; vector data are compact, precise and store topology but overlay is more complex.
cards.w: Hook: 'raster is faster, vector is corrector'. The choice depends on the type of data and analysis.

cards.t: Geographic Information System (GIS) - principles and applications
cards.a: Topology in GIS is the set of spatial relationships between features that do not change with stretching: adjacency, connectivity and containment.
cards.w: It tells which polygons share a boundary and which lines join at a node. It allows network tracing and error checking.

cards.t: Geographic Information System (GIS) - principles and applications
cards.a: Overlay analysis combines two or more map layers of the same area to create a new layer; common vector overlays are union, intersect and identity.
cards.w: Intersect keeps only the common area; union keeps everything. Overlay is the core tool in groundwater potential and site-selection studies.

cards.t: Geographic Information System (GIS) - principles and applications
cards.a: A digital elevation model (DEM) is a raster grid of elevation values; a TIN (triangulated irregular network) is a vector surface built from triangles joining irregularly spaced points.
cards.w: From a DEM a GIS derives slope, aspect, hill-shade, drainage network and watershed boundaries.

cards.t: Geographic Information System (GIS) - principles and applications
cards.a: Common free DEM sources are SRTM (radar interferometry), ASTER GDEM (optical stereo) and CartoDEM (ISRO, from Cartosat-1 stereo images).
cards.w: Stereo pairs or radar phase give height. CartoDEM for India is available through Bhuvan.

cards.t: Geographic Information System (GIS) - principles and applications
cards.a: The UTM projection divides the Earth into 60 north-south zones, each 6° of longitude wide; Kerala lies in UTM zone 43 North (72°E to 78°E).
cards.w: Zone number = whole part of (longitude + 180) / 6, plus 1. For 76°E this gives 43.

cards.t: Satellite remote sensing - data products and their interpretation
cards.a: Reflectance of dry bare soil rises gently and steadily from visible to near- and shortwave-infrared; moisture, organic matter, iron oxide and surface roughness all lower it.
cards.w: Wet soil looks darker than dry soil. The soil curve has no sharp peaks like the vegetation curve, only water absorption dips near 1.4 and 1.9 µm.

cards.t: Satellite remote sensing - data products and their interpretation
cards.a: The ground resolution cell of a scanner = IFOV (in radians) x flying height; an IFOV of 0.1 milliradian from 700 km gives a 70 m cell.
cards.w: IFOV (instantaneous field of view) is the tiny cone angle seen by one detector. A higher orbit or a wider angle gives a coarser pixel.

cards.t: Satellite remote sensing - data products and their interpretation
cards.a: Mie scattering is caused by particles about as large as the wavelength (dust, smoke); non-selective scattering by much larger water droplets affects all visible wavelengths equally, so clouds and fog look white.
cards.w: Three types by particle size: gas molecules (Rayleigh), dust and smoke (Mie), water droplets (non-selective). Equal scattering of all colours gives white.

cards.t: Satellite remote sensing - data products and their interpretation
cards.a: Stefan-Boltzmann law: the total energy emitted by a blackbody per unit area is proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature (M = σT^4).
cards.w: Doubling the temperature gives 16 times the energy. Real surfaces emit less than a blackbody (a perfect emitter); that fraction is called emissivity.

cards.t: Concepts and principles of aerial photography and photogrammetry
cards.a: Photogrammetry is the science of obtaining reliable measurements of objects and terrain (distances, heights, maps) from photographs, mainly overlapping vertical aerial photographs.
cards.w: Photo = light, gram = drawing, metry = measurement. Standard mapping photos are 23 cm x 23 cm, usually taken with a 152 mm lens.

cards.t: Concepts and principles of aerial photography and photogrammetry
cards.a: An orthophoto is an aerial photograph from which camera tilt and relief displacement have been removed, so it has a uniform scale and can be measured like a map.
cards.w: It keeps the picture detail of a photo but has the geometry of a map. A digital elevation model is needed to make it.

cards.t: Concepts and principles of aerial photography and photogrammetry
cards.a: Air base (ground distance between successive exposure stations) = ground length covered by one photo x (1 - forward overlap); with 60% overlap it is 40% of the photo coverage.
cards.w: Example: a 23 cm photo at 1:20,000 covers 4.6 km, so the air base is 0.4 x 4.6 = 1.84 km.

cards.t: Satellite remote sensing - data products and their interpretation
cards.a: Satellite scenes are indexed by path and row numbers (e.g. Landsat's Worldwide Reference System) and supplied at processing levels from raw data to radiometrically corrected, georeferenced and orthorectified products.
cards.w: Path is the orbit track and row is the position along it. Users normally order corrected products as digital files such as GeoTIFF.

cards.a: Image fusion (pan-sharpening) merges a high-resolution panchromatic image with lower-resolution multispectral bands to give a sharp colour image; IHS and Brovey transforms are common methods.
cards.w: A panchromatic band is one broad band, so it can have smaller pixels. Fusion borrows its sharpness, e.g. Landsat 8's 15 m band sharpens the 30 m colour bands.

cards.a: Principal component analysis (PCA) converts correlated spectral bands into uncorrelated components; the first component (PC1) holds the largest share of the total variance.
cards.w: Neighbouring bands often repeat the same information. PCA packs most of it into the first two or three components, so fewer images need study.

cards.t: Remote sensing in landform and land use mapping
cards.a: Land cover is what physically covers the ground (forest, water, bare rock); land use is how people use it (farming, housing). Images record land cover directly, and land use is inferred.
cards.w: A grassy area is one land cover but may be a pasture, a park or an airfield. So field checks are needed for land use maps.

cards.t: Remote sensing in landform and land use mapping
cards.a: Change detection compares co-registered images of the same area from two or more dates to map changes such as urban growth, forest loss, shoreline shift and conversion of wetlands or paddy fields.
cards.w: The images must overlay exactly and be of the same season, or false changes appear. The regular revisit of satellites makes this possible.

cards.t: Remote sensing in landform and land use mapping
cards.a: Landforms are identified on images from their shape and relief (seen in stereo or on a DEM), drainage pattern, tone and texture, and the vegetation and land use on them.
cards.w: Example: a flat, dark-toned, cultivated strip along a stream is a valley fill; a bare, light-toned isolated hill is an inselberg.

cards.t: Remote sensing in landform and land use mapping
cards.a: The Kerala State Remote Sensing and Environment Centre (KSREC), Thiruvananthapuram, is the State Government's nodal agency for remote sensing and GIS applications.
cards.w: It prepares land use, watershed and other resource maps for State departments from satellite data.

cards.a: Faults are recognised on images by straight scarps, abrupt offset or truncation of beds, ridges and streams, and sharp linear breaks in tone or vegetation.
cards.w: A fault cuts and shifts whatever it crosses. So look for features that end suddenly or are displaced along a straight line.

cards.a: Dolerite dykes usually appear on images as narrow, straight, dark-toned linear features cutting across the country rock; they can act as underground barriers to groundwater flow.
cards.w: Dolerite is a dark, basic rock, so its tone is dark. Wells on the upstream side of a dyke often hold more water.

cards.a: Remote sensing cannot detect groundwater directly; it maps surface indicators (landforms, lineaments, vegetation, soil moisture, springs), which must be confirmed by geophysical survey and drilling.
cards.w: Most sensors see only the ground surface. So images narrow down the target area, and resistivity survey then fixes the well site.

cards.a: Thermal infrared images can locate springs, seeps and submarine groundwater discharge, because groundwater has a nearly constant temperature that contrasts with surface water.
cards.w: Groundwater is cooler than sea or lake water on a summer day and warmer on a cold night. The plume shows as a different tone.

cards.a: On dry-season images, lines or patches of healthy vegetation (bright red on a standard FCC) in otherwise dry ground point to shallow groundwater or moist fracture zones.
cards.w: Plants stay green in summer only where roots reach water. A straight line of such vegetation often follows a water-bearing fracture.

cards.a: Geobotanical remote sensing finds mineralised ground through stressed vegetation: metal-rich soil shifts the 'red edge' of the leaf reflectance curve towards shorter wavelengths (blue shift).
cards.w: The red edge is the steep rise in reflectance near 0.7 µm. This helps in forested areas where rocks and soil are hidden.

cards.a: HysIS, India's hyperspectral imaging satellite, was launched on 29 November 2018 by PSLV-C43; it images in visible, near-infrared and shortwave-infrared bands at 30 m resolution.
cards.w: 'Hys' is short for hyperspectral. Its many narrow bands help in mineral, soil and crop studies.

cards.a: Landsat sensors evolved from MSS (4 bands, about 80 m) to TM (7 bands, 30 m; Landsat 4 and 5), ETM+ (Landsat 7; adds a 15 m panchromatic band) and OLI plus TIRS (Landsat 8 and 9).
cards.w: MSS = Multispectral Scanner, TM = Thematic Mapper, OLI = Operational Land Imager, TIRS = Thermal Infrared Sensor. Landsat 6 (1993) failed to reach orbit.

cards.a: Since 2020 ISRO names its earth observation satellites 'EOS': EOS-01 (2020), EOS-04 or RISAT-1A (2022), EOS-06 or Oceansat-3 (2022) and EOS-08 (16 August 2024, by SSLV-D3).
cards.w: SSLV is ISRO's Small Satellite Launch Vehicle. EOS-09 (RISAT-1B) was lost when PSLV-C61 failed on 18 May 2025.

cards.a: INSAT-3D (2013), INSAT-3DR (2016) and INSAT-3DS (17 February 2024, by GSLV-F14) are India's geostationary weather satellites, each carrying an imager and an atmospheric sounder.
cards.w: From geostationary orbit they watch India continuously, which suits cyclone and monsoon tracking. The sounder gives temperature and humidity profiles.

cards.a: India's space programme began at Thumba, Thiruvananthapuram, where the first sounding rocket was launched on 21 November 1963; the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC) there is ISRO's lead centre for launch vehicles.
cards.w: Thumba lies close to the magnetic equator. Satellites are launched from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre at Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh.

cards.a: PSLV is ISRO's workhorse rocket for placing remote sensing satellites in sun-synchronous polar orbit; GSLV and LVM3 carry heavier satellites, mainly to geosynchronous transfer orbit.
cards.w: P stands for Polar and G for Geosynchronous. Chandrayaan-1, Mangalyaan and Aditya-L1 also flew on PSLV; Chandrayaan-3 flew on LVM3.

cards.a: Global navigation satellite systems are GPS (USA), GLONASS (Russia), Galileo (European Union) and BeiDou (China); NavIC (India) and QZSS (Japan) are regional systems.
cards.w: GNSS is the common name for all of them. A modern receiver uses several systems together to get more satellites in view.

cards.a: Differential GPS (DGPS) uses a base receiver at a precisely known point to compute corrections for a roving receiver, improving accuracy from several metres to sub-metre level.
cards.w: Both receivers see nearly the same satellite and atmosphere errors, so these cancel. India's GAGAN system (ISRO and Airports Authority of India) sends similar corrections by satellite.

cards.t: Geographic Information System (GIS) - principles and applications
cards.a: A datum is a reference ellipsoid fixed to the Earth for defining coordinates; GPS uses the global WGS 84 datum, while older Survey of India maps used the Everest ellipsoid.
cards.w: The same point gets slightly different latitude and longitude on different datums, so all layers must share one. New Survey of India Open Series Maps use WGS 84 with UTM.

cards.t: Geographic Information System (GIS) - principles and applications
cards.a: A map projection transfers the curved Earth to a flat sheet and always distorts something: conformal projections keep shape (angles), equal-area projections keep area; no projection keeps both.
cards.w: UTM is a conformal (transverse Mercator) projection. Old Survey of India toposheets used the polyconic projection.

cards.t: Geographic Information System (GIS) - principles and applications
cards.a: Buffering creates a zone (a polygon) of chosen distance around a point, line or polygon feature, for example a 500 m protection zone around a drinking-water well.
cards.w: The output is always an area, whatever the input shape. It answers 'what lies within this distance of that feature?'

cards.t: Geographic Information System (GIS) - principles and applications
cards.a: Spatial interpolation estimates values at unsampled places from point data; common methods are inverse distance weighting (IDW) and kriging, used to make water-table and rainfall maps from well and rain-gauge data.
cards.w: IDW simply gives nearer points more weight. Kriging is a geostatistical method based on the semivariogram and also gives the likely error.

cards.t: Geographic Information System (GIS) - principles and applications
cards.a: A digital surface model (DSM) includes the tops of trees and buildings; a digital terrain model (DTM) shows the bare ground. LiDAR, which times laser pulses, gives very detailed elevation models.
cards.w: Some laser pulses pass through gaps in the tree canopy and reach the ground, so LiDAR can map the bare earth under forest.

cards.t: Geographic Information System (GIS) - principles and applications
cards.a: A GIS stores information as separate thematic layers (e.g. geology, drainage, wells, land use) registered to one common coordinate system so that they can be overlaid and analysed together.
cards.w: Think of transparent map sheets stacked exactly one over another. Each layer holds one theme only.

cards.t: Measurement of strain in deformed rocks
cards.a: Stress is force per unit area (SI unit: pascal). Strain is the change in shape or volume that stress produces, and it has no units.
cards.w: Stress is the cause, strain is the effect. Strain is a ratio (change in length / original length), so the units cancel.

cards.t: Measurement of strain in deformed rocks
cards.a: The strain ellipsoid is the shape a sphere takes after homogeneous strain. Its axes are X ≥ Y ≥ Z: longest, intermediate and shortest.
cards.w: Think of squeezing a ball of clay: it becomes an egg or a disc. X is the stretch direction, Z is the squeeze direction.

cards.t: Measurement of strain in deformed rocks
cards.a: Pure shear is coaxial (non-rotational) strain. Simple shear is non-coaxial (rotational) strain.
cards.w: Pure shear = squeezing a block flat; the strain axes do not turn. Simple shear = pushing the top of a pack of cards sideways; the strain axes rotate.

cards.t: Measurement of strain in deformed rocks
cards.a: Elongation e = (final length − original length) / original length. Stretch S = 1 + e. Quadratic elongation λ = (1 + e)².
cards.w: Example: a 10 cm fossil stretched to 15 cm has e = 0.5, S = 1.5 and λ = 2.25. Shortening gives a negative e.

cards.t: Measurement of strain in deformed rocks
cards.a: The Flinn diagram plots the axial ratio a = X/Y on the vertical axis against b = Y/Z on the horizontal axis.
cards.w: It shows the shape of any strain ellipsoid as one point on a graph. An unstrained sphere plots at the origin (1, 1).

cards.t: Measurement of strain in deformed rocks
cards.a: Flinn's k = (a − 1)/(b − 1). k = 0 means oblate (pancake) strain, k = 1 plane strain, and k = infinity prolate (cigar) strain.
cards.w: Below the k = 1 line is the flattening field, above it the constriction (stretching) field. Pancakes give strong foliation; cigars give strong lineation.

cards.t: Measurement of strain in deformed rocks
cards.a: Strain markers are objects of known original shape, such as ooids, reduction spots, pebbles, vesicles and fossils.
cards.w: If we know the shape before deformation (for example a sphere), the shape now tells us how much the rock was strained.

cards.t: Measurement of strain in deformed rocks
cards.a: The Fry method finds the strain ellipse from the centre-to-centre distances between neighbouring grains or ooids.
cards.w: Before strain, grain centres are evenly spaced in all directions. After strain they are closer along the squeeze direction, and a plot of the centres shows an elliptical gap.

cards.t: Measurement of strain in deformed rocks
cards.a: Wellman's method measures strain from deformed fossils that had known original angles, such as brachiopods and trilobites.
cards.w: These fossils have bilateral symmetry (left and right halves match), so the hinge line and median line were at 90°. Strain changes that angle.

cards.t: Behaviour of minerals and rocks under deformation conditions
cards.a: With rising stress a rock first deforms elastically (recoverable), then plastically after the yield point (permanent), and finally ruptures.
cards.w: Like a steel wire: a small pull springs back, a bigger pull bends it for good, and a still bigger pull snaps it.

cards.t: Behaviour of minerals and rocks under deformation conditions
p: TNPSC Geology paper (code 394, year not stated)
cards.a: A brittle rock breaks after very little plastic strain. A ductile rock takes a large plastic strain before it breaks.
cards.w: Brittle = glass (snaps). Ductile = warm wax (flows). Faults and joints are brittle structures; folds and shear zones are ductile ones.

cards.t: Behaviour of minerals and rocks under deformation conditions
cards.a: Rocks become more ductile with higher confining pressure, higher temperature, the presence of fluids and a slower strain rate.
cards.w: Deep rocks are hot, tightly confined and deformed slowly, so they fold and flow. Shallow, cold, quickly loaded rocks crack.

cards.t: Behaviour of minerals and rocks under deformation conditions
cards.a: Pore-fluid pressure lowers the effective normal stress (normal stress minus pore pressure), so it weakens rock and helps faults to slip.
cards.w: Water pressure in the pores pushes the grains apart and partly carries the load. On a Mohr diagram the stress circle moves left toward failure.

cards.t: Behaviour of minerals and rocks under deformation conditions
p: TNPSC Geology paper (code 394, year not stated)
cards.a: Boudinage forms when a competent layer is stretched and breaks into sausage-shaped pieces. If the layer only necks without separating, it is pinch-and-swell structure.
cards.w: Competent means strong and stiff. The stiff layer cannot stretch as much as the soft rock around it, so it necks or pulls apart.

cards.t: Behaviour of minerals and rocks under deformation conditions
cards.a: Mylonite is a fine-grained, foliated rock made by ductile shearing in a shear zone. Fault breccia, gouge and cataclasite are made by brittle crushing.
cards.w: In mylonite the grains get smaller by recrystallising while the rock flows. In breccia and gouge the grains are simply broken.

cards.t: Behaviour of minerals and rocks under deformation conditions
cards.a: Wavy (undulose) extinction in quartz under the microscope shows that the crystal lattice has been bent by plastic strain.
cards.w: A bent crystal goes dark in a sweeping wave instead of all at once when the stage is turned. It is a quick sign of a deformed rock.

cards.a: At any point there are three mutually perpendicular principal stresses, σ1 ≥ σ2 ≥ σ3. The planes they act on carry no shear stress.
cards.w: σ1 is the greatest squeeze, σ3 the least. All fault and joint theory starts from the directions of these three.

cards.a: The Mohr circle plots shear stress against normal stress. Its centre is at (σ1 + σ3)/2 and its radius is (σ1 − σ3)/2.
cards.w: Each point on the circle is one plane in the rock. Centre = mean stress; diameter = differential stress. A bigger circle means the rock is closer to breaking.

cards.a: Maximum shear stress equals (σ1 − σ3)/2 and acts on planes at 45° to σ1.
cards.w: It is the top point of the Mohr circle, so its value is the radius. Example: σ1 = 100 MPa, σ3 = 40 MPa gives 30 MPa.

cards.a: Real shear fractures form at about 30° to σ1, not 45°, because of internal friction (Coulomb criterion: τ = C + σn tan φ).
cards.w: C is cohesion (built-in strength) and φ the friction angle. Friction makes it easier to slip on planes closer to σ1, where the normal stress is lower.

cards.a: In conjugate shear fractures, σ1 bisects the acute angle, σ3 bisects the obtuse angle, and the line of intersection is parallel to σ2.
cards.w: Conjugate means a matching pair formed together, like an X. The squeeze direction (σ1) points into the narrow part of the X.

cards.a: Anderson's theory: the Earth's surface carries no shear stress, so one principal stress is vertical. σ1 vertical gives normal faults, σ2 strike-slip faults, σ3 thrust faults.
cards.w: Hook: 1-2-3 = Normal, Strike-slip, Thrust. In normal faults gravity is the biggest stress; in thrusts the horizontal squeeze is biggest and the vertical load is least.

cards.a: Anderson's theory predicts dips of about 60° for normal faults, about 30° for thrust faults, and vertical for strike-slip faults.
cards.w: Faults form at about 30° to σ1. With σ1 vertical that is a 60° dip; with σ1 horizontal it is a 30° dip.

cards.a: Buckling is folding by compression parallel to the layers. Bending is folding by forces acting across the layers, as over a rising intrusion or fault block.
cards.w: Push the two ends of a ruler together and it buckles. Push up under the middle of a sheet and it bends.

cards.a: In flexural-slip folding, layers slide past each other along bedding planes, like a bent pack of cards. It gives parallel folds.
cards.w: Each bed keeps its thickness. Proof in the field: slickensides (scratch marks) on bedding planes at right angles to the fold hinge.

cards.a: In passive (shear) folding the layers are only markers; slip on closely spaced planes parallel to the axial plane produces similar folds.
cards.w: The layering has no strength of its own here. This happens in hot, soft rocks and gives thick hinges and thin limbs.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
p: TNPSC Geology paper (code 394, year not stated)
cards.a: Strike is the direction of a horizontal line on an inclined plane. Dip is the steepest angle of slope of the plane, measured at right angles to strike.
cards.w: On a sloping roof, the ridge line is the strike and the path rainwater takes is the dip direction.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: True dip is the maximum dip. Apparent dip in any other direction is smaller: tan(apparent dip) = tan(true dip) × sin(angle between section and strike).
cards.w: Along the strike the apparent dip is zero; at right angles to strike it equals the true dip. Example: true dip 45°, section 30° from strike, apparent dip about 27°.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: Plunge is the angle between a line and the horizontal, measured in a vertical plane. Pitch (rake) is the angle between a line and the strike, measured within the plane holding the line.
cards.w: Plunge is for any line (fold axis, lineation). Pitch is used for a line lying on a plane, such as scratches on a fault surface.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: Structure contours (strike lines) join points of equal height on a geological surface. tan(dip) = contour interval / horizontal spacing between contours.
cards.w: They work like topographic contours, but for a buried bed. Closely spaced contours mean a steep dip.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: Rule of V's: outcrops of horizontal beds follow the topographic contours and V upstream; outcrops of vertical beds run straight across valleys.
cards.w: A horizontal bed is at one height everywhere, just like a contour. A vertical bed is not shifted sideways by any change in ground height.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: Rule of V's: a bed dipping downstream more steeply than the valley floor Vs downstream; a bed dipping upstream Vs upstream.
cards.w: Short rule: the V points in the direction of dip. The one exception is a bed dipping downstream more gently than the stream bed; it Vs upstream.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: On level ground a plunging anticline's outcrop closes (noses) in the direction of plunge; a plunging syncline's outcrop closes in the opposite direction.
cards.w: Non-plunging folds give straight parallel bands. Plunge makes the bands meet in a V or U shape.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: The Wulff net is equal-angle; the Schmidt (Lambert) net is equal-area. Structural geologists use the Schmidt net with lower-hemisphere projection for contouring data.
cards.w: Equal-area keeps the density of points true, which is needed for statistics. The Wulff net keeps angles true and is preferred in crystallography.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: On a stereonet a plane plots as a great circle and a line as a point. A plane can also be shown by its pole, the point 90° from its great circle.
cards.w: A horizontal plane is the outer circle; a vertical plane is a straight line through the centre; a vertical line is the centre point.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: For a cylindrical fold, poles to bedding lie on a great circle (π-circle) whose pole is the fold axis. In a β-diagram, bedding great circles cross at the fold axis.
cards.w: π-diagram uses poles; β-diagram uses the planes themselves. Both find the fold axis from many dip readings.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: The hinge is the line of maximum curvature of a folded layer. The axial plane (axial surface) joins the hinge lines of successive layers.
cards.w: The axial plane splits the fold into two limbs. Its attitude and the plunge of the hinge together describe how the fold sits in space.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: An anticline has the oldest rocks in its core and a syncline the youngest. Antiform and synform describe only the shape (closing up or closing down).
cards.w: Shape and age can disagree in overturned regions. An arch with the youngest rocks in the core is an antiformal syncline.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: Fleuty's interlimb-angle classes: gentle 180–120°, open 120–70°, close 70–30°, tight 30–0°, isoclinal 0° (parallel limbs).
cards.w: The interlimb angle is the angle between the two limbs. Smaller angle = tighter fold = more shortening.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: An upright fold has a vertical axial plane; a recumbent fold has a horizontal axial plane; a reclined fold has a hinge plunging down the dip of its inclined axial plane.
cards.w: Fleuty named folds by the dip of the axial plane and the plunge of the hinge. In a reclined fold the hinge has a pitch of about 90° on the axial plane.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
p: TNPSC Geology paper (code 394, year not stated)
cards.a: In an overturned fold both limbs dip the same way, and one limb is upside down (rotated past vertical).
cards.w: On the upside-down limb, older beds lie on top of younger beds. Way-up clues such as graded bedding and cross-bedding reveal this.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: Ramsay's fold classification uses dip isogons: lines joining points of equal dip on the upper and lower surfaces of a folded layer.
cards.w: The isogon pattern shows how layer thickness changes from hinge to limb. Three patterns: convergent (Class 1), parallel (Class 2), divergent (Class 3).

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: Ramsay Class 1 folds have convergent isogons. Class 1B is the parallel (concentric) fold, with constant thickness measured at right angles to the layer.
cards.w: In Class 1B the isogons are perpendicular to the layer. Parallel folds form by buckling of strong (competent) beds.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: Ramsay Class 2 folds have parallel isogons and are similar folds. Class 3 folds have divergent isogons.
cards.w: In a similar fold every layer has the same shape, so thickness measured parallel to the axial plane is constant. Hinges are thick, limbs thin.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
p: TNPSC Geology paper (code 394, year not stated)
cards.a: A chevron fold has straight limbs and a sharp hinge. A box fold has two hinges and three limbs. A fan fold has both limbs overturned.
cards.w: Chevron looks like a zigzag (V). Box looks like a flat-topped rectangle. Fan looks like an open hand-fan, pinched at the base.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: Foliation is any planar fabric that runs through a rock; lineation is any linear fabric. Slaty cleavage is a foliation made by parallel, very fine platy minerals.
cards.w: Foliation = sheets (like pages). Lineation = lines (like pencils in a box). Slate splits into thin plates along its cleavage.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: Axial-plane cleavage lies roughly parallel to fold axial planes. It forms at right angles to the direction of greatest shortening (parallel to the XY plane of the strain ellipsoid).
cards.w: Platy minerals turn or grow flat-on to the squeeze, like cards flattened by a press. So cleavage tells you the squeeze direction.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: Crenulation cleavage forms by microfolding (crenulation) of an earlier foliation, so it records a later deformation.
cards.w: Tiny wrinkles form in an older cleavage, and their limbs line up as a new cleavage. Seeing it means the rock was deformed at least twice.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: Where bedding and axial-plane cleavage dip the same way: cleavage steeper than bedding means a normal limb; bedding steeper than cleavage means an overturned limb.
cards.w: This lets you tell which way up the beds are from one outcrop, even when the whole fold is not visible.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: The lineation made by the intersection of bedding and axial-plane cleavage is parallel to the fold axis.
cards.w: Both planes contain the fold axis direction, so the line where they meet points along it. It is a quick way to find the plunge of a large fold.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: Common lineations are mineral (stretching) lineation, intersection lineation, crenulation lineation, slickenlines, boudin axes, mullions and quartz rods.
cards.w: Mullions are pillar-like ribs on the surface of a strong bed. Rods are pencil-like bodies of quartz. Both usually lie parallel to fold axes.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: A joint is a fracture with no visible movement parallel to its surface. Parallel joints make a joint set; two or more sets make a joint system.
cards.w: If the two sides have slid past each other, it is a fault, not a joint. Joints control groundwater flow in hard rocks.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: In folded rocks, longitudinal joints run parallel to the fold axis, cross (transverse) joints run at right angles to it, and diagonal joints are oblique.
cards.w: Relative to bedding the same idea gives strike joints, dip joints and oblique joints. Diagonal joints often come as conjugate shear pairs.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: Columnar joints form by shrinkage during cooling of lava flows, sills and dykes. The columns grow at right angles to the cooling surface.
cards.w: Cooling rock shrinks and cracks into polygons, like drying mud. Indian examples: Deccan Trap flows and St Mary's Islands off Karnataka.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: Sheet (exfoliation) joints lie parallel to the ground surface and form by unloading. Mural joints are three sets at right angles, cutting granite into cubes.
cards.w: When erosion removes the rock above, a granite body expands and peels in sheets. Mural joints make granite easy to quarry as blocks.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: Hanging wall = block above an inclined fault; down in a normal fault, up in a reverse fault. A thrust is a low-angle reverse fault (under 45° in Billings; some books say under 30°).
cards.w: Miners named them: the hanging wall hangs over your head, the footwall is under your feet. Normal = pulling apart; reverse = pushing together.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: Throw is the vertical component and heave the horizontal component of dip-slip displacement, so tan(fault dip) = throw / heave. Hade is the angle between the fault plane and the vertical.
cards.w: Hade = 90° − dip. Example: throw 173 m and heave 100 m give tan(dip) = 1.73, so the dip is 60° and the hade 30°.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: A horst is an uplifted block and a graben a down-dropped block, each bounded by normal faults.
cards.w: Both form where the crust is pulled apart. A graben makes a rift valley; the Rhine valley is the classic example.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: Slickensides are polished, grooved fault surfaces. The grooves (slickenlines) lie parallel to the direction of slip.
cards.w: The two blocks grind against each other and scratch the surface. The scratches show the line of movement on the fault.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: Field signs of faults include offset, repeated or missing beds, fault breccia and gouge, drag folds, fault scarps, triangular facets and lines of springs.
cards.w: Triangular facets are the cut-off ends of ridges along a fault scarp. Springs line up because crushed rock along the fault carries or dams groundwater.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: A nappe is a large rock sheet moved far from its source by thrusting or recumbent folding. Moved rocks are allochthonous; rocks still in place are autochthonous.
cards.w: Nappe is French for tablecloth: a sheet spread over other rocks. Allo = other place; auto = same place.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
p: TNPSC Geology paper (code 394, year not stated)
cards.a: A klippe is an erosional remnant (outlier) of a thrust sheet. A window (fenster) is a hole eroded through a thrust sheet, exposing the rocks below.
cards.w: Klippe = an island of the upper sheet left behind. Window = a hole in the upper sheet that lets you see the lower rocks.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: Himalayan thrusts from north to south are the Main Central Thrust (MCT), Main Boundary Thrust (MBT) and Main Frontal Thrust (MFT). The MBT puts Lesser Himalayan rocks over the Siwaliks.
cards.w: The thrusts get younger toward the south (C-B-F in order). The MCT carries the Higher Himalayan crystalline rocks over the Lesser Himalaya.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: In Kerala, the NW–SE Achankovil Shear Zone separates the Madurai Block from the Trivandrum Block; the Palghat Gap lies along the E–W Palghat–Cauvery Shear Zone.
cards.w: A shear zone is a belt of strongly sheared rock, the deep (ductile) form of a fault. These two are the main crustal breaks of Kerala's basement.

cards.a: Ramsay Type 1 interference is the dome-and-basin ('egg-carton') pattern. It forms when two sets of upright folds cross at a high angle.
cards.w: Superposed folding means later folds (F2) bend earlier folds (F1). Where two arches cross you get a dome; where two troughs cross, a basin.

cards.a: Ramsay Type 2 interference is the dome–crescent–mushroom pattern. It forms when early recumbent or overturned folds are refolded by upright folds with axes at a high angle.
cards.w: Because the first folds were lying down, their axial planes get folded too. Erosion then cuts crescent and mushroom shapes on the map.

cards.a: Ramsay Type 3 interference is the hook-shaped (convergent–divergent) pattern. It forms by coaxial refolding: fold axes nearly parallel, axial planes at a high angle.
cards.w: Coaxial means both fold sets share the same axis direction. The first fold is simply bent again about that axis, giving a hook in cross-section.

cards.a: A porphyroblast is a large crystal grown in the solid state during metamorphism. A phenocryst is a large crystal grown from magma.
cards.w: -blast means grown in a metamorphic rock (garnet, staurolite). The tiny inclusions trapped inside a porphyroblast record the fabric at the time it grew.

cards.a: Pre-tectonic porphyroblasts are wrapped by the foliation and show pressure shadows, cracks, bending or wavy extinction.
cards.w: The crystal was already there when the squeeze came, so the foliation had to flow around it and the crystal itself got damaged.

cards.a: Syn-tectonic porphyroblasts have curved or spiral inclusion trails (Si) that continue into the matrix foliation (Se); snowball garnet is the classic example.
cards.w: Si = foliation inside the crystal, Se = foliation outside. The crystal rotated while it grew, so it trapped a spiral, like a rolling snowball.

cards.a: Post-tectonic porphyroblasts grow across the foliation without bending it. Their inclusion trails are straight, or preserve earlier microfolds (helicitic texture), and match the matrix foliation.
cards.w: Deformation had stopped, so the crystal quietly grew over the finished fabric. No pressure shadows, no wrapping, often random orientation.

cards.a: An unconformity is a buried surface of erosion or non-deposition between older and younger rocks. The missing time is called a hiatus.
cards.w: It is a gap in the rock record, like torn-out pages in a book. It shows uplift and erosion happened before deposition restarted.

cards.a: In an angular unconformity, older beds were tilted or folded and eroded before younger beds were laid across them at a different dip.
cards.w: The dips above and below do not match. Order of events: deposit, tilt, erode, deposit again.

cards.a: In a disconformity, beds above and below are parallel but an uneven erosion surface separates them.
cards.w: There was erosion but no tilting. Look for an irregular surface, old soil or a pebble bed between parallel layers.

cards.a: In a paraconformity, beds are parallel and no erosion surface is visible; the gap is known only from fossils or dating.
cards.w: It looks like a normal bedding plane. Only missing fossil zones show that a long time is not recorded.

cards.a: In a nonconformity, sedimentary beds rest on eroded plutonic igneous or massive metamorphic rocks.
cards.w: Granite forms deep down. For sediments to lie on it, kilometres of rock were eroded first, so the time gap is very large.

cards.a: An inlier is an area of older rocks surrounded by younger rocks. An outlier is an area of younger rocks surrounded by older rocks.
cards.w: Inliers appear where erosion cuts a hole through younger cover (valleys, eroded anticlines). Outliers are caps of younger rock left on hilltops.

cards.a: The Eparchaean Unconformity separates Archaean basement from the overlying Proterozoic (Purana) rocks. It is well exposed at Tirumala, Andhra Pradesh, below Cuddapah quartzite.
cards.w: Ep-Archaean means 'after the Archaean'. It is a nonconformity (sediments on granite and gneiss) and a GSI national geological monument.

cards.a: In Kerala, Tertiary sediments such as the Warkalli Formation rest unconformably on Precambrian crystalline basement of khondalite, charnockite and gneiss.
cards.w: This is Kerala's own basement–cover contact. Nearly the whole Palaeozoic and Mesozoic record is missing in between.

cards.a: Basement is the older crystalline (igneous and metamorphic) rock below a major unconformity; cover is the younger sedimentary sequence lying on it.
cards.w: Basement is stiff and already deformed; cover is layered and weaker. So the two often deform in different ways.

cards.a: In thin-skinned tectonics the cover folds and thrusts above a décollement (detachment surface) and the basement is not involved; in thick-skinned tectonics basement is faulted too.
cards.w: A décollement usually follows a weak layer such as salt or shale, like a rug sliding on a floor. The Jura Mountains are the classic case.

cards.t: Structural behaviour of igneous rocks, diapirs and salt domes
cards.a: Concordant intrusions (sill, laccolith, lopolith, phacolith) lie parallel to the layering of the country rock. Discordant intrusions (dyke, batholith, stock) cut across it.
cards.w: Concordant = agrees with the bedding. Discordant = disagrees. Sill is parallel to beds; dyke cuts across beds.

cards.t: Structural behaviour of igneous rocks, diapirs and salt domes
cards.a: A laccolith has a flat floor and a domed roof. A lopolith is saucer-shaped. A phacolith is a lens along the crest or trough of a fold.
cards.w: Laccolith lifts the roof (thick magma). Lopolith sags like a saucer (Bushveld, South Africa). Phacolith fills the gap that opens at a fold hinge.

cards.t: Structural behaviour of igneous rocks, diapirs and salt domes
cards.a: A batholith is a large discordant pluton with over 100 km² of exposed area; a stock is smaller than 100 km².
cards.w: Batholiths are mostly granite and form the cores of mountain belts. A round stock is called a boss.

cards.t: Structural behaviour of igneous rocks, diapirs and salt domes
cards.a: Ring dykes are vertical or dip steeply outward and form by cauldron subsidence. Cone sheets dip inward toward a magma centre.
cards.w: Ring dyke: a block sinks and magma rises around it. Cone sheet: magma pushes up and fills cone-shaped cracks, like stacked funnels.

cards.t: Structural behaviour of igneous rocks, diapirs and salt domes
cards.a: Flow foliation and flow lineation in a pluton are primary structures made by moving magma; near the margins they usually lie parallel to the contacts.
cards.w: Platy and rod-shaped crystals line up in flowing magma, like logs in a river. They are 'primary' because they form before the rock is fully solid.

cards.t: Structural behaviour of igneous rocks, diapirs and salt domes
cards.a: A diapir is a body of light, mobile rock (salt, mud or magma) that rises and pierces the denser rocks above it.
cards.w: Diapir comes from Greek 'to pierce'. It rises by buoyancy, like oil rising through water, only very slowly.

cards.t: Structural behaviour of igneous rocks, diapirs and salt domes
cards.a: Salt domes rise because buried salt (density about 2.2 g/cm³) is lighter than compacted sediments and flows as a plastic solid.
cards.w: Sediments get denser as they are buried and squeezed; salt does not. Below some depth the salt is the lighter layer and pushes upward.

cards.t: Structural behaviour of igneous rocks, diapirs and salt domes
cards.a: A salt-dome cap rock has anhydrite at the base, gypsum in the middle and calcite on top; native sulphur occurs in the calcite zone.
cards.w: Groundwater dissolves the salt at the top of the dome and leaves the less soluble anhydrite. Anhydrite then alters to gypsum, calcite and sulphur.

cards.t: Structural behaviour of igneous rocks, diapirs and salt domes
cards.a: Salt domes usually give a gravity low. Oil and gas are trapped in the upturned and faulted beds against their flanks and above them.
cards.w: Salt is lighter than the rocks around it, so gravity is slightly weaker over it. Salt does not let fluids pass, so it seals the traps. Classic area: US Gulf Coast.

cards.t: Measurement of strain in deformed rocks
cards.a: In plane strain the intermediate axis Y keeps its original length, so all the shape change is in the XZ plane. At constant volume it plots on the k = 1 line of the Flinn diagram.
cards.w: Pure shear and simple shear are both plane strains. Think of a sheared card deck: it changes shape in one plane only, and its width along the cards stays the same.

cards.t: Measurement of strain in deformed rocks
cards.a: The Rf/φ method finds strain from markers that were already elliptical before deformation, such as pebbles, using each marker's final axial ratio (Rf) and long-axis direction (φ).
cards.w: Pebbles do not start as perfect spheres. Plotting shape against direction for many pebbles separates the original shape from the tectonic strain.

cards.t: Measurement of strain in deformed rocks
cards.a: In homogeneous strain, straight lines stay straight and parallel lines stay parallel, so a circle becomes an ellipse. In heterogeneous strain, straight lines become curved.
cards.w: A fold is heterogeneous strain. Geologists pick small areas where strain is nearly homogeneous so that the strain-ellipse idea can be used.

cards.t: Behaviour of minerals and rocks under deformation conditions
cards.a: An elastic solid obeys Hooke's law: stress is proportional to strain. In a viscous (Newtonian) fluid, stress is proportional to strain rate. A plastic body flows only above a yield stress.
