cards.w: Models: a spring is elastic, a dashpot (piston in oil) is viscous, a block that slides only when pushed hard enough is plastic. Rocks behave as mixes of these.

cards.t: Behaviour of minerals and rocks under deformation conditions
cards.a: Young's modulus is axial stress divided by axial strain. Poisson's ratio is lateral strain divided by axial strain; it is about 0.25 for many rocks.
cards.w: Young's modulus tells how stiff a rock is. Poisson's ratio tells how much it bulges sideways when squeezed lengthwise.

cards.t: Behaviour of minerals and rocks under deformation conditions
cards.a: Competent beds (quartzite, massive sandstone, limestone) are strong and buckle or fracture. Incompetent beds (shale, rock salt, phyllite) are weak and flow.
cards.w: Competence means relative strength under the same conditions. In a folded pile the strong beds set the fold shape and the weak beds flow to fill the gaps.

cards.t: Behaviour of minerals and rocks under deformation conditions
cards.a: Pressure solution dissolves minerals at highly stressed grain contacts and redeposits them where stress is low. It produces stylolites and spaced solution cleavage.
cards.w: It works through a water film around grains at fairly low temperature. Stylolites are the dark, toothed seams seen in limestone and marble.

cards.t: Behaviour of minerals and rocks under deformation conditions
cards.a: Calcite deforms easily by mechanical twinning and micas by kinking. Quartz deforms by dislocation creep, giving undulose extinction, deformation bands and subgrains.
cards.w: Each mineral has its own easiest way to change shape. Dislocations are line defects that move through a crystal and let it flow without breaking.

cards.t: Behaviour of minerals and rocks under deformation conditions
cards.a: Creep is slow, continuous strain under a constant stress below the rock's short-term strength. Its stages are primary (slowing), secondary (steady-state) and tertiary (speeding up to failure).
cards.w: Given geological time, rocks flow under stresses far too small to break them quickly. This is why strain rate matters so much.

cards.t: Behaviour of minerals and rocks under deformation conditions
cards.a: Tectonites are rocks whose fabric was made by deformation. S-tectonites have a dominant foliation, L-tectonites a dominant lineation, and L-S tectonites have both.
cards.w: S = surface (planes), L = line. Flattening strain gives S-tectonites, constriction (stretching) gives L-tectonites, and plane strain gives L-S tectonites.

cards.a: In tangential longitudinal strain (neutral-surface) folding, the outer arc of a competent layer is stretched, the inner arc is shortened, and a neutral surface between them has no strain.
cards.w: Bend a thick rubber eraser: the outside of the bend stretches and the inside wrinkles. Tension cracks can open on the outer arc of such folds.

cards.a: In buckle folds, wavelength increases with the thickness of the competent layer and with its viscosity contrast against the host rock (Biot–Ramberg theory).
cards.w: Thick, stiff beds make large, widely spaced folds; thin beds make small, closely spaced folds. So thick and thin beds in one outcrop fold at different sizes.

cards.a: Ptygmatic folds are tight, lobate, meandering folds of thin competent veins (quartz, pegmatite) in a much weaker host such as migmatite or gneiss.
cards.w: They look like coiled intestines. They form by buckling when the vein is far stiffer than the rock around it.

cards.a: Parasitic (minor) folds are S- or Z-shaped on the limbs and M-shaped at the hinge of a larger fold. Their axes are parallel to the larger fold's axis (Pumpelly's rule).
cards.w: S and Z shapes occur on opposite limbs, so they show on which side the nearest antiform lies. Older books call them drag folds.

cards.a: A listric fault is a curved normal fault, concave upward, that flattens with depth. Its hanging wall commonly bends into a rollover anticline.
cards.w: Listric means shovel-shaped. Growth faults in deltas are listric faults that move during deposition, so beds are thicker on the downthrown side. Rollovers trap oil and gas.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: A strike-slip fault is dextral (right-lateral) if the block across the fault appears to have moved to the right, and sinistral (left-lateral) if it moved to the left.
cards.w: The answer is the same from either side of the fault. Wrench, tear and transcurrent faults are other names for strike-slip faults. The San Andreas Fault is dextral.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
p: TNPSC Geology paper (code 394, year not stated)
cards.a: Relative to the beds it cuts, a strike fault runs parallel to the strike of the beds, a dip fault parallel to their dip direction, and an oblique fault diagonally.
cards.w: A strike fault is also called a longitudinal fault and a dip fault a transverse fault. This naming is about map direction only, not about normal or reverse movement.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: Strike faults make beds repeat or go missing at the surface. Folds repeat beds in mirror-image order (A-B-C-B-A); faults repeat them in the same order (A-B-C-A-B-C).
cards.w: A fold bends the same beds back, so the order reverses about the axis. A fault just shifts the pile, so the order starts again.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: An imbricate (schuppen) zone is a stack of overlapping thrust slices that all dip the same way. A duplex is such a stack bounded by a floor thrust below and a roof thrust above.
cards.w: Imbricate means overlapping like roof tiles. Thrusts climb in steps: flats along weak beds and ramps across strong beds.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: Pseudotachylite is a dark, glassy vein rock made by frictional melting during very fast (earthquake) slip on a fault.
cards.w: It looks like tachylite (basalt glass) but is not volcanic, hence 'pseudo'. It is sometimes called a fossil earthquake.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: Extension (tension) joints open at right angles to σ3 and are parallel to σ1. Their faces often show plumose (feather-like) markings. Shear joints form as conjugate pairs.
cards.w: A crack opens in the direction of least squeeze. Plumose marks fan out from where the crack started and prove the walls pulled apart instead of sliding.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
p: TNPSC Geology paper (code 394, year not stated)
cards.a: In spaced (disjunctive) cleavage, thin cleavage domains are separated by slabs of less-deformed rock called microlithons. In continuous cleavage, such as slaty cleavage, the fabric runs through the whole rock.
cards.w: Fracture cleavage and crenulation cleavage are spaced types. If you can see separate cleavage planes with rock between them, it is spaced.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: Cleavage refraction: cleavage changes angle from bed to bed, lying at a high angle to bedding in competent beds (sandstone) and at a lower angle in incompetent beds (shale).
cards.w: Weak beds take up more shear, which turns their cleavage closer to bedding. In a graded bed the cleavage curves smoothly, which also shows the way up.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: S-C fabric in mylonites has S (foliation) planes oblique to C (shear) planes. The acute angle between S and C points in the direction of shear.
cards.w: From French: schistosité and cisaillement (shear). Other shear-sense indicators are tailed porphyroclasts (σ and δ types) and mica fish. Stretching lineation gives the line of movement.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: Way-up (top-and-bottom) criteria include graded bedding (coarse at the base), cross-bedding (cut off at the top), mud cracks (wide at the top), sole marks (on the base) and convex tops of pillow lava.
cards.w: In folded country beds may be upside down. These primary structures show which side was up when the rock formed, so overturned limbs can be found.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
p: TNPSC Geology paper (code 394, year not stated)
cards.a: Disharmonic folds change in shape or wavelength from layer to layer. Conjugate folds are a pair with axial planes dipping toward each other; a box fold is one example.
cards.w: Disharmony comes from beds of different thickness and strength folding in their own way, often above a weak layer that takes up the misfit.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: A monocline is a step-like bend with one steep limb in otherwise flat or gently dipping beds. A homocline is a set of beds dipping evenly in one direction.
cards.w: Mono = one limb. Monoclines often form in cover beds draped over a fault in the basement below.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: The Narmada–Son Lineament is an ENE–WSW zone of deep faults across central India. The Narmada flows west in its rift valley; the Tapi follows a parallel rift to the south (SONATA zone).
cards.w: It lies between the Vindhyan country to the north and the Satpura–Gondwana country to the south. It is old but still active: the 1997 Jabalpur earthquake occurred on it.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: The Great Boundary Fault of Rajasthan trends NE–SW near Chittorgarh and brings the older rocks of the Aravalli belt against the Vindhyan Supergroup.
cards.w: It marks the western edge of the Vindhyan basin in Rajasthan. Vindhyan beds near it are dragged and steeply tilted.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: The Palghat–Cauvery Shear Zone system (with the Moyar and Bhavani shear zones) crosses southern India roughly east–west and separates the Dharwar Craton–Nilgiri region from the Madurai Block.
cards.w: It is the main crustal boundary inside the Southern Granulite Terrain. In Kerala its surface expression is the Palghat Gap, the widest break in the Western Ghats.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: The Indus–Tsangpo Suture Zone, with its ophiolites, marks where the Indian and Eurasian plates joined. The South Tibetan Detachment is a normal-sense fault at the top of the Higher Himalayan crystalline rocks.
cards.w: Suture = stitch line between two plates; ophiolites are slices of old ocean floor caught in it. Order from north to south: suture, detachment, MCT, MBT, MFT.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: Himalayan examples: the Almora klippe (Kumaun) is a remnant of a crystalline thrust sheet; the Kishtwar and Kulu–Rampur windows expose Lesser Himalayan rocks below the Main Central Thrust sheet.
cards.w: Klippe = island of the upper sheet; window = hole through the upper sheet. Both prove that the crystalline sheet once travelled far over the Lesser Himalaya.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: Regional strike of Indian Precambrian belts: Dharwar NNW–SSE, Aravalli NE–SW, Eastern Ghats NE–SW and Satpura ENE–WSW.
cards.w: These old trends guide later structures too. For example, the Narmada–Son zone follows the Satpura trend.

cards.t: Structural analysis of folds, cleavages, lineations, joints and faults
cards.a: The Singhbhum Shear Zone (Copper Belt Thrust) of Jharkhand is an arcuate ductile shear zone about 200 km long. It hosts copper (Mosabani) and uranium (Jaduguda) deposits.
cards.w: Sheared, crushed rock gave easy paths for ore fluids. It runs along the northern edge of the Singhbhum craton.

cards.a: In repeatedly deformed areas, S0 is bedding, S1 and S2 are successive foliations, F1 and F2 fold generations, L1 and L2 lineations, and D1 and D2 the deformation phases.
cards.w: The number gives the order in time. Example: S1 is the axial-plane cleavage of F1 folds, both made during D1.

cards.a: Signs of superposed folding: folded axial planes and cleavages, refolded fold hinges, bent early lineations, crenulation of an early foliation, and dome, crescent or hook outcrop patterns.
cards.w: An axial plane or cleavage starts flat or planar. If it is now folded, a second folding must have happened after it formed.

cards.a: In Ramsay Type 1 interference the axial planes of the first folds stay nearly planar. In Types 2 and 3 the first axial planes are themselves folded.
cards.w: In Type 1 only the early hinge lines are bent up and down. In Type 3 the early hinges stay straight but the axial planes are bent. In Type 2 both are bent.

cards.a: A culmination is a high point and a depression a low point along a fold hinge whose plunge changes direction. A doubly plunging fold is called a pericline.
cards.w: A doubly plunging anticline makes an elongate dome on the map, with beds dipping away on all sides. Such folds are non-cylindrical.

cards.a: A pressure shadow (strain shadow) is a low-strain zone on two opposite sides of a rigid grain, filled with new quartz, calcite or chlorite and drawn out along the foliation.
cards.w: The hard grain shields the rock beside it from the squeeze, and minerals grow in the sheltered gap. Pyrite and garnet often have them.

cards.a: A porphyroclast is a large relict grain that survived grain-size reduction in a mylonite, such as a feldspar 'augen' (eye). A porphyroblast is a newly grown metamorphic crystal.
cards.w: -clast = broken remnant, -blast = new growth. Porphyroclasts are older than the shearing, and their tails show the shear sense.

cards.a: If straight inclusion trails (Si) in a porphyroblast are cut off sharply and lie at an angle to the outside foliation (Se), the crystal grew between two deformation phases (inter-tectonic).
cards.w: The crystal overgrew the first foliation after D1. Then D2 turned the crystal or built a new foliation around it, so inside and outside no longer match.

cards.a: Bent micas, kinked crystals and undulose extinction show deformation outlasted crystallization. Strain-free polygonal grains meeting at 120° triple junctions show recrystallization outlasted deformation.
cards.w: Heat heals strained crystals (annealing). A polygonal arc, a microfold outlined by straight, unbent mica flakes, likewise shows the micas recrystallized after folding.

cards.a: Randomly oriented contact-metamorphic porphyroblasts (andalusite, cordierite) that overprint a regional foliation show that the granite intrusion is post-tectonic.
cards.w: If the granite had come before or during the deformation, its aureole minerals would be wrapped, broken or lined up by the foliation.

cards.a: Overlap (onlap): during transgression each younger bed extends farther onto the old land surface than the bed below. Offlap: during regression each younger bed covers a smaller area.
cards.w: Rising sea = beds spread landward (overlap). Falling sea = beds retreat seaward (offlap). Overstep is different: one bed rests on the cut edges of several older beds.

cards.a: Field signs of an unconformity: a basal conglomerate with pebbles of the rocks below, an old weathered zone (palaeosol), a difference in dip, cut-off dykes or faults, and a jump in fossil age or metamorphic grade.
cards.w: All of them show that the lower rocks were exposed and eroded before the upper rocks were laid down.

cards.a: A mantled gneiss dome (Eskola) has a core of older granitic gneiss basement, remobilised and domed up, wrapped by a mantle of younger metamorphosed cover rocks.
cards.w: During a later mountain-building event the old basement became hot and light and rose as a dome, lifting its cover like a cloak.

cards.a: In Rajasthan the Banded Gneissic Complex (BGC) is the Archaean basement on which the Proterozoic Aravalli Supergroup was deposited, with an erosional unconformity between them.
cards.w: This is a classic Indian basement–cover pair, described by A. M. Heron. The Peninsular Gneiss plays a similar basement role for the Dharwar belts.

cards.t: Structural behaviour of igneous rocks, diapirs and salt domes
cards.a: Hans Cloos's primary joints in granite plutons: cross (Q) joints at right angles to the flow lines, longitudinal (S) joints steep and parallel to the flow lines, and flat-lying (L) joints.
cards.w: Q joints open by stretching along the flow and often carry aplite or pegmatite dykes. Quarrymen use the related rift, grain and hardway splitting directions.

cards.t: Structural behaviour of igneous rocks, diapirs and salt domes
cards.a: In magmatic stoping, blocks of roof rock break off and sink into the magma, leaving xenoliths. A roof pendant is a remnant of roof rock hanging down into a batholith.
cards.w: Stoping is passive emplacement: magma makes room by swallowing its roof. Forceful emplacement instead pushes the wall rocks aside and bends their foliation parallel to the contact.

cards.t: Structural behaviour of igneous rocks, diapirs and salt domes
cards.a: Dykes open at right angles to σ3, the least compressive stress, so a dyke swarm trends parallel to the σ1–σ2 plane. Radial dykes fan out from a volcanic centre.
cards.w: Magma wedges rock apart in the easiest direction. A swarm of parallel dykes therefore records the direction of crustal stretching.

cards.t: Structural behaviour of igneous rocks, diapirs and salt domes
cards.a: Salt structures grow from salt pillows (cover not pierced) into salt domes or stocks (piercing plugs) and salt walls (long ridges). Salt withdrawal forms a rim syncline around a dome.
cards.w: Salt flows sideways into the rising dome, so the ground around it sinks. Beds over the crest are arched and cut by radial normal faults and a central graben.

cards.t: Structural behaviour of igneous rocks, diapirs and salt domes
cards.a: Classic salt-dome provinces are the US Gulf Coast, the Zechstein basin of north Germany and the North Sea, and the Zagros–Persian Gulf region, where Hormuz salt reaches the surface as salt glaciers.
cards.w: All have a thick, deeply buried salt layer under younger sediments. In the dry climate of Iran the salt is not dissolved, so it flows out over the ground.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.t: Nomenclature and the modern stratigraphic code
p: Calicut Univ M.Sc. Applied Geology 'Stratigraphy and Indian Geology' Nov 2024
Kerala University M.Sc. Geology model questions (GL 231)
cards.a: Nicolaus Steno (1669) gave three basic laws of stratigraphy: superposition, original horizontality and lateral continuity.
cards.w: Steno = S for Strata. Superposition means that in an undisturbed pile the lowest bed is the oldest.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.t: Nomenclature and the modern stratigraphic code
p: Kerala University M.Sc. Geology model questions (GL 231)
cards.a: William Smith stated the principle of faunal succession: fossil assemblages follow one another in a fixed, recognisable order. He made the first geological map of England and Wales (1815).
cards.w: Smith was a canal surveyor who saw the same fossils in the same order everywhere. This lets us match beds by fossils.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.t: Nomenclature and the modern stratigraphic code
cards.a: Walther's Law of facies: facies found one above another in a conformable vertical sequence were deposited side by side at the same time.
cards.w: Environments shift sideways as the sea advances or retreats, so side-by-side belts end up stacked. It fails across an unconformity (a break in deposition).

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.t: Nomenclature and the modern stratigraphic code
cards.a: James Hutton founded uniformitarianism ('the present is the key to the past') and first recognised an angular unconformity, at Siccar Point, Scotland.
cards.w: The same slow processes seen today shaped old rocks. The opposite idea, catastrophism, is linked to Cuvier.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.t: Nomenclature and the modern stratigraphic code
p: Kerala University M.Sc. Geology model questions (GL 231)
cards.a: Principle of cross-cutting relationships: a dyke, fault or erosion surface is younger than the rocks it cuts. Principle of inclusions: fragments are older than the rock that contains them.
cards.w: You cannot cut a cake before it is baked. A pebble must exist before it is caught up in a conglomerate.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.t: Nomenclature and the modern stratigraphic code
cards.a: The term 'facies' was introduced by Amanz Gressly in 1838 for the total rock and fossil character of a sedimentary unit.
cards.w: Facies means 'face' or appearance of a rock. Gressly worked in the Jura Mountains of Switzerland.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.t: Nomenclature and the modern stratigraphic code
p: UPSC Geologist Exam 2019 Geology Paper I (descriptive)
cards.a: Lithostratigraphic units in descending rank are Supergroup, Group, Formation, Member and Bed.
cards.w: These units are based only on rock type, not on age or fossils. Big to small: S-G-F-M-B.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.t: Nomenclature and the modern stratigraphic code
p: UPSC Geologist Exam 2019 Geology Paper I (descriptive)
cards.a: The Formation is the fundamental unit of lithostratigraphy; it must be mappable at the surface or traceable in the subsurface.
cards.w: Geological maps are built from formations. A formation name has a place name plus a rock name or the word Formation, e.g. Narji Limestone.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.t: Nomenclature and the modern stratigraphic code
cards.a: Chronostratigraphic (rock) units Eonothem, Erathem, System, Series and Stage match the geochronologic (time) units Eon, Era, Period, Epoch and Age.
cards.w: Rock units are the rocks formed during the matching time unit. System pairs with Period, Series with Epoch, Stage with Age.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.t: Nomenclature and the modern stratigraphic code
cards.a: For chronostratigraphic (rock) units we use Lower, Middle and Upper; for geochronologic (time) units we use Early, Middle and Late.
cards.w: Rocks have a position, so lower or upper. Time has no position, so early or late. Example: Upper Cretaceous rocks formed in Late Cretaceous time.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.t: Nomenclature and the modern stratigraphic code
p: UPSC Geologist Exam 2019 Geology Paper I (descriptive)
cards.a: The biozone is the basic unit of biostratigraphy. Main kinds are range zone, interval zone, assemblage zone, abundance (acme) zone and lineage zone.
cards.w: A biozone is a body of rock defined by its fossils. An assemblage zone uses a natural association of three or more taxa (kinds of fossils).

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.t: Nomenclature and the modern stratigraphic code
p: Calicut Univ M.Sc. Applied Geology 'Stratigraphy and Indian Geology' Nov 2024
cards.a: A stratotype (type section) is the designated reference section that defines a stratigraphic unit or boundary. The original one named by the author is the holostratotype.
cards.w: It works like a standard metre bar for a rock unit. Later substitutes are called lectostratotype or neostratotype.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.t: Nomenclature and the modern stratigraphic code
p: Kerala University M.Sc. Geology model questions (GL 231)
cards.a: A GSSP (Global Boundary Stratotype Section and Point), the 'golden spike', fixes the base of a stage at one point in one rock section. It is ratified by the IUGS.
cards.w: Only the base is defined; the top of a stage is the base of the next. The first GSSP was the Silurian-Devonian boundary at Klonk, Czech Republic (1972).

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.t: Nomenclature and the modern stratigraphic code
cards.a: Most Precambrian boundaries are fixed by a GSSA (Global Standard Stratigraphic Age), a round number in years, not by a point in rock. Example: Archean-Proterozoic at 2500 Ma.
cards.w: Old rocks lack good fossils for a spike, so an agreed age is used. The Ediacaran is an exception: it has a GSSP in South Australia.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.t: Nomenclature and the modern stratigraphic code
cards.a: The International Stratigraphic Guide (ed. Hedberg 1976; 2nd ed. Salvador 1994) of the International Commission on Stratigraphy is the world standard for stratigraphic classification and naming.
cards.w: It keeps rock (litho), fossil (bio) and time-rock (chrono) units as separate, independent categories.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.t: Nomenclature and the modern stratigraphic code
cards.a: India follows the Code of Stratigraphic Nomenclature of India, published by the Geological Survey of India as Miscellaneous Publication No. 20 (1971).
cards.w: After this code the old words 'System' and 'Series' for rock packages were replaced, e.g. Cuddapah System became Cuddapah Supergroup.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.t: Nomenclature and the modern stratigraphic code
cards.a: Lithostratigraphic boundaries can be diachronous (cut across time), but chronostratigraphic boundaries are isochronous (same age everywhere).
cards.w: A beach sand laid down by an advancing sea is older at one end than the other. So rock boundaries are not time lines.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: Radioactive decay follows N = N0 e^(-lambda t); half-life = 0.693 / lambda. After n half-lives the fraction of parent left is 1/2^n.
cards.w: Lambda is the decay constant (chance of decay per year). Example: after 3 half-lives only 1/8 (12.5%) of the parent remains.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: Uranium-238 decays to lead-206 with a half-life of about 4.47 billion years, releasing 8 alpha and 6 beta particles.
cards.w: The half-life is close to the age of the Earth, so about half of the original U-238 is still present.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: Uranium-235 decays to lead-207 (half-life about 704 million years) and thorium-232 decays to lead-208 (half-life about 14 billion years).
cards.w: Odd goes to odd: 235 to 207. Lead-204 is the only lead isotope that is not made by decay.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: Zircon is the best mineral for U-Pb dating: it takes in uranium but rejects lead when it grows, and it survives weathering and metamorphism.
cards.w: So nearly all lead in a zircon is from decay. Its closure temperature (below which lead cannot escape) is above 900 degrees C.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: On a concordia diagram (Wetherill) 206Pb/238U is plotted against 207Pb/235U. Samples that lost lead fall on a discordia line; its upper intercept gives the crystallisation age.
cards.w: Concordia is the curve where both uranium clocks agree. The lower intercept of the discordia line often marks the time of lead loss.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: Potassium-40 (half-life about 1.25 billion years) decays two ways: about 89% to calcium-40 by beta emission and about 11% to argon-40 by electron capture.
cards.w: Only the argon branch is used for dating, because common calcium-40 is everywhere in rocks and hides the radiogenic part.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: K-Ar dating suits micas, hornblende, sanidine, whole-rock basalt and glauconite. Loss of argon gas on reheating gives ages that are too young.
cards.w: Argon is a gas and is not bound in the crystal, so heat lets it leak out. Glauconite lets us date sedimentary rocks directly.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: In the 40Ar/39Ar method the sample is irradiated with fast neutrons in a reactor to turn potassium-39 into argon-39; step-heating then gives a plateau age.
cards.w: Only argon isotope ratios are measured on one sample piece, so it is more precise than K-Ar. A flat plateau shows no argon loss.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: Rubidium-87 decays to strontium-87 by beta emission with a very long half-life of about 49 billion years. It suits micas, K-feldspar and whole-rock granites.
cards.w: Rubidium follows potassium in minerals, so K-rich rocks are best. The long half-life makes it good for old rocks.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: In an Rb-Sr isochron plot (87Sr/86Sr against 87Rb/86Sr) the slope gives the age and the intercept gives the initial 87Sr/86Sr ratio.
cards.w: A low initial ratio (about 0.703) points to a mantle source. A high ratio (above about 0.710) points to melted old crust.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
p: UPSC Geologist Exam 2019 Geology Paper I (descriptive)
cards.a: Samarium-147 decays to neodymium-143 by alpha emission with a half-life of about 106 billion years. It is used for mafic and ultramafic rocks and garnet.
cards.w: Sm and Nd are rare-earth elements that do not move easily during weathering or metamorphism, so the clock stays reliable in old altered rocks.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: Carbon-14 forms in the upper atmosphere when cosmic-ray neutrons hit nitrogen-14, and it decays back to nitrogen-14 by beta emission.
cards.w: Living things keep taking in C-14. At death the intake stops and the clock starts.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5,730 years and dates organic matter (wood, charcoal, shell, bone) and groundwater up to about 50,000 years. W. F. Libby developed it.
cards.w: After about 9 half-lives too little C-14 is left to measure. Libby won the 1960 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: Fission-track dating counts damage trails made by spontaneous fission of uranium-238 in apatite, zircon, titanite, mica and volcanic glass.
cards.w: Tracks heal (anneal) on heating; in apatite they fade above about 110 degrees C. So the method records cooling and uplift history.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: Closure (blocking) temperature is the temperature below which a mineral keeps its daughter isotope. It falls in the order zircon U-Pb > hornblende K-Ar > biotite K-Ar > apatite fission track.
cards.w: A radiometric age is the time since the mineral cooled below this temperature. Different minerals from one rock therefore give a cooling path.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: Tritium (hydrogen-3) has a half-life of about 12.3 years and is used to identify and date young groundwater recharged in the last few decades.
cards.w: Nuclear bomb tests in the 1950s-60s put a tritium spike in rain. Water with tritium is therefore modern recharge.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: Clair Patterson (1956) fixed the age of the Earth at about 4.55 billion years using lead isotopes in meteorites.
cards.w: Earth's first rocks are destroyed, so he dated meteorites that formed with the Earth. He used the Canyon Diablo iron meteorite as the starting lead.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: The oldest known Earth mineral grains are detrital zircons from Jack Hills, Western Australia (about 4.4 Ga); the oldest known rock is the Acasta Gneiss, Canada (about 4.03 Ga).
cards.w: Detrital means the zircons were eroded from a lost older rock. The Acasta age is used as the base of the Archean Eon.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: Luminescence dating (TL and OSL) measures the time since quartz or feldspar grains were last exposed to sunlight or heat. It is used for Quaternary sands, loess and pottery.
cards.w: Buried grains store energy from natural radiation, and light resets them to zero. OSL = optically stimulated luminescence.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: Rhenium-187 decays to osmium-187 (Re-Os method), which directly dates molybdenite, other sulphide ores and black shales.
cards.w: Re and Os enter sulphide and organic-rich material, unlike most other clocks which need silicate minerals. So it dates ore deposits directly.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
p: Kerala University M.Sc. Geology model questions (GL 231)
cards.a: The four eons from oldest to youngest are Hadean, Archean, Proterozoic and Phanerozoic. The first three together form the Precambrian, about 88% of Earth history.
cards.w: Phanerozoic means 'visible life'. It began with the Cambrian Period.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: Hadean starts about 4600 Ma (ICS 4567), Archean about 4000 Ma (ICS 4031) and Proterozoic at 2500 Ma.
cards.w: 4567 is easy to recall (4-5-6-7). Exam keys mostly use the round 4600 and 4000 Ma; pick the ICS number only if it is the option offered.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: Proterozoic eras: Paleoproterozoic 2500-1600 Ma, Mesoproterozoic 1600-1000 Ma, Neoproterozoic 1000 to about 541 Ma (ICS now 538.8 Ma).
cards.w: 2500, 1600 and 1000 are round because they are agreed ages (GSSA). The top is the Cambrian base, fixed by a GSSP: 541 Ma in most books, 538.8 Ma on the current ICS chart.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: The Neoproterozoic has three periods: Tonian, Cryogenian (from about 720 Ma) and Ediacaran (from about 635 Ma).
cards.w: Cryogenian = 'cold birth', the time of Snowball Earth glaciations. Ediacaran has the first large soft-bodied animals.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: The base of the Cambrian (and Phanerozoic) is about 541 Ma in most textbooks (538.8 Ma on the current ICS chart). GSSP: Fortune Head, Newfoundland; marker trace fossil Treptichnus pedum.
cards.w: Older books give 570 or 542 Ma; ICS revised 541 to 538.8 Ma in 2022. A trace fossil is a burrow or track, not a body.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: Palaeozoic periods in order are Cambrian, Ordovician, Silurian, Devonian, Carboniferous and Permian. Mesozoic periods are Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous.
cards.w: Memory hook for the Palaeozoic: 'Camels Often Sit Down Carefully, Perhaps'.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: Base ages of Palaeozoic periods, textbook (ICS 2026 in brackets): Ordovician 485 (486.9), Silurian 444 (443.1), Devonian 419 (419.6), Carboniferous 359 (358.9), Permian 299 (298.9) Ma.
cards.w: Rough hooks: 485, 444, 419, 359, 299. ICS shifted three of these slightly in Dec 2024. Exam options usually differ by tens of millions of years, so the round value is enough.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: Base ages of Mesozoic periods: Triassic 252 Ma (ICS 251.9), Jurassic 201 Ma (ICS 201.4) and Cretaceous 145 Ma (ICS now 143.1).
cards.w: Most textbooks and answer keys use 145 Ma for the base of the Cretaceous; ICS revised it to 143.1 Ma in Dec 2024. Choose 145 unless only 143.1 is offered.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: The Cenozoic began 66 Ma (older books 65). Periods: Paleogene (Paleocene, Eocene, Oligocene), Neogene (Miocene, Pliocene; from about 23 Ma, ICS 23.04) and Quaternary (Pleistocene, Holocene; from 2.58 Ma).
cards.w: Epoch hook: 'Put Eggs On My Plate Please, Honey'. The Quaternary base was lowered from 1.8 to 2.58 Ma in 2009.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: The Holocene began 11,700 years ago. Its youngest stage, the Meghalayan (from about 4,200 years ago), has its GSSP in a stalagmite from Mawmluh Cave, Meghalaya, India (ratified 2018).
cards.w: It is the only stage named after an Indian state. The boundary marks a worldwide drought seen in the cave deposit.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
p: UPSC Geologist Exam 2019 Geology Paper I (descriptive)
cards.a: The 'Big Five' mass extinctions are end-Ordovician, Late Devonian, end-Permian, end-Triassic and end-Cretaceous. The end-Permian (about 252 Ma) was the largest.
cards.w: The end-Permian event killed about 90% of marine species, including the last trilobites. It is linked to the Siberian Traps eruptions.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
p: UPSC Geologist Exam 2019 Geology Paper I (descriptive)
cards.a: The end-Cretaceous extinction (66 Ma) removed non-avian dinosaurs and ammonites. It is marked worldwide by an iridium-rich clay layer and linked to the Chicxulub impact and Deccan volcanism.
cards.w: Iridium is rare in the crust but common in meteorites. Alvarez and others (1980) found the layer at Gubbio, Italy.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: Cambrian was named by Sedgwick (1835), Silurian (1835) and Permian (1841) by Murchison, and Ordovician by Lapworth (1879).
cards.w: Lapworth created the Ordovician to settle the Sedgwick-Murchison quarrel over overlapping rocks in Wales. Cambria = Latin for Wales; Silures and Ordovices were Welsh tribes; Permian from Perm in Russia.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: In March 2024 the IUGS and ICS rejected the proposal to make the Anthropocene a formal epoch, so the Holocene remains the current epoch.
cards.w: The proposal wanted a start around 1952 with a marker at Crawford Lake, Canada. The word is still used informally.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.t: Stratigraphic procedures of correlation of unfossiliferous rocks
cards.a: Unfossiliferous rocks are correlated by lithological similarity, marker beds, position in sequence, unconformities, structural and metamorphic relations, radiometric ages, palaeomagnetism, geochemistry and well logs.
cards.w: Without fossils we use physical and chemical 'fingerprints'. Radiometric dating is the most reliable of these for Precambrian rocks.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.t: Stratigraphic procedures of correlation of unfossiliferous rocks
cards.a: A good marker (key) bed is thin, distinctive, widespread and deposited quickly. Volcanic ash (tephra or bentonite) beds are the best examples.
cards.w: An ash fall settles in days over a huge area, so it is a true time line. Toba ash (about 74,000 years old) is such a marker across peninsular India.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.t: Stratigraphic procedures of correlation of unfossiliferous rocks
p: Kerala University M.Sc. Geology model questions (GL 231)
Calicut Univ M.Sc. Applied Geology 'Stratigraphy and Indian Geology' Nov 2024
cards.a: Magnetostratigraphy correlates rocks by their record of geomagnetic polarity reversals, which are worldwide and occur at the same time everywhere.
cards.w: Iron minerals lock in the field direction when the rock forms. The pattern of normal and reversed zones works like a barcode.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.t: Stratigraphic procedures of correlation of unfossiliferous rocks
cards.a: The present Brunhes normal polarity chron began about 0.78 Ma. Before it came the Matuyama (reversed), Gauss (normal) and Gilbert (reversed) chrons.
cards.w: Going back in time: B-M-G-G. The Gauss-Matuyama reversal at 2.58 Ma is used as the base of the Quaternary.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.t: Stratigraphic procedures of correlation of unfossiliferous rocks
p: Calicut Univ M.Sc. Applied Geology 'Stratigraphy and Indian Geology' Nov 2024
cards.a: Chemostratigraphy correlates strata using chemical signals such as carbon-13, oxygen-18 and 87Sr/86Sr ratios, or element spikes like the iridium layer.
cards.w: Seawater chemistry changes with time and is the same across the oceans, so rocks of the same age carry the same signal.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.t: Stratigraphic procedures of correlation of unfossiliferous rocks
cards.a: In the marine oxygen-isotope record, odd-numbered stages are warm interglacials and even-numbered stages are cold glacials. Stage 1 is the Holocene.
cards.w: Ice sheets lock up light oxygen-16, so seawater and shells become rich in oxygen-18 in cold times.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.t: Stratigraphic procedures of correlation of unfossiliferous rocks
p: Calicut Univ M.Sc. Applied Geology 'Stratigraphy and Indian Geology' Nov 2024
cards.a: In sequence stratigraphy a depositional sequence is a package of related strata bounded above and below by unconformities or their correlative conformities.
cards.w: A sequence records one cycle of sea-level fall and rise. Its parts are the lowstand, transgressive and highstand systems tracts.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.t: Stratigraphic procedures of correlation of unfossiliferous rocks
cards.a: The maximum flooding surface marks the greatest landward advance of the sea; it separates the transgressive systems tract below from the highstand systems tract above.
cards.w: It is often a thin, clay-rich, slowly deposited layer and gives a strong gamma-ray peak on well logs.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.t: Stratigraphic procedures of correlation of unfossiliferous rocks
cards.a: A varve is one year's deposit in a glacial lake: a light, coarse summer layer plus a dark, fine winter layer. De Geer used varve counting for dating in Sweden.
cards.w: Counting pairs is like counting tree rings. It gives absolute ages for late Quaternary deposits.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.t: Stratigraphic procedures of correlation of unfossiliferous rocks
cards.a: In boreholes, unfossiliferous beds are correlated with geophysical well logs, mainly gamma-ray and resistivity (electric) logs.
cards.w: Shale gives high gamma-ray counts and sandstone low, so each bed has a log shape that can be matched from well to well.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
p: Kerala University M.Sc. Geology model questions (GL 231)
cards.a: Peninsular India has five main Archean cratons: Dharwar, Bastar, Singhbhum, Bundelkhand and Aravalli. They are joined by mobile belts such as the Eastern Ghats and Satpura belts.
cards.w: A craton is an old, stable block of crust. A mobile belt is a long zone of strong folding and metamorphism between cratons.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: The Eparchaean Unconformity separates Archean basement from the overlying Proterozoic 'Purana' basins. It is best seen at Tirumala (Tirupati), where Cuddapah quartzite rests on Archean granite.
cards.w: It marks a very long gap of erosion. The Tirumala site is a National Geological Monument.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
p: Calicut Univ M.Sc. Applied Geology 'Stratigraphy and Indian Geology' Nov 2024
cards.a: The Dharwar craton has a western block (older gneisses, wide schist belts rich in sediments) and an eastern block (younger granites, narrow gold-bearing volcanic belts such as Kolar and Hutti).
cards.w: The two blocks meet along the Chitradurga shear zone; older books use the Closepet Granite as the divide.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: The Sargur Group (older than 3.0 Ga) is the oldest supracrustal unit of the Dharwar craton. It occurs as high-grade enclaves in the Peninsular Gneiss.
cards.w: Supracrustal means rocks first laid down at the surface (lavas and sediments). Sargur ultramafic rocks host chromite at Nuggihalli, Karnataka.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: The Peninsular Gneiss of Karnataka is a tonalite-trondhjemite-granodiorite (TTG) gneiss complex aged about 3.4-3.0 Ga. It is the basement to the Dharwar Supergroup.
cards.w: TTG are sodium-rich granitic rocks typical of Archean crust. The name was given by W. F. Smeeth.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
p: Calicut Univ B.Sc. Geology 'Indian Geology' Nov 2018
cards.a: The Dharwar Supergroup (about 2.9-2.6 Ga) has a lower Bababudan Group and an upper Chitradurga Group.
cards.w: B before C. It lies unconformably on the Peninsular Gneiss. R. Bruce Foote introduced the name Dharwar in 1886.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
p: Calicut Univ B.Sc. Geology 'Indian Geology' Nov 2018
cards.a: The Bababudan Group starts with a uranium- and pyrite-bearing quartz-pebble conglomerate and has thick banded iron formation. The Chitradurga Group has polymict conglomerate, greywacke, carbonates and iron-manganese formations.
cards.w: Bababudan and Kudremukh iron ores come from these banded iron formations. Polymict means pebbles of many rock types.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: The Closepet Granite is a north-south, potassium-rich granite belt about 400 km long in Karnataka, aged about 2.5 Ga (end of the Archean).
cards.w: It is named after Closepet, now Ramanagara. Its intrusion marks the final stabilisation of the Dharwar craton.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
p: Calicut Univ B.Sc. Geology 'Indian Geology' Nov 2018
Calicut Univ M.Sc. Applied Geology 'Stratigraphy and Indian Geology' Nov 2024
cards.a: Dharwar schist belts are India's richest metal source: gold at Kolar and Hutti, iron and manganese at Sandur-Ballari, iron at Bababudan and Kudremukh, and chromite at Nuggihalli.
cards.w: Schist (greenstone) belts are old volcanic-sedimentary belts. Hot fluids moving along their shear zones deposited the gold.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: Charnockite (orthopyroxene-bearing granite) was named by T. H. Holland after Job Charnock; its type area is St. Thomas Mount-Pallavaram, Chennai.
cards.w: Job Charnock's tombstone in Kolkata is made of this rock. Orthopyroxene (hypersthene) shows very hot, dry granulite-facies conditions.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: Khondalite is a garnet-sillimanite-graphite gneiss named by T. L. Walker after the Khond tribe of Odisha. It is a metamorphosed clay-rich sediment.
cards.w: Sillimanite and graphite show the parent was an aluminium- and carbon-rich mud. It is typical of the Eastern Ghats and south Kerala.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
p: UPSC Geologist Exam 2019 Geology Paper I (descriptive)
Calicut Univ M.Sc. Applied Geology 'Stratigraphy and Indian Geology' Nov 2024
cards.a: The Southern Granulite Terrain lies south of the Dharwar craton and is cut by the Moyar-Bhavani, Palghat-Cauvery and Achankovil shear zones. South of Palghat-Cauvery it is also called the Pandyan Mobile Belt.
cards.w: Blocks north of Palghat-Cauvery had granulite metamorphism about 2.5 Ga. The Madurai and Trivandrum blocks to the south were reworked about 550 Ma (Pan-African).

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
p: Calicut Univ M.Sc. Applied Geology 'Stratigraphy and Indian Geology' Nov 2024
cards.a: The Kerala Khondalite Belt (Trivandrum Block) lies south of the Achankovil shear zone. It has khondalite, garnet-biotite gneiss (leptynite) and charnockite, metamorphosed about 550 Ma.
cards.w: It shows 'incipient charnockite' patches formed in gneiss by CO2-rich fluids, classic at Ponmudi. The rocks supply sillimanite, monazite and zircon to Kerala beach sands.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
p: Calicut Univ M.Sc. Applied Geology 'Stratigraphy and Indian Geology' Nov 2024
cards.a: In Kerala the Wayanad Group (schists and ultramafics, Sargur equivalent) is the oldest unit; the Vengad Group of Kannur district (conglomerate, quartzite, mica schist) is equated with the Dharwar Supergroup.
cards.w: Charnockite is the most widespread Precambrian rock of Kerala. Younger granites include Ambalavayal, Kalpetta and Munnar.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
p: UPSC Geologist Exam 2019 Geology Paper I (descriptive)
cards.a: In the Singhbhum craton the oldest units are the Older Metamorphic Group and Older Metamorphic Tonalite Gneiss (about 3.5-3.4 Ga), intruded by the Singhbhum Granite (about 3.3-3.1 Ga).
cards.w: 'Older Metamorphic' is literally the oldest. The granite forms a large batholith (very big intrusion) in Jharkhand and Odisha.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
p: UPSC Geologist Exam 2019 Geology Paper I (descriptive)
cards.a: The Iron Ore Group of Singhbhum-Odisha holds banded hematite jasper and India's major hematite ores (Noamundi, Joda, Barbil, Kiriburu) in a horseshoe-shaped syncline. The Kolhan Group is the youngest cover.
cards.w: Banded hematite jasper is a banded iron formation. Leaching of silica from it left rich hematite ore.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: The arcuate Singhbhum Shear Zone (about 200 km long) hosts copper at Mosabani, Rakha and Surda and uranium at Jaduguda, India's first uranium mine.
cards.w: It is also called the Singhbhum copper belt thrust. Hot fluids moving along the sheared rocks deposited the metals.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
p: Calicut Univ B.Sc. Geology 'Indian Geology' Nov 2018
cards.a: In the Bastar craton and central India the Bailadila Group has rich iron ore, the Sausar Group has manganese ore with gondite, and Malanjkhand granitoid hosts India's largest copper deposit.
cards.w: Gondite is a spessartine garnet-quartz rock named by Fermor after the Gond tribe. The Dongargarh Supergroup of Bastar has Bijli rhyolite.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: The Bundelkhand craton is mainly Bundelkhand granite and gneiss (granite about 2.5 Ga), cut by giant quartz reefs trending NE-SW and mafic dyke swarms trending NW-SE.
cards.w: The quartz reefs stand out as long ridges. The Vindhyan basin wraps around the craton; the Bijawar and Gwalior groups lie on its edges.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
p: Calicut Univ B.Sc. Geology 'Indian Geology' Nov 2018
cards.a: In Rajasthan the order from oldest to youngest is Banded Gneissic Complex (basement), Aravalli Supergroup, Delhi Supergroup (Alwar and Ajabgarh groups), Erinpura Granite and Malani Igneous Suite.
cards.w: A. M. Heron set up this sequence. The Banded Gneissic Complex is Archean (about 3.3-2.5 Ga).

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: The Aravalli Supergroup hosts Zawar lead-zinc and Jhamarkotra stromatolitic rock phosphate; the Delhi Supergroup hosts Khetri copper; the older Bhilwara rocks host Rampura-Agucha lead-zinc.
cards.w: Stromatolites are layered mounds built by microbes. Jhamarkotra near Udaipur is India's largest rock phosphate mine.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
p: Calicut Univ B.Sc. Geology 'Indian Geology' Nov 2018
cards.a: The Erinpura Granite (about 850 Ma) marks the close of the Delhi orogeny. The Malani Igneous Suite (about 750 Ma) of western Rajasthan is mainly rhyolite and granite.
cards.w: Malani is the largest felsic (silica-rich) volcanic province of India. It is overlain by the Marwar Supergroup.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: The Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh is a granulite belt of khondalite, charnockite, anorthosite and alkaline rocks, metamorphosed mainly about 1000 Ma.
cards.w: Its khondalite weathers to the East Coast bauxite (Panchpatmali). It also has manganese ore (kodurite) and graphite.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
p: Calicut Univ B.Sc. Geology 'Indian Geology' Nov 2018
cards.a: The Cuddapah Supergroup of Andhra Pradesh fills a crescent-shaped basin. Its groups, upward, are Papaghni, Chitravati and Nallamalai; the Kurnool Group lies unconformably above.
cards.w: Hook: P-C-N then K. The Papaghni Group starts with Gulcheru Quartzite followed by Vempalle dolomite. W. King named it in 1872.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
p: Calicut Univ B.Sc. Geology 'Indian Geology' Nov 2018
cards.a: Cuddapah basin minerals: baryte at Mangampeta (among the world's largest deposits), uranium at Tummalapalle in Vempalle dolomite, and chrysotile asbestos at Pulivendla.
cards.w: The asbestos formed where dolerite sills baked the Vempalle dolomite. Mangampeta baryte lies in Cumbum (Pullampet) shales of the Nallamalai Group.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: The Kurnool Group, upward, has Banganapalle Quartzite, Narji Limestone, Owk Shale, Paniam Quartzite, Koilkuntla Limestone and Nandyal Shale. Banganapalle conglomerates carry diamonds.
cards.w: It is Neoproterozoic and much thinner than the Cuddapah. Narji Limestone is used for cement and as flooring slabs.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
p: UPSC Geologist Exam 2019 Geology Paper I (descriptive)
Calicut Univ M.Sc. Applied Geology 'Stratigraphy and Indian Geology' Nov 2024
cards.a: The Vindhyan Supergroup has a Lower Vindhyan Semri Group and, above an unconformity, the Upper Vindhyan Kaimur, Rewa and Bhander groups (in upward order).
cards.w: Hook: S-K-R-B. It is more than 4 km thick and mostly unmetamorphosed and little deformed. T. Oldham named it in 1856.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
p: Calicut Univ B.Sc. Geology 'Indian Geology' Nov 2018
cards.a: Vindhyan economic products: diamonds at Panna (Majhgawan pipe and Rewa Group conglomerates), cement-grade limestone (Rohtas, Bhander) and red building sandstone.
cards.w: The Majhgawan pipe cuts Kaimur sandstone and is about 1.07 Ga old. Vindhyan sandstone built the Red Fort and Sanchi Stupa.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: The Chhattisgarh Supergroup on the Bastar craton has a lower sandy Chandarpur Group and an upper limestone-shale Raipur Group, a major cement-limestone source.
cards.w: It is a 'Purana' basin like the Cuddapah and Vindhyan: flat-lying Proterozoic sediments on Archean basement.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.a: In north Karnataka the Kaladgi Supergroup has a lower Bagalkot Group and an upper Badami Group. The Bhima Group of Kalaburagi is mostly limestone (Shahabad Limestone).
cards.w: Badami cave temples are cut in flat Badami sandstone. Shahabad stone is used for cement and flooring; uranium occurs at Gogi in the Bhima basin.

cards.a: A good index (zone) fossil has a short time range, a wide geographic spread, is abundant and is easy to identify.
cards.w: A short life pins down the age; a wide spread lets far-apart rocks be matched. Ammonites, graptolites and planktonic foraminifera are classic examples.

cards.a: Body fossils are actual remains of an organism or their moulds and casts; trace fossils (ichnofossils) record activity - tracks, trails, burrows, borings and coprolites (fossil dung). The study of traces is ichnology.
cards.w: A trace shows behaviour, not the body. Traces are almost always found where they were made, so they are good guides to the old environment.

cards.a: Fossilisation is favoured by hard parts (shell, bone, wood) and by quick burial in fine sediment with little oxygen.
cards.w: Burial shuts out scavengers and decay. That is why shelled sea-floor animals dominate the fossil record and soft-bodied land animals are rare.

cards.a: In permineralisation (petrifaction), minerals such as silica or calcite fill the pores of wood or bone; in replacement they substitute the original material, as in pyritised shells.
cards.w: Permineralised wood keeps its cell structure, so it looks like wood but is stone. Pyrite replacement is common in black, oxygen-poor muds.

cards.a: Carbonisation (distillation) drives off the volatile parts of an organism and leaves a thin carbon film; it is the usual preservation of leaves and graptolites.
cards.w: Heat and pressure squeeze out water and gases, so only carbon stays - like a pressed black print of the leaf.

cards.a: A mould is the impression left by a shell in the sediment; a cast forms when that hollow is later filled, copying the shape of the shell.
cards.w: Mould = the negative (like a jelly mould). Cast = the positive copy made inside it. An internal mould of a shell is called a steinkern.

cards.a: Taphonomy is the study of everything that happens to an organism between its death and its discovery as a fossil - decay, transport, burial and chemical change.
cards.w: From Greek 'taphos' = burial. It tells us how much of the original community is missing from a fossil bed.

cards.a: Living fossils are present-day organisms almost unchanged from very old relatives: Lingula (brachiopod), Nautilus, Limulus (horseshoe crab), Latimeria (coelacanth fish) and Ginkgo (tree).
cards.w: They evolved very slowly, so they have long time ranges. That makes them poor index fossils.

cards.a: Principle of faunal succession (William Smith): fossil groups follow one another through the rock pile in a definite, non-repeating order, so beds with the same fossils are of the same age.
cards.w: Smith was an English canal surveyor (about 1800). This principle is the base of biostratigraphy and of the geological time-scale.

cards.a: The 'Big Five' mass extinctions occurred at the end-Ordovician, Late Devonian, end-Permian, end-Triassic and end-Cretaceous.
cards.w: Memory order: O-D-P-T-K. They explain several of the big breaks in the geological time-scale.

cards.a: The end-Permian extinction (about 252 million years ago) was the largest; it finished off trilobites, rugose and tabulate corals, fusulinid foraminifera and blastoids.
cards.w: It is called 'the Great Dying' and marks the Palaeozoic-Mesozoic boundary. It is linked to the huge Siberian Traps eruptions.

cards.a: The end-Cretaceous extinction (66 million years ago) removed ammonites, belemnites, rudist bivalves and non-avian dinosaurs; it is tied to the Chicxulub impact and an iridium-rich boundary clay.
cards.w: It marks the Mesozoic-Cenozoic boundary. Deccan Trap volcanism in India was erupting at about the same time.

cards.a: In the Cambrian explosion (from about 540 million years ago) most animal phyla with hard parts appear abruptly; the Middle Cambrian Burgess Shale of Canada preserves its soft-bodied animals.
cards.w: Hard shells fossilise easily, so the record suddenly becomes rich. This is why the Phanerozoic ('visible life') starts with the Cambrian.

cards.a: The Devonian is the 'Age of Fishes'; amphibians first appeared in the Late Devonian and reptiles in the Carboniferous. The Mesozoic is the 'Age of Reptiles', the Cenozoic the 'Age of Mammals'.
cards.w: Order of backboned animals: fish, amphibians, reptiles, then mammals and birds. Each step moved life further away from water.

cards.a: Dinosaurs and mammals both first appeared in the Triassic; the earliest known bird, Archaeopteryx, comes from the Late Jurassic Solnhofen Limestone of Germany.
cards.w: Archaeopteryx had feathers like a bird but teeth and a long bony tail like a reptile - a classic connecting link.

cards.a: Vascular land plants first appeared in the Silurian, coal-forming forests peaked in the Carboniferous, and flowering plants (angiosperms) appeared in the Early Cretaceous.
cards.w: Plants colonised the land before backboned animals did. Angiosperms came late but dominate the Cenozoic.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: In brachiopods each valve is bilaterally symmetrical but the two valves are unequal; in a typical bivalve the two valves are mirror images but each valve is lopsided.
cards.w: Hook: a brachiopod valve looks the same on its left and right, like a face. In a clam the symmetry plane runs between the valves instead.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: A brachiopod has a larger pedicle (ventral) valve with an opening for its fleshy stalk - a round pedicle foramen or a triangular notch, the delthyrium - and a brachial (dorsal) valve carrying the lophophore support.
cards.w: Pedicle = stalk that anchors the animal. Lophophore = coiled feeding organ; its calcareous support is called the brachidium.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: Brachiopods range from Cambrian to Recent but dominated Palaeozoic sea floors; Productus (spiny) and Spirifer (wide, wing-like hinge) are typical Late Palaeozoic genera.
cards.w: After the end-Permian extinction bivalves largely took their place. Lingula survives today almost unchanged.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: In bivalves the pallial line marks where the mantle was attached; an embayment in it, the pallial sinus, shows the animal had retractable siphons and burrowed.
cards.w: Siphons are breathing and feeding tubes. A deep sinus means long siphons, so a deep burrower.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: Bivalve hinge types include taxodont (many small similar teeth, e.g. Arca, Nucula), heterodont (cardinal and lateral teeth, e.g. Venus) and schizodont (e.g. Trigonia).
cards.w: Dentition = the pattern of hinge teeth that keeps the two valves aligned. It is a main basis of bivalve classification.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: Bivalve life habits: Mytilus lives attached by byssus threads, Pecten can swim by clapping its valves, Mya burrows deeply and Ostrea cements one valve to the sea floor.
cards.w: Shell shape follows life habit. Byssus = bundle of tough threads used as an anchor.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: Inoceramus is a key Cretaceous zone bivalve; Trigonia is a Mesozoic genus common in the Jurassic of Kutch; rudists were Cretaceous reef-building bivalves that died out at the end of the Cretaceous.
cards.w: Bivalves range from Cambrian to Recent but became dominant only in the Mesozoic and Cenozoic.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: A gastropod shell is one unchambered coiled tube: the spire (older whorls) plus the large body whorl ending in the aperture, coiled around a central pillar called the columella. Range: Cambrian to Recent.
cards.w: No chambers and no siphuncle - that separates a snail shell from a coiled cephalopod shell.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: Most gastropod shells coil dextrally (aperture on the right when the apex points up); Physa coils sinistrally, and Physa prinsepii is a typical fossil of the Deccan Inter-trappean beds.
cards.w: Physa is a freshwater snail, so it shows the inter-trappean beds were laid in lakes between lava flows.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: A cephalopod shell is divided by septa into chambers linked by a tube called the siphuncle; the chambered part is the phragmocone and the animal lives in the last (body) chamber.
cards.w: The siphuncle moves liquid in and out of the chambers to control buoyancy, like ballast tanks. It is central in Nautilus but near the outer edge in ammonoids.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: Ammonoid sutures: goniatitic (simple zigzag, unfrilled lobes and saddles) - Devonian to Permian; ceratitic (frilled lobes, smooth saddles) - mainly Triassic; ammonitic (both frilled) - Jurassic and Cretaceous.
cards.w: Suture = the line where a septum meets the shell wall. Saddles point to the aperture, lobes point away. Hook: G-C-A, in order of time and frilliness.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: Ammonoids ranged from the Devonian to the end of the Cretaceous; nautiloids appeared in the Late Cambrian, have simple gently curved sutures, and survive today as Nautilus.
cards.w: Nautilus is the only living cephalopod with a coiled external shell, so it is the living model for how ammonite shells worked.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: Belemnites were squid-like cephalopods with an internal shell; the usual fossil is the solid, bullet-shaped calcite guard (rostrum). They are common in the Jurassic and Cretaceous and died out at the end-Cretaceous.
cards.w: The guard acted as a counterweight at the tail end. Its calcite is widely used for oxygen-isotope sea-temperature studies.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: Trilobites (marine arthropods, Cambrian to Permian) are divided lengthwise into an axial lobe and two pleural lobes, and crosswise into cephalon, thorax and pygidium.
cards.w: 'Tri-lobe' refers to the three lengthwise lobes, not head-body-tail. Cephalon = head shield; pygidium = tail shield.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: The trilobite cephalon has a raised central glabella, cheeks crossed by facial sutures, compound eyes, and often genal spines drawn out from its rear corners.
cards.w: Trilobites were among the first animals with eyes; the lenses were made of calcite. The glabella covered the stomach.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: Trilobites grew by moulting; the facial sutures were lines of weakness along which the old head shield split open.
cards.w: Like crabs today, they shed the hard outer skeleton to grow. So one animal could leave many fossil moults.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: Trilobite facial sutures: proparian cuts the side margin in front of the genal angle, opisthoparian cuts the rear margin behind it, and gonatoparian passes through the genal angle.
cards.w: Genal angle = rear corner of the cheek. 'Pro' = in front, 'opistho' = behind, 'gonato' = at the angle.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: Classic Cambrian trilobite zones are Olenellus (Lower), Paradoxides (Middle) and Olenus (Upper); in India, Redlichia marks the Cambrian of the Salt Range and Spiti.
cards.w: Trilobites are the main index fossils of the Cambrian because they evolved fast and had hard, easily preserved shields.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: Graptolites were colonial, mostly floating hemichordates; graptoloids are the prime zone fossils of the Ordovician and Silurian, usually preserved as carbon films in black shales.
cards.w: They drifted across oceans and evolved quickly - ideal index fossils. A colony (rhabdosome) has branches (stipes) carrying cups (thecae).

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: Graptolite evolution shows reduction of stipes: many-branched Dictyonema, four-stiped Tetragraptus, two-stiped Didymograptus (Ordovician), then single-stiped Monograptus (Silurian).
cards.w: Hook: many - 4 - 2 - 1. Didymograptus looks like a tuning fork; Monograptus has cups on one side only.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: Regular echinoids (e.g. Cidaris) have five-fold radial symmetry with the anus inside the apical disc; irregular echinoids (e.g. Micraster, Hemiaster) are bilateral with the anus outside it.
cards.w: Regular forms graze on the surface; irregular forms burrow, so they gained a front and a back. Echinoids are Ordovician to Recent; irregular ones appear in the Jurassic.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: An echinoid test has five ambulacral areas pierced by pore pairs for the tube feet, alternating with five interambulacral areas; its jaw apparatus is called Aristotle's lantern.
cards.w: Tube feet are small water-filled 'legs' used for moving and breathing. Echinoderm plates are made of calcite, each plate a single crystal.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: Crinoids ('sea lilies') are stalked echinoderms with a stem, calyx and arms; their broken stem pieces build Palaeozoic crinoidal limestones. Blastoids such as Pentremites died out in the Permian.
cards.w: Crinoids look like plants but are animals. They were most abundant in the Palaeozoic, though some still live today.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: Rugose corals (septa inserted in fours) and tabulate corals (colonial, with strong tabulae) are Ordovician to Permian; scleractinian corals (septa in sixes) range from Triassic to Recent.
cards.w: Rugosa and Tabulata died in the end-Permian extinction; all modern reef corals are scleractinians. Rugose corals are also called tetracorals, scleractinians hexacorals.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: Coral skeleton parts: septa (vertical radial plates), tabulae (horizontal floors) and dissepiments (small curved plates). Favosites (honeycomb coral) and Halysites (chain coral) are tabulate; Zaphrentis and Calceola are rugose.
cards.w: Each polyp sits in a cup called a corallite. Calceola is the Devonian 'slipper coral' with a lid.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: Foraminifera are single-celled, mostly marine protists whose tests are agglutinated (cemented grains), microgranular (fusulinids), porcelaneous (miliolids) or glassy hyaline calcite (rotaliids, globigerinids).
cards.w: Wall type is the first step in classifying forams. They range from Cambrian to Recent and are the most used microfossils.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: Many foraminifera are dimorphic: the megalospheric form has a large first chamber (proloculus) but a small test; the microspheric form has a tiny proloculus but a large test.
cards.w: The two forms come from alternating asexual and sexual generations. Nummulites shows this clearly.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: Fusulinids are spindle-shaped larger foraminifera restricted to the Carboniferous and Permian, which makes them excellent index fossils for the Late Palaeozoic.
cards.w: They look like grains of wheat. They died out in the end-Permian extinction, so any fusulinid limestone is Late Palaeozoic.

cards.t: Morphology and time-ranges of fossil groups
cards.a: Nummulites, a coin-shaped larger foraminifer, ranges from Paleocene to Oligocene and peaks in the Eocene; it builds the Eocene nummulitic limestones of Kutch, Jaisalmer, Subathu and Meghalaya.
cards.w: 'Nummulus' = little coin. The Eocene sea that left these limestones was the shrinking Tethys.

cards.t: Evolutionary changes in molluscs and mammals in geological time
cards.a: Ammonoid sutures grew more complex through time; in the Cretaceous many ammonites became uncoiled 'heteromorphs' such as straight Baculites, hooked Scaphites and helical Turrilites.
cards.w: More folded septa are thought to have strengthened the shell against water pressure. Turrilites looks like a snail but has chambers and sutures.

cards.t: Evolutionary changes in molluscs and mammals in geological time
cards.a: Bivalves replaced brachiopods as the main shelled sea-floor animals after the end-Permian extinction; in the Mesozoic, burrowing bivalves with siphons diversified strongly as shell-crushing predators increased.
cards.w: Hiding in the sediment is a defence. This rise of predators and burrowers is called the Mesozoic marine revolution.

cards.t: Evolutionary changes in molluscs and mammals in geological time
cards.a: Mammals arose from mammal-like reptiles (therapsids, of the cynodont group) in the Late Triassic, stayed small through the Mesozoic, and diversified rapidly in the Paleocene and Eocene.
cards.w: Dinosaurs held the big-animal roles until 66 million years ago. Their extinction left empty niches for mammals to fill.

cards.t: Evolutionary changes in molluscs and mammals in geological time
cards.a: Textbook horse lineage: Eohippus or Hyracotherium (Eocene), Mesohippus (Oligocene), Merychippus (Miocene), Pliohippus (Pliocene), Equus (Pleistocene to Recent) - evolved mainly in North America.
cards.w: Hook: E-M-M-P-E, one genus per epoch. Eohippus means 'dawn horse' and was only the size of a fox.

cards.t: Evolutionary changes in molluscs and mammals in geological time
cards.a: Horse evolution shows increase in body size, reduction of toes from four (front foot of Eohippus) to one, a longer face and limbs, and high-crowned (hypsodont) grazing teeth.
cards.w: Forests gave way to open grassland, so horses became fast runners and grass eaters. Gritty grass wears teeth, so tall crowns helped.

cards.t: Evolutionary changes in molluscs and mammals in geological time
cards.a: Mesohippus had three toes on each foot; Merychippus was the first grazing horse with high-crowned teeth; Pliohippus was the first one-toed horse.
cards.w: Browsing = eating soft leaves (low-crowned teeth). Grazing = eating grass (high-crowned teeth). The switch came in the Miocene.

cards.t: Evolutionary changes in molluscs and mammals in geological time
cards.a: Textbook elephant lineage: Moeritherium (Eocene of Fayum, Egypt), Palaeomastodon (Oligocene), Gomphotherium or Trilophodon (Miocene), Stegodon, then Elephas and Mammuthus (Pleistocene).
cards.w: Moeritherium was pig-sized with no trunk. Proboscideans started in Africa and later spread to Asia, Europe and America.

cards.t: Evolutionary changes in molluscs and mammals in geological time
cards.a: Elephant evolution trends: bigger body, nose and upper lip lengthened into a trunk, second incisors became tusks, the jaw shortened, and molars grew larger with more cross-ridges (plates).
cards.w: A heavy head on a short neck cannot reach the ground, so the trunk does the reaching. More enamel ridges grind tough grass better.

cards.t: Evolutionary changes in molluscs and mammals in geological time
cards.a: Hominin sequence: Australopithecus (Africa), Homo habilis (traditionally the first stone-tool maker), Homo erectus (Java and Peking Man, used fire), Homo sapiens; brain size rose from about 450 to about 1350 cc.
cards.w: Upright walking came first, big brains later. Homo erectus was the first to spread out of Africa.

cards.t: Evolutionary changes in molluscs and mammals in geological time
cards.a: Key hominin finds: 'Taung child' (Australopithecus africanus, Raymond Dart, South Africa, 1924); 'Lucy' (Australopithecus afarensis, Ethiopia, 1974); Java Man (Homo erectus, Eugene Dubois, 1891); Homo habilis from Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania.
cards.w: Africa holds the oldest hominins, which is why it is called the cradle of humankind. Java Man was first named Pithecanthropus erectus.

cards.t: Evolutionary changes in molluscs and mammals in geological time
cards.a: India's best-known ancient hominin fossil is the 'Narmada Man' skull cap, found at Hathnora in the Narmada valley (Madhya Pradesh) by Arun Sonakia of GSI in 1982.
cards.w: It came from Middle Pleistocene river gravels with stone tools. It is classed as Homo erectus or archaic Homo sapiens.

cards.a: Darwin's theory of natural selection ('On the Origin of Species', 1859) says heritable variations that improve survival and reproduction accumulate over generations; A. R. Wallace reached the same idea independently.
cards.w: More young are born than can survive, so the better-fitted leave more offspring. Fossils give the time dimension of this change.

cards.a: Lamarck (1809) proposed evolution by inheritance of acquired characters through use and disuse of organs - a mechanism now rejected.
cards.w: His example: giraffes stretching their necks and passing longer necks to their young. Changes gained in life are not passed on through genes.

cards.a: Neo-Darwinism (the Modern Synthesis) joins natural selection with Mendelian genetics: mutation and gene recombination supply the variation, and selection acts on populations. Hugo de Vries proposed the mutation theory in 1901.
cards.w: Darwin did not know how variation arises or is inherited. Genetics filled that gap.

cards.a: Cope's rule: body size tends to increase within an evolving lineage over geological time, as seen in horses and elephants.
cards.w: Fox-sized Eohippus to modern horse is the standard example. It is a trend with exceptions, not a strict law.

cards.a: Dollo's law: evolution is irreversible - a complex structure once lost is not regained in its original form.
cards.w: Whales went back to the sea but did not regain gills; they still breathe with lungs.

cards.a: Punctuated equilibrium (Eldredge and Gould, 1972): species stay almost unchanged for long periods (stasis), with change concentrated in brief speciation events - the opposite of phyletic gradualism.
cards.w: It explains why fossil species often appear suddenly with few intermediate forms. Gradualism expects slow, steady change instead.

cards.a: Adaptive radiation is the rapid diversification of one ancestral group into many ways of life, e.g. mammals in the early Cenozoic after the dinosaurs died out.
cards.w: Empty niches after an extinction are quickly filled. Darwin's finches are the living example.

cards.a: Convergent evolution gives unrelated groups similar shapes for similar lifestyles, e.g. ichthyosaurs (reptiles), sharks (fish) and dolphins (mammals); look-alike shells from unrelated stocks are called homeomorphs.
cards.w: Same problem, same solution: fast swimming needs a streamlined body. Look-alike fossils from different groups can mislead correlation.

cards.a: Homologous organs share a common origin but differ in use (human arm, bat wing, whale flipper); analogous organs do the same job but arose separately (bird wing, insect wing).
cards.w: Homology points to common ancestry (divergent evolution). Analogy points to convergent evolution.

cards.a: Haeckel's biogenetic law says 'ontogeny recapitulates phylogeny': the growth stages of an individual repeat the history of its ancestors. Ammonoid inner whorls with simpler sutures were the classic fossil example.
cards.w: Ontogeny = growth of one individual. Phylogeny = history of the group. Today it is treated as a loose tendency, not a strict law.

cards.t: Use of species and genera of foraminifera and echinodermata in biostratigraphic correlation
cards.a: Planktonic foraminifera give the standard zonation of Cretaceous and Cenozoic marine rocks; Globotruncana marks the Late Cretaceous (as in the Cauvery basin) and died out at the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary.
cards.w: Floating forms spread across whole oceans and evolve fast. Globigerina and Globorotalia take over in the Cenozoic.
