cards.t: Use of species and genera of foraminifera and echinodermata in biostratigraphic correlation
cards.a: Planktonic foraminifera first appear in the Jurassic. Cenozoic tropical zones are numbered P (Paleogene) and N (Neogene); the first appearance of Orbulina (the 'Orbulina datum') lies near the base of the Middle Miocene.
cards.w: A datum is a first or last appearance of a species used as a time line. Orbulina is a simple sphere, easy to spot.

cards.t: Use of species and genera of foraminifera and echinodermata in biostratigraphic correlation
cards.a: Among larger benthic foraminifera, Orbitoides marks the Late Cretaceous, Assilina, Alveolina and Discocyclina the Eocene, Lepidocyclina the Oligocene-Miocene and Miogypsina the Miocene.
cards.w: Larger forams lived in warm shallow seas and are used where planktonic forms are scarce, as in the shelf limestones of Kutch.

cards.t: Use of species and genera of foraminifera and echinodermata in biostratigraphic correlation
cards.a: Benthic (bottom-living) foraminifera are tied to particular facies, so they are used mainly to read old water depth and environment; a higher planktonic-to-benthic ratio means deeper, more open sea.
cards.w: Planktonic forms rain down everywhere in open sea, but few bottom forms live in deep water. So the ratio rises offshore.

cards.t: Use of species and genera of foraminifera and echinodermata in biostratigraphic correlation
cards.a: The heart-urchin Micraster shows gradual evolutionary change through the Upper Cretaceous Chalk of England and is used to zone it (Rowe, 1899).
cards.w: It is the textbook case of slow, step-by-step evolution in one lineage, tied to deeper burrowing.

cards.t: Use of species and genera of foraminifera and echinodermata in biostratigraphic correlation
cards.a: The stemless crinoids Marsupites and Uintacrinus are short-ranged, widespread zone fossils of the Upper Cretaceous Chalk.
cards.w: Being free-floating or free-lying, they spread widely. Most other echinoderms are tied to one facies, so they are used only for local zoning.

cards.t: Use of species and genera of foraminifera and echinodermata in biostratigraphic correlation
cards.a: In India, echinoids serve as local guide fossils of the marine Cretaceous: Hemiaster in the Bagh Beds of the Narmada valley and Stigmatopygus elatus in the Ariyalur Group of the Cauvery basin.
cards.w: Echinoids live on or in the sea bed, so they do not spread as widely as floating forms. They work best within one basin.

cards.t: Use of species and genera of foraminifera and echinodermata in biostratigraphic correlation
cards.a: The Um Sohryngkew River section in Meghalaya exposes a marine Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary, marked by a turnover of planktonic foraminifera and an iridium anomaly.
cards.w: It is India's best-known marine record of the end-Cretaceous extinction. Cretaceous planktonic forams vanish at the boundary clay.

cards.t: Siwalik vertebrate fauna and Gondwana flora
cards.a: The Siwalik Group (Middle Miocene to Early Pleistocene) is a freshwater molasse famous for its mammal fossils - elephants, horses, giraffes, pigs, apes - first described by Falconer and Cautley in 'Fauna Antiqua Sivalensis'.
cards.w: Molasse = river sediment shed from a rising mountain chain. There are no dinosaurs: the beds are far too young.

cards.t: Siwalik vertebrate fauna and Gondwana flora
cards.a: Lower Siwalik (Kamlial-Chinji) fauna includes the pig Listriodon, Deinotherium, Gomphotherium (Trilophodon), the giraffid Giraffokeryx and the ape Sivapithecus.
cards.w: These are forest and woodland animals, showing a warm, humid climate in the Miocene foothills.

cards.t: Siwalik vertebrate fauna and Gondwana flora
cards.a: The three-toed horse Hipparion is the characteristic fossil of the Middle Siwalik (Nagri and Dhok Pathan formations); it migrated in from North America.
cards.w: Its arrival (the 'Hipparion datum') is used to correlate Late Miocene land deposits across the Old World.

cards.t: Siwalik vertebrate fauna and Gondwana flora
cards.a: Upper Siwalik (Tatrot-Pinjor) fauna is of modern type: Equus, Elephas, Bos or Leptobos, Camelus, Stegodon, Hippopotamus (Hexaprotodon) and the giant tortoise Colossochelys atlas.
cards.w: True one-toed horse, true elephant and true cattle arrive together. Hook: Equus-Elephas-Bos = Pinjor.

cards.t: Siwalik vertebrate fauna and Gondwana flora
cards.a: Stegodon, an extinct elephant relative with low-crowned molars bearing roof-like ridges, is common in the Upper Siwalik; Stegodon ganesa had enormous, long tusks.
cards.w: 'Stegodon' means 'roof tooth'. It links the mastodon-like forms to true elephants in textbook lineages.

cards.t: Siwalik vertebrate fauna and Gondwana flora
cards.a: Sivatherium giganteum was a huge, short-necked giraffid with horn-like ossicones, known from the Upper Siwalik.
cards.w: The name means 'Shiva's beast'. It looked more like a giant moose than a modern giraffe.

cards.t: Siwalik vertebrate fauna and Gondwana flora
cards.a: Ramapithecus, described by G. E. Lewis from the Siwaliks at Haritalyangar (Himachal Pradesh), was once thought a human ancestor; it is now merged with Sivapithecus, a relative of the orangutan.
cards.w: Only jaw pieces were known at first, and they looked human-like. Better skulls later showed an orangutan-like face.

cards.t: Siwalik vertebrate fauna and Gondwana flora
cards.a: The Siwalik Fossil Park at Saketi (Sirmaur district, Himachal Pradesh), run by the Geological Survey of India, displays life-size models of Siwalik mammals at a real fossil site.
cards.w: Saketi lies in the Markanda valley, where Upper Siwalik beds are rich in vertebrate fossils.

cards.t: Siwalik vertebrate fauna and Gondwana flora
cards.a: Lower Gondwana (Permian) rocks carry the Glossopteris flora: Glossopteris, Gangamopteris, Vertebraria, Schizoneura, Noeggerathiopsis and Sphenophyllum.
cards.w: This cool-climate flora followed the Talchir glaciation and formed India's main coal seams.

cards.t: Siwalik vertebrate fauna and Gondwana flora
cards.a: Glossopteris is a tongue-shaped leaf with a distinct midrib and net-like veins; Gangamopteris is similar but has no midrib and dominates the oldest beds (Talchir and Karharbari).
cards.w: 'Glossa' = tongue. Hook: Gangamopteris came first and has no midrib; Glossopteris takes over in the Barakar and Raniganj.

cards.t: Siwalik vertebrate fauna and Gondwana flora
cards.a: Vertebraria is the root-like underground axis of the Glossopteris plant, while Glossopteris, Dicroidium and Ptilophyllum are names for leaves.
cards.w: Fossil plant parts found separately get separate names. Vertebraria looks like a row of vertebrae, hence the name.

cards.t: Siwalik vertebrate fauna and Gondwana flora
cards.a: Separate plant organs carry separate names in the Gondwana flora: Dadoxylon is fossil wood (stem), and Samaropsis and Cordaicarpus are detached seeds.
cards.w: A whole plant is rarely fossilised in one piece. So leaf, wood, root and seed each got their own genus name.

cards.t: Siwalik vertebrate fauna and Gondwana flora
cards.a: Glossopteris was a seed fern (pteridosperm, a gymnosperm), not a true fern; its remains formed the Permian coal of the Barakar and Raniganj formations.
cards.w: Seed ferns had fern-like leaves but reproduced by seeds. Growth rings in Gondwana wood show a seasonal, cool-temperate climate.

cards.t: Siwalik vertebrate fauna and Gondwana flora
cards.a: The Glossopteris flora occurs in India, Australia, South Africa, South America and Antarctica - key fossil evidence that these lands once formed Gondwanaland.
cards.w: Its seeds were too heavy to cross oceans. Wegener used this distribution as evidence for continental drift.

cards.t: Siwalik vertebrate fauna and Gondwana flora
cards.a: Dicroidium (earlier called Thinnfeldia), a seed fern with forked fronds, typifies the Triassic or 'Middle' Gondwana, e.g. the Panchet and Parsora beds.
cards.w: After the end-Permian extinction the Glossopteris flora declined and Dicroidium replaced it across Gondwanaland.

cards.t: Siwalik vertebrate fauna and Gondwana flora
cards.a: Upper Gondwana (Jurassic to Early Cretaceous) rocks carry the Ptilophyllum flora of cycad-like plants, conifers and ferns: Ptilophyllum, Otozamites, Williamsonia, Brachyphyllum, Araucarites and Cladophlebis.
cards.w: Classic localities: Rajmahal Hills, Jabalpur, Kota, Athgarh, Sriperumbudur and Kutch. Hook: Lower = Glossopteris, Middle = Dicroidium, Upper = Ptilophyllum.

cards.t: Siwalik vertebrate fauna and Gondwana flora
cards.a: Birbal Sahni reconstructed the Williamsonia sewardiana plant and described Pentoxylon from the Rajmahal Hills; he founded the palaeobotany institute at Lucknow in 1946.
cards.w: Williamsonia is the 'flower' of the plant that bore Ptilophyllum leaves. Sahni is called the father of Indian palaeobotany.

cards.t: Siwalik vertebrate fauna and Gondwana flora
cards.a: Lepidodendron and Sigillaria (giant club-mosses) and Calamites (giant horsetail) formed the Carboniferous coal forests of Europe and North America; they are not part of the Glossopteris flora.
cards.w: Northern coal is Carboniferous and tropical; Indian Gondwana coal is Permian and cool-climate. Stigmaria is the root of Lepidodendron.

cards.t: Evidence of life in Precambrian times
cards.a: Stromatolites are laminated mounds built when mats of cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) trap and bind sediment; they are the commonest evidence of Precambrian life.
cards.w: They are layered structures made by microbes, not body fossils. Their oxygen-making builders slowly changed the early atmosphere.

cards.t: Evidence of life in Precambrian times
cards.a: The oldest widely accepted stromatolites, about 3.5 billion years old, are in the Pilbara craton of Western Australia; living ones grow today at Shark Bay.
cards.w: This shows microbial life existed in the early Archaean. Shark Bay is too salty for grazing snails, so the mats survive.

cards.t: Evidence of life in Precambrian times
cards.a: The Gunflint Chert of Ontario, Canada (about 1.9 billion years old) gave the first well-preserved Precambrian microfossils, described by Tyler and Barghoorn in 1954.
cards.w: Chert (fine silica) seals in tiny cells before they decay. Older microfossils are reported from the Fig Tree cherts of South Africa (over 3 billion years).

cards.t: Evidence of life in Precambrian times
cards.a: The earliest life was prokaryotic (cells without a nucleus). Oxygen released by cyanobacteria caused the Great Oxidation Event about 2.4 billion years ago; eukaryotes (cells with a nucleus) appear later, in the Proterozoic.
cards.w: Banded iron formations formed as this oxygen combined with dissolved iron in the sea. Complex cells needed an oxygen-bearing world.

cards.t: Evidence of life in Precambrian times
cards.a: In India stromatolites are common in Proterozoic carbonates of the Vindhyan, Cuddapah, Kaladgi, Chhattisgarh and Aravalli basins; at Jhamarkotra (Udaipur) they host rock phosphate.
cards.w: Form-types such as Collenia and Conophyton (cone-shaped) help in broad correlation of these otherwise unfossiliferous basins.

cards.t: Evidence of life in Precambrian times
cards.a: Stromatolites were most abundant and varied in the Proterozoic and declined sharply towards its end, probably because newly evolved animals grazed and burrowed the microbial mats.
cards.w: Today they survive only where grazers cannot live, such as very salty lagoons.

cards.t: Evidence of life in Precambrian times
cards.a: Archaean stromatolites occur in the Dharwar Supergroup of Karnataka (Chitradurga, Sandur, Shimoga belts) and the Iron Ore Group of Odisha - among the oldest evidence of life in India.
cards.w: These Archaean carbonates are over 2.5 billion years old, far older than the Vindhyan or Cuddapah stromatolites.

cards.t: Evidence of life in Precambrian times
cards.a: Acritarchs are organic-walled microfossils of uncertain affinity (probably cysts of planktonic algae); they are the main biostratigraphic tool for the Proterozoic and are also common in the Lower Palaeozoic.
cards.w: 'Acritarch' means 'of uncertain origin'. They are freed from rock by dissolving it in acid, like pollen.

cards.t: Evidence of life in Precambrian times
cards.a: The Ediacaran fauna - soft-bodied animals such as Dickinsonia, Spriggina and Charnia - lived just before the Cambrian (about 575 to 539 million years ago) and is named after the Ediacara Hills of South Australia.
cards.w: These are the oldest large, many-celled animals. They had no shells, so they are preserved only as impressions in sandstone.

cards.t: Evidence of life in Precambrian times
cards.a: A 2021 report of Dickinsonia from Bhimbetka (Upper Vindhyan, Madhya Pradesh) was disproved in 2023: the 'fossil' was a decayed beehive, and the original authors accepted this.
cards.w: A re-visit found the impression peeling off the rock, with wax still present. A reminder that pseudofossils (false fossils) can fool experts.

cards.t: Evidence of life in Precambrian times
cards.a: Vindhyan rocks yield Precambrian carbonaceous megafossils: disc-shaped Chuaria, sausage-shaped Tawuia, and coiled Grypania from the Rohtas Formation, regarded as an early eukaryote.
cards.w: Eukaryote = cell with a nucleus. These thin carbon films are visible to the naked eye, unlike most Precambrian fossils.

cards.t: Evidence of life in Precambrian times
cards.a: The base of the Cambrian is defined by the first appearance of the burrow trace fossil Treptichnus pedum; small shelly fossils of this age occur in the Tal Formation of the Lesser Himalaya.
cards.w: A complex burrow shows animals that could dig in three dimensions. The underlying Krol beds are Ediacaran in age.

cards.t: Different microfossil groups and their distribution in India
cards.a: Microfossils grouped by wall material: calcareous (foraminifera, ostracods, coccoliths), siliceous (radiolaria, diatoms), phosphatic (conodonts) and organic-walled (spores, pollen, dinoflagellate cysts, acritarchs).
cards.w: The wall material decides the lab method: acids destroy calcareous forms but free the organic-walled and siliceous ones.

cards.t: Different microfossil groups and their distribution in India
cards.a: Ostracods are tiny bivalved crustaceans with a calcareous carapace, living since the early Palaeozoic in marine, brackish and fresh water - useful for salinity studies and non-marine correlation.
cards.w: They look like microscopic clams but are relatives of shrimps. Different species prefer different salinity.

cards.t: Different microfossil groups and their distribution in India
cards.a: Radiolaria are marine planktonic protists with an opaline silica skeleton (Cambrian to Recent): Spumellaria are spherical, Nassellaria cone- or helmet-shaped. They form deep-sea ooze and chert, as in the ophiolite belts of Ladakh, Nagaland and Andaman.
cards.w: Silica survives below the depth where carbonate dissolves, so radiolarian chert marks old deep ocean floor.

cards.t: Different microfossil groups and their distribution in India
cards.a: Diatoms are single-celled algae with a two-part silica shell (frustule), round (centric) or elongate (pennate), found in marine and fresh water mainly from the Cretaceous onward; their deposits form diatomite.
cards.w: The frustule fits together like a pill-box. Being plants, they need light and live only in the sunlit upper water.

cards.t: Different microfossil groups and their distribution in India
cards.a: Conodonts are tooth-like microfossils of calcium phosphate (apatite) from an extinct eel-like chordate, ranging from Cambrian to Triassic; their colour (Conodont Alteration Index) records how strongly the rock was heated.
cards.w: They are key index fossils for Palaeozoic and Triassic marine rocks. Pale = cool, black = heated, so they show if oil could survive.

cards.t: Different microfossil groups and their distribution in India
cards.a: The Permian-Triassic boundary is defined by the first appearance of the conodont Hindeodus parvus; in India it is studied with conodonts at Guryul Ravine (Kashmir) and in Spiti.
cards.w: Ammonoids like Otoceras were used earlier, but conodonts are found in more sections and give finer zones.

cards.t: Different microfossil groups and their distribution in India
cards.a: Spores and pollen have a tough sporopollenin wall and are carried into both land and sea deposits, so palynology is the main tool for correlating non-marine beds such as Gondwana coal seams.
cards.w: Palynology = study of spores and pollen. Striped two-sac (striate bisaccate) pollen of the Glossopteris plants is typical of the Indian Permian.

cards.t: Different microfossil groups and their distribution in India
cards.a: Dinoflagellate cysts are organic-walled marine plankton fossils useful from the Late Triassic onward; chitinozoans are flask-shaped organic-walled microfossils of the Ordovician to Devonian.
cards.w: Both are studied on the same slides as spores and pollen, so together they are called palynomorphs.

cards.t: Different microfossil groups and their distribution in India
cards.a: Calcareous nannofossils (coccoliths) are calcite plates of planktonic algae, only a few micrometres across, ranging from Late Triassic to Recent; they are the main ingredient of chalk.
cards.w: They are so small that a tiny chip of rock holds thousands. Star-shaped discoasters are typical Cenozoic forms.

cards.t: Different microfossil groups and their distribution in India
cards.a: Microfossils suit oil exploration because they are abundant and survive whole in small drill cuttings, giving the age, correlation and depositional depth of subsurface beds.
cards.w: Big fossils are broken by the drill bit; microfossils are not. Foraminifera, nannofossils and palynomorphs are the main groups used in Indian basins.

cards.t: Different microfossil groups and their distribution in India
cards.a: Freshwater microfossils - charophyte fruiting bodies (gyrogonites of the alga Chara) and ostracods - are typical of the Lameta and Deccan Inter-trappean beds.
cards.w: They prove these beds were laid in lakes and ponds, not in the sea. They also help fix the latest Cretaceous to earliest Paleocene age.

cards.t: Different microfossil groups and their distribution in India
cards.a: The marine Cretaceous of the Cauvery basin (Uttattur, Trichinopoly, Ariyalur groups) is rich in foraminifera; the Ariyalur Group carries Globotruncana and larger forms such as Orbitoides, Siderolites and Lepidorbitoides.
cards.w: These are Late Cretaceous (Campanian-Maastrichtian) markers. The Cauvery basin is India's reference area for Cretaceous marine microfossils.

cards.t: Different microfossil groups and their distribution in India
cards.a: Kutch is the reference area for Indian Tertiary larger foraminifera: Nummulites, Assilina, Alveolina and Discocyclina in the Eocene; Nummulites fichteli and Lepidocyclina in the Oligocene; Miogypsina in the Lower Miocene.
cards.w: Shallow warm shelf limestones there are packed with larger forams. Similar zones are used in the Mumbai offshore basin.

cards.t: Different microfossil groups and their distribution in India
cards.a: The Sylhet Limestone (Jaintia Group) of Meghalaya and Assam is a Paleocene-Eocene shelf limestone rich in Nummulites, Assilina, Alveolina and Discocyclina.
cards.w: It is the nummulitic limestone of north-east India, quarried for cement. It was laid on a shallow shelf at the edge of the Shillong Plateau.

cards.t: Different microfossil groups and their distribution in India
cards.a: In the Upper Assam oilfields the oil-bearing Barail and Tipam beds are poor in marine microfossils, so subsurface correlation there relies mainly on palynology (spores and pollen).
cards.w: These sands were laid by rivers and deltas, where forams are rare but pollen is plentiful.

cards.t: Different microfossil groups and their distribution in India
cards.a: The Andaman-Nicobar islands (for example Neill and Havelock islands) expose India's best Neogene deep-water marine sequence, rich in planktonic foraminifera, radiolaria and calcareous nannofossils.
cards.w: Open-ocean plankton settled here, away from river mud. So Indian Neogene planktonic zones are tied to Andaman sections.

cards.t: Different microfossil groups and their distribution in India
cards.a: Kerala's Quilon Limestone (Lower Miocene, Burdigalian; type area Padappakkara near Kollam) carries larger foraminifera - Miogypsina, Lepidocyclina, Austrotrillina and Pseudotaberina (Orbiculina) malabarica - with corals and molluscs.
cards.w: Miogypsina fixes the Early Miocene age. The fauna records a warm, shallow sea over the Kerala coast.

cards.t: Different microfossil groups and their distribution in India
cards.a: The lignite and carbonaceous clays of Kerala's Warkalli Formation are poor in shelly fossils; they are dated as Miocene (to Mio-Pliocene) mainly from spores and pollen, which show warm, humid coastal vegetation.
cards.w: Lignite forms from land plants in swamps, so pollen is the fossil to look for. The marine Quilon beds below are dated by forams instead.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Palaeozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Spiti valley in the Tethys Himalaya holds India's most complete marine fossil-bearing sequence, running from the Cambrian to the Cretaceous.
cards.w: Spiti lay under the Tethys sea for most of that time, so beds piled up with few breaks. It is the reference section for Himalayan stratigraphy.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Palaeozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Cambrian of Spiti is the Haimanta Group; its upper beds in the Parahio valley carry trilobites.
cards.w: Haimanta means 'snow-covered'. Trilobites (extinct sea arthropods) prove the Cambrian age.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Palaeozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Muth Quartzite of Spiti is a hard, white, almost unfossiliferous quartzite of Devonian age (possibly starting in the late Silurian).
cards.w: It is a clean shore sand turned to quartzite. White and barren, it is an easy marker between fossil-rich units.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Palaeozoic formations of India
cards.a: In Spiti the Carboniferous is the Kanawar Group: Lipak Formation (limestone) below and Po Formation (shale and quartzite, ending in Fenestella Shales) above.
cards.w: Fenestella is a lace-like bryozoan (tiny colony animal). Order hook: Lipak is Lower, Po is on top.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Palaeozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Kuling Group is the Permian of Spiti; its upper part is the black Productus Shales.
cards.w: Productus is a spiny brachiopod (lamp shell) typical of Permian seas. The Triassic Lilang beds follow directly above.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Palaeozoic formations of India
cards.a: Cambrian of the Salt Range, bottom to top: Purple Sandstone, Neobolus Shales, Magnesian Sandstone, Salt Pseudomorph Shales.
cards.w: Hook: P-N-M-S. Neobolus is a small brachiopod. Salt pseudomorphs are clay casts of salt cubes from a drying lagoon.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Palaeozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Saline Series of the Salt Range (rock salt, gypsum, marl; mined at Khewra) lies below the Cambrian Purple Sandstone and is latest Precambrian to earliest Cambrian.
cards.w: Its age was argued for decades (Cambrian or Eocene). It is now taken as lying in normal order under the Cambrian.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Palaeozoic formations of India
cards.a: In the Salt Range the Ordovician to Middle Carboniferous is missing: the glacial Talchir Boulder Bed rests straight on Cambrian rocks.
cards.w: The area stayed above sea level, so nothing was laid down. This big gap (unconformity) is a favourite exam point.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Palaeozoic formations of India
cards.a: Late Palaeozoic of the Salt Range, bottom to top: Boulder Bed (glacial, Talchir equivalent), Speckled Sandstone, Productus Limestone (Permian).
cards.w: Ice first, then a sandy shallow sea, then a clear warm sea full of brachiopods. Hook: Boulder - Speckled - Productus.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Palaeozoic formations of India
cards.a: In Kashmir the Syringothyris Limestone is Lower Carboniferous and the Fenestella Shales above it are Middle Carboniferous.
cards.w: Both are named after their index fossils: Syringothyris is a brachiopod, Fenestella a bryozoan.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Palaeozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Panjal Volcanics of Kashmir are the Agglomeratic Slate (below) and the Panjal Trap basalt flows (above), of Late Carboniferous to Permian age.
cards.w: Explosive ash and fragments came first, then quiet lava. Do not confuse with the far younger Deccan Traps.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Palaeozoic formations of India
cards.a: In Kashmir the Gangamopteris beds (Lower Gondwana plants) lie above the Panjal volcanics and below the marine Upper Permian Zewan beds.
cards.w: Land plants under dated sea beds prove the Lower Gondwana flora is Permian. This ties Peninsular and Himalayan stratigraphy together.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Palaeozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Guryul Ravine near Srinagar exposes a continuous Permian-Triassic boundary section, from the Zewan Formation up into the Khunamuh Formation.
cards.w: Few places on Earth show this boundary without a break. It records the biggest mass extinction.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Palaeozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Umaria marine bed (Madhya Pradesh) is a thin Lower Permian marine layer with Productus, lying just above the Talchir beds inside a Gondwana basin.
cards.w: It records a short invasion of the sea into the land-locked troughs. Peninsular India otherwise has almost no marine Palaeozoic.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Mesozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Triassic of Spiti is the Lilang Group: thick limestone and shale, very rich in ammonoids.
cards.w: Named after Lilang village. Ammonoids (coiled cephalopod shells) evolved fast, so the Spiti Triassic is zoned in fine detail.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Mesozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Otoceras zone, with Otoceras woodwardi, is the lowest Triassic zone of Spiti and marks the Permian-Triassic boundary there.
cards.w: It sits right on the Permian Productus Shales. Hook: O for Otoceras, O for opening of the Triassic.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Mesozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Kioto (Megalodon) Limestone tops the Triassic of Spiti and continues from the latest Triassic into the Lower-Middle Jurassic.
cards.w: Megalodon here is a thick-shelled bivalve, not the shark. The cliff-forming limestone crosses the Triassic-Jurassic boundary.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Mesozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Spiti Shales are black Upper Jurassic shales (reaching the earliest Cretaceous) with ammonite-bearing concretions called saligrams.
cards.w: Saligrams are round nodules that split to show an ammonite. They are collected as sacred stones.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Mesozoic formations of India
cards.a: Above the Spiti Shales come the Giumal Sandstone (Lower Cretaceous) and the Chikkim limestone and shale (Upper Cretaceous).
cards.w: These are the last sea beds of Spiti before the Tethys closed. Hook going up: Spiti - Giumal - Chikkim.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Mesozoic formations of India
cards.a: The marine Jurassic of Kutch has four classical series, oldest to youngest: Patcham, Chari, Katrol, Umia.
cards.w: Hook: 'Please Come Kutch, Uncle'. The sea entered Kutch from the west in the Middle Jurassic.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Mesozoic formations of India
cards.a: Kutch ages: Patcham is Bathonian, Chari is Callovian-Oxfordian, Katrol is Kimmeridgian-Tithonian, and Umia runs from latest Jurassic into the Lower Cretaceous.
cards.w: Patcham to Katrol are Middle to Upper Jurassic. Only the Umia crosses into the Cretaceous.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Mesozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Dhosa Oolite, a thin Oxfordian marker bed rich in ammonites, forms the top of the Chari Series in Kutch.
cards.w: Oolite is limestone made of tiny round grains. This bed can be traced across Kutch, so it is used for correlation.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Mesozoic formations of India
cards.a: Modern formation names for the Kutch Mesozoic (S.K. Biswas), oldest to youngest: Jhurio, Jumara, Jhuran, Bhuj. Roughly, Jhurio = Patcham and Jumara = Chari.
cards.w: All four start with J-J-J-B. The Bhuj Formation is the sandy, plant-bearing Lower Cretaceous top (upper Umia).

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Mesozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Umia (Bhuj) plant beds of Kutch carry the Upper Gondwana Ptilophyllum flora and are interbedded with marine beds holding ammonites.
cards.w: Sea fossils give a firm date. So these beds help fix the age of the Upper Gondwana as Jurassic to Lower Cretaceous.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Mesozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Jurassic of Jaisalmer (Rajasthan), oldest to youngest: Lathi, Jaisalmer, Baisakhi, Bedesar formations. The Jaisalmer Formation is a golden-yellow limestone.
cards.w: The yellow limestone is the stone of Jaisalmer fort. The Lathi beds below hold the fossil wood of Akal.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Mesozoic formations of India
cards.a: Cretaceous of the Trichinopoly area (Cauvery basin), oldest to youngest: Uttatur, Trichinopoly, Ariyalur, with the Niniyur beds on top.
cards.w: Hook: U-T-A-N. They record the great mid-Cretaceous sea flooding (transgression) of the east coast.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Mesozoic formations of India
cards.a: Trichinopoly ages: Uttatur is Albian-Cenomanian, Trichinopoly is Turonian-Coniacian, Ariyalur is Campanian-Maastrichtian, and Niniyur is Danian (earliest Paleocene).
cards.w: So the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary lies between the Ariyalur and Niniyur. Ammonites stop at the top of the Ariyalur.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Mesozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Uttatur Group starts with coral-reef limestone (quarried at Dalmiapuram) and has clays with gypsum and phosphatic nodules; it is very rich in ammonites.
cards.w: Reefs grew on the newly drowned shore, then mud covered them. The reef limestone feeds cement plants.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Mesozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Trichinopoly Group contains a shell limestone packed with white bivalve and gastropod shells, polished as the ornamental 'Trichinopoly marble'.
cards.w: It is not a true marble, only a hard shelly limestone. Shell banks show a shallow, near-shore sea.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Mesozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Ariyalur Group has yielded dinosaur bones (Kallamedu beds); the Niniyur beds above carry Nautilus danicus and algae but no ammonites.
cards.w: Ammonites and dinosaurs died out at the end of the Cretaceous. Their absence marks the Niniyur as Danian.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Mesozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Bagh Beds are marine Cretaceous (Cenomanian-Turonian) rocks of the lower Narmada valley: Nimar Sandstone at the base, then Nodular Limestone, then Coralline Limestone.
cards.w: A narrow arm of the sea reached inland along the Narmada from the west. Hook going up: N-N-C.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Mesozoic formations of India
cards.a: Bagh Bed fossils resemble those of Arabia and southern Europe, while Trichinopoly fossils are of Indo-Pacific type.
cards.w: The two seas did not mix freely. A land barrier across the Peninsula kept the western (Tethyan) and eastern faunas apart.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Mesozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Lameta Beds are thin river and lake deposits of Maastrichtian (latest Cretaceous) age lying just below the Deccan Traps; they hold dinosaur bones and eggs. Type area: Lameta Ghat, Jabalpur.
cards.w: They are 'infra-trappean' (under the traps). Dinosaurs such as Titanosaurus prove a Cretaceous age for the base of the lavas.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Mesozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Deccan Traps are tholeiitic flood basalts erupted through fissures about 66 million years ago, across the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary; they now cover about 500,000 square km.
cards.w: 'Trap' comes from a Swedish word for stairs: flat flows weather into steps. Tholeiitic means a silica-saturated basalt.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Mesozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Deccan lava pile is thickest (over 2000 m) near the west coast around Mumbai and the Western Ghats, and thins to the east and north.
cards.w: The feeding fissures lay in the west. Thin edges far away, like Rajahmundry and Belgaum, are the tips of long flows.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Mesozoic formations of India
cards.a: Deccan volcanism is linked to the Reunion hotspot, over which India passed as it drifted north; the Rajmahal Traps are linked to the Kerguelen hotspot.
cards.w: A hotspot is a fixed hot plume under the moving plate. Deccan = Reunion, Rajmahal = Kerguelen is a common pairing question.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Mesozoic formations of India
cards.a: Classical division of the Deccan Traps: Lower (eastern Madhya Pradesh), Middle (Malwa and central India), Upper (Mumbai and Kathiawar). Inter-trappean beds are common in Lower and Upper Traps, almost absent in the Middle.
cards.w: The Middle Traps are the thickest yet have few sediment layers. That odd gap is the usual exam catch.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Mesozoic formations of India
cards.a: Inter-trappean beds are thin freshwater lake sediments (chert, limestone, clay) between Deccan flows; the snail Physa prinsepii is the typical fossil.
cards.w: Lakes formed on a cooled flow in quiet gaps, then the next flow buried them. Inter = between flows; infra = below all flows.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Mesozoic formations of India
cards.a: The inter-trappean beds of Mumbai (Upper Traps) yield fossil frogs and tortoises; those near Rajahmundry have estuarine and marine fossils.
cards.w: Frogs mean ponds on the lava plain. Sea shells at Rajahmundry show the east coast shoreline was close by.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Mesozoic formations of India
cards.a: Modern stratigraphy splits the Western Ghats lava pile (Deccan Basalt Group) into three subgroups, oldest to youngest: Kalsubai, Lonavala, Wai.
cards.w: Flows are told apart by chemistry and marker beds. The Wai Subgroup includes the Ambenali and Mahabaleshwar formations.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Mesozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Mahadek Formation is the Upper Cretaceous sandstone on the southern edge of the Shillong Plateau, Meghalaya; it hosts the Domiasiat uranium deposit.
cards.w: It is the north-east record of the same Cretaceous sea flooding seen at Trichinopoly and Bagh.

cards.a: The name Gondwana was given by H.B. Medlicott in 1872, after the Gond kingdom of central India; it first appeared in print in 1876 (Feistmantel).
cards.w: Gondwana means 'land of the Gonds'. Medlicott named the rocks; Suess later named the supercontinent after them.

cards.a: The Gondwana Supergroup ranges from latest Carboniferous (Permo-Carboniferous) to Lower Cretaceous.
cards.w: It starts with the Talchir ice age and ends just before the east-coast seas and the Deccan lavas arrive.

cards.a: Gondwana rocks are mainly river and lake sediments laid in fault-bounded, slowly sinking troughs (rift basins or grabens) within the Peninsular shield.
cards.w: Sinking along faults let thick sediment and coal collect and saved them from later erosion.

cards.a: The main Gondwana basins follow river valleys: Damodar-Koel, Son-Mahanadi, Pranhita-Godavari and Satpura, with outliers in the Rajmahal hills and along the east coast.
cards.w: Today's rivers follow the old rift lines. That is why India's coalfields sit along these same valleys.

cards.a: Two-fold: Lower Gondwana (Glossopteris flora; Talchir, Damuda, Panchet) and Upper Gondwana (Ptilophyllum flora; Mahadeva, Rajmahal, Jabalpur). Three-fold adds a Middle Gondwana for Triassic red beds (Panchet, Mahadeva).
cards.w: Two-fold rests on plant fossils, so Panchet stays in the Lower. Three-fold rests on rock type and reptiles, as the Triassic beds are red and coal-free.

cards.a: Damodar valley sequence, oldest to youngest: Talchir, Karharbari, Barakar, Barren Measures, Raniganj (all Lower Gondwana), then Panchet and Supra-Panchet (Mahadeva).
cards.w: Hook: 'Tall Kings Bring Big Rewards, Please'. The Damodar valley is the type area for the Lower Gondwana.

cards.a: The Damuda Group is the coal-bearing Permian part of the Lower Gondwana: Barakar, Barren Measures and Raniganj formations.
cards.w: Damuda is the old spelling of the Damodar river. Coal seams lie in the Barakar and Raniganj, not in the Barren Measures.

cards.a: The Talchir Formation is the base of the Gondwana: a glacial boulder bed (tillite) with striated, faceted boulders, overlain by green needle shales and varves, resting on Precambrian basement.
cards.w: Scratched boulders and varves (thin yearly layers from meltwater lakes) are sure signs of ice. Named after Talchir in Odisha.

cards.a: The Karharbari Formation (Lower Permian) lies above the Talchir, is best developed in the Giridih coalfield, carries good coal seams and is rich in Gangamopteris.
cards.w: It is the first coal after the ice melted. The climate was still cool, so Gangamopteris outnumbers Glossopteris.

cards.a: The Barakar Formation (Lower Permian) is India's chief coal-bearing unit: sandstone, shale, fireclay and thick coal seams, including the prime coking coal of Jharia.
cards.w: Warm, wet swamps gave thick peat. Named after the Barakar river. Think Barakar = bulk of Indian coal.

cards.a: The Barren Measures lie between the Barakar and Raniganj formations and have no workable coal; in the Raniganj coalfield they are called the Ironstone Shales.
cards.w: 'Barren' means barren of coal. The shales carry clay-ironstone (siderite) nodules instead.

cards.a: The Raniganj Formation is Upper Permian and coal-bearing; rough equivalents are the Kamthi (Godavari-Wardha), Bijori (Satpura) and Himgir (Mahanadi) formations.
cards.w: Same age, different basin, different local name. Raniganj coal is mostly non-coking and high in volatile matter.

cards.a: The Panchet Formation is Lower Triassic: red and chocolate clays with greenish sandstones, no coal, and the reptile Lystrosaurus.
cards.w: Red colour and no coal mean a drier climate. Lystrosaurus also occurs in South Africa and Antarctica, a link across Gondwanaland.

cards.a: The Mahadeva Group of the Satpura basin has three formations, oldest to youngest: Pachmarhi, Denwa, Bagra; the massive Pachmarhi Sandstone forms the Pachmarhi scarps.
cards.w: Named after the Mahadeva hills of Madhya Pradesh. Thick red and buff sandstones with no coal point to a dry climate.

cards.a: In the Pranhita-Godavari basin the Maleri Formation (Upper Triassic red clays with reptiles) is followed by the Dharmaram and then the Kota Formation (Lower Jurassic, with fish and the dinosaur Barapasaurus).
cards.w: Hook going up: M-D-K. The Kota has a thin limestone band with the fish Lepidotes.

cards.a: The Rajmahal Formation of Jharkhand is a pile of Lower Cretaceous basalt flows (Rajmahal Traps) with inter-trappean plant beds carrying the Ptilophyllum flora.
cards.w: It is an Upper Gondwana unit. Older books call it Jurassic; radiometric dates of about 117 million years put it in the Early Cretaceous.

cards.a: The Jabalpur Formation (Upper Jurassic to Lower Cretaceous) of the Satpura-Jabalpur area is an Upper Gondwana unit of white clays and soft sandstones with thin coal.
cards.w: It is the youngest Gondwana unit of central India. It lies below the Lameta Beds and the Deccan Traps.

cards.a: East-coast Upper Gondwana outcrops include the Athgarh Sandstone (Cuttack), the Golapalli-Raghavapuram-Tirupati beds (Godavari) and the Sriperumbudur and Sivaganga beds (Tamil Nadu); some have marine layers.
cards.w: The sea was starting to enter along the new east coast as India broke away. Marine fossils help date these beds.

cards.a: Gondwana climate story: glacial (Talchir), cool and wet (Karharbari), warm humid swamps (Barakar, Raniganj), dry semi-arid (Panchet, Mahadeva), then humid again (Upper Gondwana).
cards.w: Read the rocks: boulder bed = ice, coal = wet swamp, red beds without coal = dry.

cards.a: Gondwana coal forms nearly all (about 98 per cent) of India's coal resources; it is mainly bituminous, of drift origin, high in ash and low in sulphur.
cards.w: Drift origin means plant matter was washed in with mud, so ash is high. The small remainder is Tertiary coal.

cards.a: Key Gondwana coalfields: Raniganj (West Bengal, India's oldest, mined since 1774), Jharia and Bokaro (Jharkhand), Korba (Chhattisgarh), Singrauli (Madhya Pradesh-Uttar Pradesh), Talcher (Odisha), Singareni (Telangana).
cards.w: Jharia gives prime coking coal. Singareni, in the Godavari valley, is the only major coalfield in South India.

cards.a: Gondwanaland (name by Eduard Suess) was the southern supercontinent of South America, Africa, Madagascar, India, Australia and Antarctica.
cards.w: Suess took the name from the Indian Gondwana rocks, since the same rocks and fossils occur on all these lands.

cards.a: Evidence for Gondwanaland: the shared Glossopteris flora, Permo-Carboniferous tillites on every fragment, and land reptiles such as Lystrosaurus in India, Africa and Antarctica.
cards.w: Land plants and reptiles cannot cross oceans, and ice sheets do not form at the equator. So the lands were once joined near the south pole.

cards.a: Karoo (South Africa) equivalents of the Gondwana: Dwyka tillite = Talchir, Ecca coal measures = Damuda, Beaufort beds with Lystrosaurus = Panchet.
cards.w: Same ice, same coal, same reptile, in the same order. Hook: D-E-B in Africa matches T-D-P in India.

cards.a: Gondwanaland began to break up in the Jurassic; India left Antarctica-Australia in the Early Cretaceous, Madagascar about 88-90 million years ago, and the Seychelles about 65 million years ago.
cards.w: Each split has its lava: Rajmahal for the first, Deccan for the Seychelles split.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Cenozoic formations of India
cards.a: Tertiary of Assam, oldest to youngest: Jaintia (Eocene), Barail (Oligocene), Surma (Lower Miocene), Tipam (Miocene), Dupi Tila (Mio-Pliocene), Dihing (Plio-Pleistocene).
cards.w: Hook: 'Just Bring Some Tea, Dear Deepa'. Beds change upward from marine to river deposits as the sea withdrew.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Cenozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Jaintia Group (Eocene shelf beds of Meghalaya-Assam) has three parts: Therria Sandstone, Sylhet Limestone (nummulitic) and Kopili Shale; its deep-water equivalent is the Disang Shale.
cards.w: Nummulites are coin-shaped foraminifera typical of the Eocene. Shelf limestone passes into basin mud toward the Naga Hills.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Cenozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Tertiary coal of Upper Assam (Makum field) lies in the Oligocene Barail Group; unlike Gondwana coal it is low in ash but high in sulphur.
cards.w: It formed in coastal swamps touched by sea water, which adds sulphur. Low ash, high sulphur is the Tertiary coal signature.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Cenozoic formations of India
cards.a: At Digboi (Assam) oil is produced from the Tipam Sandstone (Miocene); the Girujan Clay above it is the cap rock. At Naharkatiya, Barail (Oligocene) sands are the main producers.
cards.w: Oil needs a porous sandstone to hold it and a tight clay to seal it. Tipam = tank, Girujan = lid.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Cenozoic formations of India
cards.a: Sub-Himalayan Tertiary of Himachal (Sirmur Group), oldest to youngest: Subathu (marine, nummulitic, Paleocene-Eocene), Dagshai (red continental beds), Kasauli (grey sandstone with plant fossils).
cards.w: Subathu is the last sea deposit of the foothills. After it only rivers laid sediment, so the land had risen.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Cenozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Murree Group of the Jammu and Potwar foothills is a thick Oligocene-Lower Miocene pile of red and purple continental sandstone and clay, equivalent to the Dagshai and Kasauli; the Siwalik Group lies above it.
cards.w: It is the first river debris shed from the young Himalaya. Order: Subathu (sea), Murree (river), Siwalik (river).

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Cenozoic formations of India
cards.a: Classical Tertiary sequence of Sind, oldest to youngest: Ranikot (Paleocene), Laki and Kirthar (Eocene), Nari (Oligocene), Gaj (Lower Miocene), Manchhar (Mio-Pliocene, Siwalik equivalent).
cards.w: The older units are marine, with nummulitic limestones. The Manchhar on top is river-laid, like the Siwaliks.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Cenozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Tertiary of Kutch rests on weathered Deccan Trap and runs from Paleocene to Pliocene; its Eocene Fulra Limestone is packed with larger foraminifera such as Nummulites.
cards.w: Kutch is the reference section for the marine Tertiary of western India. Biswas gave the modern formation names.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Cenozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Cuddalore Sandstone (Mio-Pliocene) of Tamil Nadu holds the Neyveli lignite, India's largest lignite deposit; the Palana lignite of Bikaner (Rajasthan) is of Paleocene-Eocene age.
cards.w: Lignite is young, soft brown coal. At Neyveli, sands under the seam hold water under pressure and must be pumped during mining.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Cenozoic formations of India
cards.a: In Kerala, sedimentary rocks are limited to Tertiary and Quaternary beds of the coastal belt, resting unconformably on Precambrian crystalline rocks.
cards.w: Kerala has no exposed Palaeozoic or Mesozoic sediments. The Ghats and midlands are charnockite, khondalite and gneiss.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Cenozoic formations of India
cards.a: Tertiary sequence of Kerala, oldest to youngest: Vaikom Formation, Quilon Formation, Warkalli Formation, usually capped by laterite.
cards.w: Hook: V-Q-W, alphabetical going up. Older books list only the Quilon and Warkalli beds.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Cenozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Vaikom Formation is gravel, coarse sandstone and clay with carbonaceous clay and thin lignite seams, lying below the Quilon beds.
cards.w: It is a river-laid, non-marine unit. Named after Vaikom in Kottayam district.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Cenozoic formations of India
cards.a: Boreholes in the Alappuzha area show an older buried unit below the Vaikom, the Alleppey beds: carbonaceous clay with lignite, thought to be Eocene and nowhere exposed.
cards.w: It is known only from drilling by groundwater agencies. So the full subsurface order is Alleppey, Vaikom, Quilon, Warkalli.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Cenozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Quilon Formation is a marine, fossil-rich limestone with marl and clay of Lower Miocene age; its type area is Padappakkara near Kollam.
cards.w: It is the only clearly marine Tertiary unit exposed in Kerala. Its corals, molluscs and foraminifera record a short sea advance.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Cenozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Warkalli Formation (Mio-Pliocene) is sandstone and variegated clay with carbonaceous clay, lignite and marcasite; its type section is the Varkala cliff, Thiruvananthapuram district.
cards.w: Marcasite is an iron sulphide formed in swampy, oxygen-poor mud. The cliff is a GSI national geological monument; W. King named the beds in 1882.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Cenozoic formations of India
cards.a: The Warkalli Formation of Kerala is correlated with the Cuddalore Sandstone of Tamil Nadu and the Ratnagiri beds of Maharashtra.
cards.w: All three are young coastal sands and clays with lignite, laid at about the same time on the two coasts.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Cenozoic formations of India
cards.a: Kerala's Tertiary lignite occurs as thin seams in the Warkalli beds, as at Varkala and in the Madayi-Pazhayangadi area of Kannur and at Nileswaram; the same beds give china clay at Kundara and Madayi.
cards.w: Coastal swamps left thin lignite, too thin for large mining. The white clays feed Kerala's ceramic industry.

cards.t: Stratigraphy of the Cenozoic formations of India
cards.a: The sands of the Warkalli and Vaikom formations are the main confined (pressure) aquifers of coastal Kerala; the Warkalli aquifer is the most widely developed, while the Quilon limestone-clay unit is a poor aquifer.
cards.w: Sand and gravel store and pass water well. Clay and marl do not, so they act as confining layers. Alappuzha's water supply taps these Tertiary sands.

cards.t: Rise of the Himalaya and evolution of Siwalik basin
cards.a: Himalayan belts from south to north: Sub-Himalaya (Siwalik), Lesser Himalaya, Higher (Great) Himalaya, Tethys Himalaya, Indus-Tsangpo Suture Zone, Trans-Himalaya.
cards.w: Each belt is a slice of crust stacked on the one to its south. The suture is the join between India and Asia.

cards.t: Rise of the Himalaya and evolution of Siwalik basin
cards.a: Thrusts from south to north: HFT (plains against Siwalik), MBT (Siwalik against Lesser Himalaya), MCT (Lesser against Higher Himalaya); the South Tibetan Detachment, a normal fault, separates the Higher Himalaya from the Tethyan sediments.
cards.w: HFT = Himalayan Frontal Thrust, MBT = Main Boundary Thrust, MCT = Main Central Thrust. Hook going north: F-B-C.

cards.t: Rise of the Himalaya and evolution of Siwalik basin
cards.a: The Indus-Tsangpo Suture Zone marks where India joined Asia; it contains ophiolites (slices of Tethys ocean floor), melange and the Dras island-arc volcanics.
cards.w: A suture is the scar left when an ocean closes. Ophiolite = ocean crust pushed up on land.

cards.t: Rise of the Himalaya and evolution of Siwalik basin
cards.a: The Trans-Himalayan (Ladakh) batholith is a belt of Cretaceous-Eocene granitic rocks formed above the subducting Tethys ocean floor, before India and Asia collided.
cards.w: It is an Andes-type magmatic arc on the Asian edge. It lies just north of the Indus suture.

cards.t: Rise of the Himalaya and evolution of Siwalik basin
cards.a: India collided with Asia about 50-55 million years ago (Early Eocene), closing the Tethys sea.
cards.w: The last marine beds (Eocene nummulitic limestone of Ladakh, Subathu of the foothills) show when the sea finally left.

cards.t: Rise of the Himalaya and evolution of Siwalik basin
cards.a: Main phases of Himalayan uplift (Wadia): end of Eocene to Oligocene, Middle Miocene (the strongest), and end of Pliocene to Pleistocene, which folded the Siwaliks and tilted the Karewas.
cards.w: Each push is dated by the youngest beds it folded. Krishnan adds an earlier Late Cretaceous phase and a latest sub-Recent one.

cards.t: Rise of the Himalaya and evolution of Siwalik basin
cards.a: The Himalayan thrusts get younger southward: MCT (Early Miocene), MBT (Late Miocene), HFT (Quaternary and still active).
cards.w: As India keeps pushing north, the mountain front steps out toward the plains. The newest break is at the foot of the hills.

cards.t: Rise of the Himalaya and evolution of Siwalik basin
cards.a: The Himalayan arc ends in two sharp hairpin bends called syntaxes: the north-western at Nanga Parbat and the north-eastern at Namcha Barwa.
cards.w: The mountain chains wrap around the two corners of the Indian plate. D.N. Wadia described the north-western syntaxis.

cards.t: Rise of the Himalaya and evolution of Siwalik basin
cards.a: The Higher Himalaya is made of high-grade Central Crystallines intruded by Miocene tourmaline-bearing leucogranites, such as the Gangotri (Badrinath) and Manaslu granites.
cards.w: Leucogranite is a pale granite formed by melting of thickened crust. Its Miocene age dates the peak of mountain building.

cards.t: Rise of the Himalaya and evolution of Siwalik basin
cards.a: The Siwalik Group is a 5-6 km thick pile of freshwater river sediment (molasse) laid in the foreland basin in front of the rising Himalaya, from Middle Miocene to Lower Pleistocene.
cards.w: A foreland basin is the trough made when the mountain load bends the crust down. Molasse = debris shed from a rising range.

cards.t: Rise of the Himalaya and evolution of Siwalik basin
cards.a: Siwalik divisions: Lower (Kamlial, Chinji), Middle (Nagri, Dhok Pathan), Upper (Tatrot, Pinjor, Boulder Conglomerate).
cards.w: Hook: 'Kamal Chose Nagpur, Dad Took Pinky By car'. All names are places in the Potwar-Punjab foothills.

cards.t: Rise of the Himalaya and evolution of Siwalik basin
cards.a: Siwalik rocks coarsen upward: Lower = sandstone with red-purple mudstone; Middle = thick grey 'pepper-and-salt' sandstone; Upper = sand, clay and boulder conglomerate.
cards.w: Coarser debris on top means the mountains were rising and coming closer. Boulders at the top record the last big uplift.

cards.t: Rise of the Himalaya and evolution of Siwalik basin
cards.a: Flysch is deep-marine mud and turbidite sand laid before and during mountain building; molasse is the later, mostly continental, coarse debris. The Siwaliks and Murrees are molasse; the Indus Flysch is flysch.
cards.w: Flysch = sea, early. Molasse = land, late. Both are Alpine terms applied to the Himalaya.

cards.t: Rise of the Himalaya and evolution of Siwalik basin
cards.a: Pascoe and Pilgrim (1919) explained the long, narrow Siwalik belt as the deposit of one great river, the 'Indobrahm' or 'Siwalik River', flowing north-west along the Himalayan foot.
cards.w: Later workers prefer many south-flowing rivers building joined alluvial fans. The old single-river idea is still asked by name.

cards.t: Rise of the Himalaya and evolution of Siwalik basin
cards.a: After the Siwaliks were folded and uplifted in the Pleistocene, the foreland basin shifted south to become the present Indo-Gangetic trough.
cards.w: The foredeep (trough in front of a mountain) moves outward as the thrust front advances. The Ganga plain is today's 'Siwalik basin'.

cards.a: The Quaternary (Pleistocene + Holocene) begins 2.58 million years ago, at the base of the Gelasian Stage (ratified by IUGS in 2009); the Holocene begins 11,700 years ago.
cards.w: The 2.58 mark is when northern ice sheets began to grow strongly. The Holocene is the warm time after the last ice age.

cards.a: The Holocene has three ages (ratified 2018): Greenlandian, Northgrippian and Meghalayan. The Meghalayan began 4,200 years ago; its reference record is a stalagmite from Mawmluh Cave, Meghalaya.
cards.w: It starts with a widespread drought recorded in the cave deposit. It is the only age named after an Indian state.

cards.a: The Middle Pleistocene is now the Chibanian Age (ratified 2020), beginning about 774,000 years ago near the Brunhes-Matuyama magnetic reversal.
cards.w: Named after Chiba in Japan. A magnetic reversal is a world-wide time marker, handy for dating Quaternary beds.

cards.a: At the Last Glacial Maximum, about 20,000 years ago, global sea level stood roughly 120 m lower than today.
cards.w: Water was locked in ice sheets. Rising Holocene seas later drowned river mouths and built today's coastal plains.

cards.a: The Karewas are Plio-Pleistocene lake and river deposits of the Kashmir valley forming flat-topped terraces: Lower Karewa (Hirpur Formation) and Upper Karewa (Nagum Formation).
cards.w: Kashmir was once a big lake dammed by the rising Pir Panjal. Karewa soil is famous for saffron.

cards.a: De Terra and Paterson (1939) recognised four Pleistocene glacial stages separated by three interglacial stages in Kashmir.
cards.w: They read the story from moraines (ice-dumped debris) and river terraces. Interglacial = warm gap between ice advances.

cards.a: Bhangar is the older alluvium of the Indo-Gangetic plain (Pleistocene, above flood level, with kankar nodules); Khadar is the newer flood-plain alluvium (Holocene).
cards.w: Kankar = lime nodules that need a long time to grow, so they mark old alluvium. Khadar is renewed by every flood.

cards.a: Bhabar is the porous gravel belt along the Siwalik foothills where streams sink underground; Terai is the marshy belt just south of it where the water comes out again.
cards.w: Coarse gravel drops first at the hill foot and lets water soak in. Finer beds further out force it back to the surface.

cards.a: Ash from the Toba super-eruption of Sumatra (Youngest Toba Tuff, about 74,000 years old) forms a marker bed in the Quaternary alluvium of the Son, Narmada and other Indian valleys.
cards.w: One ash fall landed everywhere at the same moment. So it ties far-apart river sections to one date.

cards.a: The Miliolite Limestone of coastal Saurashtra (Porbandar stone) is a Pleistocene calcareous sand rock rich in miliolid foraminifera.
cards.w: Named after the tiny Miliolid shells. It is a popular soft building stone of Gujarat.

cards.a: Teri sands are red, wind-blown Late Quaternary dune sands of the south Tamil Nadu coast (Tirunelveli-Thoothukudi), stained by iron oxide and carrying heavy minerals.
cards.w: The red colour is a thin iron-oxide coat on the grains. They carry ilmenite and garnet.

cards.a: The term laterite was coined by Francis Buchanan in 1807 for the rock at Angadipuram, Malappuram district, Kerala.
cards.w: Latin 'later' means brick: the soft rock is cut into blocks that harden in air. The site is a GSI national geological monument.

cards.a: Laterite is a residual weathering product of hot climates with alternate wet and dry seasons, rich in iron and aluminium hydroxides; high-level laterite caps plateaus, low-level laterite covers coastal lowlands.
cards.w: Rain washes out silica and bases; iron and aluminium stay behind. Residual means formed in place, not transported.

cards.a: In Kerala laterite caps the Precambrian crystalline rocks of the midlands and also the Tertiary Warkalli beds of the coast.
cards.w: So lateritisation went on after the Warkalli beds were laid, into the Quaternary. Laterite here is a key shallow aquifer for dug wells.

cards.a: Quaternary coastal sediments of Kerala are beach and dune sands, old beach ridges, lagoon and backwater clays, peat and river alluvium; the Chavara beach sands hold ilmenite, rutile, zircon and monazite.
cards.w: Rising Holocene seas and longshore drift built sand barriers. Lagoons (kayals) such as Vembanad were trapped behind them.

cards.a: GSI divides the Quaternary of coastal Kerala by origin: Guruvayur Formation (old beach ridges), Viyyam Formation (tidal flats), Periyar Formation (river alluvium), Kadappuram Formation (present beaches).
cards.w: Each name tells the setting: old beach, tidal mud, river, modern beach. Kadappuram simply means seashore in Malayalam.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Crystals are grouped into seven crystal systems: cubic (isometric), tetragonal, hexagonal, trigonal, orthorhombic, monoclinic and triclinic. Older books count six by placing trigonal inside hexagonal.
cards.w: Systems are defined by the lengths of the crystal axes and the angles between them. Symmetry falls from cubic (highest) to triclinic (lowest).

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: There are 32 crystal classes (point groups), 14 Bravais lattices and 230 space groups.
cards.w: Hook: 7 systems - 14 lattices - 32 classes - 230 space groups. Classes describe the outer symmetry of a crystal; space groups describe the inner arrangement of atoms.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: The symmetry elements of crystals are the plane (mirror), the axis of rotation and the centre. Rotation axes can only be 2-, 3-, 4- or 6-fold; a 5-fold axis is impossible.
cards.w: Five-fold units cannot fill space without gaps, just as regular pentagon tiles cannot cover a floor. So a repeating crystal lattice cannot have a 5-fold axis.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: The cubic system has three equal axes at right angles (a = b = c). Its diagnostic symmetry is four 3-fold axes, which run along the body diagonals of the cube.
cards.w: Every cubic class keeps the four 3-fold axes, even classes such as pyrite's that have no 4-fold axis. Examples: galena, garnet, halite, fluorite, magnetite.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: The normal (galena-type) class of the cubic system has the highest symmetry of any crystal: 9 planes, 13 axes (three 4-fold, four 3-fold, six 2-fold) and a centre.
cards.w: Hook: 9 + 13 + 1 = 23 symmetry elements. The 9 planes are 3 axial planes plus 6 diagonal planes.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Tetragonal crystals have a = b but c different, with all angles 90°, and one 4-fold axis. Examples: zircon, rutile, cassiterite, chalcopyrite.
cards.w: Think of a cube stretched or squashed along one axis. That special axis (c) is the single 4-fold axis.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Hexagonal crystals use four axes: three equal horizontal axes at 120° and a vertical c axis. The hexagonal division has one 6-fold axis (beryl, apatite); the trigonal division has one 3-fold axis (quartz, calcite, tourmaline, corundum).
cards.w: It is the only system described with four axes. Hook: beryl and apatite are 'six-siders'; quartz and calcite are 'three-siders'.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Orthorhombic crystals have three unequal axes, all at 90°. Their symmetry is three 2-fold axes, or one 2-fold axis with two mirror planes. Examples: olivine, barite, topaz, sulphur, aragonite.
cards.w: Think of a matchbox: three different edge lengths but all corners square. No axis is higher than 2-fold.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Monoclinic crystals have three unequal axes with one oblique angle (beta is not 90°). The highest symmetry is one 2-fold axis, one plane and a centre. Examples: orthoclase, gypsum, augite, hornblende, micas.
cards.w: Mono-clinic means 'one inclination': only one axis leans. More common minerals belong to this system than to any other.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Triclinic crystals have three unequal axes and no right angles between them. The highest possible symmetry is only a centre. Examples: plagioclase, microcline, kyanite, axinite.
cards.w: Tri-clinic means 'three inclinations': all three axes lean. It is the least symmetric system.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Miller indices of a crystal face are the reciprocals of its intercepts on the crystal axes, cleared of fractions. A face parallel to an axis gets the index 0 for that axis.
cards.w: Example: intercepts 1a, 2b and parallel to c. Reciprocals are 1, 1/2, 0. Multiply by 2 to get (210). Parallel means the intercept is infinity, and 1/infinity = 0.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Steno's law of constancy of interfacial angles: in all crystals of the same mineral, the angles between corresponding faces are the same. These angles are measured with a goniometer.
cards.w: Faces can grow large or small, but the atomic framework fixes the angles between them. A contact goniometer suits large crystals; a reflecting goniometer suits small bright ones.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: A crystal form is a set of faces related by symmetry. Closed forms enclose space (cube, octahedron, dipyramid). Open forms do not: pedion (1 face), pinacoid (2 parallel faces), prism, pyramid.
cards.w: An open form must combine with another form to make a whole crystal. A prism needs a basal pinacoid {001} or a pyramid to close its ends.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Common cubic forms: the cube {100} has 6 faces, the octahedron {111} has 8 faces and the rhombic dodecahedron {110} has 12 faces.
cards.w: A cube face cuts one axis and is parallel to two. An octahedron face cuts all three equally. A dodecahedron face cuts two axes and is parallel to the third.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Three cubic forms have 24 faces: tetrahexahedron {hk0}, trapezohedron {hll} and trisoctahedron {hhl}. The hexoctahedron {hkl} has 48 faces, the largest number in any crystal form.
cards.w: Trapezohedron is the usual shape of leucite and analcime crystals and is common in garnet. 48 is the 'general form' of the highest-symmetry class.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Mohs scale of hardness: talc 1, gypsum 2, calcite 3, fluorite 4, apatite 5, orthoclase 6, quartz 7, topaz 8, corundum 9, diamond 10.
cards.w: Hook: 'The Girls Can Flirt And Other Queer Things Can Do'. The scale is only relative: diamond is many times harder than corundum, not just one step.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Kyanite has two hardnesses: about 4.5-5 along the length of the blade and about 6.5-7 across it. Its old name, disthene, refers to this.
cards.w: Disthene means 'two strengths'. A knife scratches a kyanite blade lengthwise but not crosswise. It is the classic example of hardness varying with direction.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Cleavage directions: micas 1 (basal); pyroxenes, amphiboles and feldspars 2; halite and galena 3 at 90° (cubic); calcite 3 not at 90° (rhombohedral); fluorite 4 (octahedral); sphalerite 6 (dodecahedral).
cards.w: Cleavage is smooth breaking along planes of weak atomic bonds. Hook: 1 mica - 2 chains and feldspars - 3 cubes and rhombs - 4 fluorite - 6 sphalerite.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Quartz has no cleavage and breaks with a conchoidal (shell-like) fracture, while calcite has perfect rhombohedral cleavage. Cleavage is the best hand-specimen property to tell the two apart.
cards.w: In quartz every direction has equally strong Si-O bonds, so there is no weak plane to split along. Hardness helps too: quartz 7, calcite 3.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Streak is the colour of a mineral's fine powder, obtained by rubbing it on an unglazed porcelain plate. It is much more constant than body colour, which is the least reliable property.
cards.w: Impurities change the colour of a lump but hardly change the colour of its powder. Hematite can be black, grey or red, yet its streak is always red.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Diagnostic streaks: hematite cherry red to red-brown; magnetite black; chromite brown; limonite yellow-brown; pyrite and chalcopyrite greenish black; cinnabar scarlet; sphalerite pale yellow to brown.
cards.w: Streak separates look-alike black ores quickly: magnetite black, chromite brown, hematite red. Gold gives a golden streak, but 'fool's gold' (pyrite) gives a dark one.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Lustre types: metallic (galena, pyrite); adamantine (diamond); vitreous (quartz); resinous (sphalerite); pearly (talc, mica cleavage); silky (asbestos, satin spar); greasy (nepheline); earthy or dull (kaolin).
cards.w: Lustre is how a surface reflects light. Silky lustre comes from parallel fibres; pearly lustre comes from light reflected off many thin cleavage sheets.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Specific gravity is the weight of a mineral divided by the weight of an equal volume of water. Quartz 2.65, calcite 2.71, barite 4.5, pyrite 5.0, galena 7.5.
cards.w: Most common rock-forming minerals fall between 2.6 and 3.4. Metallic ores are much heavier. Barite is called 'heavy spar' because it is so heavy for a non-metallic mineral.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Specific gravity is measured with Jolly's spring balance, Walker's steelyard balance or a pycnometer (density bottle). Bromoform (specific gravity 2.89) is the usual heavy liquid for separating heavy minerals.
cards.w: All the balances weigh the mineral in air and then in water. In bromoform, quartz and feldspar float while 'heavy minerals' such as zircon and garnet sink.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Special properties: magnetite is strongly magnetic; halite tastes salty; talc feels soapy; clear calcite (Iceland spar) shows double refraction; quartz is piezoelectric; tourmaline is pyroelectric and piezoelectric.
cards.w: Piezoelectric means the crystal develops electric charge when squeezed. It needs a crystal with no centre of symmetry. This is why quartz plates are used in watches and radios.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Olivine is a complete solid solution between forsterite (Mg2SiO4) and fayalite (Fe2SiO4): Mg2+ and Fe2+ replace each other freely in the same structure.
cards.w: The two ions have the same charge and almost the same size, so the structure does not notice the swap. Such a series is also called an isomorphous series.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Plagioclase is a complete solid solution from albite (NaAlSi3O8) to anorthite (CaAl2Si2O8) by coupled substitution: Na+ with Si4+ is replaced by Ca2+ with Al3+.
cards.w: Na+ and Ca2+ are similar in size but differ in charge. Swapping one Si4+ for Al3+ at the same time keeps the total charge balanced.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Polymorphs have the same chemical composition but different crystal structures: diamond-graphite (C), calcite-aragonite (CaCO3), pyrite-marcasite (FeS2), sphalerite-wurtzite (ZnS), and quartz-tridymite-cristobalite (SiO2).
cards.w: Poly-morph means 'many forms'. Which form is stable depends on pressure and temperature. High pressure favours the denser form, such as diamond.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Isomorphous minerals have the same crystal structure and similar formula type but different compositions, for example the calcite group: calcite CaCO3, magnesite MgCO3, siderite FeCO3, rhodochrosite MnCO3.
cards.w: Iso-morph means 'same form'. It is the opposite idea to polymorphism: here the shape stays the same and the chemistry changes.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Exsolution is the unmixing of a solid solution during slow cooling. Perthite is a potassium feldspar host with sodic feldspar (albite) lamellae; antiperthite is a plagioclase host with potassium feldspar lamellae.
cards.w: At high temperature K and Na feldspar mix fully. On slow cooling they separate, like oil and water. On a phase diagram the curve below which unmixing starts is called the solvus.

cards.a: The building block of all silicates is the (SiO4)4- tetrahedron: one small Si4+ ion surrounded by four O2- ions at the corners, leaving a net charge of -4.
cards.w: Charge: +4 from silicon and 4 x (-2) from oxygen gives -4. Tetrahedra balance this charge by bonding to metal ions or by sharing oxygens with each other.

cards.a: Silicates are classified by how many oxygens each tetrahedron shares: neso 0, soro 1, cyclo 2, single chain 2, double chain 2 and 3 alternately, phyllo 3, tecto 4.
cards.w: More sharing means more linking (polymerisation) and less oxygen per silicon. So the Si:O ratio rises from 1:4 in olivine to 1:2 in quartz.

cards.a: Nesosilicates (orthosilicates) have isolated (SiO4)4- tetrahedra with Si:O = 1:4. Examples: olivine, garnet, zircon, kyanite, sillimanite, andalusite, staurolite, topaz, sphene.
cards.w: Neso means 'island'. The tetrahedra share no oxygens and are held together only by metal ions. The tight packing makes these minerals dense and hard.

cards.a: Sorosilicates have pairs of tetrahedra sharing one oxygen, giving (Si2O7)6- groups with Si:O = 2:7. Examples: epidote, hemimorphite, melilite, lawsonite, vesuvianite.
cards.w: Soro means 'group'; the pair looks like a bow-tie. Epidote and vesuvianite contain both paired groups and single tetrahedra.

cards.a: Cyclosilicates have rings of tetrahedra, each sharing two oxygens, with Si:O = 1:3; the common six-member ring is (Si6O18)12-. Examples: beryl, tourmaline, cordierite.
cards.w: Cyclo means 'ring'. Rings stacked on one another make channels, which is why beryl and tourmaline grow as long prisms.

cards.a: Single-chain inosilicates have tetrahedra sharing two oxygens in an endless chain, with Si:O = 1:3, written (SiO3)2- or (Si2O6)4-. The pyroxenes are the main examples.
cards.w: Ino means 'thread'. The chains run parallel to the c axis and are bonded sideways by weaker metal-oxygen bonds. That gives two cleavages at nearly 90°.

cards.a: Double-chain inosilicates have two linked chains in which tetrahedra share two and three oxygens alternately, with Si:O = 4:11, written (Si4O11)6-. The amphiboles are the examples, and they contain (OH).
cards.w: The wider double chain makes the cleavage angle 56° and 124° instead of about 90°. Hook: amphibole = 4:11 and hydrous; pyroxene = 1:3 and dry.

cards.a: Phyllosilicates have sheets in which each tetrahedron shares three oxygens, with Si:O = 2:5, written (Si2O5)2- or (Si4O10)4-. Examples: micas, chlorite, talc, serpentine, clay minerals.
cards.w: Phyllo means 'leaf'. Bonds inside a sheet are strong but bonds between sheets are weak. This gives one perfect basal cleavage and soft, flaky minerals.

cards.a: Tectosilicates have a three-dimensional framework in which all four oxygens of every tetrahedron are shared, with (Si,Al):O = 1:2. Examples: quartz, feldspars, feldspathoids, zeolites.
cards.w: Tecto means 'framework'. In feldspars some Si4+ is replaced by Al3+; the missing charge is made up by K+, Na+ or Ca2+ sitting in the framework holes.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Olivine (Mg,Fe)2SiO4 is an orthorhombic nesosilicate: olive-green, glassy, hardness 6.5-7, with no good cleavage and conchoidal fracture. The gem variety is peridot.
cards.w: It is the main mineral of dunite and peridotite and of the upper mantle. It alters easily to serpentine and is the first common silicate to weather.

cards.t: Common minerals of igneous and metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Magnesium-rich olivine does not occur in equilibrium with free quartz: forsterite reacts with silica to form enstatite (Mg2SiO4 + SiO2 = 2MgSiO3).
cards.w: Olivine is silica-poor (undersaturated), so any spare silica is used up to make pyroxene. The same rule bars nepheline and leucite from occurring with quartz.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Garnets are cubic nesosilicates with the general formula X3Y2(SiO4)3. They form dodecahedral or trapezohedral crystals, have no cleavage, and have hardness 6.5-7.5.
cards.w: X is a large 2+ ion (Mg, Fe, Mn, Ca); Y is a smaller 3+ ion (Al, Fe, Cr). Being hard with no cleavage, garnet is used as an abrasive.

cards.t: Common minerals of igneous and metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Garnet species. Pyralspite series: pyrope Mg3Al2, almandine Fe3Al2, spessartine Mn3Al2. Ugrandite series: uvarovite Ca3Cr2, grossular Ca3Al2, andradite Ca3Fe2 (each with Si3O12).
cards.w: The series names are built from the first letters. Almandine is the usual garnet of schists; pyrope occurs in kimberlite and eclogite; grossular and andradite occur in metamorphosed limestones (skarns).

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Pyroxenes are single-chain silicates with the general formula XYZ2O6. They show two cleavages at about 87° and 93° and a four- or eight-sided cross-section.
cards.w: The narrow single chains stack like bricks, so the cleavages meet at almost a right angle. This is the quickest way to tell pyroxene from amphibole.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Orthopyroxenes (enstatite MgSiO3, hypersthene, ferrosilite FeSiO3) are orthorhombic. Clinopyroxenes (diopside CaMgSi2O6, hedenbergite CaFeSi2O6, augite, pigeonite) are monoclinic.
cards.w: Calcium-poor pyroxenes are mostly ortho; calcium-bearing ones are clino. Augite is the common pyroxene of basalt and gabbro. Hypersthene is the essential mineral of charnockite.

cards.t: Common minerals of igneous and metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Sodic pyroxenes: jadeite NaAlSi2O6 (high-pressure rocks), aegirine NaFe3+Si2O6 (alkaline igneous rocks) and omphacite (eclogite). Spodumene LiAlSi2O6 is the lithium pyroxene of pegmatites.
cards.w: Eclogite is made of green omphacite and red pyrope-rich garnet. Spodumene is an ore of lithium.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Amphiboles are hydrous double-chain silicates. They show two cleavages at about 56° and 124° and a six-sided, diamond-shaped cross-section.
cards.w: Hook: amphibole angles are 'far from 90' (56/124); pyroxene angles are 'near 90' (87/93). Amphiboles contain (OH), pyroxenes do not.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Amphibole species: anthophyllite (orthorhombic, Mg-Fe); tremolite Ca2Mg5Si8O22(OH)2 and actinolite (calcic); hornblende (calcic, aluminous, the commonest); glaucophane and riebeckite (sodic, blue).
cards.w: Glaucophane is the blue amphibole of blueschists (high pressure, low temperature). Hornblende is the usual amphibole of diorite and amphibolite.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Asbestos is of two kinds: chrysotile (fibrous serpentine, 'white asbestos', the main commercial type) and amphibole asbestos such as crocidolite (blue asbestos, fibrous riebeckite) and amosite.
cards.w: Serpentine Mg3Si2O5(OH)4 forms by alteration of olivine and pyroxene in ultramafic rocks. Its three forms are antigorite (platy), lizardite and chrysotile (fibrous).

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
