cards.a: Micas are monoclinic sheet silicates with one perfect basal {001} cleavage. They split into thin flakes that are flexible and elastic; hardness is only 2-3.
cards.w: Layers are held together by K+ ions, a weak link, so sheets peel off easily. Elastic means a bent flake springs back; chlorite flakes bend but stay bent.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Mica species: muscovite KAl2(AlSi3O10)(OH)2 (white, potash mica); biotite K(Mg,Fe)3(AlSi3O10)(OH)2 (black); phlogopite (magnesium mica); lepidolite (lithium mica, lilac); glauconite (green, marine).
cards.w: Muscovite is dioctahedral (two Al fill three sites); biotite and phlogopite are trioctahedral (three Mg or Fe fill three sites). Sericite is fine-grained muscovite.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Talc Mg3Si4O10(OH)2 and pyrophyllite Al2Si4O10(OH)2 are sheet silicates with no ions between the layers, so they are very soft (hardness 1-2) and feel soapy.
cards.w: The layers are neutral and held only by very weak (van der Waals) forces, so they slide over each other. Massive talc is called soapstone or steatite.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Clay minerals: kaolinite has a 1:1 (T-O) layer and does not swell; illite is a 2:1 non-swelling clay with fixed K+; montmorillonite (smectite) is a 2:1 clay that swells and has high cation exchange capacity.
cards.w: T = tetrahedral sheet, O = octahedral sheet. Water and ions enter between the weakly held layers of montmorillonite. Bentonite and black cotton soil are rich in it.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Kaolinite Al2Si2O5(OH)4 forms by weathering or hydrothermal alteration of feldspar (kaolinisation). Kerala's china clay deposits at Kundara (Kollam) and Thonnakkal (Thiruvananthapuram) are well known.
cards.w: Water and CO2 remove K, Na and Ca from feldspar and leave an aluminium silicate clay. China clay (kaolin) is used in ceramics and paper.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Feldspars are framework silicates with three end members: orthoclase KAlSi3O8 (Or), albite NaAlSi3O8 (Ab) and anorthite CaAl2Si2O8 (An). Or-Ab is the alkali feldspar series; Ab-An is the plagioclase series.
cards.w: K+ is too big and Ca2+ too different to mix, so there is almost no Or-An series. Feldspars are the most abundant minerals of the Earth's crust.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Plagioclase is divided by anorthite content: albite An0-10, oligoclase An10-30, andesine An30-50, labradorite An50-70, bytownite An70-90, anorthite An90-100.
cards.w: Hook: 'All Old Aunts Love Baking Apples'. Basalt and gabbro carry labradorite; granite carries oligoclase. Fine parallel striations on cleavage faces identify plagioclase in hand specimen.

cards.t: Common minerals of igneous and metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Potassium feldspar KAlSi3O8 has three polymorphs: sanidine (monoclinic, high temperature, in volcanic rocks), orthoclase (monoclinic, intermediate) and microcline (triclinic, low temperature, in granites and pegmatites).
cards.w: Fast cooling in lavas freezes the disordered high-temperature form, sanidine. Slow cooling at depth lets Al and Si order into triclinic microcline. Amazonite is green microcline.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Feldspars have hardness 6, specific gravity 2.55-2.76 and two good cleavages at or near 90°: exactly 90° in orthoclase and about 86° in plagioclase.
cards.w: Ortho-clase means 'straight break'; plagio-clase means 'oblique break'. Hardness 6 and blocky cleavage separate feldspar from quartz, which has no cleavage.

cards.t: Common minerals of igneous and metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Feldspathoids are silica-poor framework silicates that take the place of feldspar in silica-undersaturated rocks: nepheline (Na,K)AlSiO4, leucite KAlSi2O6, sodalite and kalsilite KAlSiO4. They never occur with quartz.
cards.w: With free silica they would react to make feldspar (nepheline + silica = albite). Leucite forms trapezohedral crystals that look cubic but are tetragonal at room temperature.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: At 1 atmosphere, low (alpha) quartz inverts to high (beta) quartz at 573 °C; tridymite is stable from 870 to 1470 °C, and cristobalite from 1470 °C to melting at 1713 °C.
cards.w: Alpha quartz is trigonal; beta quartz is hexagonal. The 573 °C change only bends bonds (displacive), so it is fast and reversible. Quartz to tridymite breaks bonds (reconstructive) and is slow.

cards.t: Common minerals of igneous and metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Coesite and stishovite are the high-pressure polymorphs of SiO2. Coesite marks ultra-high-pressure metamorphism and meteorite impact; stishovite, with silicon in six-fold coordination, is found at impact sites.
cards.w: Pressure squeezes silica into denser structures. Quartz 2.65, coesite about 2.9, stishovite about 4.3. In stishovite each Si has six oxygen neighbours instead of four.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Chalcedony, agate, jasper, chert and flint are cryptocrystalline (very fine-grained) quartz. Opal is hydrous, non-crystalline silica (SiO2.nH2O) and is a mineraloid, not a true mineral.
cards.w: A mineral must have an ordered atomic structure; opal has none. Coloured crystalline quartz varieties are amethyst (purple), citrine (yellow), rose quartz and smoky quartz.

cards.t: Common minerals of igneous and metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Of the three Al2SiO5 polymorphs, kyanite is triclinic and the densest (specific gravity about 3.6); andalusite (orthorhombic, about 3.15) is the least dense; sillimanite is orthorhombic and fibrous.
cards.w: Density explains the stability: dense kyanite is the high-pressure form and light andalusite the low-pressure form. Chiastolite is andalusite with a dark cross of carbon inclusions.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Beryl Be3Al2Si6O18 is a hexagonal cyclosilicate that forms six-sided prisms with hardness 7.5-8; emerald (green) and aquamarine (blue-green) are its gem varieties.
cards.w: Beryl occurs mainly in granite pegmatites and is the chief ore of beryllium. Do not confuse: ruby and sapphire are corundum, not beryl.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.a: Zeolites are hydrated aluminosilicate framework minerals with open channels, such as natrolite, stilbite, heulandite, chabazite and analcime. They show cation exchange and lose and regain water reversibly.
cards.w: The name means 'boiling stone' because they froth when heated. They fill gas cavities in Deccan basalts (Pune, Nashik) and are used as water softeners and molecular sieves.

cards.t: Common minerals of igneous and metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Zircon ZrSiO4 is a tetragonal nesosilicate (hardness 7.5, specific gravity about 4.7) found as an accessory mineral in granites; it is the main mineral used for U-Pb dating.
cards.w: Zircon takes uranium into its structure but rejects lead, and it survives weathering. So it also collects in beach sands such as those of Chavara, Kerala.

cards.t: Common minerals of igneous and metamorphic rocks
cards.a: In an igneous rock, essential minerals decide the rock name (quartz and feldspar in granite); accessory minerals occur in small amounts (zircon, apatite, magnetite, sphene); secondary minerals form by later alteration (chlorite, sericite, serpentine, kaolinite).
cards.w: Felsic (light) minerals are quartz, feldspars, feldspathoids and muscovite. Mafic (dark, Fe-Mg rich) minerals are olivine, pyroxene, amphibole and biotite.

cards.t: Common minerals of igneous and metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Staurolite, kyanite, andalusite, sillimanite, cordierite, glaucophane and wollastonite are characteristic minerals of metamorphic rocks; leucite, nepheline and sanidine are essentially igneous minerals.
cards.w: Metamorphic minerals grow in the solid state from aluminous or limy rocks under heat and pressure. Feldspathoids and sanidine need a hot silicate melt.

cards.t: Minerals of the carbonate, phosphate, sulphide and halide groups
cards.a: Calcite CaCO3 is trigonal, with hardness 3, specific gravity 2.71 and perfect rhombohedral cleavage in three directions. It effervesces briskly in cold dilute HCl.
cards.w: The acid releases CO2 gas, seen as fizzing. Clear calcite (Iceland spar) shows strong double refraction. Pointed 'dog-tooth spar' crystals are scalenohedra.

cards.t: Minerals of the carbonate, phosphate, sulphide and halide groups
cards.a: Aragonite is the orthorhombic polymorph of CaCO3. It is harder (3.5-4) and denser (2.95) than calcite, lacks rhombohedral cleavage, and slowly changes to calcite with time.
cards.w: It is the denser, high-pressure form, so it is metastable (not truly stable) at the surface. Many shells and pearls are aragonite. It fizzes in cold acid like calcite.

cards.t: Minerals of the carbonate, phosphate, sulphide and halide groups
cards.a: Dolomite CaMg(CO3)2 has hardness 3.5-4, specific gravity 2.85 and curved, saddle-shaped rhombohedral crystals. It effervesces in cold dilute HCl only when powdered, or in warm acid.
cards.w: Powdering gives more surface for the weak reaction. In thin section, the stain Alizarin Red S turns calcite pink-red but leaves dolomite unstained.

cards.t: Minerals of the carbonate, phosphate, sulphide and halide groups
cards.a: Carbonates of small cations (Mg, Fe, Mn, Zn) have the rhombohedral calcite structure; carbonates of large cations (Sr, Ba, Pb) have the orthorhombic aragonite structure. CaCO3 forms both.
cards.w: Calcite group: magnesite, siderite, rhodochrosite, smithsonite ZnCO3. Aragonite group: strontianite SrCO3, witherite BaCO3, cerussite PbCO3. Calcium is the in-between size.

cards.t: Minerals of the carbonate, phosphate, sulphide and halide groups
cards.a: Siderite FeCO3 is a brown rhombohedral carbonate with specific gravity about 3.9. It becomes magnetic on heating and is an ore of iron (about 48% Fe), called spathic iron ore.
cards.w: Hook: sideros is Greek for iron. It is the heaviest of the rock-forming carbonates (calcite, dolomite, magnesite, siderite) and reacts with acid only when the acid is hot.

cards.t: Minerals of the carbonate, phosphate, sulphide and halide groups
cards.a: Magnesite MgCO3 usually occurs as white, compact, porcelain-like masses formed by alteration of ultramafic rocks. It is used for refractory bricks; the Chalk Hills of Salem, Tamil Nadu, are the classic Indian locality.
cards.w: CO2-bearing water attacks Mg-rich serpentinite and deposits veins of magnesite. Refractory means it withstands very high furnace temperatures.

cards.t: Minerals of the carbonate, phosphate, sulphide and halide groups
cards.a: Apatite Ca5(PO4)3(F,Cl,OH) is hexagonal with hardness 5. It is the commonest phosphate mineral, an accessory in most igneous rocks, and the main source of phosphorus for fertilisers.
cards.w: Sedimentary rock phosphate (phosphorite) is made of very fine apatite called collophane, as at Jhamarkotra, Rajasthan. Bones and teeth are also a form of apatite.

cards.t: Minerals of the carbonate, phosphate, sulphide and halide groups
cards.a: Monazite (Ce,La,Nd,Th)PO4 is a monoclinic, yellow-brown, resinous, heavy (specific gravity about 5) rare-earth phosphate. It is the chief ore of thorium and occurs in the beach sands of Chavara, Kerala.
cards.w: It is radioactive because of thorium. Being heavy and resistant, it collects with ilmenite, rutile, zircon and sillimanite in the placers of Kerala and Manavalakurichi (Tamil Nadu).

cards.t: Minerals of the carbonate, phosphate, sulphide and halide groups
cards.a: Pyrite FeS2 is cubic and pale brass-yellow, with a greenish-black streak, hardness 6-6.5 and specific gravity 5.0. It forms striated cubes and pyritohedra and is called fool's gold.
cards.w: It is too hard for a knife to scratch, which is unusual for a sulphide. Real gold is soft, bends, and gives a golden streak. Pyrite is used for sulphuric acid, not as an iron ore.

cards.t: Minerals of the carbonate, phosphate, sulphide and halide groups
cards.a: Chalcopyrite CuFeS2 is tetragonal, deep brass-yellow and often tarnished, with a greenish-black streak and hardness 3.5-4. It is the most important ore of copper (34.6% Cu).
cards.w: A knife scratches chalcopyrite but not pyrite. It is the main ore mineral at Khetri (Rajasthan), Malanjkhand (Madhya Pradesh) and Singhbhum (Jharkhand).

cards.t: Minerals of the carbonate, phosphate, sulphide and halide groups
cards.a: Galena PbS is cubic and lead-grey with bright metallic lustre, perfect cubic cleavage, hardness 2.5 and very high specific gravity (about 7.5). It is the chief ore of lead and often carries silver.
cards.w: It breaks into tiny cubes because it has the same structure as halite. In India it is mined with sphalerite at Zawar and Rampura-Agucha, Rajasthan.

cards.t: Minerals of the carbonate, phosphate, sulphide and halide groups
cards.a: Sphalerite ZnS (zinc blende) is cubic, with resinous to adamantine lustre, perfect dodecahedral cleavage in six directions, hardness 3.5-4 and a streak paler than its body colour. It is the chief ore of zinc.
cards.w: Iron-rich sphalerite is black ('black jack') yet still gives a pale brown streak. Its hexagonal polymorph is wurtzite. It commonly occurs with galena.

cards.t: Minerals of the carbonate, phosphate, sulphide and halide groups
cards.a: Other sulphides: cinnabar HgS (red, mercury ore), molybdenite MoS2 (soft, greasy), stibnite Sb2S3 (antimony), argentite Ag2S (silver), realgar AsS (red), orpiment As2S3 (yellow), pentlandite (nickel), pyrrhotite Fe1-xS (magnetic).
cards.w: Sulphides are mostly soft, heavy, metallic ore minerals. Pyrrhotite is the one common magnetic sulphide; marcasite is the orthorhombic polymorph of pyrite.

cards.t: Minerals of the carbonate, phosphate, sulphide and halide groups
cards.a: Halite NaCl (rock salt) is cubic, with perfect cubic cleavage, hardness 2.5, specific gravity 2.16 and a salty taste. It dissolves in water and forms in evaporite deposits.
cards.w: Evaporite means a rock left behind when salty water dries up. Because it is light and flows, buried salt rises as salt domes. India mines rock salt at Mandi, Himachal Pradesh.

cards.t: Minerals of the carbonate, phosphate, sulphide and halide groups
cards.a: Fluorite CaF2 is cubic and commonly forms cubes, but its perfect cleavage is octahedral (four directions). Hardness is 4 and specific gravity 3.18; it is used as a flux in steel making.
cards.w: The word fluorescence comes from fluorite, which often glows under ultraviolet light. India's main fluorite deposit is at Amba Dongar, Gujarat.

cards.t: Minerals of the carbonate, phosphate, sulphide and halide groups
cards.a: Other halide minerals: sylvite KCl (bitter taste, potash source), carnallite KMgCl3.6H2O (potash evaporite) and cryolite Na3AlF6 (flux in aluminium smelting, from Ivigtut, Greenland).
cards.w: Halides are compounds of metals with chlorine or fluorine. Most are soft, light, and many dissolve in water. Sylvite looks like halite but tastes bitter.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.a: A polarising (petrological) microscope has two polarising filters: the polariser below the stage and the analyser above the objective, with their vibration directions at 90° to each other.
cards.w: The lower filter makes light vibrate in one plane. The upper one tests what the mineral did to that light. With no mineral in between, the crossed filters give darkness.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.a: In plane polarised light (analyser out) we study colour, pleochroism, relief, cleavage and form; under crossed polars (analyser in) we study interference colours, extinction and twinning.
cards.w: Hook: plane light shows what the mineral looks like; crossed polars show what the mineral does to light.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.a: The Bertrand lens is inserted, together with the condenser and a high-power objective, to see interference figures (conoscopic view).
cards.w: Conoscopic means using a cone of converging light. The interference figure forms at the back of the objective, and the Bertrand lens brings it into focus for the eye.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.a: A Nicol prism is clear calcite (Iceland spar) cut and re-cemented with Canada balsam; the ordinary ray is totally reflected away and the extraordinary ray passes through as polarised light.
cards.w: Calcite splits light into two rays. The balsam has a lower index than the ordinary ray, so that ray is thrown out sideways. Hook: O = Out, E = Emerges.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.a: A standard rock thin section is 0.03 mm (30 micrometres) thick and is mounted in a medium of refractive index about 1.54 (Canada balsam).
cards.w: Interference colour depends on thickness, so one fixed thickness lets us compare minerals. Quartz (first-order grey to white at 0.03 mm) is the usual thickness check.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.a: Refractive index (n) is the speed of light in vacuum divided by its speed in the mineral; a higher index means light travels more slowly in the mineral.
cards.w: Example: n = 1.5 means light moves at 3 × 10^8 / 1.5 = 2 × 10^8 m/s inside the mineral. Dense minerals usually have higher indices.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.a: Relief is how strongly a mineral's outline stands out in plane polarised light; it depends on the difference between the refractive indices of the mineral and the mounting medium.
cards.w: Big difference = bold dark borders and a rough-looking surface (garnet, zircon). Small difference = the grain is almost invisible (quartz in balsam).

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.a: The Becke line is a bright line at a grain edge that moves into the material of higher refractive index when the stage is lowered (focus raised).
cards.w: Hook: 'Lower the stage, the line goes to the Higher index.' It tells whether the mineral's index is above or below that of the balsam.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.a: Minerals with index above the balsam show positive relief (garnet, olivine, zircon); those with index below it show negative relief (fluorite, sodalite, opal).
cards.w: Fluorite (n = 1.434) is the classic negative-relief mineral. Positive or negative is decided with the Becke line, not by eye alone.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.a: Calcite 'twinkles': its relief changes from high to low as the stage is rotated in plane polarised light, because its two indices (1.658 and 1.486) are very different.
cards.w: One index is well above the balsam and the other is below it. So the grain looks bold in one position and faint 90° away.

cards.a: Isotropic substances - cubic minerals (garnet, spinel, fluorite) and glass - have a single refractive index and stay dark under crossed polars through a full rotation of the stage.
cards.w: Light travels at the same speed in every direction, so it is not split into two rays. Nothing gets through the analyser.

cards.a: Anisotropic minerals split light into two rays that vibrate at right angles to each other and travel at different speeds; this is double refraction, seen best in Iceland spar (calcite).
cards.w: A dot seen through clear calcite looks double. The speed difference between the two rays is what later produces interference colours.

cards.a: Cubic crystals are isotropic; tetragonal, hexagonal and trigonal crystals are uniaxial; orthorhombic, monoclinic and triclinic crystals are biaxial.
cards.w: One special axis (3-, 4- or 6-fold) gives one optic axis. Lower symmetry gives two optic axes. The highest (cubic) symmetry gives no special direction at all.

cards.a: A uniaxial mineral has one optic axis, parallel to the c crystallographic axis, and two principal indices: omega (ω, ordinary ray) and epsilon (ε, extraordinary ray).
cards.w: The ordinary ray vibrates at right angles to c and always has index ω. The extraordinary ray's index changes with direction and reaches ε when it vibrates parallel to c.

cards.a: Along an optic axis there is no double refraction, so a section cut perpendicular to it (such as a basal section of quartz) stays dark under crossed polars.
cards.w: Looking down the optic axis the mineral behaves like an isotropic one. This same section gives the centred optic-axis interference figure.

cards.a: Uniaxial positive means ε > ω (quartz, zircon, rutile); uniaxial negative means ε < ω (calcite, tourmaline, apatite, beryl, nepheline, corundum).
cards.w: Hook: quartz is positive, calcite is negative. Most other common uniaxial rock-forming minerals are negative.

cards.a: A biaxial mineral has three principal indices alpha < beta < gamma, for light vibrating along X, Y and Z; its two optic axes lie in the XZ plane (optic axial plane).
cards.w: Y, the beta direction, is at right angles to the optic plane and is called the optic normal.

cards.a: 2V is the angle between the two optic axes; the mineral is biaxial positive if Z is the acute bisectrix and biaxial negative if X is the acute bisectrix.
cards.w: Acute bisectrix = the line that halves the smaller angle between the optic axes. In positive minerals beta is closer to alpha; in negative ones beta is closer to gamma.

cards.a: The optical indicatrix is a sphere for isotropic minerals, an ellipsoid of revolution for uniaxial minerals and a triaxial ellipsoid for biaxial minerals.
cards.w: Indicatrix = a 3-D shape whose radius in any direction equals the refractive index for light vibrating in that direction.

cards.a: The uniaxial positive indicatrix is prolate (stretched along the optic axis, like an egg); the uniaxial negative indicatrix is oblate (flattened along it, like a pumpkin).
cards.w: In positive minerals ε, the index measured along c, is the larger one, so the shape is long along c. In negative minerals ε is the smaller one.

cards.t: Birefringence of minerals and their relation with mineral composition
cards.a: Birefringence is the difference between the largest and smallest refractive indices of a mineral: the difference between ε and ω for uniaxial minerals, and gamma minus alpha for biaxial minerals.
cards.w: It measures how strongly the mineral splits light. A grain shows this maximum only when cut parallel to the optic axis (uniaxial) or to the optic plane (biaxial).

cards.t: Birefringence of minerals and their relation with mineral composition
cards.a: Retardation = thickness × birefringence. A 30 micrometre (30,000 nm) quartz section with birefringence 0.009 gives 270 nm, a first-order white.
cards.w: Retardation is the distance by which the slow ray lags behind the fast ray. Keep thickness and retardation in the same unit (nm) when calculating.

cards.t: Birefringence of minerals and their relation with mineral composition
cards.a: The Michel-Lévy chart links section thickness, birefringence and retardation (interference colour); each colour order spans about 550 nm and ends in a red band.
cards.w: Know any two of the three and read off the third. First order has greys, white, yellow and red; blues and greens start only in the second order.

cards.t: Birefringence of minerals and their relation with mineral composition
cards.a: In a standard section quartz and feldspars show first-order greys and whites (about 0.007-0.010); olivine and muscovite show bright second- to third-order colours; calcite (0.172) shows high-order pearly whites.
cards.w: Low birefringence = dull greys. High = bright rainbow colours. Very high = washed-out creamy white, because many colours overlap.

cards.t: Birefringence of minerals and their relation with mineral composition
cards.a: Chlorite often shows anomalous interference colours (inky 'Berlin blue' or brown) that are not on the Michel-Lévy chart; zoisite and clinozoisite also show anomalous blues.
cards.w: Their birefringence is different for different colours of light. So the normal first-order grey is replaced by an odd blue or brown.

cards.t: Birefringence of minerals and their relation with mineral composition
cards.a: Accessory plates: the gypsum plate (sensitive tint, first-order red) adds about 550 nm; the mica plate adds a quarter wavelength (about 150 nm); the quartz wedge gives variable retardation.
cards.w: They are pushed in at 45° to the polarisers. Their slow direction is marked, so they reveal the slow direction of the mineral and the order of its colour.

cards.t: Birefringence of minerals and their relation with mineral composition
cards.a: With an accessory plate, interference colours rise (addition) when the slow directions of mineral and plate are parallel, and fall (subtraction) when slow lies over fast.
cards.w: Example with the gypsum plate: a 150 nm grey grain becomes 700 nm (second-order blue) on addition and 400 nm (first-order yellow) on subtraction.

cards.t: Birefringence of minerals and their relation with mineral composition
cards.a: A mineral is length-slow (positive elongation) if the slow ray vibrates parallel to its length and length-fast (negative elongation) if the fast ray does; sillimanite is length-slow, andalusite and tourmaline are length-fast.
cards.w: It is found with the gypsum plate on an elongate grain turned to 45°. It quickly separates look-alike prismatic minerals.

cards.a: A centred uniaxial optic-axis figure is a black cross (isogyres) with circular colour rings (isochromes) that stays fixed on rotation; its centre, where the optic axis emerges, is the melatope.
cards.w: Thicker sections or higher birefringence give more colour rings. A cross that never breaks up on rotation means the mineral is uniaxial.

cards.a: In a uniaxial optic-axis figure with the gypsum plate (slow direction NE-SW), a positive mineral shows blue in the NE and SW quadrants and yellow in the NW and SE quadrants; a negative mineral shows the reverse.
cards.w: Blue means addition and yellow means subtraction. The extraordinary ray vibrates radially, and in positive minerals that radial direction is the slow one.

cards.a: A biaxial acute-bisectrix figure shows a cross that splits into two curved isogyres (hyperbolas) on rotation; their separation at the 45° position increases with 2V.
cards.w: The two melatopes mark the two optic axes. A uniaxial cross never splits - that is the quick uniaxial versus biaxial test.

cards.a: A centred biaxial optic-axis figure shows a single isogyre, straight when 2V is 90° and strongly curved when 2V is small; with an accessory plate it gives the optic sign.
cards.w: The convex side of the curved isogyre points towards the acute bisectrix. This figure comes from grains showing the lowest interference colours.

cards.a: Under crossed polars an anisotropic grain goes dark (extinct) four times in a 360° rotation, at 90° intervals, when its vibration directions are parallel to the polariser and analyser.
cards.w: In those positions light passes through the grain unchanged and the analyser blocks it. The grain is brightest at 45° from extinction.

cards.a: Extinction types: parallel (straight) - dark when cleavage or length is parallel to a cross-hair; oblique (inclined) - dark at an angle to it; symmetrical - cross-hairs bisect the angle between two cleavages.
cards.w: Symmetrical extinction is seen in basal sections of amphibole and pyroxene and in calcite rhombs, where two cleavage sets cross.

cards.a: Undulose (wavy) extinction is a dark shadow that sweeps across a single grain during rotation; it is typical of strained quartz in deformed rocks.
cards.w: Stress bends the crystal lattice, so different parts of one grain go dark at slightly different positions.

cards.a: The extinction angle is the angle between a crystal direction (cleavage trace, length or twin plane) and the nearest extinction position, commonly quoted as Z^c or X^c.
cards.w: To measure: put the cleavage along a cross-hair and note the stage reading, rotate to darkness and note again. The difference is the extinction angle.

cards.a: Prismatic sections of tetragonal, hexagonal and orthorhombic minerals give parallel extinction; monoclinic minerals give oblique extinction in most sections; triclinic minerals give oblique extinction in all sections.
cards.w: In higher-symmetry crystals the vibration directions line up with the crystal axes. In monoclinic crystals only the b axis is fixed, so the largest angle is seen on the (010) section.

cards.a: Maximum extinction angle (Z^c): clinopyroxene such as augite about 35°-48°; hornblende about 12°-30°; orthopyroxenes (enstatite, hypersthene) show parallel extinction.
cards.w: Hook: pyroxene = big angle (near 45°); amphibole = small angle; orthopyroxene = zero, because it is orthorhombic.

cards.a: The Michel-Lévy method finds plagioclase composition (anorthite %) from the maximum symmetrical extinction angle of albite twin lamellae in sections cut perpendicular to (010).
cards.w: In such sections the two sets of lamellae go dark at nearly equal angles to the left and right. Average the two, repeat on several grains and use the largest value on the curve.

cards.a: In the Michel-Lévy method, extinction angles below about 20° are ambiguous (sodic or intermediate plagioclase); the Becke line settles it, because albite and sodic oligoclase have indices below balsam.
cards.w: The curve falls from about 16° at pure albite to 0° near An20 and then rises again. So one small angle fits two different compositions.

cards.t: Birefringence of minerals and their relation with mineral composition
cards.a: In plagioclase the refractive indices rise steadily from albite (about 1.53) to anorthite (about 1.58) as calcium increases; extinction angle and 2V also vary with composition.
cards.w: Because the change is steady, optics alone can give the composition of a plagioclase without a chemical analysis.

cards.t: Birefringence of minerals and their relation with mineral composition
cards.a: In olivine, refractive indices and birefringence rise with iron content; magnesian forsterite is biaxial positive (2V near 90°) while iron-rich fayalite is biaxial negative (2V about 50°).
cards.w: Iron raises the indices of most ferromagnesian minerals. The sign changes at roughly Fo85-90, so common rock olivine has 2V close to 90°.

cards.t: Birefringence of minerals and their relation with mineral composition
cards.a: In orthopyroxenes, indices and pleochroism increase with iron: enstatite is colourless and optically positive, while hypersthene is pleochroic (pink to green) and optically negative.
cards.w: The same rule holds widely: iron and titanium raise the index and deepen the colour. Compare colourless tremolite with green hornblende, or pale phlogopite with dark biotite.

cards.a: Pleochroism is the change in colour of a mineral as the stage is rotated in plane polarised light, caused by unequal absorption of light along different vibration directions.
cards.w: It is seen with the analyser out. Colour changes under crossed polars are interference colours, which is a different thing.

cards.a: Isotropic minerals are never pleochroic; coloured uniaxial minerals can show two extreme colours (dichroism) and coloured biaxial minerals three (trichroism).
cards.w: One index = one colour. Two principal vibration directions (ω, ε) = two colours. Three (X, Y, Z) = three colours.

cards.a: Biotite is darkest when its cleavage is parallel to the polariser's vibration direction; tourmaline is darkest when its length is perpendicular to that direction.
cards.w: This opposite behaviour separates the two common brown pleochroic minerals. Biotite is so reliable that it is used to find the polariser direction of a microscope.

cards.a: Pleochroic haloes are dark, strongly pleochroic spots around tiny radioactive inclusions such as zircon, monazite and allanite, seen mainly in biotite and also in cordierite (yellow haloes).
cards.w: Alpha particles from uranium and thorium damage the host mineral in a small sphere around the inclusion. Monazite, the thorium mineral of Kerala's beach sands, is one such inclusion.

cards.a: Diagnostic pleochroism: hypersthene pink to pale green; glaucophane lavender to blue; staurolite colourless to golden yellow; andalusite weak patchy pink; piemontite yellow-red-violet.
cards.w: These colour schemes are almost fingerprints. Piemontite is the manganese-bearing epidote; glaucophane is the blue amphibole of blueschists.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.a: Quartz in thin section is colourless, clear and unaltered, with low relief, no cleavage and no visible twinning; it is uniaxial positive with first-order grey to white colours.
cards.w: Feldspars look similar but show cleavage, twinning and cloudy alteration. Quartz stays 'clean'.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.a: Orthoclase has low negative relief, cloudy (kaolinised) alteration and simple Carlsbad twins; microcline shows cross-hatched twinning; sanidine is clear with a small 2V and occurs in volcanic rocks.
cards.w: All three are potassium feldspars with first-order grey colours and indices below balsam. The twinning and the rock type tell them apart.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.a: Plagioclase is recognised by polysynthetic albite twinning - parallel light and dark stripes under crossed polars - and often shows compositional zoning in volcanic rocks.
cards.w: Polysynthetic = many thin twin slabs repeated side by side. Alternate slabs go dark at different positions, giving the striped look.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.a: Olivine is colourless with high relief, curved irregular cracks, no good cleavage, parallel extinction and bright second- to third-order colours; it alters to serpentine or iddingsite along the cracks.
cards.w: Hook: 'cracked, clean and colourful'. Augite, its usual neighbour, has cleavage, oblique extinction and lower colours.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.a: Augite is pale and weakly pleochroic with two cleavages near 90° (87° and 93°) in basal sections; hornblende is strongly pleochroic green-brown with cleavages at 56° and 124°.
cards.w: Pyroxene = single silicate chains, nearly square cleavage. Amphibole = double chains, diamond-shaped cleavage. Add the extinction angle and the two are easily separated.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.a: Micas show one perfect cleavage, parallel extinction and mottled 'bird's-eye' extinction; muscovite is colourless with 2V of 30°-45°, while biotite is brown, strongly pleochroic and nearly uniaxial (2V 0°-25°).
cards.w: Bird's-eye = a speckled, pebbly look near the extinction position. Both micas are optically negative with bright second- to third-order colours.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.a: Garnet is isotropic with very high relief, no cleavage and irregular fractures; it is colourless to pale pink in plane light and stays black under crossed polars.
cards.w: Garnet is cubic, so it has one refractive index. High relief plus permanent darkness is the giveaway.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.a: Calcite is uniaxial negative with extreme birefringence (0.172), rhombohedral cleavage, lamellar twinning and high-order pearl-grey to creamy interference colours.
cards.w: It is also the 'twinkling' mineral. No common silicate has such high birefringence, so the pale high-order colours point to a carbonate.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.a: Al2SiO5 minerals: kyanite - high relief, oblique extinction up to about 30°; sillimanite - slender needles, parallel extinction, length-slow, small positive 2V; andalusite - parallel extinction, length-fast, optically negative.
cards.w: Kyanite is triclinic, so its extinction is inclined. The other two are orthorhombic and are separated by the sign of elongation. Sillimanite is the needle mineral of Kerala's khondalites.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.a: Tourmaline is uniaxial negative and strongly pleochroic, with parallel extinction, negative elongation (length-fast), poor cleavage and rounded triangular basal sections.
cards.w: It can look like biotite or hornblende, but it has no good cleavage and is darkest when its length lies across the polariser direction.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.a: Accessory minerals: zircon - tiny prisms, very high relief, third-order or higher colours, uniaxial positive; apatite - moderate relief, first-order grey, uniaxial negative; sphene - wedge-shaped, extreme relief and birefringence.
cards.w: Zircon is bright, apatite is dull grey. Sphene (titanite) is brownish with a typical diamond or wedge outline.

cards.a: A twin is a symmetrical intergrowth of two or more crystals of the same mineral, related by a twin law: reflection across a twin plane, rotation about a twin axis, or inversion through a twin centre.
cards.w: A twin plane can never be a symmetry plane of the single crystal. If it were, the two parts would simply be one and the same crystal.

cards.a: Contact twins meet on a flat composition plane; penetration twins grow through each other; polysynthetic twins repeat on parallel planes; cyclic twins repeat on non-parallel planes (aragonite, chrysoberyl).
cards.w: Composition plane = the surface where the two individuals are joined. Cyclic aragonite twins look six-sided (pseudo-hexagonal).

cards.a: Orthoclase twin laws: Carlsbad - twin axis is the c axis, usually a penetration twin; Baveno - twin plane (021); Manebach - twin plane (001).
cards.w: Under crossed polars a Carlsbad twin shows as two halves, one bright and one dark. Baveno and Manebach are contact twins and are much rarer.

cards.a: Albite law: twin plane (010), repeated polysynthetically; it occurs only in triclinic feldspars (plagioclase, microcline) because (010) is a mirror plane in monoclinic orthoclase.
cards.w: A plane that is already a symmetry plane cannot act as a twin plane. So striped albite twinning means the feldspar is triclinic.

cards.a: Pericline law: the twin axis is the b axis [010]; albite and pericline twins together give the cross-hatched (tartan) pattern of microcline.
cards.w: The two twin sets cross nearly at right angles. They form when monoclinic potassium feldspar changes to triclinic microcline on slow cooling.

cards.a: Quartz twins: the Brazil law joins right- and left-handed quartz (optical twin); the Dauphiné law is a 180° rotation about c joining crystals of the same hand (electrical twin).
cards.w: Either twin spoils quartz for use in oscillators, which need untwinned crystal. Only Brazil twins can be seen with polarised light.

cards.a: Japan-law quartz twins are flat contact twins with the two c axes at about 84.5°; Dauphiné twins commonly form when quartz cools through the high-low inversion at 573 °C.
cards.w: Japan twins look like a flat V or heart. Dauphiné twins are 'transformation twins' - they appear when the structure changes on cooling.

cards.a: Spinel law: the twin plane is the octahedron face {111}; it is seen in spinel, magnetite and diamond (flat triangular 'macles').
cards.w: It is the common twin law of cubic minerals that grow as octahedra. Hook: spinel = one-one-one.

cards.a: Named twins: swallow-tail - gypsum; cross-shaped (cruciform, at about 90° or 60°) - staurolite; iron cross - pyrite; knee-shaped (elbow) - rutile and cassiterite; interpenetrating cubes - fluorite.
cards.w: Staurolite takes its name from the Greek for cross. The dark cross of chiastolite (andalusite) is made of inclusions and is not a twin.

cards.a: Twins form in three ways: growth twins (Carlsbad), transformation twins (Dauphiné quartz, microcline cross-hatching, leucite) and deformation or glide twins (calcite lamellae, some plagioclase).
cards.w: Growth = an accident while the crystal grows. Transformation = the structure changes on cooling. Deformation = stress makes layers of the lattice slip.

cards.a: Dispersion is the variation of refractive index with wavelength; in normal dispersion the index is higher for violet (short wavelength) than for red light.
cards.w: This is why a prism spreads white light into colours. For the same reason standard indices are quoted for one colour: yellow sodium light (589 nm).

cards.a: Strong dispersion gives 'fire' in gemstones such as diamond; fluorite has very low dispersion and is therefore used in high-quality microscope and camera lenses.
cards.w: Fire = flashes of rainbow colour as white light is split. A lens needs the opposite: little splitting, so that colours focus together.

cards.a: In biaxial minerals 2V differs for red and violet light (dispersion of the optic axes); it is written r > v or r < v and is seen as colour fringes on the isogyres.
cards.w: r > v means the optic angle is larger for red light than for violet. Isotropic and uniaxial minerals cannot show it, as they have no 2V.

cards.a: Dispersion types: orthorhombic minerals show rhombic dispersion; monoclinic minerals show inclined, horizontal (parallel) or crossed dispersion; triclinic minerals show asymmetric dispersion.
cards.w: In monoclinic crystals only b is fixed: inclined if b is the optic normal (Y), horizontal if b is the obtuse bisectrix, crossed if b is the acute bisectrix.

cards.a: Brookite shows crossed axial plane dispersion: its optic plane for red light is at right angles to that for blue light. Sphene shows strong dispersion (r > v) and so incomplete extinction.
cards.w: When dispersion is very strong, the extinction position differs for each colour. The grain then never goes fully black in white light.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.a: Light going from a higher-index to a lower-index medium is totally reflected beyond the critical angle C, where sin C = lower index / higher index.
cards.w: Example: from a mineral of index 2.0 into air, sin C = 1/2, so C = 30°. The Nicol prism uses this effect to throw out the ordinary ray.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.a: Brewster's law: light reflected from a transparent surface is fully plane polarised when tan i = n (i = angle of incidence); the reflected and refracted rays are then at 90°.
cards.w: This is polarisation by reflection. For glass of index 1.5 the polarising angle is about 56° (tan 56.3° = 1.5). It is why polarised sunglasses cut glare from water and roads.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.a: Polarisation by absorption: tourmaline and Polaroid sheet absorb one of the two rays almost fully and pass the other; modern microscopes use Polaroid filters instead of Nicol prisms.
cards.w: Tourmaline absorbs the ordinary ray strongly. Three ways to polarise light: reflection (Brewster), double refraction (Nicol prism) and absorption (Polaroid).

cards.t: Birefringence of minerals and their relation with mineral composition
cards.a: The quartz wedge is a quartz plate that thickens along its length, giving steadily rising retardation; it is used to find the order of an interference colour and the optic sign.
cards.w: Push it in over a grain at 45°. If the colours fall to black (compensation), count the red bands passed - that number is the order of the grain's colour.

cards.t: Birefringence of minerals and their relation with mineral composition
cards.a: Under crossed polars a wavelength is cut out when the retardation equals a whole number of that wavelength; the remaining wavelengths give the interference colour.
cards.w: At 550 nm retardation, green light is removed and we see red-violet. This is the 'sensitive tint' of the gypsum plate, where a tiny change gives a clear blue or yellow.

cards.a: A biaxial indicatrix has two circular sections of radius beta, and the two optic axes are perpendicular to them; a uniaxial indicatrix has only one circular section, of radius omega.
cards.w: A circular section means one index for all vibration directions in it. So light travelling at right angles to it (along an optic axis) is not split.

cards.a: Sections cut parallel to the optic axis (uniaxial) or to the optic plane (biaxial) show the maximum interference colour and give a flash figure.
cards.w: Flash figure = a broad, fuzzy cross that fills the field and leaves it after only a few degrees of rotation. Lowest-colour grains give optic-axis figures instead.

cards.t: Birefringence of minerals and their relation with mineral composition
cards.a: Normally zoned plagioclase has a calcium-rich core and a sodium-rich rim; under crossed polars the zones show as concentric bands that go extinct at different positions.
cards.w: Extinction angle changes with composition, so each zone goes dark at its own angle. Calcic plagioclase forms first, at higher temperature. Oscillatory zoning is common in andesites.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.a: Cordierite looks like quartz or untwinned feldspar (low relief, first-order greys) but is biaxial, shows sector or lamellar twinning, alters to yellowish pinite and has yellow pleochroic haloes.
cards.w: Pinite = a fine mica-chlorite alteration product. Cordierite gneisses occur in the Kerala Khondalite Belt, so this look-alike matters locally.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.a: Leucite has very low refractive index (about 1.51) and very weak birefringence, so it looks almost isotropic; it shows eight-sided outlines and complex lamellar twinning in several directions.
cards.w: It is cubic when hot and becomes tetragonal on cooling, which creates the fine twins. Nepheline, the other common feldspathoid, is uniaxial negative with no twinning.

cards.a: An ore is a natural mineral aggregate from which one or more metals can be extracted at a profit; the worthless minerals mixed with it are called gangue.
cards.w: Ore is defined by economics, not chemistry. Quartz and calcite are the commonest gangue (waste) minerals.

cards.a: Tenor (grade) is the metal content of an ore, stated in percent for base metals and in grams per tonne for precious metals.
cards.w: Cheap metals need a high tenor: iron ore needs over 50% Fe, copper ore can pay near 1% Cu, gold ore at a few grams per tonne.

cards.a: Syngenetic deposits form at the same time as their host rock; epigenetic deposits are introduced into the host rock after it has formed.
cards.w: Syn = together, epi = after. A coal seam or banded iron formation is syngenetic; a vein cutting across beds is epigenetic.

cards.a: Hypogene ores are primary ores deposited by rising (ascending) fluids; supergene ores are secondary ores formed by descending surface waters.
cards.w: Hypo = from below, super = from above. Supergene processes rework an older hypogene ore near the surface.

cards.a: Lindgren's genetic classification divides hydrothermal deposits by temperature and depth: hypothermal (300-500 °C, deep), mesothermal (200-300 °C) and epithermal (50-200 °C, shallow).
cards.w: Hypo = deep and hot, meso = middle, epi = shallow and cool. Hook: H-M-E going upward like floors of a building.

cards.a: Bateman classified mineral deposits by forming process: magmatic concentration, sublimation, contact metasomatism, hydrothermal processes, sedimentation, evaporation, residual and mechanical concentration, supergene enrichment and metamorphism.
cards.w: Lindgren sorts by temperature and depth of the fluid. Bateman sorts by the process that made the ore, so it is easier to use in the field.

cards.a: Chromite is the classic early magmatic segregation ore: it crystallises early from mafic-ultramafic magma and settles to form layers (stratiform, as in Bushveld) or pods (podiform, in ophiolites).
cards.w: Chromite is heavy and forms early, so it sinks in the magma chamber. Its hosts are ultramafic-mafic rocks: dunite, peridotite, serpentinite, and pyroxenite-anorthosite layers in Bushveld.

cards.a: Nickel-copper sulphide ores such as Sudbury (Canada) form by liquid immiscibility: a dense sulphide liquid separates from mafic magma and sinks, collecting Ni, Cu and platinum-group metals.
cards.w: Like oil and water, sulphide liquid and silicate magma do not mix. Ni, Cu and PGE are chalcophile (sulphur-loving) and move into the sulphide liquid.

cards.a: Pegmatites crystallise from the last water-rich fraction of granitic magma and yield sheet mica, feldspar, beryl, lithium minerals (spodumene, lepidolite), columbite-tantalite and gem tourmaline.
cards.w: Rare elements do not fit into common minerals, so they stay in the last melt. Water in that melt lets very large crystals grow.

cards.a: Skarn (contact metasomatic) deposits form where granitic intrusions react with limestone or dolomite, giving garnet-pyroxene-wollastonite rock with ores of tungsten (scheelite), iron, copper or tin.
cards.w: Hot fluids from the magma swap material with the carbonate rock (metasomatism = change of composition). Calcium from limestone plus tungsten from granite gives scheelite, CaWO4.

cards.a: Porphyry copper deposits are large-tonnage, low-grade ores with disseminated and stockwork Cu (with Mo or Au) in felsic porphyry intrusions above subduction zones.
cards.w: Grade is often below 1% Cu, but the huge volume makes open-pit mining pay. Alteration is zoned from a potassic core outward to phyllic, argillic and propylitic zones.

cards.a: Volcanogenic massive sulphide (VMS) deposits form on the sea floor from hot volcanic springs: Cyprus type is Cu-rich in ophiolitic basalt, Kuroko type is Zn-Pb-Cu in felsic arc volcanics.
cards.w: Modern black smokers at mid-ocean ridges are VMS deposits forming today. The metal mix follows the volcanic rock below.

cards.a: SEDEX (sedimentary exhalative) deposits are layered Zn-Pb-Ag sulphides in shales and carbonates of rift basins, formed where metal-bearing brines vented on the sea floor; Rampura-Agucha is an Indian example.
cards.w: VMS needs volcanic rocks; SEDEX sits in sediments with little or no volcanic rock. Both are laid down on the sea floor, so the ore is bedded.

cards.a: Placers are mechanical concentrations of heavy, hard, chemically stable minerals such as gold, platinum, cassiterite, diamond, ilmenite, rutile, zircon and monazite in stream, beach or hill-slope deposits.
cards.w: Water or wind carries away light quartz and leaves heavy grains behind. A placer mineral must be heavy, tough and resistant to weathering.

cards.a: Residual concentration under hot, wet tropical weathering removes silica and bases and leaves insoluble oxides, forming bauxite, laterite and nickel laterite.
cards.w: The valuable part is what is left behind after leaching (washing out by rain water). Good drainage and alternate wet and dry seasons help.

cards.a: A weathered sulphide ore body shows, from the top down: gossan, leached and oxidised zone, supergene enriched zone near the water table, and unaltered primary sulphide zone.
cards.w: Rain water with oxygen dissolves metals above the water table. Below it, with no oxygen, the metals are dropped again as rich secondary sulphides.

cards.a: Gossan (iron hat) is a rusty, cellular cap of limonite and goethite left after sulphides are oxidised and leached; it guides prospectors to sulphide ore hidden below.
cards.w: Pyrite rusts to iron hydroxide, which stays at the surface while copper, zinc and sulphur are washed down. The empty box-like holes are called boxwork.

cards.a: In copper deposits the oxidised zone carries malachite, azurite, cuprite and native copper, while the supergene enriched zone below the water table carries chalcocite and covellite.
cards.w: Oxides and carbonates form where oxygen is present. Copper-rich sulphides form below, where copper in solution replaces iron in pyrite and chalcopyrite.

cards.a: Banded iron formations are Precambrian chemical sediments of alternating iron oxide and chert bands: Algoma type is small and volcanic-related, Superior type is large and formed on continental shelves.
cards.w: Most BIF formed about 2.5-1.8 billion years ago, when rising oxygen made dissolved iron in the sea precipitate. In India they are called BHQ, BHJ or BMQ.

cards.a: When sea water evaporates, salts precipitate in order of rising solubility: calcite, then gypsum, then halite, and last the potassium-magnesium salts (sylvite, carnallite).
cards.w: The least soluble salt comes out first. Potash salts are the most soluble, so they form only when the basin is almost dry, which is why they are rare.

cards.a: Ore localisation is governed by structural, lithological (physical and chemical nature of the host rock), stratigraphic and igneous (magmatic) controls.
cards.w: Ore fluids need a path, an opening and a reason to drop their load. Structures give the path, and the host rock gives the trap or the chemical trigger.

cards.a: Structural controls such as faults, shear zones, joints, breccias and fold hinges give pathways and open space for ore fluids; saddle reefs at anticlinal crests (Bendigo, Australia) are a classic case.
cards.w: When beds fold, gaps open at the crest between layers, shaped like a horse saddle. Quartz and gold fill these gaps.

cards.a: Lithological control: reactive limestone and dolomite favour replacement ores, brittle rocks fracture and hold veins, and impermeable shale or fault gouge can pond rising fluids so ore collects beneath.
cards.w: Carbonate rocks neutralise acidic ore fluids, which forces the metals to precipitate. Brittle rocks crack open; soft rocks flow and seal.

cards.a: Hydrothermal districts show metal zoning around the heat source; in Cornwall (England) the order outward from the granite is tin, then copper, then lead-zinc.
cards.w: Each metal drops out at its own temperature as the fluid cools away from the intrusion. Zoning is the order in space; paragenesis is the order in time.

cards.a: A metallogenic epoch is a span of geological time in which particular ores formed widely; a metallogenic province is a region marked by a characteristic group of mineral deposits.
cards.w: Epoch = when, province = where. Example: the Permian is India's coal epoch; the Dharwar craton is a gold province.

cards.a: The Precambrian is India's most important metallogenic era: it holds the iron, manganese, chromite, gold, copper, lead-zinc, uranium and mica deposits of the Peninsular shield.
cards.w: Old shield rocks have gone through many cycles of volcanism, sedimentation and metamorphism, each giving a chance to concentrate metals.

cards.a: Later Indian metallogenic epochs: Permian (Gondwana) for coal, Tertiary for petroleum and lignite, Tertiary-Quaternary weathering for bauxite and laterite, and Quaternary for beach placers.
cards.w: Fuels need buried plants or plankton, so they are in younger sedimentary basins. Bauxite and placers are surface products and are the youngest.

cards.a: Indian metallogenic provinces include the Dharwar gold province, Singhbhum copper-uranium belt, Aravalli-Delhi lead-zinc-copper belt of Rajasthan, Sausar manganese belt and Jharkhand-Bihar mica belt.
cards.w: Link each belt to one flagship mine: Kolar and Hutti, Mosabani and Jaduguda, Zawar and Khetri, Balaghat, Koderma.

cards.a: Plate setting controls ore type: porphyry copper at subduction zones, podiform chromite and Cyprus-type VMS in ophiolites, tin with collision granites, and diamond in kimberlites of old stable cratons.
cards.w: Ophiolites are slices of old ocean floor pushed onto land. Diamonds need very thick, cold, old lithosphere, found only under cratons.

cards.a: Kolar Gold Fields (Karnataka) worked gold-quartz lodes such as the Champion reef in hornblende schists of the Kolar schist belt to over 3 km depth; mining closed in 2001.
cards.w: It was one of the deepest mines in the world. The lodes follow shear zones in an Archaean greenstone belt of the Dharwar craton.

cards.a: Hutti mine (Hutti-Maski schist belt, Raichur, Karnataka) is India's main working gold mine; Karnataka gave about 99% of primary gold in 2021-22 (IBM).
cards.w: After Kolar closed in 2001, Hutti became the chief producer. Figure from Indian Minerals Yearbook 2022 (IBM) for 2021-22; the balance came from Jharkhand. Production data change yearly.

cards.a: In India silver is won mainly as a by-product of Rajasthan lead-zinc ores, and platinum-group elements occur with chromite in the Baula-Nuasahi ultramafic complex of Odisha.
cards.w: Galena often carries silver (argentiferous galena). Platinum metals worldwide follow mafic-ultramafic rocks, as in the Merensky Reef of Bushveld.

cards.a: In Kerala, gold occurs in the Nilambur valley (Malappuram) as placer gold in gravels of the Chaliyar river system and as primary gold-quartz veins of the Wayanad-Nilambur belt.
cards.w: Rivers wash gold out of the veins in the hills and drop the heavy grains in gravel beds. Local people have panned it for generations.

cards.a: Copper ore minerals: chalcopyrite CuFeS2 (the chief ore), bornite Cu5FeS4, chalcocite Cu2S, covellite CuS, cuprite Cu2O, malachite and azurite (green and blue copper carbonates).
cards.w: Chalcopyrite has about 34.6% Cu and is brass yellow. Bornite is called peacock ore for its purple-blue tarnish.

cards.a: Lead ore minerals are galena PbS, cerussite PbCO3 and anglesite PbSO4; zinc ore minerals are sphalerite ZnS, smithsonite ZnCO3 and zincite ZnO.
cards.w: Galena and sphalerite almost always occur together, so we speak of lead-zinc deposits. The carbonates and sulphate form in the oxidised zone.

cards.a: Bauxite (gibbsite, boehmite, diaspore) is a residual aluminium ore; Odisha holds about 41% of India's resources (IBM, IMY 2022, as on 1.4.2020), mainly East Coast bauxite capping khondalite hills such as Panchpatmali.
cards.w: Gibbsite is Al(OH)3; boehmite and diaspore are AlO(OH). In central and western India bauxite caps Deccan basalt instead (Amarkantak, Lohardaga, Gujarat).

cards.a: The Khetri copper belt (Jhunjhunu district, Rajasthan) has chalcopyrite-pyrrhotite ore in metasedimentary rocks of the Delhi Supergroup; mines include Khetri and Kolihan.
cards.w: Hook: Khetri = Rajasthan copper, in the Delhi fold belt. Zawar, also in Rajasthan, is lead-zinc and sits in the older Aravalli rocks.

cards.a: Malanjkhand (Balaghat district, Madhya Pradesh) is India's largest open-pit copper mine; chalcopyrite occurs in a quartz reef within Proterozoic granitoid and is often compared with porphyry copper.
cards.w: Khetri ore is in metasediments, Malanjkhand ore is in granite. This contrast is a favourite exam comparison.

cards.a: The Singhbhum copper belt (Mosabani, Rakha, Surda; Jharkhand) lies along the arc-shaped Singhbhum Shear Zone, which also hosts the Jaduguda uranium deposit.
cards.w: A shear zone is a belt of crushed, sheared rock. It acted as the channel for ore fluids, a clear case of structural control.

cards.a: In Rajasthan, Zawar (Udaipur) has lead-zinc ore in Aravalli dolomite, while Rampura-Agucha (Bhilwara) is a world-class SEDEX zinc-lead deposit in graphite-mica-sillimanite schist.
cards.w: Zawar is also famous for ancient zinc smelting. Rampura-Agucha, Zawar and Rajpura-Dariba are all worked by Hindustan Zinc Ltd.

cards.a: Iron ore minerals by iron content: magnetite Fe3O4 (72.4% Fe), hematite Fe2O3 (about 70%), goethite and limonite (hydrated oxides, about 60%), siderite FeCO3 (48.2%).
cards.w: Magnetite is black and magnetic with a black streak. Hematite has a cherry-red streak and is India's main ore.

cards.a: Most Indian iron ore is hematite formed by natural enrichment of Precambrian banded iron formations (BHQ, BHJ), where silica was leached out and iron stayed.
cards.w: BHQ = banded hematite quartzite, BHJ = banded hematite jasper. Remove the silica bands and what is left is rich hematite.

cards.a: Bailadila (Dantewada, Bastar region, Chhattisgarh) has very high-grade hematite worked by NMDC; Noamundi, Gua and Kiriburu lie in the horse-shoe shaped Iron Ore Group syncline of Jharkhand-Odisha.
cards.w: Bailadila means hump of an ox, from the shape of the range. Noamundi feeds Tata Steel at Jamshedpur.

cards.a: Kudremukh (Chikkamagaluru district, Karnataka) is a large low-grade magnetite quartzite deposit; mining there stopped at the end of 2005 to protect the Western Ghats forests.
cards.w: Kudremukh means horse face. Unlike most Indian mines its ore is magnetite, not hematite, so it had to be concentrated and made into pellets.

cards.a: Kerala's iron ore is low-grade banded magnetite quartzite in Kozhikode district (Cheruppa, Nanminda, Naduvallur, Eleyettimala) and in Malappuram district; it has not been mined commercially.
cards.w: The bands lie within the Precambrian gneisses and charnockites. Same ore type as Kudremukh: magnetite plus quartz.

cards.a: Manganese ore minerals are pyrolusite MnO2, psilomelane, braunite and manganite; rhodochrosite MnCO3 and rhodonite MnSiO3 are the pink manganese minerals.
cards.w: Pyrolusite is soft, black and soils the fingers. Manganese is used mostly in steel making, to remove sulphur and oxygen.

cards.a: Gondite is a spessartite garnet-quartz rock with the manganese ores of the Sausar Group (Balaghat, Nagpur, Bhandara); kodurite is the manganese-bearing rock of the Eastern Ghats of Andhra Pradesh.
cards.w: Both names were given by Fermor. Gondite is named after the Gond people of central India, kodurite after Kodur village.

cards.a: Chromite FeCr2O4 is the only ore of chromium; the Sukinda valley (Jajpur) and Baula-Nuasahi in Odisha hold about 96% of India's chromite resources (IBM, Indian Minerals Yearbook 2022).
cards.w: The chromite lies in ultramafic rocks. Nickel-bearing laterite over the same Sukinda rocks holds most of India's nickel resources too.

cards.a: Coal rank rises from peat to lignite, sub-bituminous, bituminous and anthracite; fixed carbon and heating value increase while moisture and volatile matter decrease.
cards.w: Burial heat and pressure drive off water and gases, leaving more carbon. Rank is measured by vitrinite reflectance (shine of the main coal component).

cards.a: Almost all of India's coal is Gondwana coal of Permian age, in the Barakar and Raniganj Formations (Damuda Group) of the Damodar, Son-Mahanadi and Godavari valley basins.
cards.w: The Barakar Formation has the most and the best seams. Gondwana coal is bituminous, high in ash and low in sulphur.

cards.a: Jharia (Dhanbad, Jharkhand) is India's chief source of prime coking coal; Raniganj (West Bengal) is the oldest coalfield, where mining began in 1774.
cards.w: Coking coal is needed to make steel. Other big Gondwana fields are Bokaro, Talcher, Korba, Singrauli and Singareni.

cards.a: Tertiary coals occur in Assam (Makum), Meghalaya, Nagaland and Arunachal Pradesh; they are of Eocene-Oligocene age and high in sulphur.
cards.w: They formed in swamps near the sea, and sea water supplies sulphur. Gondwana coal formed in river basins, so it has little sulphur.

cards.a: Neyveli (Cuddalore district, Tamil Nadu) is India's largest lignite field, of Miocene age; a confined aquifer under pressure below the seam must be pumped continuously for safe mining.
cards.w: If the artesian pressure is not lowered, water can burst through the mine floor. Other lignite fields: Kutch, and Barmer and Bikaner in Rajasthan.

cards.a: Digboi in Upper Assam is India's oldest oil field (oil struck in 1889, refinery from 1901); Assam oil comes from Tertiary sandstones such as the Tipam and Barail.
cards.w: Other Upper Assam fields are Naharkatiya, Moran and Rudrasagar. Hook: the name is said to come from the cry: dig, boy, dig.

cards.a: Mumbai High, an offshore field found in 1974, produces from Miocene limestone; Cambay basin fields (Ankleshwar) produce from Eocene sandstone; the Krishna-Godavari basin has the Ravva oil field and deep-water KG-D6 gas.
cards.w: Every oil field needs a source rock, a porous reservoir rock, a tight cap rock and a trap. Mumbai High is India's largest oil field.

cards.a: Uranium deposits of India: Jaduguda (Singhbhum Shear Zone, Jharkhand, the first mine), Tummalapalle (in Vempalle dolostone of the Cuddapah basin, Andhra Pradesh) and Domiasiat (in Cretaceous Mahadek sandstone, Meghalaya).
cards.w: Three different host rocks: sheared schist, dolostone and sandstone. The main uranium mineral is uraninite (pitchblende), UO2.

cards.a: China clay (kaolin) is mainly kaolinite, Al2Si2O5(OH)4, formed by weathering or hydrothermal alteration of feldspar; a ceramic body needs clay for plasticity, feldspar as flux and quartz as filler.
cards.w: Flux means it melts first and glues the body together. Good china clay is white because it has almost no iron.

cards.a: Ball clay is a very plastic sedimentary clay, fire clay is a refractory clay often found under coal seams, and bentonite is montmorillonite clay formed from altered volcanic ash.
cards.w: Bentonite swells in water and is used in drilling mud. In India it comes mainly from Barmer (Rajasthan) and Kutch (Gujarat).

cards.a: Kerala's best-known china clay deposit is at Kundara (Kollam district); the state holds about 23% of India's china clay resources (IBM, IMY 2022; inventory as on 1.4.2015).
cards.w: The clay occurs in the Tertiary Warkalli beds and as residual clay over weathered gneiss. Thonnakkal near Thiruvananthapuram is another centre.

cards.a: Portland cement is made from limestone (low in magnesia) and clay burnt to clinker; about 3-5% gypsum (CaSO4.2H2O) is added during grinding to slow down setting.
cards.w: Without gypsum, cement would set almost at once (flash set). Heated gypsum loses water and becomes plaster of Paris.

cards.a: Famous Indian building stones: Makrana marble (Rajasthan) of the Taj Mahal, Vindhyan red sandstone of Red Fort, Kota stone (Vindhyan limestone) and Cuddapah slabs; granite, charnockite and basalt give road metal.
cards.w: A good building stone is strong, dense, low in porosity and resists weathering. In Kerala, charnockite and gneiss are the main crushed stone.

cards.a: Laterite was named by Francis Buchanan in 1807 at Angadipuram (Malappuram, Kerala), where the soft rock is cut into bricks that harden on exposure to air.
cards.w: Later is Latin for brick. Laterite caps much of the Kerala midlands and is the traditional building stone of Malabar.

cards.a: Refractories resist very high temperatures: acid types are silica (quartzite) and fire clay, basic types are magnesite and dolomite, and neutral types are chromite and graphite.
cards.w: The furnace lining must match the slag. Basic slag eats an acid lining, so basic steel furnaces are lined with magnesite or dolomite.

cards.a: Limestone and dolomite are the fluxes of the iron blast furnace, and fluorspar (CaF2) is a flux in steel making; India's main fluorite deposit is at Ambadongar, Gujarat, in carbonatite.
cards.w: A flux joins with silica gangue to make a liquid slag that floats and is tapped off. Carbonatite is a rare igneous rock made of carbonate minerals.

cards.a: Magnesite (MgCO3) at Salem, Tamil Nadu (Chalk Hills) occurs as white veins in dunite and peridotite, formed when CO2-bearing waters altered the magnesium-rich ultramafic rock.
cards.w: The white veins on the hills look like chalk, hence the name. Magnesite in Uttarakhand (Almora, Pithoragarh) instead replaces dolomite.

cards.a: Kyanite and sillimanite (both Al2SiO5) are high-alumina refractories that turn to mullite on heating; Lapsa Buru (Singhbhum, Jharkhand) is the classic kyanite deposit and Sonapahar (Meghalaya) the classic sillimanite deposit.
cards.w: Mullite stays strong at very high heat, so these minerals go into furnace bricks and spark plugs. Both are metamorphic minerals.

cards.a: Graphite is metamorphosed carbon, found as flakes in khondalite of the Eastern Ghats (Odisha) and of Kerala (Thiruvananthapuram, Kollam, Kottayam, Idukki, Ernakulam); it is used in crucibles and electrodes.
cards.w: Khondalite is garnet-sillimanite-graphite gneiss. Graphite does not melt and conducts heat and electricity, so it suits crucibles.

cards.a: Fertilizer elements are N, P and K: phosphorus comes from rock phosphate and apatite, potassium from potash salts (sylvite KCl, carnallite, polyhalite), and nitrogen mostly from the air.
cards.w: Rock phosphate is treated with sulphuric acid to make superphosphate. Gypsum and pyrite (for sulphur) are also counted as fertilizer minerals.

cards.a: Jhamarkotra (Udaipur, Rajasthan) is India's largest rock phosphate deposit: stromatolitic phosphorite in dolomite of the Proterozoic Aravalli Supergroup.
cards.w: Stromatolites are layered mounds built by algae-like microbes, which trapped the phosphate. The Mussoorie phosphorite is younger (Tal Formation).

cards.a: India has no working potash mine and imports its potash; potash salts (polyhalite, sylvite) are known in the buried evaporites of the Nagaur-Ganganagar basin, Rajasthan.
cards.w: Potash salts form only in the last stage of sea water evaporation and dissolve easily, so they survive only deep underground. Status as known in 2025.

cards.a: Natural abrasives in order of hardness: diamond (10), corundum (9), emery (corundum mixed with magnetite) and garnet (6.5-7.5); softer ones include quartz sand, pumice and diatomite.
cards.w: An abrasive must be harder than the thing it grinds. Garnet is used in sandpaper and in water-jet cutting.

cards.a: In India, abrasive garnet is recovered from beach sands of Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Odisha, and corundum occurs with sillimanite at Pipra (Madhya Pradesh) and Sonapahar (Meghalaya).
cards.w: Garnet is a heavy mineral, so it collects in the same placers as ilmenite. Corundum and sillimanite are both alumina-rich metamorphic minerals.

cards.a: Ruby (red, coloured by chromium) and sapphire (blue, by iron and titanium) are gem corundum, Al2O3; emerald (green) and aquamarine (blue) are gem beryl, Be3Al2Si6O18.
cards.w: Same mineral, different trace element, different gem. India's famous sapphire comes from Paddar in Kashmir and emerald from the Ajmer-Udaipur belt of Rajasthan.

cards.a: Chrysoberyl (BeAl2O4, hardness 8.5) has two gem varieties, alexandrite (colour-changing) and cat's eye; in Kerala it occurs in pegmatites and gem gravels of Thiruvananthapuram and Kollam districts.
cards.w: Alexandrite looks green in daylight and red in lamp light. The pegmatites cut the khondalite belt of south Kerala.

cards.a: Diamond comes from kimberlite and lamproite pipes and their placers; in India the Majhgawan pipe at Panna (Madhya Pradesh) is the site of NMDC's diamond mine, and Wajrakarur (Anantapur, Andhra Pradesh) has kimberlite pipes.
cards.w: Kimberlite brings diamonds up fast from over 150 km depth. The old Golconda diamonds came from Krishna river gravels.

cards.a: The Chavara beach placer (Neendakara to Kayamkulam, Kollam district, Kerala) is rich in ilmenite, rutile, zircon, monazite, sillimanite and garnet, and is mined by IREL and KMML.
cards.w: Formulae: ilmenite FeTiO3, rutile TiO2, zircon ZrSiO4, sillimanite Al2SiO5. Chavara ilmenite is prized for its high TiO2 (about 60%).

cards.a: Kerala's beach heavy minerals come from weathered khondalite, charnockite, gneiss and pegmatite of the hinterland, carried by rivers and sorted by waves; monazite in them is India's thorium source.
cards.w: Waves and longshore currents wash away light quartz and leave heavy black sand. Monazite is a rare-earth and thorium phosphate, so it is a nuclear mineral.

cards.a: Other Kerala minerals: glass-grade silica sand in the Cherthala-Alappuzha belt, bauxite at Nileshwaram (Kasaragod), lime shell in Vembanad Lake, and lignite at Madayi (Kannur).
cards.w: Kerala has no coal, oil or big metal mines. Its strength is beach sand, china clay and silica sand.

cards.a: Muscovite mica comes from pegmatites cutting mica schist; the Koderma-Giridih-Hazaribagh belt (Jharkhand-Bihar) yields ruby mica, with other belts at Nellore (Andhra Pradesh) and Bhilwara (Rajasthan).
cards.w: Koderma is called the mica capital of India. Sheet mica splits thin and does not conduct electricity, so it is an insulator.

cards.a: Mangampet (Kadapa region, Andhra Pradesh) has one of the world's largest single barytes (BaSO4) deposits, bedded in Pullampet shales of the Cuddapah Supergroup; barytes is used as oil-well drilling mud.
cards.w: Barytes is very heavy (specific gravity about 4.5). Heavy mud holds down gas and oil pressure in a well.

cards.a: A sill is a sheet-like (tabular) concordant intrusion: it lies parallel to the bedding or foliation of the country rock.
cards.w: Concordant means it follows the layers. Memory hook: a window sill lies flat, like the beds.

cards.a: A dyke is a tabular discordant intrusion: it cuts across the bedding or foliation of the country rock.
cards.w: Discordant means it cuts the layers. Dykes fill cracks, so they are usually steep. Dolerite is the commonest dyke rock.

cards.a: A laccolith is a concordant intrusion with a flat floor and a domed roof, usually built by viscous acid (silica-rich) magma.
cards.w: Thick, sticky magma cannot spread far sideways. It piles up and lifts the roof beds, like a mushroom cap.

cards.a: A lopolith is a very large, saucer-shaped (basin-like) concordant intrusion, usually of mafic rock; the Bushveld Complex is the classic example.
cards.w: Lopo = basin. The centre sags under the weight of heavy mafic magma. Laccolith bulges up; lopolith sags down.

cards.a: A phacolith is a lens-shaped concordant intrusion found at the crests of anticlines and the troughs of synclines in folded strata.
cards.w: Folding opens low-pressure gaps at fold hinges, and magma moves into them. Phaco = lens.

cards.a: A batholith is the largest discordant pluton, mostly granite or granodiorite, with exposed area above 100 square km and no visible floor; a smaller one is a stock.
cards.w: Batho = deep. The 100 square km limit separates batholith from stock. A stock with a round outline is called a boss.

cards.a: Ring dykes are vertical or steeply outward-dipping and form by cauldron subsidence; cone sheets dip inward to a common centre and form by upward magma pressure.
cards.w: Ring dyke: a roof block sinks and magma rises around it. Cone sheet: magma pushes the roof up and opens inward-dipping cracks. Both are classic on Mull, Scotland.

cards.a: By crystallinity, igneous rocks are holocrystalline (all crystals), holohyaline (all glass, like obsidian) or hypocrystalline (crystals plus glass).
cards.w: Holo = whole, hyaline = glassy. Glass forms when lava cools too fast for crystals to grow.

cards.a: Slow cooling at depth gives coarse (phaneritic) grains because few nuclei form and grow large; fast cooling of lava gives fine (aphanitic) grains or glass.
cards.w: Nuclei are the tiny starting points of crystals. Slow cooling = few nuclei, big crystals. Fast cooling = many nuclei, tiny crystals.

cards.a: Porphyritic texture has large crystals (phenocrysts) set in a finer groundmass, usually recording two stages of cooling; with a glassy groundmass it is called vitrophyric.
cards.w: The big crystals grew slowly at depth. Then the magma rose and the rest cooled quickly around them.

cards.a: In ophitic texture, plagioclase laths are wholly enclosed in large augite crystals; it is the typical texture of dolerite.
cards.w: Plagioclase started growing first as many small laths. Augite grew later as a few big crystals that wrapped around them.

cards.a: In poikilitic texture, a large host crystal (oikocryst) encloses many small, randomly oriented crystals (chadacrysts) of other minerals.
cards.w: Oikos = house: the big crystal houses the small ones. Ophitic texture is a special kind of poikilitic texture.

cards.a: Graphic texture is a regular intergrowth of quartz in alkali feldspar that looks like ancient wedge-shaped writing; it is typical of granite pegmatites.
cards.w: Quartz and K-feldspar crystallise at the same time from the last melt. The microscopic version is called granophyric.

cards.a: Perthite is K-feldspar hosting exsolved lamellae of albite; antiperthite is the reverse, a plagioclase host with K-feldspar blebs.
cards.w: Hot Na- and K-feldspar mix into one crystal. On slow cooling they unmix (exsolution), like oil separating from water.

cards.a: Myrmekite is an intergrowth of worm-like (vermicular) quartz in sodic plagioclase, usually found next to K-feldspar in granitic rocks.
cards.w: Myrmex = ant; the quartz looks like ant tunnels. Do not confuse with graphic texture, where quartz sits in K-feldspar.

p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Mains 2020 Geology Paper II
cards.a: Rapakivi texture shows large rounded K-feldspar (orthoclase) crystals mantled by a rim of plagioclase (oligoclase); it is named from Proterozoic granites of Finland.
cards.w: Rapakivi is Finnish for crumbly stone. Hook: pink egg with a white shell. These granites are anorogenic (A-type).

cards.a: Spinifex texture consists of long skeletal blades of olivine (or pyroxene) formed by rapid cooling of ultramafic lava; it is diagnostic of komatiite.
cards.w: Named after spiky Australian spinifex grass. Komatiite is a magnesium-rich lava (over 18% MgO), almost all of Archaean age.

cards.a: In basaltic rocks, intersertal texture has glass filling the gaps between plagioclase laths, while intergranular texture has small pyroxene grains in those gaps.
cards.w: Same framework of laths, different filling. Glass filling = cooled faster. Granules filling = had time to crystallise.

cards.a: A reaction rim (corona) is a shell of a new mineral around an earlier crystal that reacted with the melt, such as orthopyroxene around olivine.
cards.w: Early olivine is no longer stable as the melt gets richer in silica. It reacts at its edge to make pyroxene, as Bowen's series predicts.

cards.a: Vesicular structure is formed by escaping gas bubbles; scoria is dark vesicular basaltic rock, and pumice is light frothy silicic glass that can float on water.
cards.w: Gas comes out of lava when pressure drops, like opening a soda bottle. Pumice has so many holes that it is lighter than water.

cards.a: When vesicles are later filled by secondary minerals such as zeolites, calcite or agate, the fillings are amygdales and the structure is amygdaloidal.
cards.w: Amygdale = almond-shaped. Deccan Trap basalts are famous for cavities filled with zeolites.

cards.a: Pillow structure forms when basaltic lava erupts under water; each pillow has a convex top and a glassy chilled skin.
cards.w: Water chills the lava into bag-like lobes. Pillows prove underwater eruption and show which way was up. Sodium-rich pillow basalt with albite is called spilite.
