cards.a: Columnar joints are polygonal, commonly six-sided columns formed by contraction of cooling lava or shallow intrusions; the columns grow at right angles to the cooling surface.
cards.w: Rock shrinks as it cools and cracks like drying mud. Indian example: St. Mary's Islands off Udupi, Karnataka; also seen in Deccan basalts.

cards.a: Pahoehoe is basaltic lava with a smooth, ropy surface; aa lava has a rough, jagged, clinkery surface and is more viscous.
cards.w: Both are Hawaiian words. Pahoehoe is hot and runny, so its skin wrinkles like rope. Aa is cooler and stiffer, so its crust breaks into rubble.

cards.a: Flow structure (flow banding) is a streaky layering produced by movement of viscous lava; it is best developed in rhyolite and obsidian.
cards.w: Sticky lava smears out bands of different colour or crystal content as it creeps. The name rhyolite itself comes from the Greek for flow.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.a: Bowen's discontinuous reaction series runs olivine, then pyroxene, then amphibole, then biotite, with falling temperature.
cards.w: Each mineral reacts with the melt to form the next one. Hook: O-P-A-B. Silicate structure also grows: islands, chains, double chains, sheets.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.a: Bowen's continuous reaction series is the plagioclase feldspars, changing smoothly from calcium-rich (anorthite) at high temperature to sodium-rich (albite) at low temperature.
cards.w: Continuous = same mineral structure, only the composition shifts. That is why basalt has calcic plagioclase and granite has sodic plagioclase.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.a: In Bowen's reaction series, K-feldspar, muscovite and quartz crystallise last, at the lowest temperatures; quartz is the final mineral.
cards.w: Goldich's weathering series follows the same order as Bowen's: first-formed olivine weathers fastest, last-formed quartz resists longest. High-temperature minerals are least stable at the surface.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.a: Fractional crystallisation, in which early crystals separate from the melt (for example by gravity settling), is the main process of magmatic differentiation.
cards.w: Removing early Mg-Fe minerals leaves the remaining melt richer in silica and alkalis. Heavy chromite or olivine sinking to the floor makes layered rocks.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.a: Assimilation is the incorporation and digestion of country rock by magma, which changes the magma composition; partly digested xenoliths are its field evidence.
cards.w: Xenolith = foreign rock piece inside an igneous rock. Melting wall rock uses up heat, so assimilation usually goes with crystallisation.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.a: Magma viscosity increases with silica content and decreases with higher temperature and dissolved water; rhyolitic magma is far more viscous than basaltic magma.
cards.w: Silica tetrahedra link into long chains and networks that resist flow. So basalt makes quiet flows and rhyolite makes domes and explosions.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.a: By silica content, igneous rocks are ultrabasic (below 45% SiO2), basic (45-52%), intermediate, and acid (above 66% in the classical scheme; 63% in the TAS diagram).
cards.w: Examples in order: peridotite, basalt, andesite, granite. Acid here means silica-rich, not low pH.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.a: Colour index is the volume percentage of dark (mafic) minerals in a rock; leucocratic rocks are light with a low index and melanocratic rocks are dark with a high index.
cards.w: Leuco = white, melano = black, meso = in between. Granite is leucocratic; gabbro is mesocratic to melanocratic.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.a: The IUGS (Streckeisen) QAPF classification uses modal quartz (Q), alkali feldspar (A), plagioclase (P) and feldspathoids (F), and applies when mafic minerals are below 90%.
cards.w: Modal = actually measured minerals. It is a double triangle because quartz and feldspathoids never occur together. Above 90% mafics, ultramafic diagrams are used.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.a: The TAS diagram plots total alkalis (Na2O + K2O) against SiO2 and is used to name volcanic rocks whose minerals are too fine or glassy to count.
cards.w: TAS = Total Alkali-Silica. When you cannot see the minerals, you use chemistry instead of the QAPF mode.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.a: In Shand's silica saturation scheme, oversaturated rocks have free quartz and undersaturated rocks have feldspathoids or Mg-olivine; quartz never coexists with nepheline or leucite.
cards.w: Feldspathoids are silica-poor stand-ins for feldspar. If spare silica were present, it would react with them to make feldspar instead.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.a: Peraluminous rocks have molar Al2O3 greater than CaO + Na2O + K2O (muscovite, garnet, cordierite); peralkaline rocks have Al2O3 less than Na2O + K2O (aegirine, riebeckite).
cards.w: Extra alumina makes Al-rich minerals. Extra alkalis make sodium-rich pyroxene and amphibole. Metaluminous rocks lie in between (hornblende).

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.a: The CIPW norm is a set of ideal anhydrous minerals calculated from a rock's chemical analysis; the mode is the mineral content actually measured in the rock.
cards.w: Named after Cross, Iddings, Pirsson and Washington. Normative quartz means silica-oversaturated; normative nepheline means undersaturated.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.a: Diopside-anorthite at 1 atmosphere is a simple binary eutectic with no solid solution; the eutectic lies at about 1274 °C and 42% anorthite.
cards.w: Eutectic = the lowest-melting mixture, where both minerals crystallise together. It is the simple model for basalt (pyroxene + plagioclase).

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Mains 2020 Geology Paper II
cards.a: Albite-anorthite (plagioclase) shows complete solid solution with a liquidus-solidus loop between 1118 °C (albite) and 1553 °C (anorthite), and has no eutectic.
cards.w: Crystals are always richer in anorthite than the melt they grow from. If they cannot re-react, you get zoned plagioclase: calcic core, sodic rim.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Mains 2020 Geology Paper II
cards.a: In the forsterite-silica system, enstatite melts incongruently to forsterite plus liquid at a peritectic point (about 1557 °C at 1 atmosphere).
cards.w: Incongruent = the solid breaks into a different solid plus melt. On cooling, olivine reacts with melt to make pyroxene, so Mg-olivine and quartz do not occur together.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.a: Basaltic magma forms by partial melting of mantle peridotite: by decompression at mid-ocean ridges and hotspots, and by water-induced (flux) melting above subduction zones.
cards.w: The mantle is solid. It melts when pressure drops as it rises, or when water lowers its melting point. Only a small part melts, and that part is basalt.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.a: Plutonic-volcanic equivalents are granite-rhyolite, granodiorite-dacite, diorite-andesite and gabbro-basalt.
cards.w: Same chemistry, different cooling speed. Plutonic = slow and coarse; volcanic = fast and fine. Dacite and granodiorite are the pair most often confused.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.a: Dolerite (diabase) is the medium-grained hypabyssal equivalent of basalt and gabbro, made of calcic plagioclase and augite, and typically forms dykes and sills.
cards.w: Hypabyssal = shallow intrusion, between plutonic and volcanic. Medium cooling speed gives medium grain size and ophitic texture.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of basalts
cards.a: Basalt consists essentially of calcic plagioclase (labradorite) and augite, with or without olivine; quartz is not an essential mineral.
cards.w: Basalt is a basic rock (45-52% SiO2), so there is no spare silica to form quartz. Olivine-bearing types are called olivine basalt.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of basalts
cards.a: Mid-ocean ridge basalt (MORB) is tholeiitic, low in potassium and depleted in incompatible elements, and forms by decompression melting of depleted upper mantle.
cards.w: Incompatible elements (K, Rb, light rare earths) prefer melt over crystals. Earlier melting had already removed them from this mantle source.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of basalts
cards.a: Ocean island basalts (OIB), as in Hawaii and Réunion, are enriched in incompatible elements and are linked to hotspots fed by mantle plumes.
cards.w: Plumes tap a deeper, less depleted mantle source than ridges do. So OIB is richer in K and light rare earths than MORB, and often alkaline.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of basalts
cards.a: Continental flood basalts are huge piles of mainly tholeiitic lava erupted from fissures in a short time; examples are the Deccan, Siberian, Columbia River and Paraná provinces.
cards.w: They are large igneous provinces, usually tied to a plume head and often to continental break-up. Fluid basalt spreads as wide flat sheets.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of basalts
p: Uttarakhand PSC Geology paper 2017 (exam name not shown)
cards.a: The Deccan Traps are tholeiitic flood basalts covering about 500,000 square km of western and central India, erupted through fissures and forming step-like hills.
cards.w: Trap comes from a Swedish word for stairs. Flat lava flows weather into terraces, as seen in the Western Ghats of Maharashtra.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of basalts
cards.a: The main Deccan eruptions took place about 66 million years ago, at the Cretaceous-Palaeogene boundary, when India passed over the Réunion hotspot.
cards.w: Same time as the dinosaur extinction. The hotspot track runs from the Deccan through the Lakshadweep-Chagos ridge to Réunion island today.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of basalts
cards.a: The Rajmahal Traps of Jharkhand, with the Sylhet Traps, are Early Cretaceous basalts about 117 million years old, linked to the Kerguelen hotspot.
cards.w: Older than the Deccan. Remember: Rajmahal = Kerguelen = Early Cretaceous; Deccan = Réunion = end Cretaceous.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites
cards.a: I-type granites come from melting of igneous source rocks, are metaluminous with hornblende, sphene and magnetite, and typify subduction-related (Cordilleran) batholiths.
cards.w: I = igneous source. The I and S types were defined by Chappell and White in the Lachlan Fold Belt of Australia.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites
cards.a: S-type granites form by melting of sedimentary rocks, are peraluminous with muscovite, garnet or cordierite, and typify continental collision belts such as the Himalaya.
cards.w: S = sedimentary source. Clay-rich sediments are rich in alumina, so the melt grows Al-rich minerals. Crustal melting is called anatexis.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites
cards.a: A-type granites are anorogenic, alkali-rich and relatively dry, found in rifts and plate interiors; M-type granites are mantle-derived plagiogranites of island arcs and ophiolites.
cards.w: A = anorogenic (not linked to mountain building) and alkaline. M = mantle. Rapakivi granites are A-type.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites
cards.a: The Malani Igneous Suite of western Rajasthan is Neoproterozoic (about 750 million years old) and dominated by rhyolite with granites; it is India's largest felsic volcanic province.
cards.w: Felsic = rich in feldspar and silica. Its granites include the Jalor and Siwana granites. Contrast with the basaltic Deccan.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites
cards.a: Younger granites of Kerala include the Ambalavayal and Kalpetta granites of Wayanad and the Munnar granite of Idukki; all are Neoproterozoic intrusions.
cards.w: They cut the older charnockite and gneiss basement, so they are younger than it. Hook: Wayanad has two (Ambalavayal, Kalpetta), Idukki has Munnar.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites
cards.a: Charnockite is an orthopyroxene (hypersthene)-bearing rock of granitic composition, named by T.H. Holland after Job Charnock, whose tombstone in Kolkata is made of it.
cards.w: Type area: St. Thomas Mount near Chennai. With khondalite it is the main rock of Kerala's highlands. Its quartz looks greasy and blue-grey.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of andesites
cards.a: Andesite is an intermediate volcanic rock (about 57-63% SiO2) made of andesine plagioclase with pyroxene or hornblende, named after the Andes mountains.
cards.w: It is the volcanic equivalent of diorite. It is often porphyritic, with zoned plagioclase phenocrysts.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of andesites
cards.a: Andesites belong to the calc-alkaline series of subduction zones, where water released from the sinking slab lowers the melting point of the overlying mantle wedge.
cards.w: Water acts like salt on ice: it makes hot mantle melt. The calc-alkaline series is basalt, andesite, dacite, rhyolite, with no iron enrichment.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of alkaline rocks
cards.a: Syenite is a plutonic rock dominated by alkali feldspar with little or no quartz, usually with hornblende or biotite; its volcanic equivalent is trachyte.
cards.w: Think of it as granite without the quartz. It is a silica-saturated rock: no quartz, no feldspathoid.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of alkaline rocks
cards.a: Nepheline syenite is a silica-undersaturated plutonic rock of alkali feldspar and nepheline with no quartz; its volcanic equivalent is phonolite.
cards.w: It is used in glass and ceramics. Indian examples: Kishangarh (Rajasthan) and Sivamalai (Tamil Nadu). Phonolite = clinkstone, it rings when struck.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of alkaline rocks
cards.a: Alkaline rocks occur mainly in continental rifts and intraplate hotspots, such as the East African Rift, and form by low-degree partial melting of enriched mantle.
cards.w: A small amount of melting pulls out mostly the alkalis (Na, K) and volatiles first. So small melt fractions are alkali-rich and silica-poor.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of alkaline rocks
cards.a: The Angadimogar syenite of Kasaragod district is a well-known alkaline pluton of Kerala; Peralimala in Kannur district is an alkali granite-syenite body.
cards.w: Both are in north Kerala and intrude the Precambrian basement. Hook: syenite sits in the northernmost district, Kasaragod.

cards.a: Gabbro is a plutonic rock of calcic plagioclase and clinopyroxene; norite has orthopyroxene instead, and troctolite is plagioclase plus olivine.
cards.w: All three are basic plutonic rocks. Only the main mafic mineral changes: augite, hypersthene, or olivine.

p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Mains 2020 Geology Paper II
cards.a: The Bushveld Complex of South Africa is the world's largest layered mafic intrusion and the main source of platinum-group elements (Merensky Reef) and chromite.
cards.w: Heavy minerals settled in layers on the chamber floor. It is also the classic lopolith and has vanadium-bearing magnetite layers.

cards.a: The Skaergaard intrusion of East Greenland is the classic example of closed-system fractional crystallisation of tholeiitic magma, showing strong iron enrichment.
cards.w: One batch of magma cooled without refilling, so its layers record the full crystallisation history. Studied by Wager and Deer.

cards.a: The Stillwater Complex of Montana, USA, is an Archaean layered intrusion mined for palladium and platinum (J-M Reef) and known for its chromite seams.
cards.w: Hook for the big three: Bushveld = South Africa, Skaergaard = Greenland, Stillwater = USA.

cards.a: Layered intrusions are built of cumulates (accumulated crystals); cryptic layering is a gradual upward change in mineral composition, and such bodies lie mostly in stable cratons.
cards.w: Cryptic = hidden: you need chemical analysis to see it. Rhythmic layering is the visible repetition of light and dark bands.

cards.a: Mafic (dolerite and gabbro) dykes cutting Kerala's Precambrian basement trend mainly NNW-SSE to NW-SE; the younger ones are Late Cretaceous-Palaeocene, around Deccan Trap age.
cards.w: The trend is roughly parallel to the west coast. The dykes record stretching of the crust when India rifted and the Arabian Sea opened.

p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Mains 2020 Geology Paper II
Uttarakhand PSC Geology paper 2017 (exam name not shown)
cards.a: Kimberlite is a potassic, volatile-rich ultramafic rock with olivine, phlogopite, pyrope garnet and ilmenite; it occurs in carrot-shaped pipes and is the main primary host of diamond.
cards.w: Named after Kimberley, South Africa. Volatiles (CO2, H2O) make it erupt explosively, drilling pipes called diatremes.

cards.a: Kimberlite magma rises from depths greater than about 150 km and carries mantle xenoliths; diamond-bearing pipes are confined to old, thick cratons (Clifford's rule).
cards.w: Diamond is stable only at very high pressure. Only cold, thick, ancient continental roots reach that depth.

cards.a: Lamproite is an ultrapotassic, magnesium-rich rock with phlogopite and leucite; it can also carry diamond, as at Argyle in Western Australia.
cards.w: So kimberlite is not the only diamond host. Lamproite is richer in potassium and poorer in CO2 than kimberlite.

cards.a: The Wajrakarur kimberlite field lies in Anantapur district, Andhra Pradesh, in the Eastern Dharwar Craton; its pipes are Mesoproterozoic, about 1100 million years old.
cards.w: Vajra means diamond. India's main primary diamond source, however, is the Majhgawan pipe at Panna, Madhya Pradesh.

cards.a: Anorthosite is a plutonic rock with more than 90% plagioclase feldspar.
cards.w: It is almost a one-mineral rock, so its colour index is below 10. The light-coloured highlands of the Moon are anorthosite.

p: Uttarakhand PSC Geology paper 2017 (exam name not shown)
cards.a: Archaean anorthosites are layered and very calcic (bytownite-anorthite); Proterozoic massif-type anorthosites have andesine-labradorite and carry ilmenite-magnetite deposits.
cards.w: Two ages, two styles. Massif-type bodies are large Proterozoic plutons, often found with charnockitic rocks, and are a source of titanium.

cards.a: The Sittampundi Complex in Namakkal district, Tamil Nadu, is an Archaean layered anorthosite with chromitite layers and very calcic plagioclase (anorthite).
cards.w: It is the Indian type example of the Archaean layered kind. Its rocks have been used as a stand-in for lunar highland material.

cards.a: Massif-type anorthosites of India include Chilka Lake (Odisha), Bankura (West Bengal) and Oddanchatram (Tamil Nadu); Kerala has the Perinthatta anorthosite in Kannur district.
cards.w: Most lie in the Eastern Ghats and the Southern Granulite Terrain, the high-grade belts of Proterozoic age.

cards.a: Carbonatite is an igneous rock containing more than 50% carbonate minerals such as calcite or dolomite.
cards.w: It looks like marble but came from magma. Calcite-rich coarse carbonatite is called sovite; dolomite-rich is beforsite.

cards.a: Ol Doinyo Lengai in Tanzania is the only active carbonatite volcano and erupts sodium-rich natrocarbonatite lava.
cards.w: Its lava is very cool and runny for a lava, and looks black, then turns white on weathering. It sits in the East African Rift.

cards.a: Carbonatites occur with alkaline rocks such as nepheline syenite and ijolite in ring complexes of continental rifts; the alkali-metasomatised halo around them is called fenite.
cards.w: Metasomatism = chemical change by hot fluids. Fenite is named after the Fen complex in Norway. Sodium and potassium soak into the wall rock.

cards.a: Carbonatites are the chief source of rare earth elements (bastnäsite, as at Bayan Obo and Mountain Pass) and niobium (pyrochlore, as at Araxá).
cards.w: Carbonatite melt gathers elements that do not fit in common silicate minerals. They also supply phosphate (apatite), fluorite and vermiculite.

cards.a: Amba Dongar in Chhota Udepur district, Gujarat, is a carbonatite ring complex of Deccan Trap age that hosts India's largest fluorite deposit and rare earth minerals.
cards.w: It formed at the end of Deccan volcanism, about 65 million years ago. Hook: Amba Dongar = fluorite; Sevattur = vermiculite.

cards.a: The Sevattur carbonatite in northern Tamil Nadu is Neoproterozoic, mainly dolomitic, and is mined for vermiculite; it also carries apatite and pyrochlore.
cards.w: It is much older than Amba Dongar. It lies close to the Samalpatti carbonatite, with syenite and pyroxenite around it.

cards.a: The Majhgawan pipe near Panna, Madhya Pradesh, mined by NMDC, is India's main primary diamond source; long called kimberlite, its rock is now often classed as lamproite.
cards.w: Panna = diamonds. The pipe cuts Vindhyan sandstone of the Bundelkhand region. Lamproite is a potassium-rich cousin of kimberlite that can also carry diamond.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites
cards.a: The Closepet Granite of Karnataka is a north-south linear belt, about 400 km long, of potassium-rich granite about 2.5 billion years old (late Archaean) in the Dharwar Craton.
cards.w: Closepet is the old name of Ramanagara town. The belt runs like a spine through the craton, close to the join between its western and eastern blocks.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of alkaline rocks
cards.a: The Sivamalai alkaline complex near Kangayam, Tamil Nadu, is made mainly of nepheline syenite and syenite, some of it corundum-bearing; T.H. Holland named it the 'Sivamalai series' in 1901.
cards.w: Nepheline forms only when silica is short, so these rocks have no quartz. Excess alumina with little silica gives corundum (Al2O3).

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites
cards.a: The type area of charnockite is Pallavaram-St Thomas Mount near Chennai; in Kerala, charnockite is the most widespread basement rock, and patchy 'incipient charnockite' is seen in southern Kerala quarries.
cards.w: Type area = the place where a rock was first described. Incipient charnockite means dark greasy patches where gneiss was caught turning into charnockite.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.a: On an AFM diagram (alkalis, iron oxide, magnesia), tholeiitic magmas show early iron enrichment (Fenner trend), while calc-alkaline magmas show no iron enrichment (Bowen trend).
cards.w: Calc-alkaline magmas are wet and oxidised, so magnetite forms early and removes iron. Dry tholeiitic magma keeps its iron in the melt for longer.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of basalts
cards.a: Tholeiitic basalt is silica-saturated (hypersthene in the norm) and carries low-calcium pyroxene; alkali basalt is silica-undersaturated (nepheline in the norm) with olivine and titanium-rich augite.
cards.w: Norm = minerals calculated from the chemistry. Hypersthene in the norm means enough silica; nepheline in the norm means silica is short.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of andesites
cards.a: Andesite is typically porphyritic with zoned plagioclase phenocrysts and builds steep composite volcanoes (stratovolcanoes) around the Pacific 'Ring of Fire'.
cards.w: Andesite lava is sticky and gas-rich, so eruptions are explosive and pile up steep cones of lava and ash. Zoning records changing conditions in the magma chamber.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites
cards.a: In the IUGS QAPF diagram, granite has 20-60% quartz among its felsic (light) minerals, with plagioclase forming 10-65% of the total feldspar.
cards.w: Less than 20% quartz moves the rock towards syenite or monzonite. More plagioclase than 65% of the feldspar makes it granodiorite.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.a: By the phase rule (F = C - P + 2), a eutectic or peritectic point of a binary system at fixed pressure has three coexisting phases and zero degrees of freedom (an invariant point).
cards.w: At fixed pressure the rule becomes F = C - P + 1 = 2 - 3 + 1 = 0. So temperature and liquid composition stay fixed until one phase is used up.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.a: Metamorphism is the solid-state change in the minerals and texture of a rock caused by changes in temperature, pressure and chemically active fluids.
cards.w: The rock stays solid. If it melts, the process is no longer metamorphic but igneous (anatexis = partial melting).

p: UPSC Geologist Exam 2018 Geology Paper II (descriptive)
cards.a: The three agents of metamorphism are heat, pressure (uniform confining pressure plus directed stress) and chemically active fluids.
cards.w: Heat drives mineral reactions. Directed stress lines minerals up (foliation). Fluids carry ions and speed reactions up.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.a: Contact (thermal) metamorphism is caused mainly by heat from an igneous intrusion; the baked zone of country rock around the intrusion is called the contact aureole.
cards.w: Heat is the main agent and stress is small, so the rocks are usually not foliated. A bigger, hotter intrusion gives a wider aureole.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.a: Regional (dynamothermal) metamorphism acts over large areas of orogenic belts under both heat and directed pressure, giving foliated rocks such as slate, schist and gneiss.
cards.w: Mountain building squeezes and heats rocks together. Squeezing makes platy minerals grow parallel, so the rocks split in layers.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.a: Cataclastic (dynamic) metamorphism occurs along fault and shear zones, where rocks are crushed and sheared mechanically with little rise in temperature.
cards.w: Stress is the main agent here, not heat. Products are fault breccia, cataclasite and mylonite.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.a: Burial metamorphism occurs at the base of thick sedimentary or volcanic piles without strong deformation and typically produces zeolite-facies minerals.
cards.w: Only the weight of overlying rock and gentle heat act. So original bedding survives and no foliation forms.

p: UPSC Geologist Exam 2018 Geology Paper II (descriptive)
cards.a: Shock (impact) metamorphism is recognised by the very high-pressure silica polymorphs coesite and stishovite and by shatter cones.
cards.w: A meteorite impact gives extreme pressure for a split second. Ordinary crustal metamorphism cannot make stishovite.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
p: UPSC Geologist Mains 2020 Geology Paper II (descriptive)
cards.a: Retrograde metamorphism (diaphthoresis) changes a high-grade assemblage to a lower-grade one during cooling, for example garnet to chlorite or pyroxene to amphibole.
cards.w: Low-grade minerals contain water. So retrograde change happens only where water gets back into the rock, usually along shear zones.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Metamorphic textures are called crystalloblastic: the suffix '-blastic' means grown during metamorphism, while the prefix 'blasto-' marks a relict texture inherited from the parent rock.
cards.w: Example: porphyroblastic is a new metamorphic texture, but blastoporphyritic is an old igneous porphyritic texture still visible.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Granoblastic texture is a mosaic of equidimensional grains with no preferred orientation, typical of quartzite, marble, hornfels and granulite.
cards.w: Quartz, calcite and feldspar are not platy, so they grow as equal-sized grains. Grain boundaries often meet at 120 degree triple junctions.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Lepidoblastic texture is the parallel arrangement of platy minerals such as muscovite, biotite and chlorite, as seen in mica schist.
cards.w: Lepido = scale or flake. Flaky micas grow at right angles to the squeezing direction.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Nematoblastic texture is the parallel arrangement of prismatic or needle-like minerals such as hornblende, actinolite and sillimanite, as in hornblende schist.
cards.w: Nema = thread. Think of needles lying side by side.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Porphyroblastic texture has large metamorphic crystals (porphyroblasts) such as garnet or staurolite set in a finer-grained matrix.
cards.w: It is the metamorphic twin of porphyritic texture. Phenocrysts grow from magma, porphyroblasts grow in solid rock.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Poikiloblastic (sieve) texture is shown by porphyroblasts crowded with small inclusions of other minerals, common in staurolite, cordierite and garnet.
cards.w: The fast-growing crystal swallows matrix grains instead of pushing them out. The igneous equivalent is poikilitic.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Idioblastic crystals show their own crystal faces and xenoblastic crystals do not; garnet, staurolite, sphene and rutile stand high in the crystalloblastic series.
cards.w: Minerals high in the series (Becke) have strong crystallising force and keep good shapes. Quartz and feldspar stand low and stay shapeless.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Relict (palimpsest) textures are features of the parent rock that survive metamorphism, for example blastoporphyritic, blastophitic and blastopsammitic textures.
cards.w: Palimpsest = old writing showing through new writing. They tell us what the parent rock was.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Mylonitic texture forms in ductile shear zones: grain size is reduced by dynamic recrystallisation, giving a fine foliated matrix around surviving porphyroclasts.
cards.w: Porphyroclasts are old broken survivors, not new growths like porphyroblasts. Lapworth named mylonite from the Moine Thrust, Scotland.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Decussate texture is a random criss-cross arrangement of platy or prismatic crystals, typical of contact metamorphic rocks formed without directed stress.
cards.w: No squeezing means no alignment. Micas in hornfels point in all directions.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
p: UPSC Geologist Mains 2020 Geology Paper II (descriptive)
cards.a: Helicitic texture is curved or S-shaped trails of inclusions inside a porphyroblast; spiral trails in 'snowball' garnet show growth during deformation (syn-tectonic).
cards.w: The crystal rotated while it grew, so the trapped foliation is wound up like a rolled snowball.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Slaty cleavage is the perfect, closely spaced splitting of fine-grained slate, caused by parallel microscopic flakes of mica and chlorite.
cards.w: The flakes are too small to see, but all lie parallel, so the rock splits into thin sheets. It is usually parallel to fold axial planes.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Schistosity is foliation formed by parallel, visible flakes of mica or other platy and prismatic minerals in a medium- to coarse-grained rock (schist).
cards.w: Same cause as slaty cleavage, but higher grade makes the flakes big enough to see with the naked eye.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Gneissosity (gneissose banding) is the alternation of light quartz-feldspar bands and dark mafic bands; eye-shaped feldspars give augen gneiss.
cards.w: At high grade, minerals separate into bands (metamorphic segregation). Augen = eyes in German.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
p: UPSC Geologist Mains 2020 Geology Paper II (descriptive)
cards.a: Hornfelsic structure is fine-grained, tough and non-foliated with a granoblastic mosaic; it is typical of contact metamorphism.
cards.w: Heat without squeezing gives interlocking equal grains. The rock breaks with a splintery, horn-like fracture.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.a: With rising grade a shale changes in the order slate, phyllite, schist, gneiss; phyllite is known by its silky sheen.
cards.w: Mica flakes grow bigger at each step. Sheen in phyllite comes from mica just too fine to see singly.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.a: Limestone changes to marble and quartz sandstone changes to quartzite; both are granoblastic and normally non-foliated.
cards.w: They are made of one mineral that is not platy (calcite or quartz). So the grains only recrystallise and enlarge.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.a: A basalt changes with rising grade to greenschist, then amphibolite, then basic granulite; under very high pressure it becomes blueschist and eclogite.
cards.w: Mafic rocks show facies best because their minerals change clearly. Most facies are named after metabasalts.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.a: The prefix 'para-' means a metamorphic rock derived from a sedimentary parent and 'ortho-' means derived from an igneous parent, as in paragneiss and orthogneiss.
cards.w: Memory hook: ortho = original igneous. Para = from sediments.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.a: Pelitic rocks are metamorphosed clay-rich, alumina-rich sediments (shale, mudstone); psammitic rocks come from sandstones and calcareous rocks from limestones and marls.
cards.w: Pelites are the best grade indicators. Their high alumina lets many index minerals form.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
p: UPSC Geologist Mains 2020 Geology Paper II (descriptive)
cards.a: Barrow's zones in pelitic rocks of the Scottish Highlands, in order of rising grade, are chlorite, biotite, garnet (almandine), staurolite, kyanite and sillimanite.
cards.w: Memory hook: 'Can Big Girls Stay Kind Still'. George Barrow mapped them in the Dalradian rocks.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
p: UPSC Geologist Exam 2018 Geology Paper II (descriptive)
cards.a: An isograd is a line on a map joining points of first appearance of an index mineral; the term was introduced by C. E. Tilley.
cards.w: Iso = equal, grad = grade. An index mineral is one whose first appearance marks a certain grade.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.a: Buchan zones (north-east Scotland) are a low-pressure sequence in pelites: biotite, cordierite, andalusite, sillimanite. Kyanite, the marker of the Barrovian type, does not appear.
cards.w: Andalusite and cordierite are low-pressure minerals. Their presence shows a hotter, shallower crust than in Barrow's area.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.a: In high-grade pelites, muscovite + quartz break down to K-feldspar + sillimanite + water; this marks the second sillimanite (sillimanite-K-feldspar) isograd.
cards.w: Muscovite cannot survive with quartz at very high temperature. It is a dehydration reaction (water is driven off).

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: Grubenmann's depth zones of metamorphism are the epizone (shallow, low temperature), mesozone (intermediate) and katazone (deep, high temperature).
cards.w: Old depth-based scheme, later replaced by the facies concept. Epi = upon, meso = middle, kata = down.

cards.a: Harker called kyanite, staurolite and chloritoid 'stress minerals' and andalusite and cordierite 'anti-stress minerals'.
cards.w: He thought the first group needs directed stress to form. Today this is explained by pressure-temperature stability, but the terms are still asked.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
p: UPSC Geologist Mains 2020 Geology Paper II (descriptive)
cards.a: Eskola (1915) defined a metamorphic facies as all rocks that reached equilibrium under the same pressure-temperature conditions, so that mineral assemblage depends only on bulk composition.
cards.w: Same P-T plus same chemistry gives the same minerals. So the minerals tell us the P-T conditions.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: Eskola first named five facies (greenschist, amphibolite, hornfels, sanidinite, eclogite) and later added granulite, epidote-amphibolite and glaucophane-schist (blueschist) facies.
cards.w: Zeolite and prehnite-pumpellyite facies were added still later by Coombs from New Zealand.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: The zeolite facies is the lowest-grade facies, marked by zeolites such as laumontite and heulandite; the prehnite-pumpellyite facies comes next.
cards.w: It bridges diagenesis and true metamorphism. Zeolites are water-rich and break down with only a little more heat.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: Greenschist facies metabasites carry chlorite + actinolite + albite + epidote; the facies represents low-grade regional metamorphism at roughly 300-500 °C.
cards.w: Chlorite, actinolite and epidote are all green. That gives the rock and the facies their name.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: Amphibolite facies metabasites carry hornblende + plagioclase (more calcic than albite) with or without garnet; it is medium to high grade, roughly 500-700 °C.
cards.w: The change from greenschist is marked by actinolite turning to hornblende and albite turning to oligoclase-andesine. Epidote-amphibolite facies is the step between.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
p: UPSC Geologist Exam 2018 Geology Paper II (descriptive)
cards.a: Granulite facies is marked by orthopyroxene (hypersthene) with clinopyroxene, plagioclase and often garnet; assemblages are nearly anhydrous and form above about 700 °C.
cards.w: Hydrous minerals like hornblende and mica break down. Charnockite and khondalite of South India are granulite-facies rocks.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: Blueschist facies is marked by glaucophane with lawsonite (also jadeite + quartz, aragonite); it forms at high pressure and low temperature.
cards.w: Glaucophane is a blue sodic amphibole. Such cold but deep conditions exist only in subduction zones.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: Eclogite is made of omphacite (sodic clinopyroxene) and pyrope-rich garnet, with no plagioclase; it forms from basic rocks at very high pressure.
cards.w: At high pressure plagioclase is unstable. Its sodium goes into omphacite and its calcium and aluminium into garnet, giving a very dense rock.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: The contact (low-pressure) facies in order of rising temperature are albite-epidote hornfels, hornblende hornfels, pyroxene hornfels and sanidinite.
cards.w: They are the low-pressure cousins of greenschist, amphibolite and granulite facies. They form in contact aureoles.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: Sanidinite facies represents very high temperature at very low pressure, seen in xenoliths in basic magma; typical minerals are sanidine, tridymite and mullite.
cards.w: This is pyrometamorphism (baking by direct contact with lava). Some glass (buchite) may also form.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
p: UPSC Geologist Mains 2020 Geology Paper II (descriptive)
cards.a: Miyashiro's three facies series (baric types) are low-pressure andalusite-sillimanite type, medium-pressure kyanite-sillimanite (Barrovian) type and high-pressure jadeite-glaucophane type.
cards.w: Each series is a different geothermal gradient (rate of heating with depth). Abukuma or Buchan is low P, Barrovian is medium P, Sanbagawa or Franciscan is high P.

cards.a: The Al2SiO5 polymorphs kyanite, andalusite and sillimanite coexist at a triple point of about 500 °C and about 0.38 GPa (3.8 kbar) (Holdaway, 1971).
cards.w: This most-quoted value is a fixed reference point on the P-T grid. Finding all three together pins both pressure and temperature.

cards.a: Among the Al2SiO5 polymorphs, kyanite is the high-pressure form, andalusite the low-pressure low-temperature form, and sillimanite the high-temperature form.
cards.w: Kyanite is the densest, so pressure favours it. Andalusite is the least dense, so it is found in shallow contact aureoles.

cards.a: By Gibbs' phase rule F = C - P + 2, the Al2SiO5 triple point is invariant (F = 0), a boundary between two polymorphs is univariant (F = 1) and a single-polymorph field is divariant (F = 2).
cards.w: C = 1 component here. F is the number of things (P, T) we can change freely without losing a phase.

cards.a: Goldschmidt's mineralogical phase rule states that in a rock at equilibrium the number of mineral phases cannot exceed the number of components (P ≤ C).
cards.w: A rock normally forms over a range of P and T, so F is at least 2. Put F ≥ 2 into F = C - P + 2 and P ≤ C follows.

p: UPSC Geologist Mains 2020 Geology Paper II (descriptive)
cards.a: In Eskola's ACF diagram, A = Al2O3 + Fe2O3 - (Na2O + K2O), C = CaO (corrected for apatite) and F = FeO + MgO + MnO; quartz is assumed in excess.
cards.w: It squeezes rock chemistry into a triangle. It works best for basic and calcareous rocks.

cards.a: In the AKF diagram, A = Al2O3 + Fe2O3 - (Na2O + K2O + CaO), K = K2O and F = FeO + MgO + MnO; it is used for potassium-bearing pelitic rocks.
cards.w: ACF cannot show muscovite, biotite and K-feldspar. AKF gives potassium its own corner.

cards.a: Thompson's AFM diagram (1957) for pelites is projected from muscovite: A = Al2O3 - 3K2O, F = FeO, M = MgO (from K-feldspar at high grade, A = Al2O3 - K2O).
cards.w: ACF and AKF lump FeO and MgO together. AFM separates them, so it shows iron-magnesium differences between garnet, biotite, staurolite and chlorite.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.a: Contact metamorphism of pelitic rocks gives, towards the intrusion, spotted slate and then andalusite-cordierite hornfels; sillimanite and K-feldspar may appear at the inner contact.
cards.w: Spots are early clots of cordierite, andalusite or carbon. Low pressure in aureoles favours andalusite and cordierite.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.a: Chiastolite is a variety of andalusite with dark carbonaceous inclusions arranged in a cross; it is typical of contact-metamorphosed carbon-rich slates.
cards.w: Chi is the Greek letter X. The cross is seen in the square cross-section of the crystal.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.a: Skarn (tactite) is a calc-silicate rock formed by metasomatism where a granitic intrusion meets limestone or dolomite; typical minerals are grossular-andradite garnet, diopside-hedenbergite and wollastonite.
cards.w: Hot fluids from the magma add silica, iron and aluminium to the carbonate rock. Skarns host ores of tungsten (scheelite), copper, iron and tin.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.a: In siliceous limestone at high temperature, calcite + quartz react to wollastonite + CO2 (CaCO3 + SiO2 = CaSiO3 + CO2).
cards.w: This is a decarbonation reaction (CO2 is driven off). If CO2 cannot escape, the reaction needs a higher temperature.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.a: One common order in siliceous dolomite: talc, tremolite, diopside, forsterite, wollastonite, periclase, monticellite. Bowen's list differs: tremolite, forsterite, diopside, periclase, wollastonite, monticellite.
cards.w: Each step drives off more CO2 (decarbonation). Order of forsterite/diopside and of periclase/wollastonite depends on rock and fluid composition and on the textbook. Talc and tremolite always come first. Rare top-end minerals: spurrite, merwinite, larnite.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.a: At high temperature and low pressure, dolomite breaks down to periclase + calcite + CO2 (dedolomitisation); periclase later hydrates to brucite, giving brucite marble.
cards.w: Periclase is MgO. It takes up water easily on cooling, so we usually see brucite, Mg(OH)2, instead.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.a: Regional metamorphism of impure limestone or marl gives calc-silicate rocks with tremolite, diopside, grossular garnet, epidote-zoisite, scapolite and calcic plagioclase.
cards.w: Clay and silica impurities react with calcite and dolomite. A pure limestone would give only marble.

p: UPSC Geologist Exam 2018 Geology Paper II (descriptive)
cards.a: Metasomatism is metamorphism with a marked change in bulk chemical composition, caused by fluids that add and remove material while the rock remains solid.
cards.w: Ordinary metamorphism is nearly isochemical (same chemistry, except loss of water and CO2). Metasomatism is not.

cards.a: Korzhinskii recognised two types of metasomatism: infiltration metasomatism (material carried by flowing fluid) and diffusion metasomatism (material moving through stationary pore fluid).
cards.w: Infiltration works over long distances along fractures. Diffusion works only over centimetres to metres at contacts.

cards.a: Fenitisation is alkali (sodium-potassium) metasomatism of country rocks around carbonatite and alkaline intrusions; the product is fenite, named after Fen in Norway.
cards.w: Alkali-rich fluids leave the carbonatite magma and soak the wall rocks. Fenite is a field guide to hidden carbonatites.

cards.a: Greisenisation changes granite to greisen, a quartz + white mica rock with topaz, tourmaline or fluorite, by fluorine-rich fluids; it is linked with tin and tungsten ores.
cards.w: Feldspar is destroyed by the acid, fluorine-bearing late fluids (pneumatolysis = alteration by hot gases).

cards.a: Other metasomatic changes are serpentinisation of ultramafic rocks, spilitisation (soda added to basalt, giving albite) and rodingite formation (calcium added to rocks within serpentinite).
cards.w: Each is named by what is added: water, sodium or calcium.

cards.a: Granitization is the conversion of pre-existing solid rocks into granite-like rock by metasomatism, without passing through a magma stage.
cards.w: It was proposed to solve the 'room problem' of huge batholiths. Transformists (Read) supported it; magmatists (Bowen) opposed it.

cards.a: H. H. Read's 'granite series' runs from autochthonous granite (formed in place) through parautochthonous to intrusive (allochthonous) granite; his phrase was 'there are granites and granites'.
cards.w: He meant that granites can form in more than one way. Deep in-place granites grade upward into moved magma bodies.

cards.a: The 'basic front' (Doris Reynolds) is a zone enriched in iron, magnesium and calcium, thought to be pushed ahead of an advancing granitization front.
cards.w: If a rock is turned into granite, the unwanted mafic elements must go somewhere. They were said to pile up just outside.

cards.a: Migmatite is a 'mixed rock' made of a dark metamorphic part and a light granitic part; the term was coined by J. J. Sederholm (1907) in Finland.
cards.w: Migma = mixture in Greek. Migmatites form at the top end of metamorphism where rocks begin to melt.

cards.a: In a migmatite, the leucosome is the light quartz-feldspar part and the melanosome is the dark mafic part rich in biotite or hornblende.
cards.w: Leuco = white, melano = black. Leucosome is the melt; melanosome is the residue left after melt was taken out.

cards.a: In a migmatite, the palaeosome is the older, unaltered parent rock and the neosome is the newly formed part (leucosome + melanosome).
cards.w: Palaeo = old, neo = new. The terms are from Mehnert's classification.

cards.a: Migmatite structures include agmatite (breccia-like, angular blocks of palaeosome in neosome), stromatic (layered), ptygmatic (tightly folded veins) and nebulitic (ghost-like, nearly homogeneous).
cards.w: Agma = fragment. Nebula = cloud; in nebulite the old rock is almost fully melted away.

cards.a: Metatexite is a migmatite formed by low-degree partial melting that keeps its older structures; diatexite is formed by extensive melting that destroys them.
cards.w: Meta-texis = partial melting, dia-texis = melting right through.

cards.a: Lit-par-lit injection is the intrusion of thin granitic sheets bed by bed along foliation; arterite has injected leucosome, venite has leucosome segregated from the rock itself.
cards.w: Lit-par-lit = 'bed by bed' in French. Arterite, like arteries, is fed from outside; venite is home-grown.

cards.a: Anatexis is the partial melting of crustal rocks during high-grade metamorphism; palingenesis is the making of new magma by complete remelting of older rocks.
cards.w: The first melt has granite composition (quartz + alkali feldspar). With water present it starts at roughly 650-700 °C.

cards.a: Blueschist-facies rocks form in subduction zones, where a cold slab is carried down quickly so that pressure rises much faster than temperature.
cards.w: The geothermal gradient there is very low, about 10 °C per km or less. So blueschist is a marker of old subduction zones.

cards.a: The facies series of a subducting oceanic slab is zeolite, prehnite-pumpellyite, blueschist, eclogite.
cards.w: This is the high-pressure, low-temperature path. Dense eclogite adds to slab pull (the sinking force on the plate).

cards.a: Continental collision belts show medium-pressure Barrovian metamorphism, magmatic arcs show low-pressure high-temperature metamorphism, and mid-ocean ridges show low-pressure hydrothermal ocean-floor metamorphism.
cards.w: Each plate setting has its own geothermal gradient. So the facies series points to the tectonic setting.

cards.a: Ultra-high-pressure (UHP) metamorphism is shown by coesite or diamond in crustal rocks; in India, coesite-bearing eclogite occurs in the Tso Morari complex, Ladakh.
cards.w: Coesite needs depths of about 90 km or more. It proves Indian continental crust was subducted and then came back up.

p: UPSC Geologist Exam 2018 Geology Paper II (descriptive)
UPSC Geologist Mains 2020 Geology Paper II (descriptive)
cards.a: Paired metamorphic belts, a concept of A. Miyashiro (1961), are two parallel belts of similar age: a high-pressure low-temperature belt and a low-pressure high-temperature belt.
cards.w: They form together at a subduction zone. One belt is the subduction complex, the other is the hot magmatic arc.

cards.a: In a paired belt the high-pressure (blueschist) belt lies on the ocean or trench side and the low-pressure high-temperature belt with granites lies on the arc or continent side.
cards.w: So the pair shows which way the old plate subducted: it dipped from the blueschist belt towards the hot belt.

cards.a: The classic paired belts of south-west Japan are the Sanbagawa belt (high pressure) and the Ryoke belt (low pressure, high temperature), separated by the Median Tectonic Line.
cards.w: Sanbagawa has glaucophane schists; Ryoke has andalusite-sillimanite rocks and granites. Another pair is Franciscan and Sierra Nevada in California.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Fault rocks are grouped as incohesive (fault breccia, gouge), cohesive brittle cataclasite, and cohesive foliated mylonite formed by ductile flow; ultramylonite has over 90% fine matrix.
cards.w: Shallow faults crush rock (brittle). Deeper, hotter shear zones make rock flow (ductile) and give mylonite.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Pseudotachylite is a dark glassy vein rock formed by frictional melting during very fast fault slip (earthquakes) or meteorite impact.
cards.w: It looks like tachylite (basalt glass) but is not volcanic. Hence 'pseudo'.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: Charnockite was named by T. H. Holland after Job Charnock, whose tombstone in St. John's Church, Kolkata, is made of this rock from St. Thomas Mount near Chennai.
cards.w: Job Charnock is regarded as the founder of Calcutta. The type area is St. Thomas Mount - Pallavaram, Tamil Nadu.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: Charnockite is a hypersthene (orthopyroxene)-bearing granite or quartz-feldspar gneiss of the granulite facies, with greasy bluish-grey quartz and feldspar.
cards.w: Orthopyroxene shows very high temperature and dry conditions. The orthopyroxene tonalite of the charnockite series is called enderbite.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: Khondalite is a quartz-garnet-sillimanite-graphite gneiss or schist, a granulite-facies metamorphosed pelitic sediment, named by T. L. Walker after the Khond people of Odisha.
cards.w: Sillimanite and graphite show the parent was an alumina-rich, carbon-bearing clay. It is common in the Eastern Ghats and south Kerala.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: Leptynite is a light-coloured, garnet-bearing quartz-feldspar granulite or gneiss, poor in mafic minerals, found with khondalite and charnockite in the Eastern Ghats and Kerala.
cards.w: Think of it as a pale garnet-quartz-feldspar rock. It lacks the sillimanite and graphite of khondalite.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: Incipient charnockite is patchy, arrested conversion of gneiss to charnockite along fractures and foliation; it is seen at Ponmudi in Kerala and Kabbaldurga in Karnataka.
cards.w: CO2-rich fluids are thought to have lowered water activity, so biotite or hornblende broke down to orthopyroxene. 'Incipient' means just beginning.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: The Kerala Khondalite Belt (Trivandrum Block) lies south of the Achankovil Shear Zone and consists of khondalite, leptynite, garnet-biotite gneiss and charnockite.
cards.w: It is the main granulite-facies metasedimentary belt of south Kerala. Graphite and incipient charnockite occur in it.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: The two great granulite terrains of India are the Southern Granulite Terrain (Tamil Nadu, Kerala, south Karnataka) and the Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt (Odisha, Andhra Pradesh).
cards.w: Both expose deep crust with charnockite and khondalite. Most of Kerala's basement belongs to the Southern Granulite Terrain.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.a: Gondite is a metamorphosed manganese-rich sediment made of spessartine garnet and quartz, named by L. L. Fermor after the Gonds; it occurs in the Sausar Group of Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra.
cards.w: Spessartine is the manganese garnet. Gondite belts host the manganese ores of Balaghat, Nagpur and Bhandara.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.a: Kodurite is a rock of K-feldspar, manganese garnet (spessartine-andradite) and apatite, named by Fermor from Kodur in the Eastern Ghats of Andhra Pradesh.
cards.w: It occurs with khondalite and hosts manganese ore. Remember: gondite = Central India, kodurite = Andhra Pradesh.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: Prograde metamorphism is the series of changes that take place as temperature (and usually pressure) rises; it drives off water and CO2, so higher-grade rocks hold fewer hydrous minerals.
cards.w: Pro = forward. Clay and chlorite hold much water; garnet, sillimanite and pyroxene hold none. Retrograde metamorphism is the return journey.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: H. G. F. Winkler replaced facies names with four temperature-based grades: very low, low, medium and high grade, each bounded by specific mineral reactions.
cards.w: He felt facies boundaries were fuzzy. In his scheme, high grade starts where muscovite breaks down in the presence of quartz.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: Prehnite-pumpellyite facies rocks carry prehnite + pumpellyite + chlorite + albite; this facies and the zeolite facies (together 'sub-greenschist', below about 300 °C) were set up by D. S. Coombs in New Zealand.
cards.w: They fill the gap between diagenesis (changes in buried sediment) and greenschist facies. Coombs worked on buried volcanic sandstones of South Island.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: Blueschist facies conditions are roughly 200-500 °C at pressures above about 0.6 GPa, equal to depths of more than about 20 km.
cards.w: This is very cold for such depth. Textbooks differ a little on the limits, so learn the pattern: cold and deep.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: Eclogite facies needs pressures above about 1.2 GPa (deeper than about 40 km) over a wide range of temperature; eclogite also comes up as xenoliths (carried fragments) in kimberlite pipes.
cards.w: It is the deepest facies. Kimberlite xenoliths prove that eclogite exists in the upper mantle.

cards.a: Quartz changes to coesite at about 2.7 GPa (about 90 km depth); in the facies scheme coesite is stable in the eclogite facies.
cards.w: Coesite in crustal rocks was first found in 1984, at Dora Maira (Western Alps) and in Norway. Diamond-bearing crustal rocks occur at Kokchetav, Kazakhstan.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.a: The first reaction in metamorphosed siliceous dolomite is dolomite + quartz + water = talc + calcite + CO2; tremolite then forms from talc + calcite + quartz.
cards.w: Dolomite gives the magnesium and quartz gives the silica. Calcite is left over at each step, so the rock stays a marble.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.a: Reactions in impure carbonate rocks release H2O and CO2, so their temperatures depend on fluid composition; they are plotted on T-XCO2 diagrams (XCO2 = share of CO2 in the fluid).
cards.w: A water-rich fluid lets a decarbonation reaction run at lower temperature. So wollastonite can form early where water flushes through an aureole.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Maculose structure is the spotted or knotted look of contact-metamorphosed clay rocks (spotted slate), caused by scattered clots or porphyroblasts of cordierite, andalusite, biotite or carbon.
cards.w: Macula = spot in Latin. Spots mark the outer aureole; nearer the contact the rock becomes hornfels.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Tyrrell's five structures of metamorphic rocks are cataclastic, maculose, schistose (including slaty), granulose and gneissose.
cards.w: Granulose means equal-sized grains with no foliation, as in quartzite and marble. It is the same idea as granoblastic texture.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Riecke's principle: under directed stress a mineral dissolves at points of greatest stress and regrows where stress is least, so grains flatten at right angles to the squeezing.
cards.w: This 'pressure solution' helps to make foliation. It needs a thin film of pore fluid to carry the dissolved material.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.a: A corona is a reaction rim of new minerals around an older grain, and a symplectite is a fine worm-like intergrowth of two minerals; kelyphite is a symplectite rim around garnet.
cards.w: They are frozen, unfinished reactions. In granulites they often show that pressure fell while the rock was still hot (decompression).

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.a: Crenulation cleavage forms when an older foliation is bent into tiny folds (crenulations) and a new cleavage develops along their limbs; it proves a second phase of deformation.
cards.w: First foliation = S1, the new one = S2. It is common in phyllites and schists.

cards.a: Lithostatic (confining) pressure rises by about 0.027-0.03 GPa per km in the crust, so 1 GPa (10 kbar) corresponds to roughly 35 km depth.
cards.w: Pressure = density x gravity x depth. With a rock density of 2800 kg/m3, each km adds about 27.5 MPa.

p: UPSC Geologist Mains 2020 Geology Paper II (descriptive)
cards.a: The slope of a reaction curve on a P-T diagram is given by the Clausius-Clapeyron equation, dP/dT = ΔS/ΔV (entropy change divided by volume change).
cards.w: Dehydration reactions have steep curves, so they mark temperature well. Solid-solid reactions with gentle slopes mark pressure well.

cards.a: A petrogenetic grid, an idea of N. L. Bowen (1940), is a P-T diagram of intersecting reaction curves that divides P-T space into fields, each with its own stable mineral assemblages.
cards.w: Find the field that matches the minerals in your rock and you have its P-T conditions. The Al2SiO5 diagram is the simplest grid.

cards.a: At high pressure albite breaks down to jadeite + quartz; this reaction is a pressure marker of the blueschist and eclogite facies.
cards.w: Jadeite is a dense sodium pyroxene. Pressure favours dense minerals, so light albite cannot survive deep in a subduction zone.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: Barrow's chlorite and biotite zones belong to the greenschist facies, while the staurolite, kyanite and sillimanite zones belong to the amphibolite facies; the garnet zone lies at the transition.
cards.w: A zone uses one index mineral in pelites. A facies uses the whole assemblage, so several zones fit inside one facies.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: Epidote-amphibolite facies metabasites carry hornblende + albite + epidote (with or without garnet); the facies is transitional between greenschist and amphibolite facies.
cards.w: The amphibole has already become hornblende, but the plagioclase is still albite with epidote. Hence the mixed name.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: In granulite-facies pelites muscovite is absent and the typical assemblage is garnet + sillimanite + K-feldspar + quartz, with or without cordierite; khondalite is an example.
cards.w: Muscovite has already broken down to K-feldspar + sillimanite. Biotite too is breaking down, to garnet or cordierite.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: Ultra-high-temperature (UHT) metamorphism is granulite-facies metamorphism above 900 °C; sapphirine + quartz is its best-known diagnostic assemblage.
cards.w: It is reported from the Eastern Ghats and the Madurai Block of South India. Spinel + quartz and orthopyroxene + sillimanite + quartz also point to UHT.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: Holland (1900) described the 'charnockite series' as hypersthene-bearing rocks ranging from acid (charnockite proper) through intermediate to basic (norite) and ultrabasic (pyroxenite), and regarded them as igneous.
cards.w: Later work showed that many are metamorphic granulites. Today both igneous and metamorphic charnockites are accepted.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: The East Coast bauxite deposits of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh were formed by lateritic weathering of khondalite.
cards.w: Khondalite is rich in alumina (sillimanite, garnet, feldspar). Tropical weathering washed away the silica and left aluminium behind.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.a: Granulite-facies metamorphism of the Kerala Khondalite Belt is of Pan-African age, about 550 million years (late Neoproterozoic to Cambrian).
cards.w: The same event is seen in Sri Lanka and Madagascar, which lay next to Kerala in Gondwana.

cards.a: Rocks of continental collision belts usually follow a clockwise P-T-t path: pressure peaks first during crustal thickening, temperature peaks later, then both fall during uplift and erosion.
cards.w: Rock conducts heat slowly, so heating lags behind burial. 'Clockwise' assumes pressure is plotted upward on the P-T diagram.

cards.a: Approximate geothermal gradients: high-pressure series about 10 °C/km or less, medium-pressure (Barrovian) series about 20-30 °C/km, low-pressure (Buchan or Abukuma) series above about 40 °C/km.
cards.w: Gradient = temperature rise per km of depth. Cold slab = low gradient; hot arc with rising magma = high gradient. Exact numbers differ between textbooks.

cards.a: In India, blueschists occur in the Indus Suture Zone of Ladakh (Sapi-Shergol area) and in the Nagaland-Manipur ophiolite belt; both mark subduction of Tethyan ocean floor.
cards.w: A suture is the scar where an ocean closed. Blueschist with ophiolite (slices of ocean floor) is its typical mark.

cards.a: Miyashiro recognised three paired belts in Japan: Sangun-Hida, Sanbagawa-Ryoke and Kamuikotan-Hidaka (high-pressure belt named first); Wakatipu-Tasman in New Zealand is another pair.
cards.w: Each pair records a separate period of subduction under the island arc. Sanbagawa-Ryoke is the one exams ask most.

cards.a: Paired belts mark old subduction zones, but the two belts need not have formed side by side; some were brought together later by large strike-slip faults such as Japan's Median Tectonic Line.
cards.w: This is the modern view. The original spacing between trench-side and arc-side belts would have been 100 km or more.

cards.a: Tuttle and Bowen (1958) showed that most granites plot near the minimum-melting composition of the quartz-albite-orthoclase-water system, strong evidence that granites crystallised from melts.
cards.w: A rock made by metasomatism need not have this special composition. The result swung the granite debate towards the magmatists.

cards.a: Field evidence cited for granitization includes gradational contacts, 'ghost stratigraphy' (relict bedding traceable through the granite) and large K-feldspar crystals grown in country rock and xenoliths.
cards.w: An intruding magma should cut and push aside the old layers. Layers passing undisturbed through granite suggested change in place. Today most such granites are explained by melting in place (anatexis).

cards.a: Lindgren's law of equal volumes: metasomatic replacement takes place volume for volume, so the shape and texture of the replaced rock, mineral or fossil can be preserved.
cards.w: The old mineral dissolves and the new one is deposited at the same moment. Pseudomorphs (false forms) and petrified wood show this.

cards.a: Exoskarn replaces the carbonate country rock outside the intrusion; endoskarn replaces the margin of the intrusion itself.
cards.w: Exo = outside, endo = inside. Most skarn ore lies in the exoskarn.

p: UPSC Geologist Mains 2019 Geology Paper II
cards.a: Provenance means the source area of a sediment: its parent rocks, relief and climate, worked out from the composition of the sediment.
cards.w: Grains carry a record of where they came from. Feldspar, rock fragments and heavy minerals point back to the parent rock.

cards.a: Heavy minerals are accessory detrital grains with specific gravity above about 2.9; they are separated from quartz and feldspar by letting them sink in bromoform (specific gravity 2.89).
cards.w: Quartz (2.65) and feldspar float in bromoform, while zircon, garnet, rutile and others sink. The sunk fraction is studied for provenance.

cards.a: The ZTR index is the percentage of zircon + tourmaline + rutile among the transparent (non-opaque) heavy minerals; a high ZTR index means a mineralogically mature sediment.
cards.w: These three are ultra-stable and survive long transport and recycling. Less stable heavy minerals get destroyed, so ZTR rises with maturity.

cards.a: Kyanite, sillimanite, staurolite and garnet as heavy minerals point to a high-grade metamorphic source; augite, hypersthene and chromite point to a basic or ultrabasic igneous source.
cards.w: Each parent rock has its own typical accessory minerals. The heavy mineral suite works like a fingerprint of the source rock.

cards.a: Abundant fresh feldspar in a sandstone (arkose) points to a granite or gneiss source with fast erosion and quick burial, usually under high relief or a dry or cold climate.
cards.w: Feldspar weathers easily to clay. It survives only when chemical weathering is weak or erosion is too fast for it to act.

cards.a: Diagenesis covers all physical, chemical and biological changes in a sediment after deposition and before metamorphism, at low temperature and pressure.
cards.w: It is the stage between loose sediment and metamorphic rock. Compaction, cementation, dissolution and replacement all belong here.

cards.a: Compaction squeezes out pore water and reduces porosity, far more in mud than in sand; compaction plus cementation turns loose sediment into rock (lithification).
cards.w: Clay flakes start with very open, watery packing and collapse under load. Sand grains already touch each other, so they compact little.

cards.a: Common sandstone cements are silica (quartz overgrowths), calcite and iron oxide; a quartz overgrowth grows in optical continuity with its host grain.
cards.w: New silica continues the crystal lattice of the old grain, so both go dark together under crossed polars. A thin dust line often marks the old grain edge.

cards.a: Authigenic minerals grow in place inside the sediment after deposition; examples are glauconite, pyrite, quartz and feldspar overgrowths and many clay minerals.
cards.w: Authigenic means 'born on the spot'. The opposite is detrital (allogenic), meaning carried in from outside.

cards.a: Dolomitisation replaces calcite or aragonite by dolomite, CaMg(CO3)2; mole-for-mole replacement shrinks the solid volume by about 12-13% and can create porosity.
cards.w: Dolomite is denser than calcite, so the same number of moles takes less space. This is why many dolomites are good oil reservoirs.

cards.a: Sanidine, glass shards and clear embayed quartz in a sandstone point to an acid volcanic source; polycrystalline quartz with strong undulose (wavy) extinction points to a metamorphic source.
cards.w: Sanidine is the high-temperature potash feldspar of rhyolites. Strained, many-crystal quartz is made by deformation during metamorphism.

cards.a: Dickinson's QFL triangle (quartz, feldspar, lithic fragments) links sandstone composition to plate-tectonic setting through three provenance types: continental block, magmatic arc and recycled orogen.
cards.w: Cratons supply quartz and feldspar, volcanic arcs supply feldspar and volcanic fragments, and uplifted fold belts supply recycled quartz and sedimentary fragments.

cards.a: With deeper burial, sand grain contacts change from point (tangential) to long, then concavo-convex, then sutured, as compaction and pressure solution increase.
cards.w: Load from above first pushes grains closer, then dissolves them where they touch. Sutured means interlocking like a jigsaw.

cards.a: In carbonate diagenesis the vadose zone lies above the water table, with air and water in the pores, and gives meniscus and pendant (hanging-drop) cements; the water-filled phreatic zone below gives even rim cements.
cards.w: Above the water table, water only clings at grain contacts or hangs under grains, so cement grows only there. Below it, cement can grow all around the grain.

cards.a: Roundness measures how sharp a grain's corners and edges are; it increases with abrasion during transport. Wadell defined it as average corner radius divided by the radius of the largest inscribed circle.
cards.w: Corners get knocked off as grains travel. So roundness tells about transport and reworking, not about the overall shape.

cards.a: Sphericity measures how closely a grain's overall form approaches a sphere; it depends mainly on the original crystal shape and is independent of roundness.
cards.w: A cube with smoothed corners is well rounded but still not a sphere. A long zircon stays long however far it travels.

cards.a: Folk's textural maturity stages: immature (over 5% clay), submature (under 5% clay but poorly sorted), mature (well sorted, grains not rounded), supermature (well sorted and rounded).
cards.w: Energy first removes clay, then sorts the sand, and last of all rounds the grains. Each step needs more reworking than the one before.

cards.a: Mineralogical (compositional) maturity is judged by the ratio of stable grains (quartz, chert) to unstable grains (feldspar, rock fragments); quartz arenite is the most mature sandstone.
cards.w: Weathering and long transport destroy weak minerals. What is left in the end is almost pure quartz.

cards.a: Textural and mineralogical maturity can differ: a wind-blown sand may be well sorted and well rounded (texturally mature) yet still rich in feldspar (mineralogically immature).
cards.w: Wind sorts and rounds grains mechanically, but in a dry climate there is little chemical weathering to destroy feldspar.

cards.t: Framework, matrix and cement of terrigenous sediments
cards.a: A terrigenous rock has three parts: framework grains (sand or gravel that carry the load), matrix (fine detrital clay and silt, under about 30 micrometres in sandstone) and cement (minerals precipitated later in pores).
cards.w: Matrix arrives with the grains during deposition. Cement is chemical and comes afterwards, during diagenesis.

cards.t: Framework, matrix and cement of terrigenous sediments
cards.a: Conglomerate has rounded clasts larger than 2 mm; breccia has angular clasts of the same size, showing very little transport.
cards.w: Rounding needs transport. Angular pieces mean the fragments were deposited close to where they broke off (scree, fault zone, collapse).

cards.t: Framework, matrix and cement of terrigenous sediments
cards.a: Orthoconglomerate is grain-supported with less than 15% matrix; paraconglomerate is matrix-supported with more than 15% matrix, such as tillite and pebbly mudstone.
cards.w: Running water washes fines away and leaves clasts touching. Glaciers and debris flows dump clasts and mud together.

cards.t: Framework, matrix and cement of terrigenous sediments
cards.a: Shale is a fissile mudrock: it splits into thin sheets because its platy clay minerals lie parallel. Mudstone is non-fissile. Mudrocks are the most abundant sedimentary rocks.
cards.w: Compaction rotates clay flakes flat, giving planes of easy splitting. Roughly half of all sedimentary rock is mudrock.

cards.t: Definition, measurement and interpretation of grain size
cards.a: Udden-Wentworth size limits: boulder over 256 mm, cobble 64-256 mm, pebble 4-64 mm, granule 2-4 mm, sand 1/16-2 mm, silt 1/256-1/16 mm, clay under 1/256 mm.
cards.w: It is a geometric scale: each main boundary is a power of 2. Memory hook: 256, 64, 4, 2, 1/16, 1/256.

cards.t: Definition, measurement and interpretation of grain size
cards.a: Krumbein's phi scale: phi = -log2(diameter in mm). So 2 mm = -1 phi, 1 mm = 0 phi, 1/16 mm = 4 phi and 1/256 mm = 8 phi; a bigger phi means a finer grain.
cards.w: The minus sign makes the common sand and mud sizes positive numbers. Phi turns the Wentworth boundaries into whole numbers that are easy to plot.

cards.t: Definition, measurement and interpretation of grain size
cards.a: Sieving is used to measure sand and gravel sizes; pipette and hydrometer methods are used for silt and clay and work on settling speed (Stokes' law).
cards.w: Silt and clay are too fine for sieves. Finer grains settle more slowly, so settling time gives the size.

cards.t: Definition, measurement and interpretation of grain size
cards.a: Stokes' law: the settling velocity of a small sphere is proportional to the square of its diameter and to the density difference between grain and fluid; it holds only for silt- and clay-size particles.
cards.w: Double the diameter and the grain settles four times faster. Larger grains create turbulence, so the law fails for sand and gravel.

cards.t: Definition, measurement and interpretation of grain size
cards.a: Folk and Ward graphic mean: Mz = (phi16 + phi50 + phi84) / 3. The median is simply phi50 read from the cumulative curve.
cards.w: Three percentiles sample the coarse third, middle and fine third of the curve. This gives a better average than the median alone.

cards.t: Definition, measurement and interpretation of grain size
cards.a: Folk and Ward sorting (inclusive graphic standard deviation) = (phi84 - phi16)/4 + (phi95 - phi5)/6.6. Under 0.35 phi is very well sorted; over 1.0 phi is poorly sorted.
cards.w: Sorting is the spread of sizes. A small spread means the current or waves selected one size, as on beaches and dunes.

cards.t: Definition, measurement and interpretation of grain size
cards.a: Skewness measures the asymmetry of the size curve: positive (fine-skewed) means a tail of excess fine grains; negative (coarse-skewed) means a tail of excess coarse grains.
cards.w: On the phi scale fine sizes have larger positive numbers. So a tail towards the fine side is a tail towards positive phi.

cards.t: Definition, measurement and interpretation of grain size
cards.a: Beach sands tend to be negatively skewed, while river and dune sands tend to be positively skewed.
cards.w: Waves wash the fines out of beach sand, leaving a coarse tail. Rivers and wind keep some fine material in suspension load, giving a fine tail.

cards.t: Definition, measurement and interpretation of grain size
