cards.a: Kurtosis measures the peakedness of the size curve: a normal curve has KG = 1.0 (mesokurtic); leptokurtic curves are sharply peaked and platykurtic curves are flat.
cards.w: Hook: 'lepto' means slender (tall peak), 'platy' means flat like a plate. It compares sorting in the centre with sorting in the tails.

cards.t: Definition, measurement and interpretation of grain size
cards.a: Sand classes on the phi scale: very coarse -1 to 0 (2-1 mm), coarse 0 to 1 (1-0.5 mm), medium 1 to 2 (0.5-0.25 mm), fine 2 to 3 (0.25-0.125 mm), very fine 3 to 4 (0.125-0.0625 mm).
cards.w: Each class is half the size of the one before, so each step is exactly one phi unit. Sand spans five phi units, from -1 to 4.

cards.t: Definition, measurement and interpretation of grain size
cards.a: Visher's log-probability plot splits a sand's cumulative size curve into straight segments for three transport populations: traction (rolling), saltation (jumping) and suspension.
cards.w: Each way of moving grains produces its own roughly normal size population, and a normal population plots as a straight line on probability paper.

p: UPSC Geologist Mains 2019 Geology Paper II
cards.a: A bed is a sedimentary layer thicker than 1 cm; a lamina is a layer thinner than 1 cm.
cards.w: The 1 cm limit is only a convention, but it is the one used in all standard textbooks.

cards.a: Cross-bedding has inclined foreset layers that dip downcurrent; planar (tabular) sets form from straight-crested bedforms and trough sets from curved-crested dunes.
cards.w: Sand avalanches down the lee (sheltered) face of a moving ripple or dune. Each avalanche layer is one foreset, so foresets point the way the current went.

cards.a: In cross-bedding the foresets curve gently (tangentially) into the lower surface and are sharply truncated at the top, so the truncated side marks the top of the bed.
cards.w: The next current erodes the upper part of the set. If the cut-off side is found at the bottom, the bed is overturned.

cards.a: Herringbone cross-bedding has foresets dipping in opposite directions in adjacent sets; it records reversing flood and ebb tidal currents.
cards.w: The tide flows in and then out, so dunes migrate both ways. The pattern looks like the bones of a fish.

cards.a: Hummocky cross-stratification (HCS) is formed by storm waves on the shelf, between fair-weather wave base and storm wave base.
cards.w: Only big storm waves reach that depth. After the storm nothing reworks the bed, so the low mounds (hummocks) are preserved.

cards.a: In graded bedding the grain size decreases upward within one bed; it forms from a waning current, typically a turbidity current, and the coarse part marks the bottom.
cards.w: As the flow slows down, the heaviest grains drop first and the finest last.

cards.a: Symmetrical (wave) ripples have sharp crests and rounded troughs, and the crests point to the top; asymmetrical (current) ripples have their steep lee side facing downcurrent.
cards.w: Waves move water to and fro, giving equal slopes. A one-way current pushes sand up the gentle side and drops it down the steep side.

cards.a: Flaser bedding is rippled sand with thin mud streaks; lenticular bedding is mud with isolated sand lenses; wavy bedding lies between. All three are typical of tidal flats.
cards.w: Sand moves when the tide runs and mud settles at slack water. The sand-to-mud ratio decides which of the three forms.

cards.a: Sole marks are casts on the underside of sandstone beds lying on mud: flute casts (current scours with a bulbous upcurrent nose) and tool marks (groove, prod, bounce, skip casts).
cards.w: The current scours or scratches the mud floor, and the next sand fills the hollows. Flute casts are the classic direction markers in turbidites.

cards.a: Groove casts and parting lineation give only the line (trend) of flow; flute casts, cross-bedding, asymmetrical ripples and pebble imbrication give the actual direction (sense) of flow.
cards.w: A straight scratch looks the same from both ends. A structure with different upcurrent and downcurrent ends shows which way the water went.

cards.a: Mud cracks (desiccation cracks) form polygons when wet mud dries in air; the cracks are V-shaped and narrow downward, so they show the top and prove subaerial exposure.
cards.w: Drying starts at the surface, so the crack is widest there. Found in tidal flats, floodplains and dried lake beds.

cards.a: Bouma sequence of a turbidite, base to top: Ta massive graded sand, Tb parallel-laminated sand, Tc ripple cross-laminated or convolute sand, Td laminated silt, Te pelagic mud.
cards.w: It records one turbidity current slowing down: fast dumping first, then traction, then quiet settling. Complete sequences are rare.

cards.a: Top-and-bottom (way-up) criteria include graded bedding, truncated cross-beds, wave-ripple crests, mud cracks, sole marks, load casts and partly filled (geopetal) cavities.
cards.w: Each of these looks different upside down. They let a geologist tell whether folded beds are the right way up or overturned.

p: UPSC Geologist Mains 2019 Geology Paper II
cards.a: A rose diagram is a circular histogram of palaeocurrent readings: unimodal for rivers and deltas, bimodal-bipolar (two peaks 180 degrees apart) for tidal settings.
cards.w: Rivers flow one way down the slope. Tides flow in and out, giving two opposite peaks. Tilted beds must first be rotated back to horizontal.

cards.a: Load casts are rounded bulges of sand that sank into the soft mud below because sand is denser; the mud squeezed up between them forms flame structures. They show the bottom of a bed but no current direction.
cards.w: Heavy wet sand on weak mud is unstable, so it sags. No current is involved, so there is no flow direction to read.

cards.a: Soft-sediment deformation structures (convolute lamination, slump folds, load casts, dish-and-pillar structures) form before lithification in water-saturated sediment and are favoured by rapid sedimentation.
cards.w: Fast deposition traps water in loose sediment. The sediment stays weak and deforms easily when loaded or shaken.

cards.a: In river gravels, flat pebbles stack like roof tiles (imbrication) with their flat faces dipping upstream; this gives the flow direction.
cards.w: A pebble leaning upstream is the most stable position against the current. Memory hook: pebbles bow down toward the source.

cards.a: Ripples and dunes belong to the lower flow regime; plane beds with parting lineation and antidunes belong to the upper flow regime. Antidunes need supercritical flow (Froude number above 1).
cards.w: As flow gets faster the bed changes from ripples to dunes to a flat bed to antidunes. Supercritical means fast, shallow, shooting flow.

cards.a: Stromatolites are laminated structures built when mats of cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) trap and bind sediment; they are common in Precambrian carbonates such as the Vindhyan and Cuddapah.
cards.w: They are the commonest sign of life in the Precambrian. They declined later when grazing animals appeared and ate the mats.

cards.a: Trace fossils (ichnofossils) are tracks, trails, burrows and borings that record animal behaviour; intense burrowing (bioturbation) mixes the sediment and destroys primary lamination.
cards.w: A trace fossil is always found where it was made, so it is a reliable guide to the environment. It cannot be transported like a shell.

cards.a: Seilacher's marine ichnofacies from shore to deep sea: Skolithos (sandy shore, vertical burrows), Cruziana (shelf), Zoophycos (slope), Nereites (deep-sea turbidites, grazing trails).
cards.w: In rough shallow water animals hide in deep vertical tubes. In the quiet deep sea they graze the mud surface in neat horizontal patterns.

p: UPSC Geologist Mains 2019 Geology Paper II
cards.a: A concretion grows by mineral precipitation around a nucleus, often in concentric layers; a nodule is an irregular lump without internal structure, such as chert (flint) nodules in limestone.
cards.w: These are chemical (diagenetic) structures. They form inside the sediment after deposition, not by currents.

cards.a: Stylolites are irregular, tooth-like (sutured) seams formed by pressure solution, most common in limestones and lined by insoluble residue such as clay and iron oxide.
cards.w: Under load the rock dissolves along a surface. The insoluble dirt stays behind as a dark zigzag line.

cards.a: A geode is a hollow, roughly spherical cavity lined with crystals (quartz, calcite) pointing inward; a septarian nodule is a concretion with radiating cracks filled by calcite.
cards.w: A geode grows inward from the wall into an empty space. A concretion grows outward from a centre and is solid.

cards.a: Facies is the sum of the lithological and fossil characters of a sedimentary unit that reflect its environment of deposition; the term was introduced by Gressly in 1838.
cards.w: Facies means 'face' or appearance of the rock. Same age rocks can have different facies in different environments.

cards.a: Walther's law: facies found in a conformable vertical succession were once deposited side by side; the law does not hold across unconformities.
cards.w: When the shoreline shifts, neighbouring environments migrate over each other. So the vertical pile repeats the sideways arrangement.

cards.a: A meandering river point bar gives a fining-upward sequence: channel lag gravel, cross-bedded sand, rippled fine sand, then floodplain mud; it builds by lateral accretion.
cards.w: Flow is strongest on the channel floor and weakest on the bank top. As the bend migrates sideways, these zones stack one above another.

cards.a: A prograding (advancing) delta gives a coarsening-upward sequence: prodelta mud, then delta-front sand, then delta-plain channel sand, mud and coal.
cards.w: As the delta builds seaward, the sandy river mouth moves over the earlier offshore mud. Coarse over fine is the delta signature.

cards.a: Aeolian (wind-blown) dune sandstones show very large-scale, steep cross-bedding, excellent sorting and rounding, frosted quartz grains, and almost no clay or mica.
cards.w: Wind carries only a narrow size range and blows clay and mica flakes away. Grain collisions in air are harsh, so grains get rounded and frosted.

cards.a: Glacial till is unsorted and unstratified; lithified till is tillite, with faceted and striated clasts. The Talchir Boulder Bed at the base of the Gondwana sequence is the Indian example.
cards.w: Ice carries boulders and clay together and drops them without sorting. Scratches (striae) on clasts come from grinding against bedrock.

cards.a: A varve is a pair of laminae laid down in one year in a glacial lake: a light, coarser summer layer and a dark, clay-rich winter layer.
cards.w: Meltwater brings silt in summer. In winter the lake freezes and only fine clay settles. Counting varves gives years.

cards.a: Turbidites are deposited by turbidity currents (dense, sediment-laden underflows), mostly on deep-sea submarine fans; the Bengal Fan is the largest submarine fan in the world.
cards.w: The muddy water is heavier than clear sea water and rushes down the slope. The Ganga-Brahmaputra feeds the Bengal Fan.

cards.a: Pelagic (open ocean) sediments: calcareous ooze above the carbonate compensation depth (CCD, about 4-5 km), siliceous ooze of radiolaria and diatoms, and red clay in the deepest basins.
cards.w: Below the CCD cold, CO2-rich water dissolves calcium carbonate shells. Only clay and silica survive there.

cards.a: A sabkha is a supratidal salt flat on an arid coast; gypsum, anhydrite and halite grow inside its sediment by capillary evaporation of saline groundwater.
cards.w: Heat draws salty groundwater up to the surface where it evaporates. Nodular anhydrite with 'chicken-wire' texture is the typical product.

cards.a: Evaporating seawater precipitates salts in order of increasing solubility: calcium carbonate first, then gypsum, then halite, and last the potassium-magnesium salts (sylvite, carnallite).
cards.w: The least soluble salt comes out first. Hook: Carbonate - Gypsum - Halite - Potash.

cards.a: Chert is a hard rock of microcrystalline quartz; bedded cherts come from siliceous oozes of radiolaria and diatoms, nodular cherts from replacement of limestone. Flint and jasper are varieties.
cards.w: Silica shells dissolve and re-precipitate as tiny quartz crystals. Flint is the dark chert of chalk; jasper is red from iron oxide.

cards.a: Banded iron formations (BIF) are thin alternating bands of iron oxide and chert, almost all Precambrian: Algoma type is small and volcanic-related, Superior type is large and shelf-deposited.
cards.w: They formed when the early oceans held dissolved iron that was precipitated as oxygen appeared. Indian BIFs (BHQ, BHJ) host the main iron ores.

cards.a: Phosphorite is a marine sedimentary rock rich in phosphate minerals (collophane, francolite), formed on shelves below upwelling water; Jhamarkotra near Udaipur has stromatolitic phosphorite in the Aravalli Supergroup.
cards.w: Upwelling brings nutrient-rich deep water to the shelf, and phosphate gets fixed in the sediment. It is the main raw material for phosphate fertiliser.

cards.a: Galloway's delta triangle: river-dominated deltas are bird's-foot shaped (Mississippi), wave-dominated deltas are smooth and arcuate (Nile, Sao Francisco), and tide-dominated deltas have funnel-shaped channels with tidal sand ridges (Ganga-Brahmaputra).
cards.w: The shape of a delta shows which force wins: the river building out, waves smoothing the front, or tides stretching sand bars along the channels.

cards.a: An alluvial fan forms where a stream leaves a mountain front onto a plain; its deposits are poorly sorted conglomerates and debris-flow beds (fanglomerate) that become finer away from the apex.
cards.w: The stream suddenly spreads out and slows down, so it drops its coarsest load first, right at the mountain front.

cards.a: A prograding beach-shoreface gives a coarsening-upward sequence: bioturbated offshore mud, hummocky cross-stratified lower shoreface sand, trough cross-bedded upper shoreface sand, and gently seaward-dipping laminated foreshore (beach) sand on top.
cards.w: Wave energy increases toward the shore, so as the coast builds seaward, higher-energy sands are stacked over lower-energy muds.

cards.a: Dropstones are isolated pebbles or boulders that fell from floating ice into fine laminated mud, bending the laminae below; they are evidence of ice-rafting in glacial lakes or seas.
cards.w: Quiet water cannot carry a boulder into mud. Only melting ice floating above can drop it there.

cards.a: In Usiglio's seawater evaporation experiment, gypsum begins to precipitate when the water is reduced to about 19% of its original volume, and halite when it is reduced to about 10%.
cards.w: Less soluble salts come out first. About four-fifths of the water must go before gypsum forms, and about nine-tenths before common salt forms.

cards.a: In the Dott (Pettijohn) scheme, sandstones with less than 15% matrix are arenites, those with 15-75% matrix are wackes, and rocks with over 75% matrix are mudstones.
cards.w: Matrix content is the first split. After that, the rock is named from its quartz, feldspar and rock fragment proportions.

cards.a: Quartz arenite has more than 95% quartz among its framework grains; it is well sorted and well rounded and forms on stable cratons, beaches and dunes after long reworking.
cards.w: It is the end product of sandstone evolution. Everything weaker than quartz has been destroyed.

cards.a: Arkose is a sandstone with more than 25% feldspar; it is derived from granite or gneiss and is often pink or red.
cards.w: The pink colour comes from potash feldspar and iron oxide. It forms close to uplifted granitic basement, often in rift basins.

cards.a: Greywacke is a dark, hard, poorly sorted sandstone with more than 15% matrix plus feldspar and rock fragments; it is typical of turbidites in orogenic belts.
cards.w: Turbidity currents dump sand and mud together without sorting. Hook: greywacke = 'dirty sandstone'.

cards.a: Folk's sandstone classification plots quartz, feldspar and rock fragments (QFR) after ignoring the matrix; its names include quartzarenite, subarkose, sublitharenite, arkose and litharenite.
cards.w: Folk treats matrix as a texture (maturity) feature, not a composition feature. Dott's scheme instead uses matrix to separate arenite from wacke.

cards.a: In Dott's scheme the sandstone name follows the dominant non-quartz grain: more feldspar than rock fragments gives arkosic (feldspathic) arenite or wacke; more rock fragments than feldspar gives lithic arenite or wacke.
cards.w: First check matrix (under or over 15%) to choose arenite or wacke. Then compare feldspar with rock fragments to choose the prefix.

cards.a: Folk's limestone scheme uses allochems (intraclasts, ooids, fossils, pellets), micrite (lime mud) and sparite (clear calcite cement); names join a prefix intra-, oo-, bio- or pel- to -micrite or -sparite, as in oosparite.
cards.w: Allochems are like sand grains, micrite like clay matrix and sparite like cement. So the idea copies sandstone description.

cards.a: Micrite (calcite mud finer than 4 micrometres) indicates quiet water; sparite cement between grains indicates agitated water that washed the mud away.
cards.w: Mud settles only where water is calm. Where waves winnow the mud, empty pores remain and are later filled by clear spar.

cards.a: Dunham's classification is based on depositional texture: mudstone, wackestone, packstone and grainstone (in order of increasing energy), plus boundstone and crystalline carbonate.
cards.w: It asks two simple questions: is there lime mud, and do the grains touch each other? This makes it easy to use in the field and on cores.

cards.a: Dunham: mudstone is mud-supported with under 10% grains; wackestone is mud-supported with over 10% grains; packstone is grain-supported with mud; grainstone is grain-supported without mud; boundstone is organically bound (reef).
cards.w: Hook in order of less mud: Mud - Wacke - Pack - Grain. Boundstone equals Folk's biolithite.

cards.a: Ooids are spherical coated grains smaller than 2 mm with concentric layers around a nucleus; they form in warm, shallow, agitated sea water. Similar grains larger than 2 mm are pisoids.
cards.w: Rolling by waves lets carbonate coat the grain evenly on all sides. A rock made of ooids is an oolite.

cards.a: Embry and Klovan extended Dunham's scheme: floatstone (matrix-supported) and rudstone (grain-supported) for limestones with over 10% grains larger than 2 mm, and bafflestone, bindstone and framestone for reef boundstones.
cards.w: Dunham had no names for very coarse grains or for different reef-building styles. Rudstone is the coarse cousin of grainstone and packstone.

cards.a: Folk's limestone scheme also has biolithite (reef rock built in place by organisms, equal to Dunham's boundstone) and dismicrite (micrite with patches of sparry calcite).
cards.w: These two types do not fit the allochem-plus-micrite-or-sparite naming, so Folk gave them separate names.

cards.a: India has 26 sedimentary basins covering about 3.36 million sq km (onland plus offshore), as listed by the Directorate General of Hydrocarbons (DGH) after the 2017 resource reassessment.
cards.w: DGH is the technical arm of the Petroleum Ministry. The figure was checked on the Ministry website in 2026.

cards.a: Since 2017 DGH uses three basin categories: Category I (commercial production, 7 basins), Category II (discoveries but no commercial production, 5 basins) and Category III (prospective only, 14 basins). The older scheme had four categories.
cards.w: The category follows the maturity of resources: reserves, contingent resources, or only prospective resources. Older books still show Category I to IV.

cards.a: The seven Category I (producing) basins are Cambay, Mumbai Offshore, Rajasthan, Krishna-Godavari, Cauvery, Assam Shelf and Assam-Arakan Fold Belt.
cards.w: These are the only basins with established commercial oil and gas production in the DGH list (as seen in 2026).

cards.a: Category II basins (DGH three-tier scheme) are Kutch, Saurashtra, Vindhyan, Mahanadi-NEC and Andaman-Nicobar; the Kerala-Konkan-Lakshadweep basin is in Category III.
cards.w: Category II has discoveries that are not yet produced commercially. Kerala-Konkan has no discovery so far. List as on the Ministry website, 2026; it can be revised.

cards.a: The Cambay Basin (Gujarat) is a narrow north-south intracratonic rift graben of Tertiary age floored by Deccan Traps; the Eocene Cambay Shale is its main source rock and Ankleshwar its best-known field.
cards.w: Intracratonic rift = a crack that opened inside the continent. Thick shale in the sinking graben generated the oil.

cards.a: The Mumbai Offshore Basin is a pericratonic rift (passive margin) basin on the western shelf; Bombay High, discovered in 1974, produces mainly from Miocene limestone.
cards.w: Pericratonic = at the edge of the craton. It formed when India rifted from Madagascar and Seychelles. Bombay High is India's largest oil field.

cards.a: Digboi in the Assam-Arakan Basin (Upper Assam) had India's first commercial oil well in 1889; the main reservoirs of Upper Assam are the Miocene Tipam Sandstone and the Oligocene Barail Group.
cards.w: It is the oldest producing petroleum province of India. The basin has a shelf part (Upper Assam) and a fold belt part (Tripura, Cachar).

cards.a: The Krishna-Godavari Basin is a pericratonic rift basin on the east coast with Permian to Recent sediments; its deepwater block KG-D6 had a major gas discovery in 2002.
cards.w: It formed when India separated from Antarctica and Australia. Ravva is its well-known offshore oil field.

cards.a: The Cauvery Basin is a pericratonic rift basin with horst-and-graben structure formed during the Late Jurassic-Early Cretaceous break-up of Gondwana; its Cretaceous rocks near Tiruchirappalli (Uttatur, Trichinopoly, Ariyalur) are richly fossiliferous.
cards.w: Horst = raised block, graben = sunken block. The marine Cretaceous of Tiruchirappalli is a classic of Indian stratigraphy.

cards.a: The Rajasthan Basin has three sub-basins: Barmer-Sanchor (Mangala oil field, discovered 2004), Jaisalmer (gas) and Bikaner-Nagaur (heavy oil in Infracambrian rocks).
cards.w: Barmer is a Tertiary rift like Cambay to its south. Mangala is the largest onland oil find in India in recent decades.

cards.a: The Kutch Basin is an east-west pericratonic rift basin famous for its marine Jurassic sequence (Patcham, Chari, Katrol, Umia) rich in ammonites.
cards.w: The sea entered the rift in Jurassic time. It is the type area for the marine Jurassic of India.

cards.a: Kerala's coastal Tertiary, oldest first: Alleppey beds (subsurface only), Vaikom beds, marine Miocene Quilon limestone, Warkalli Formation (Mio-Pliocene sandstone, clay, lignite). Vaikom is the oldest in the three-fold scheme.
cards.w: These soft sediments rest on Precambrian crystalline rocks and form the main coastal aquifers of Kerala. Warkalli cliff at Varkala is the type area.

cards.a: The Vindhyan Basin is a large intracratonic Proterozoic (Purana) basin of central India with nearly undeformed Semri, Kaimur, Rewa and Bhander groups; Cuddapah, Chhattisgarh, Bhima and Kaladgi are other Purana basins.
cards.w: Purana means 'ancient'. These basins sagged slowly inside the stable shield, so their beds stayed almost flat and unmetamorphosed.

p: UPSC Geologist Mains 2019 Geology Paper II
cards.a: Gondwana basins are intracratonic rift (graben and half-graben) basins along the Damodar, Son-Mahanadi, Pranhita-Godavari and Satpura valleys, filled by Permian to Lower Cretaceous river and lake sediments that hold almost all of India's coal.
cards.w: They follow old weak zones in the shield. The fill starts with the glacial Talchir beds and then the coal-bearing Damuda Group.

p: UPSC Geologist Mains 2019 Geology Paper II
cards.a: Not all Indian basins are rifts: the Himalayan Foreland (Siwalik) and Ganga basins are foreland basins filled with molasse, and the Andaman-Nicobar Basin is a convergent-margin island-arc (forearc) basin.
cards.w: A foreland basin forms where the plate bends down under the weight of a mountain belt. Molasse is the coarse debris shed from the rising mountains.

cards.a: The Kerala-Konkan Basin is a passive-margin (pericratonic rift) basin off the south-west coast; the Vengurla Arch separates it from the Mumbai Offshore Basin to the north. It remains a Category III basin with no commercial discovery (DGH listing, 2024).
cards.w: It formed when India rifted from Madagascar and the Seychelles. Thick Deccan basalt cover makes exploration below it difficult.

p: UPSC Geologist Mains 2019 Geology Paper II
cards.a: Sedimentary basins are grouped by tectonic setting: rift and passive-margin basins (divergent), foreland, forearc and back-arc basins (convergent), pull-apart basins (strike-slip) and intracratonic sag basins.
cards.w: The plate setting controls how a basin sinks, so it also controls its shape and its sediment fill.

cards.a: The Narmada-Son-Tapti zone is regarded as a failed rift; Cambay and Narmada rifts cross in the Gulf of Khambhat, and Kutch, Cambay and Narmada rifts surround the Saurashtra horst.
cards.w: A failed rift started to pull apart but never opened into an ocean. Kutch (Jurassic), Cambay (Early Cretaceous) and Narmada (Late Cretaceous) rifts opened one after another around the Saurashtra block.

cards.a: The Assam-Arakan Fold Belt (Tripura-Cachar-Mizoram) is a gas-rich belt of long anticlines; its main reservoirs are sandstones of the Miocene Surma Group (Bhuban and Bokabil formations).
cards.w: Squeezing between India and Burma folded the Tertiary sediments into tight anticlines, which trap gas at their crests.

cards.t: Origin of water: meteoric, juvenile, magmatic and sea waters
cards.a: Meteoric water is water derived from the atmosphere as rain or snow; almost all usable groundwater is meteoric in origin.
cards.w: It is part of the present-day hydrologic cycle. 'Meteoric' comes from meteorology (weather), not from meteorites.

cards.t: Origin of water: meteoric, juvenile, magmatic and sea waters
cards.a: Connate water is water trapped in the pores of a sedimentary rock at the time of its deposition; it is usually very old and highly saline.
cards.w: 'Connate' means 'born with' the rock. It is often old sea water, so it is also called fossil water.

cards.t: Origin of water: meteoric, juvenile, magmatic and sea waters
cards.a: Juvenile water is new water from magma or the Earth's deep interior that has never before been part of the hydrologic cycle.
cards.w: 'Juvenile' means young or new. It is joining the surface water system for the first time.

cards.t: Origin of water: meteoric, juvenile, magmatic and sea waters
cards.a: Magmatic water is water derived from magma: it is called plutonic water when it separates at great depth and volcanic water when it separates at shallow depth.
cards.w: Pluto = deep underworld, so plutonic = deep. Magmatic water may be juvenile or recycled, so the two words are not exact synonyms.

cards.t: Origin of water: meteoric, juvenile, magmatic and sea waters
cards.a: Metamorphic water is water driven out of rocks during metamorphism, for example when hydrous (water-bearing) minerals break down.
cards.w: Heat and pressure squeeze water out of minerals like clays and micas.

cards.t: Origin of water: meteoric, juvenile, magmatic and sea waters
cards.a: Sea (marine) water occurs in aquifers either by present-day intrusion along coasts or as old sea water trapped in marine sediments.
cards.w: Intrusion is a modern process; trapped sea water is connate. Both make groundwater saline.

cards.a: Oceans hold about 97% of Earth's water; groundwater is only about 0.6% of the total, yet it is the largest store of liquid fresh water.
cards.w: Most fresh water is locked in ice. Rivers and lakes together are far smaller than groundwater.

cards.a: The hydrologic cycle is the endless circulation of water between ocean, atmosphere and land, driven by solar energy and gravity.
cards.w: The Sun lifts water by evaporation; gravity brings it down as rain and moves it as runoff and groundwater.

cards.a: The water balance (hydrologic) equation is: inflow - outflow = change in storage; for a basin, P = R + ET + change in storage.
cards.w: It is simply conservation of mass. P = precipitation, R = runoff, ET = evapotranspiration.

cards.a: The Symons gauge is the standard non-recording rain gauge used in India; its collector is 127 mm in diameter.
cards.w: Non-recording means it only stores rain; a person measures it once a day. 127 mm = 5 inches.

cards.a: Recording rain gauges are of three types: tipping-bucket, weighing-bucket and natural-siphon (float) type; they give rainfall intensity as well as amount.
cards.w: They write a continuous record, so the time pattern of a storm is known.

cards.a: The arithmetic mean method of areal rainfall gives equal weight to all gauges and suits only flat areas with evenly spaced gauges.
cards.w: A simple average ignores gaps between gauges and the effect of hills.

cards.a: In the Thiessen polygon method each rain gauge is weighted by the area of its polygon, drawn using perpendicular bisectors of lines joining adjacent gauges.
cards.w: Every point in the basin is given the rainfall of its nearest gauge. Mean rain = sum(P x A) / sum(A).

cards.a: An isohyet is a line joining points of equal rainfall; the isohyetal method is the most accurate way to find mean areal rainfall, especially in hilly terrain.
cards.w: The person drawing isohyets can use knowledge of hills (orographic effect), which polygons cannot.

cards.a: A hyetograph is a bar chart of rainfall intensity against time; a mass curve is a plot of cumulative rainfall against time.
cards.w: Hyeto = rain. Do not confuse with hydrograph, which plots stream discharge.

cards.a: The double-mass curve is used to test the consistency of a rain gauge record and to correct it.
cards.w: Cumulative rain at one station is plotted against the cumulative average of nearby stations. A break in slope shows a change at the station.

cards.a: Stream flow is made of surface runoff (overland flow), interflow (shallow lateral flow through soil) and base flow (groundwater discharge).
cards.w: Surface runoff and quick interflow form 'direct runoff'. Base flow is the slow, steady part.

cards.a: Infiltration is the entry of water through the soil surface; percolation is the further downward movement of that water toward the water table.
cards.w: Infiltration is the 'gate'; percolation is the journey after the gate.

cards.a: Infiltration capacity is the maximum rate at which a soil can absorb water; Horton's equation shows it falling exponentially with time to a constant value: f = fc + (f0 - fc)e^(-kt).
cards.w: Dry soil drinks fast at first, then slows as pores fill and the surface seals. fc is the final steady rate.

cards.a: Infiltration is measured in the field with a double-ring infiltrometer; the outer ring stops water from the inner ring spreading sideways.
cards.w: With the outer buffer ring flooded, flow under the inner ring is vertical, so the reading is true.

cards.a: The phi-index is the average rainfall intensity above which the volume of rainfall equals the volume of direct runoff.
cards.w: It is a simple average loss rate. Rain above the phi line becomes runoff; rain below it is lost, mostly to infiltration.

cards.a: Evapotranspiration is evaporation from soil and water plus transpiration from plants; potential evapotranspiration (PET) is its value when water supply is unlimited.
cards.w: Actual ET can never exceed PET. The PET idea was introduced by Thornthwaite.

cards.a: A lysimeter measures evapotranspiration directly: it is a tank of soil with plants in which all water inputs and outputs are measured.
cards.w: ET = water added - water drained - change in soil moisture. A phytometer measures transpiration only.

cards.a: The US Class A evaporation pan is about 1.2 m in diameter and 25 cm deep; lake evaporation = pan evaporation x pan coefficient (about 0.7).
cards.w: A small metal pan heats up more than a lake, so it over-reads. The coefficient corrects this.

cards.a: A hydrograph is a graph of stream discharge (or stage) against time; a storm hydrograph has a rising limb, a peak (crest) and a recession (falling) limb.
cards.w: The rising limb reflects the storm; the recession limb reflects water draining out of basin storage.

cards.a: Base flow is the groundwater contribution to a stream; it keeps perennial rivers flowing in dry weather and is separated from the hydrograph to get direct runoff.
cards.w: Direct runoff hydrograph = total hydrograph - base flow.

cards.a: An effluent (gaining) stream receives groundwater because the water table is above stream level; an influent (losing) stream feeds the groundwater.
cards.w: Effluent = groundwater flows out into the stream. Influent = stream water flows into the ground.

cards.a: A unit hydrograph is the direct runoff hydrograph produced by 1 cm of effective rainfall falling uniformly over the basin in a given duration; it was proposed by Sherman (1932).
cards.w: Effective rainfall = rain that becomes direct runoff. The area under a unit hydrograph equals 1 cm depth over the basin.

cards.a: Unit hydrograph theory assumes linear response and time invariance, so ordinates are simply multiplied by the rainfall excess and hydrographs can be added.
cards.w: Linear: double the rain excess, double every ordinate. Time-invariant: the same storm always gives the same hydrograph.

cards.t: Subsurface movement and vertical distribution of groundwater
cards.a: Subsurface water is divided into the zone of aeration (vadose zone) above and the zone of saturation (phreatic zone) below; the water table separates them.
cards.w: In the vadose zone pores hold both air and water. Below the water table all pores are full of water.

cards.t: Subsurface movement and vertical distribution of groundwater
cards.a: The zone of aeration has three parts from top to bottom: soil-water zone, intermediate (vadose) zone and capillary fringe.
cards.w: Roots use the top zone; the capillary fringe sits directly on the water table.

cards.t: Subsurface movement and vertical distribution of groundwater
cards.a: Soil water is of three kinds: hygroscopic water (held tightly on grains), capillary water (held by surface tension) and gravitational water (drains freely).
cards.w: Plants can use only capillary water. Hygroscopic water is held too tightly; gravitational water drains away.

cards.t: Subsurface movement and vertical distribution of groundwater
cards.a: Field capacity is the water left in soil after gravity drainage; wilting point is the moisture at which plants wilt permanently; available water is the difference between them.
cards.w: Above field capacity water drains away. Below wilting point roots cannot pull water out.

cards.t: Subsurface movement and vertical distribution of groundwater
cards.a: The capillary fringe is thicker in fine materials: capillary rise is inversely proportional to pore size, so it is highest in silt and clay and lowest in gravel.
cards.w: Narrow tubes lift water higher. In gravel the rise is a few centimetres; in silt it can exceed a metre.

cards.t: Subsurface movement and vertical distribution of groundwater
cards.a: Pore-water pressure is less than atmospheric in the zone of aeration, equal to atmospheric at the water table and greater than atmospheric below it.
cards.w: Above the water table water is held by suction (tension). This is why water does not flow into a hole dug in the vadose zone.

cards.t: Subsurface movement and vertical distribution of groundwater
cards.a: The water table is the upper surface of the zone of saturation in an unconfined aquifer; it generally follows the land surface as a subdued (gentler) replica.
cards.w: It is high under hills and low under valleys, but with smaller relief than the ground.

cards.t: Subsurface movement and vertical distribution of groundwater
cards.a: The piezometric (potentiometric) surface is the imaginary surface to which water rises in wells tapping a confined aquifer.
cards.w: It shows the pressure head of the confined water. If it lies above ground level, wells flow by themselves.

cards.t: Subsurface movement and vertical distribution of groundwater
cards.a: Groundwater moves from points of higher hydraulic head to lower head, from recharge areas (usually uplands) to discharge areas (valleys, springs, streams, sea).
cards.w: Head = elevation + pressure head. Water follows total head, so it can even move upward in discharge areas.

cards.t: Subsurface movement of groundwater - flow nets
cards.a: A flow net is a set of flow lines and equipotential lines; in a homogeneous isotropic medium they cross at right angles and form curvilinear squares.
cards.w: Equipotential = line of equal head. Water moves along flow lines, straight down the steepest head slope.

cards.t: Subsurface movement of groundwater - flow nets
cards.a: Seepage from a flow net: q = K x H x (nf / nd) per unit width, where nf = number of flow channels and nd = number of equipotential drops.
cards.w: H is the total head loss. More flow channels mean more flow; more head drops mean a gentler gradient.

cards.t: Subsurface movement of groundwater - flow nets
cards.a: On a water table contour map groundwater flows at right angles to the contours toward lower head; closely spaced contours mean a steep gradient or low transmissivity.
cards.w: Contours bending upstream at a river show a gaining (effluent) stream.

cards.a: A spring is a concentrated natural discharge of groundwater at the land surface as flowing water; a seep (seepage area) is a slow, diffuse discharge.
cards.w: Springs appear where the water table or a water-bearing opening meets the ground surface.

cards.a: A depression spring forms where the land surface dips down and cuts the water table.
cards.w: The ground simply falls below the water level, so water flows out. Common in valleys.

cards.a: A contact spring forms where a permeable water-bearing bed overlies a less permeable bed that is exposed at the surface.
cards.w: Water cannot go down through the tight bed, so it moves sideways and comes out along the contact.

cards.a: Artesian (fault) springs release confined water through a fault or the aquifer outcrop; tubular springs issue from solution channels or lava tubes and fracture springs from joints.
cards.w: Todd's gravity spring classes are: depression, contact, artesian, impervious-rock, and tubular or fracture springs.

cards.a: A thermal spring discharges water warmer than the local mean annual air temperature; a geyser is a hot spring that erupts water and steam at intervals.
cards.w: In a geyser, deep water becomes superheated; steam pressure builds and throws the water column out.

cards.a: Meinzer classified springs by discharge into eight magnitudes; a first-magnitude spring discharges more than about 2.83 cubic metres per second (100 cubic feet per second).
cards.w: First magnitude = biggest. Such springs are mostly in limestone (karst) and basalt.

cards.a: The well-known cliff springs at Varkala (Papanasam), Kerala, emerge where permeable Warkalli sandstone and laterite rest on impermeable clay beds.
cards.w: This is a contact spring: water moving down through sandstone is stopped by clay and comes out on the cliff face.

cards.a: An aquifer is a saturated formation that both stores water and transmits it in usable quantities to wells and springs, e.g. sand, gravel, sandstone, cavernous limestone.
cards.w: Aqua = water, ferre = to bear. It needs both porosity and permeability.

cards.a: An aquiclude is a saturated formation that stores water but cannot transmit it at useful rates, e.g. clay.
cards.w: Claudere = to shut. Clay is very porous but its pores are too tiny to let water move.

cards.a: An aquifuge is a formation that neither stores nor transmits water, e.g. massive unfractured granite or compact basalt.
cards.w: Fugere = to drive away. It has no connected pores at all.

cards.a: An aquitard is a poorly permeable formation that transmits water slowly, enough for leakage between aquifers but not enough for wells, e.g. sandy clay.
cards.w: Tardus = slow. It retards flow but does not stop it.

cards.a: An unconfined aquifer has the water table as its upper boundary; it is also called a water-table, phreatic or free aquifer.
cards.w: Its top is open to the atmosphere through the pores above, so the water is at atmospheric pressure at the water table.

cards.a: A confined (artesian or pressure) aquifer is bounded above and below by impermeable beds and holds water under pressure greater than atmospheric; it is recharged mainly where it outcrops.
cards.w: Because of the pressure, water in a well rises above the top of the aquifer.

cards.a: A leaky (semi-confined) aquifer is one whose confining bed is an aquitard, so water leaks into or out of it through that bed.
cards.w: When it is pumped, part of the water comes as vertical leakage through the semi-permeable layer.

cards.a: A perched aquifer is a small saturated body held up above the main water table by a local impermeable lens, such as a clay layer.
cards.w: The clay lens acts like a saucer. Wells in perched water give small, temporary yields.

cards.a: In an artesian well water rises above the top of the confined aquifer; it becomes a flowing artesian well when the piezometric surface is above ground level.
cards.w: The name comes from Artois in France. No pumping is needed in a flowing well.

cards.a: A pumped confined aquifer stays fully saturated and releases water by compression of the aquifer and expansion of water; an unconfined aquifer releases water by gravity drainage of pores.
cards.w: This is why confined storage coefficients are thousands of times smaller than unconfined ones.

cards.t: Concepts of drainage basin and groundwater basin
cards.a: A drainage basin (catchment or watershed) is the land area that drains to a common outlet; its boundary is the topographic divide.
cards.w: All rain falling inside the divide leaves through one river mouth. It is the basic unit of surface hydrology.

cards.t: Concepts of drainage basin and groundwater basin
cards.a: A groundwater basin is a hydrogeologic unit containing one large aquifer or several connected aquifers; its boundary need not coincide with the surface drainage divide.
cards.w: Underground boundaries are set by geology (faults, rock contacts) and by groundwater divides, not only by ridges.

cards.t: Concepts of drainage basin and groundwater basin
cards.a: A groundwater divide is a ridge in the water table from which groundwater flows away in opposite directions; no flow crosses it.
cards.w: It is the underground twin of a watershed ridge, but it can shift when wells are pumped.

cards.t: Concepts of drainage basin and groundwater basin
cards.a: Safe yield of a groundwater basin is the amount of water that can be withdrawn annually without producing an undesired result; withdrawal beyond it is overdraft.
cards.w: Undesired results include falling water levels, sea water intrusion and land subsidence. Removing non-renewable storage is called groundwater mining.

cards.a: Porosity (n) is the volume of voids divided by the total volume of the rock, expressed as a percentage: n = (Vv / V) x 100.
cards.w: It tells how much water a rock can hold, not how much it will yield.

cards.a: Primary porosity forms with the rock (intergranular pores, vesicles); secondary porosity develops later (joints, fractures, faults, solution cavities, weathering).
cards.w: Hard rocks like granite and limestone depend on secondary porosity for their groundwater.

cards.a: Typical porosities: clay 45-55%, sand 30-40%, gravel 25-40%, sandstone 5-30%, fresh granite under 1-2%; clay has the highest porosity but very low permeability.
cards.w: Clay has countless tiny pores that hold water tightly. High porosity does not mean a good aquifer.

cards.a: For equal spheres, cubic packing gives the maximum porosity (about 47.6%) and rhombohedral packing the minimum (about 26%), whatever the grain size.
cards.w: Cubic = grains sit directly on top of each other (loosest). Rhombohedral = grains sit in the hollows (tightest).

cards.a: Porosity of a sediment depends on sorting, packing and grain shape; well-sorted sediments are more porous than poorly sorted ones.
cards.w: In poorly sorted sediment, small grains fill the gaps between big grains.

cards.a: Void ratio (e) is the volume of voids divided by the volume of solids; n = e / (1 + e) and e = n / (1 - n).
cards.w: Porosity compares voids with the whole; void ratio compares voids with solids only. So e is always larger than n.

cards.a: Effective porosity is the share of interconnected pore space through which water can actually flow; pumice and vesicular basalt can have high total but low effective porosity.
cards.w: Isolated bubbles hold water (or air) but are not linked, so they do not help flow.

cards.t: Hydrological properties of rocks - specific yield, specific retention
cards.a: Specific yield (Sy) is the volume of water a saturated rock releases by gravity drainage, as a fraction of the total rock volume.
cards.w: It is the usable part of the stored water. In coarse unconfined aquifers it is close to effective porosity.

cards.t: Hydrological properties of rocks - specific yield, specific retention
cards.a: Specific retention (Sr) is the water held back against gravity as a fraction of total volume; porosity = specific yield + specific retention.
cards.w: Water in the pores either drains (yield) or stays stuck to grains (retention). The two add up to all the pore water.

cards.t: Hydrological properties of rocks - specific yield, specific retention
cards.a: Specific yield is highest in coarse sand and gravel (roughly 20-30%) and very low in clay (a few percent); specific retention increases as grain size decreases.
cards.w: Fine grains have a huge surface area, so more water stays stuck to them.

cards.t: Hydrological properties of rocks - hydraulic conductivity
cards.a: Intrinsic permeability (k) is a property of the rock alone; it has dimensions of area (m2) and is measured in darcy (1 darcy is about 0.987 x 10^-12 m2).
cards.w: It depends on pore size and shape only, so it is the same for water, oil or gas.

cards.t: Hydrological properties of rocks - hydraulic conductivity
cards.a: Hydraulic conductivity (K) depends on both the rock and the fluid: K = k x density x g / viscosity; it has units of velocity (m/day).
cards.w: Warm water is less viscous, so K rises with temperature even though the rock is unchanged.

cards.t: Hydrological properties of rocks - hydraulic conductivity
cards.a: Hydraulic conductivity falls sharply with grain size: gravel (hundreds of m/day) > sand (about 1-50 m/day) > silt > clay (far below 0.001 m/day).
cards.w: Roughly, K is proportional to the square of grain diameter (Hazen: K = C x d10 squared).

cards.t: Hydrological properties of rocks - hydraulic conductivity
cards.a: An aquifer is isotropic if K at a point is the same in all directions and homogeneous if K is the same at every point.
cards.w: Isotropy is about direction; homogeneity is about place. Layered sediments are usually anisotropic, with horizontal K greater than vertical K.

cards.t: Hydrological properties of rocks - hydraulic conductivity
cards.a: For layered beds, equivalent K for flow parallel to layers is the thickness-weighted arithmetic mean; for flow across layers it is the harmonic mean, which is always smaller.
cards.w: Along the layers the best layer carries most flow. Across the layers the tightest layer controls the flow.

cards.a: Transmissivity (T) is hydraulic conductivity multiplied by saturated thickness: T = K x b; its unit is m2/day.
cards.w: It is the flow through a unit width of the whole aquifer thickness under unit gradient. The term was introduced by Theis.

cards.t: Hydrological properties of rocks - storage coefficient
cards.a: Storage coefficient (storativity, S) is the volume of water an aquifer releases per unit surface area per unit decline in head; it is dimensionless.
cards.w: Volume released = S x area x drop in head. Volume / (area x length) has no units.

cards.t: Hydrological properties of rocks - storage coefficient
cards.a: Storativity of confined aquifers is very small, about 0.00005 to 0.005; in unconfined aquifers it equals specific yield, about 0.01 to 0.30.
cards.w: Confined water comes only from squeezing; unconfined water comes from actually draining the pores.

cards.t: Hydrological properties of rocks - storage coefficient
cards.a: Specific storage (Ss) is the water released per unit volume of aquifer per unit decline in head; its unit is 1/m and S = Ss x b.
cards.w: Ss = density x g x (aquifer compressibility + porosity x water compressibility). Multiply by thickness b to get storativity.

cards.t: Hydrological properties of rocks - storage coefficient
cards.a: Hydraulic diffusivity is transmissivity divided by storativity (T/S = K/Ss); its unit is m2/day.
cards.w: It tells how fast a change in head spreads through the aquifer. Confined aquifers (small S) respond very fast.

cards.a: Water level fluctuations are grouped as secular (over many years), seasonal (monsoon recharge and summer decline) and short-term (daily or shorter); a plot of well water level against time is a well hydrograph.
cards.w: Secular trends show long-term over-use or climate change. Seasonal change shows yearly recharge.

cards.a: In most of India the water table is deepest just before the monsoon (April-May) and shallowest after it; CGWB measures levels four times a year: January, pre-monsoon, August and November.
cards.w: Monsoon rain recharges the aquifer; summer pumping and natural drainage lower it again.

cards.a: A shallow water table can show a daily cycle caused by evapotranspiration: it falls during the day and recovers at night.
cards.w: Phreatophytes (plants with roots reaching the water table) draw water in daylight. White's method uses this cycle to estimate ET.

cards.a: In wells tapping confined aquifers, water level falls when atmospheric pressure rises; barometric efficiency = change in water level / change in atmospheric pressure head.
cards.w: Air pushes directly on the water in the well, but the aquifer skeleton carries part of the load. Unconfined aquifers show almost no response.

cards.a: Tidal efficiency is the change in piezometric level divided by the change in tide level; in a confined aquifer, barometric efficiency + tidal efficiency = 1.
cards.w: A rising tide loads the aquifer and raises the well level (direct relation). Barometric response is inverse.

cards.a: Earthquakes, passing trains and other external loads cause sudden short-lived water level changes in wells tapping confined aquifers.
cards.w: The load squeezes the elastic aquifer and pushes pressure up for a moment. Earthquake-caused changes are called hydroseisms.

cards.a: Water table fluctuation method: recharge = specific yield x rise in water table x area.
cards.w: The rise fills drained pores, and specific yield is the fraction of rock volume those pores make up.

cards.a: About two-thirds of India is underlain by hard rocks (crystalline rocks, basalt and consolidated sediments), where groundwater occurs in the weathered zone and in fractures.
cards.w: These rocks have almost no primary porosity, so yields are low and vary a lot from place to place.

cards.a: The Indus-Ganga-Brahmaputra alluvium holds India's most productive aquifers: thick sand and gravel beds forming multiple unconfined and confined aquifers tapped by tube wells.
cards.w: Loose river sediments have high primary porosity and permeability, and recharge is large.

cards.a: In Deccan Trap basalts groundwater occurs in weathered, vesicular and jointed parts of flows and in intertrappean beds; massive flow cores and red bole act as barriers.
cards.w: Stacked lava flows give a layered system: each flow top can be a separate small aquifer.

cards.a: Taylor (1959) divided India into eight groundwater provinces: Precambrian crystalline, Precambrian sedimentary, Gondwana sedimentary, Deccan trap, Cenozoic sedimentary, Cenozoic fault basin, Ganga-Brahmaputra alluvial and Himalayan highland.
cards.w: The grouping follows rock type and age, because these control how water is stored. Kerala falls mainly in the Precambrian crystalline and Cenozoic sedimentary provinces.

cards.a: The Cenozoic fault basin province of India covers the alluvium-filled rift valleys of the Narmada, Tapti and Purna rivers.
cards.w: These are down-faulted troughs filled with thick, water-bearing alluvium inside hard-rock country.

cards.a: At the Himalayan foothills the Bhabar is a coarse boulder-gravel belt with a deep water table; the Terai next to it has fine sediments, a spring line and flowing artesian wells.
cards.w: Streams sink into the porous Bhabar and the water comes back up in the Terai under pressure.

cards.a: Most of Kerala is underlain by Archaean crystalline rocks (charnockite, khondalite, gneiss); sedimentary formations are limited to a narrow coastal belt.
cards.w: About 88% of the state is hard rock and about 12% is coastal sediment (CGWB). So groundwater mostly sits in the weathered layer and fractures.

cards.a: Kerala has four main aquifer systems: weathered and fractured crystalline rocks, laterite, Tertiary sedimentary formations and coastal alluvium.
cards.w: Going from the hills to the sea: crystallines (highland), laterite (midland), Tertiaries and alluvium (coast).

cards.a: The Tertiary formations of the Kerala coast, from oldest to youngest, are the Alleppey, Vaikom, Quilon and Warkalli beds.
cards.w: Memory hook: A-V-Q-W, in alphabetical order from bottom to top.

cards.a: Among Kerala's Tertiary aquifers, the Warkalli aquifer is the most extensively developed, while the Vaikom aquifer is regarded as the most potential.
cards.w: Warkalli sands are shallower and easier to tap. Vaikom beds are thick, coarse sands and gravels at greater depth.

cards.a: Warkalli beds are sandstones and clays with lignite seams; Quilon beds are mainly fossiliferous limestone and clay and are a poor aquifer.
cards.w: Sand layers give water; limestone-clay layers of the Quilon beds mostly act as confining layers.

cards.a: Laterite, which caps the midlands of Kerala, is a highly porous phreatic (water-table) aquifer tapped by open dug wells; it recharges quickly but also drains quickly.
cards.w: Its many cavities let rain in fast, but water also escapes fast to valleys, so many laterite wells go dry in summer.

cards.a: In Kerala's crystalline rocks, dug wells tap phreatic water in the weathered zone, while bore wells tap semi-confined to confined water in deeper fractures.
cards.w: Fractures show up as lineaments on satellite images, so lineaments are the usual targets for bore well siting.

cards.a: Coastal alluvium (beach and river sands) forms a potential shallow phreatic aquifer along the Kerala coast, tapped by dug wells and filter-point wells.
cards.w: Loose sand has good porosity and permeability. The risk here is salinity, since the sea and backwaters are close.

cards.a: Kerala gets about 3000 mm of rain a year, but steep slopes and 44 short rivers (41 west-flowing, 3 east-flowing) drain it quickly, so summer water scarcity is common.
cards.w: High rainfall does not mean high recharge. Much water runs off to the sea within days.

cards.a: Kerala's three physiographic zones are lowland (below 7.5 m above sea level), midland (7.5 to 75 m) and highland (above 75 m).
cards.w: Each zone has its typical aquifer: alluvium and Tertiaries in the lowland, laterite in the midland, crystallines in the highland.

cards.a: Kerala PSC key: among Kerala's crystalline rocks, charnockite is taken as the better aquifer; in reality yield depends on fractures and weathering, not rock type.
cards.w: This was the keyed answer in a Kerala PSC paper. Yield really depends on how fractured and weathered the rock is at the site.

cards.a: The Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) was formed in 1970 by renaming the Exploratory Tubewells Organisation (1954); its headquarters is at Faridabad, under the Ministry of Jal Shakti.
cards.w: It is the national agency for groundwater surveys, monitoring and assessment. Its Kerala Region office is in Thiruvananthapuram.

cards.a: The Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA) was constituted in 1997 under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 to regulate and control groundwater development.
cards.w: CGWB studies groundwater; CGWA regulates it (for example, permissions for extraction).

cards.a: In Kerala, groundwater is managed by the State Ground Water Department, and regulated under the Kerala Ground Water (Control and Regulation) Act, 2002 through the State Ground Water Authority.
cards.w: The Act (Act 19 of 2002) allows areas to be notified and wells to be permitted and registered.

cards.a: India's groundwater resources are estimated by the Groundwater Estimation Committee (GEC) methodology: first GEC-1984, revised as GEC-1997, and now GEC-2015.
cards.w: CGWB and the State groundwater departments do the assessment jointly. It has been done every year since 2022.

cards.a: Stage of groundwater extraction (%) = (annual groundwater extraction / annual extractable groundwater resource) x 100.
cards.w: It shows what share of the yearly usable recharge is being pumped out. Above 100% means pumping exceeds recharge.

cards.a: GEC-2015 categories by stage of extraction: safe up to 70%, semi-critical above 70% to 90%, critical above 90% to 100%, over-exploited above 100%.
cards.w: Memory hook: 70-90-100. Units with poor quality water are separately tagged as saline.

cards.a: In GEC-2015, annual extractable groundwater resource = total annual recharge - natural discharges; recharge is estimated by the water table fluctuation and rainfall infiltration factor methods.
cards.w: Some recharge must be left to feed streams and springs. The fluctuation method is used for the monsoon season.

cards.a: GEC-2015 recommends aquifer-wise assessment of both dynamic (annually replenished) and in-storage (static) groundwater; the unit is the watershed in hard-rock areas and the block/taluk in alluvial areas.
cards.w: Dynamic resource = the yearly recharge in the fluctuation zone. In-storage resource = water below that zone.

cards.a: National assessment 2025: annual recharge 448.52 BCM, extraction 247.22 BCM, stage of extraction 60.63%; of 6762 units, 730 (10.8%) are over-exploited and 4946 (73.1%) are safe.
cards.w: Annual extractable resource in 2025 is 407.75 BCM. Other units: 201 critical, 758 semi-critical and 127 saline. BCM = billion cubic metres.

cards.a: Kerala assessment 2024: of 152 blocks, 120 are safe, 29 semi-critical and 3 critical (Chittur and Malampuzha in Palakkad, and Kasaragod); none is over-exploited; stage of extraction is 53.78%.
cards.w: Palakkad lies in the rain-shadow Palghat Gap with heavy irrigation pumping. Kasaragod has a long record of over-use for arecanut and coconut gardens.

cards.a: Artificial recharge is the planned addition of surface water to an aquifer; methods are grouped as direct surface (spreading), direct subsurface (wells, shafts, pits) and indirect (induced recharge).
cards.w: It speeds up natural infiltration, to store surplus monsoon runoff underground.

cards.a: Spreading methods (basins, ditch-and-furrow, flooding, percolation tanks, check dams) suit unconfined aquifers with permeable soil; injection (recharge) wells are needed for confined aquifers.
cards.w: Spreading works only if water can soak straight down. A clay cover blocks it, so water must be put in through a well.

cards.a: The percolation tank, a surface pond built on permeable ground across a stream, is the most common artificial recharge structure in the hard-rock areas of India.
cards.w: It holds monsoon runoff long enough for it to seep down into weathered and fractured rock.

cards.a: Induced recharge means pumping wells near a river or lake so that the lowered water table draws surface water into the aquifer.
cards.w: The river bed acts as a natural filter. Collector wells and infiltration galleries on river banks use this idea.

cards.a: A subsurface dyke (underground dam) is an impermeable wall built below ground across a narrow valley to stop subsurface flow and store groundwater upstream.
cards.w: Nothing is flooded and nothing evaporates. It suits the narrow valleys of Kerala's midlands.

cards.a: Clogging by silt, air bubbles, bacteria and chemical precipitates is the main problem of recharge wells, so the recharge water must be clear and silt-free.
cards.w: Fine particles block the pores around the well screen and cut the intake rate.

cards.a: Mazhapolima is a programme of Thrissur district, Kerala, that recharges open dug wells with rooftop rainwater.
cards.w: Roof water is filtered and piped into the home well. It raises water levels and improves quality in summer.

cards.a: In straight-line base flow separation, direct runoff is taken to end N days after the peak, where N = 0.83 x A^0.2 and A is the drainage area in km2.
cards.w: Bigger basins keep draining storm water for longer. Base flow is cut off the hydrograph so that only storm (direct) runoff is left.

cards.a: Time of concentration is the time water takes to travel from the farthest point of a basin to its outlet; basin lag is the time from the centre of effective rainfall to the hydrograph peak.
cards.w: Both measure how fast a basin responds to rain. Small, steep basins have short lag and sharp flood peaks.

cards.a: The recession limb of a hydrograph follows Qt = Q0 x K^t, where K is the recession constant (less than 1); its shape depends on basin storage, not on the storm.
cards.w: After rain stops the stream is fed only by water draining from storage, so discharge decays like a slowly emptying tank.

cards.a: A perennial stream flows all year, an intermittent stream flows only in the wet season when the water table is high, and an ephemeral stream flows only just after rain.
cards.w: Perennial streams are fed by base flow. Ephemeral streams always lie above the water table, so they lose water to the ground (influent).

cards.a: Potential evapotranspiration is estimated by the Thornthwaite method (temperature based), the Blaney-Criddle method (temperature and daylight hours) and the Penman method (energy balance plus aerodynamic terms).
cards.w: Penman needs the most data (radiation, wind, humidity) but has the strongest physical basis. The other two are simple empirical formulas.

cards.a: Residence time of water in a reservoir = volume stored / rate of flow through it; it is about 9-10 days for the atmosphere but weeks to thousands of years for groundwater.
cards.w: Groundwater is a large store with slow flow, so water stays long. This is why polluted aquifers take so long to clean up.

cards.a: Bryan: gravity springs (depression, contact, artesian, impervious-rock, tubular or fracture springs) and non-gravitational springs (volcanic and fissure springs, usually thermal).
cards.w: Gravity springs are driven by ordinary hydraulic head. Volcanic and fissure springs bring up deep, heated water.

cards.a: Kerala assessment 2024 (CGWB): total annual groundwater recharge 5.67 BCM, annual extractable resource 5.13 BCM and annual extraction 2.76 BCM.
cards.w: Extraction is a little over half of the usable resource, which gives the stage of extraction of 53.78%. BCM = billion cubic metres.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
cards.a: Hydraulic head (h) is the sum of elevation head (z) and pressure head (p / density x g); the velocity head of groundwater is so small that it is ignored.
cards.w: Groundwater moves very slowly, so its energy of motion is negligible. Head is simply the height to which water rises in a piezometer (a small open pipe).

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Hydraulic head at a well = elevation of the measuring point minus the depth to water measured from that point.
cards.w: Depth to water alone cannot be compared between wells on different ground levels. Subtracting it from the surveyed elevation puts all wells on one datum (mean sea level).

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
cards.a: Hydraulic gradient (i) is the head loss per unit length of flow path, i = dh/dl; it is a dimensionless number.
cards.w: It is metres of head lost divided by metres travelled, so the units cancel. It is the 'slope' that drives groundwater.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Water levels in at least three wells not in a straight line are needed to find the direction of groundwater flow and the hydraulic gradient (three-point problem).
cards.w: Three points fix a plane, just as in finding strike and dip of a bed. Flow is down the 'dip' of the water table plane.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Steady groundwater flow in a homogeneous, isotropic aquifer obeys the Laplace equation: the sum of the second derivatives of head in x, y and z is zero.
cards.w: It comes from joining Darcy's law with the law of conservation of mass (continuity). Flow nets are graphical solutions of this equation.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Unsteady (transient) flow in a confined aquifer obeys the diffusion equation: Laplacian of h = (S/T) x dh/dt.
cards.w: When head changes with time, water is taken from or added to storage, so storativity S enters. With dh/dt = 0 it reduces to the Laplace equation.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: The Dupuit assumptions for unconfined flow are: flow lines are horizontal (equipotentials vertical), and the hydraulic gradient equals the slope of the water table and is constant with depth.
cards.w: They turn a hard two-dimensional free-surface problem into a simple one-dimensional one. They work well where the water table slope is gentle.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Under Dupuit assumptions, unconfined flow per unit width between two water bodies is q = K(h1^2 - h2^2) / 2L, and the water table is a parabola (Dupuit parabola).
cards.w: Saturated thickness itself falls along the flow path, so head appears as a square. This is why unconfined well equations also use h squared.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Dupuit theory fails close to a pumping well or a steep outflow face, where flow has strong vertical components and a seepage face forms above the water level in the well.
cards.w: Near the well the water table is steep, so the 'horizontal flow' assumption breaks. The real water table is higher than the Dupuit curve there.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Flow lines bend (refract) when they cross a boundary between layers of different hydraulic conductivity, following the tangent law: K1/K2 = tan(a1)/tan(a2), angles measured from the normal.
cards.w: It is like light bending between air and glass, but with tangents instead of sines. Flow lines turn nearly parallel to the boundary inside the more permeable layer.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: In an anisotropic aquifer, flow lines do not cross equipotential lines at right angles; in layered sediments horizontal K is normally greater than vertical K.
cards.w: Flat grains and thin clay layers make it easier for water to move along beds than across them. Flow is deflected toward the easy direction.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Toth (1963) showed that a groundwater basin contains three nested flow systems: local, intermediate and regional.
cards.w: Local systems run from a hill to the next valley; regional systems run from the main divide to the basin outlet. Deeper, longer paths carry older, more mineralised water.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Hubbert (1940) defined fluid potential as energy per unit mass, potential = g x h; groundwater always flows from higher to lower potential (head), not necessarily from higher to lower pressure.
cards.w: In a recharge area water moves downward toward higher pressure but lower head. Head, not pressure, is the true driving force.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: A piezometer is a small-diameter pipe open only over a short length at its bottom; it measures hydraulic head at that one point in the aquifer.
cards.w: A long-screened well averages head over its whole screen. A nest of piezometers at different depths shows whether flow is upward or downward.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2016 Hydrogeology
cards.a: Darcy's law (Henry Darcy, 1856, Dijon, France): discharge through a porous medium is Q = K i A, proportional to hydraulic gradient and cross-sectional area.
cards.w: Darcy found it by passing water through vertical sand filters for the Dijon water supply. K is the hydraulic conductivity of the sand.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: In the differential form Q = -K A (dh/dl), the negative sign shows that water flows in the direction of decreasing head.
cards.w: dh/dl is negative along the flow path because head drops. The minus sign makes the discharge come out positive.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
cards.a: Darcy velocity (specific discharge) is v = Q/A = K i; it is an apparent velocity because it assumes flow through the whole cross-section, grains included.
cards.w: Water really moves only through the pores. So Darcy velocity is a flux (volume per area per time), not the speed of a water particle.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Seepage (average linear, actual) velocity = Darcy velocity / effective porosity = K i / ne; it is always greater than the Darcy velocity.
cards.w: The same discharge is squeezed through the pore area only, which is smaller than the total area. Use it for travel time of water or a pollutant.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Darcy's law is valid only for laminar flow: Reynolds number below 1, with no serious departure up to about 10.
cards.w: In laminar flow, head loss is proportional to velocity. In turbulent flow, head loss rises roughly with velocity squared, so the straight-line law fails.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Reynolds number for groundwater flow is Re = density x v x d / viscosity, where v is Darcy velocity and d is a representative grain size, usually d10.
cards.w: It compares inertial forces with viscous forces. d10 (effective size) is the size finer than which 10% of the sample lies.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Darcy's law may not hold in large open fractures, karst solution channels, coarse gravel and right next to high-discharge wells, where flow becomes turbulent.
cards.w: Wide openings and high velocity push the Reynolds number above the laminar limit. Most natural groundwater flow, however, is laminar.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: A constant-head permeameter, K = QL/(Ah), suits coarse, permeable samples; a falling-head permeameter, K = (aL/At) ln(h0/h1), suits fine, low-permeability samples.
cards.w: Sand passes enough water to measure discharge directly. Silt and clay pass so little that it is easier to time the fall of water in a thin standpipe.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Hazen's formula estimates hydraulic conductivity of clean sand from grain size: K = C x (d10)^2, with K in cm/s, d10 in cm and C about 100.
cards.w: The finest 10% of grains fill the gaps between bigger ones, so they control how easily water passes. It is only a rough estimate.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Groundwater flow through an aquifer section is found from Darcy's law as Q = T i W, where T is transmissivity, i the hydraulic gradient and W the width of the section.
cards.w: Since T = K x b, the area term (b x W) is already built in. This is how underflow across a boundary is estimated from a water table map.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Groundwater velocity in the field can be measured directly with tracers (dyes such as fluorescein, salts, or isotopes) injected in one well and detected in another.
cards.w: Tracer travel time gives the actual seepage velocity, which can be compared with the value from Darcy's law. Good tracers do not react with the rock.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2016 Hydrogeology
cards.a: Pumping a well forms a cone of depression in the water table or piezometric surface; drawdown is the fall in water level, and the outer limit of the cone is the radius of influence.
cards.w: Water must flow toward the well, so head must slope toward it from all sides. Drawdown is greatest at the well and zero at the edge of the cone.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.a: Low transmissivity gives a deep, steep, narrow cone of depression; high transmissivity gives a shallow, flat, wide cone.
cards.w: A poor aquifer needs a steep gradient to deliver the same discharge. Cones in confined aquifers also spread much faster because storativity is very small.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.a: Thiem equation (1906) for steady radial flow to a well in a confined aquifer: T = Q ln(r2/r1) / [2 pi (s1 - s2)], using drawdowns in two observation wells.
cards.w: It is Darcy's law applied to cylindrical surfaces around the well. It needs equilibrium (steady state) and gives T but not the storage coefficient.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.a: For steady flow to a well in an unconfined aquifer (Dupuit-Thiem): Q = pi K (h2^2 - h1^2) / ln(r2/r1), where h is saturated thickness at distance r.
cards.w: The saturated thickness shrinks toward the well, so head enters as a square. The confined form uses (h2 - h1) and 2 pi T instead.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.a: Theis (1935) non-equilibrium equation for unsteady flow to a well in a confined aquifer: s = (Q / 4 pi T) W(u), where u = r^2 S / 4Tt and W(u) is the well function.
cards.w: Theis was the first to bring in time and storage, using the analogy of heat flow to a line sink. It lets T and S be found without waiting for steady state.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.a: Theis assumptions: aquifer confined, homogeneous, isotropic, uniform thickness, infinite extent; well fully penetrating, very small diameter, constant discharge; water released from storage instantly with decline in head.
cards.w: Real aquifers break some of these rules. Departures of field data from the Theis curve reveal leakage, boundaries or delayed yield.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.a: In the Theis type-curve method, field data (drawdown versus time) on log-log paper are overlaid on the type curve W(u) versus 1/u, and a match point gives T and S.
cards.w: Both plots have the same shape because s is proportional to W(u) and t to 1/u. The shift between the two sets of axes holds the unknown T and S.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
cards.a: Cooper-Jacob (1946) straight-line method: for small u (below 0.01), drawdown plots as a straight line against log time, and T = 2.303 Q / (4 pi ds), where ds is drawdown per log cycle.
cards.w: For long times or small distances the later terms of the Theis series can be dropped. No curve matching is needed, only the slope of a line.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.a: In the Cooper-Jacob time-drawdown method, storativity is S = 2.25 T t0 / r^2, where t0 is the time at which the straight line cuts the zero-drawdown axis.
cards.w: Slope gives T; the intercept gives S. Because r is needed, S can only be found from an observation well, not from the pumped well itself.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.a: In the Jacob distance-drawdown method (drawdown versus log distance at one time), T = 2.303 Q / (2 pi ds); the line cuts zero drawdown at r0, the radius of influence.
cards.w: Drawdown changes with log r twice as fast as with log t, so the constant is 2 pi instead of 4 pi. It needs at least three observation wells.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.a: Theis recovery method: after the pump stops, residual drawdown s' is plotted against log(t/t'); T = 2.303 Q / (4 pi ds'). It gives T but not a reliable S.
cards.w: Recovery is treated as an imaginary recharge well switched on at the pumped well. Recovering water levels are smooth, free of pump-rate variations, so the pumped well itself can be used.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.a: Pumping-test data from leaky (semi-confined) aquifers are analysed with the Hantush-Jacob (1955) method, using Walton's family of type curves for different r/B values.
cards.w: Leakage through the aquitard feeds the aquifer, so drawdown falls below the Theis curve and finally becomes steady. B is the leakage factor.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.a: Unconfined aquifers show delayed yield: the time-drawdown curve is S-shaped with three segments, analysed by the Boulton (1963) and Neuman (1972) methods.
cards.w: Early water comes from elastic storage like a confined aquifer; then slow gravity drainage of pores flattens the curve; later it follows a Theis curve with specific yield.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.a: A partially penetrating well has more drawdown than a fully penetrating well at the same discharge; the effect becomes negligible beyond a distance of about 1.5 to 2 times the aquifer thickness.
cards.w: Flow lines must converge vertically to reach the short screen, giving extra head loss. Far from the well, flow is horizontal again.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
