p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
cards.a: Well interference: where cones of depression of nearby wells overlap, the total drawdown at any point is the sum of the drawdowns caused by each well (principle of superposition).
cards.w: The flow equation is linear, so effects simply add. Interfering wells have more drawdown, so each yields less or costs more to pump; space wells well apart.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.a: Method of images: an impermeable (barrier) boundary is replaced by an imaginary discharging well, and a recharge boundary (river) by an imaginary recharging well, at equal distance on the other side of the boundary.
cards.w: The image well produces exactly the no-flow or constant-head condition along the boundary line. The aquifer can then be treated as infinite.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.a: On a Jacob semi-log time-drawdown plot, a barrier boundary doubles the slope of the straight line, while a recharge boundary flattens it until drawdown becomes constant.
cards.w: A barrier acts like a second pumping well, adding drawdown. A river acts like an injection well and finally supplies all the pumped water.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
cards.a: An aquifer test (constant-rate test with observation wells) gives aquifer properties T and S; a well test (step-drawdown test) gives well performance: well loss and efficiency.
cards.w: One tests the formation, the other tests the well as a structure. Water levels are measured at short intervals at first because drawdown is fastest early.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.a: A slug test finds hydraulic conductivity near a well by suddenly adding or removing a small volume of water and timing the recovery; it is analysed by the Hvorslev, Bouwer-Rice or Cooper-Bredehoeft-Papadopulos methods.
cards.w: It is quick and cheap, needs no pump or observation well, and suits low-permeability formations. But it tests only a small volume around the well.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.a: Pumping tests on large-diameter dug wells must allow for water stored in the well itself; the Papadopulos-Cooper (1967) method does this.
cards.w: Early in the test most of the pumped water comes from the well's own storage, not the aquifer. This matters for hard-rock dug wells of India.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.a: The packer (Lugeon) test measures permeability of fractured rock by injecting water under pressure into a borehole section sealed by packers; 1 Lugeon = 1 litre per minute per metre at 10 bar.
cards.w: Packers (inflatable rubber seals) isolate one stretch of the hole so single fracture zones can be tested. It is widely used at dam sites.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Specific capacity of a well is its discharge per unit drawdown, Q/s, expressed in m3/day per metre (or litres per minute per metre).
cards.w: It is the simplest measure of well productivity: how much water you get for each metre the water level is pulled down.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Specific capacity is not a constant: it decreases as pumping rate increases and as pumping time increases.
cards.w: Higher discharge adds turbulent well loss (which grows as Q squared), and longer pumping deepens the cone. So always state the rate and duration with it.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Jacob (1947): total drawdown in a pumping well is sw = BQ + CQ^2, where BQ is the formation (aquifer) loss from laminar flow and CQ^2 is the well loss from turbulent flow.
cards.w: Formation loss happens in the aquifer and follows Darcy's law. Well loss happens in the gravel pack, screen and casing where water moves fast.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Rorabaugh (1953) generalised Jacob's drawdown equation to sw = BQ + CQ^n, where the exponent n may differ from 2 (commonly about 2.5).
cards.w: Field data showed that turbulent loss does not always rise exactly as the square of discharge.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Well efficiency (%) = formation loss / total drawdown x 100 = BQ / (BQ + CQ^2) x 100; equivalently, actual specific capacity / theoretical specific capacity.
cards.w: A perfect well would have no well loss, so all drawdown would be due to the aquifer. Efficiency falls as discharge rises.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: In a step-drawdown test the well is pumped at three or more successively higher rates; a plot of s/Q against Q is a straight line with intercept B and slope C.
cards.w: Dividing sw = BQ + CQ^2 by Q gives s/Q = B + CQ, the equation of a line. Each step is run until drawdown nearly stabilises (about 1 hour or more).

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Walton's guide to the well-loss constant C (min^2/m^5): below 0.5 = well properly designed and developed; 0.5 to 1 = mild deterioration; 1 to 4 = severe clogging; above 4 = hard to restore.
cards.w: A rising C in repeat tests means the screen or gravel pack is getting clogged. Fine detail from Todd; remember 'below 0.5 is good'.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Specific capacity is roughly proportional to transmissivity, so it is used to estimate T and to compare aquifers where full pumping tests are not available.
cards.w: A more transmissive aquifer needs less drawdown to deliver the same discharge. Specific capacity maps are a quick guide to the best well sites.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: For open dug wells, specific capacity is found by a recuperation (recovery) test using Slichter's formula: C = 2.303 (A/t) log10(s1/s2), where A is the well's cross-sectional area.
cards.w: The well is pumped down and the rise of water level from depression s1 to s2 in time t is timed. Safe yield is then C multiplied by the safe working depression head.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: A steady fall in a well's specific capacity over the years, with regional water levels unchanged, signals clogging of the screen or gravel pack and the need for rehabilitation.
cards.w: The aquifer has not changed, so the extra drawdown must be well loss. Regular specific capacity checks are the main tool of well maintenance.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
cards.a: A dug (open) well is a large-diameter, shallow well, usually 1 to 10 m wide and under about 20 m deep, that taps the unconfined aquifer and also stores water.
cards.w: The big diameter acts as a storage tank that fills slowly from a poor aquifer overnight. It is the typical well of India's hard-rock and laterite areas, including Kerala.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: A bore well is a small-diameter hole drilled in hard rock, cased only through the loose overburden; a tube well is drilled in unconsolidated sediments and is fully cased, with screens against the aquifers.
cards.w: Hard rock stands on its own, so the hole is left open to let fractures feed it. Loose sand would collapse, so a tube well needs pipe and screen.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: A dug-cum-bore well is a dug well with one or more bores drilled from its bottom to tap deeper fractured or confined zones.
cards.w: It adds yield from deeper fractures while keeping the storage of the open well. It is common in the hard-rock terrain of peninsular India.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: A cavity tube well has no screen: it draws water through a hollow (cavity) formed in sand just below a strong clay roof, and flow into it is spherical, not radial.
cards.w: Sand is pumped out at first until a stable cavity forms under the clay. It is cheap and was common in the alluvial plains of north India.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: A filter-point well is a shallow, small-diameter tube well with a short screen (filter), sunk by hand boring or jetting in coastal and deltaic sands; it is common in Kerala's coastal alluvium.
cards.w: Loose sand with a shallow water table can be tapped cheaply this way, and a centrifugal pump at the surface is enough. It is also typical of the Cauvery delta.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: A collector (radial or Ranney) well has a central concrete caisson with horizontal screened pipes pushed out radially, usually built beside or under a river bed to get very large yields.
cards.w: The horizontal laterals lie in river sand and draw river water through it (induced infiltration), so the water is naturally filtered.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: An infiltration gallery is a horizontal perforated pipe or tunnel laid in permeable sand below the water table, usually along a river bank or bed, to collect groundwater by gravity.
cards.w: It skims water over a long length with very little drawdown. This makes it useful where fresh water floats on salt water.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: A qanat (karez) is a gently sloping tunnel that brings groundwater to the surface by gravity (classic in Iran); the similar horizontal tunnel wells cut in laterite hills of Kasaragod, Kerala, are called surangams.
cards.w: The tunnel taps the water table inside a hill, and the water flows out without any pumping. Surangam is the standard Kerala example.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: A driven well is made by hammering a pipe fitted with a pointed screen (well point) into soft ground; rows of well points joined to a header pipe are used to lower the water table at construction sites.
cards.w: It needs no drilling, but works only in shallow, loose, stone-free ground. Well-point systems keep excavations dry (dewatering).

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Cable-tool (percussion or churn) drilling breaks rock by repeatedly lifting and dropping a heavy string of tools: drill bit, drill stem, drilling jars and rope socket; cuttings are removed with a bailer.
cards.w: It is slow, but simple and cheap, gives good formation samples and handles boulders well. In loose ground, casing must be driven as the hole deepens.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: In direct (hydraulic) rotary drilling, a rotating bit cuts the hole while drilling mud is pumped down the drill pipe and returns up the annulus carrying the cuttings.
cards.w: The mud also plasters the wall with a thin 'mud cake' that keeps loose formations from caving, so no casing is needed while drilling. It is fast in unconsolidated sediments.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: In reverse-circulation rotary drilling, water flows down the annulus and returns up inside the drill pipe with the cuttings; it is used for large-diameter wells in soft, unconsolidated alluvium.
cards.w: The high upward velocity inside the pipe lifts even pebbles. Clear water is used instead of thick mud, so the aquifer is less clogged.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Down-the-hole (DTH) hammer drilling uses a pneumatic hammer just above the bit and compressed air to blow out cuttings; it is the fastest method in hard crystalline rock.
cards.w: The hammer strikes at the hole bottom, so no energy is lost along the drill rods. Almost all bore wells in Kerala's and peninsular India's hard rocks are DTH-drilled.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Drilling mud (usually bentonite clay in water) removes cuttings, cools and lubricates the bit, supports the hole wall with a mud cake and balances formation pressure.
cards.w: Bentonite swells and forms a gel that holds cuttings in suspension when pumping stops. The mud cake must later be removed by well development.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Auger drilling (hand or power augers) makes shallow bored wells in soft clay, silt and sand; it cannot penetrate hard rock and is difficult in caving sand below the water table.
cards.w: An auger is a large screw or bucket that cuts and lifts soil. Wells under about 30 m made with a rotary bucket auger are called bored wells.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Jetting (wash boring) sinks small-diameter shallow wells in sand by a high-velocity stream of water that loosens the material and washes it up around the pipe.
cards.w: Water does the cutting, so it works only in soft, unconsolidated ground. Filter-point wells are often installed this way.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
cards.a: The main parts of a tube well are the housing (casing) pipe that holds the pump, blank pipe against clays, the well screen against the aquifer, the gravel pack, and a cement grout sanitary seal near the top.
cards.w: Design aims at the highest yield with the least drawdown, sand-free water and long life. The seal stops polluted surface water running down outside the casing.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
cards.a: Screen length: in a homogeneous confined aquifer about 70 to 80% of the aquifer thickness is screened; in a homogeneous unconfined aquifer only the bottom one-third to one-half is screened.
cards.w: A confined aquifer stays full, so nearly all of it can be screened. In an unconfined aquifer the upper part gets dewatered by drawdown, so screen there would be wasted.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
cards.a: The total open area of a well screen should keep the entrance velocity of water at or below about 0.03 m/s (3 cm/s).
cards.w: Slow entry means little head loss, no sand movement and slower incrustation and corrosion. It is the classic design figure (0.1 foot per second).

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
cards.a: For a naturally developed well, the screen slot size is chosen from the aquifer's grain-size curve to retain about 40 to 50% of the material; the finer part is washed out during development.
cards.w: Removing the fines leaves a coarse, graded, highly permeable zone around the screen: a natural gravel pack.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
cards.a: An artificial gravel pack is used when the aquifer is fine and uniform (uniformity coefficient below about 3, effective size below about 0.25 mm) or thinly layered.
cards.w: Such sand would need impractically fine slots. A coarser pack around the screen holds the sand back while allowing wider slots and a larger effective well radius.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
cards.a: Gravel pack: clean, rounded siliceous gravel whose 30%-retained size is 4-6 times the aquifer's d30 (uniform sand; 6-9 times if non-uniform), 75-200 mm thick around the screen.
cards.w: Too fine a pack chokes the well; too coarse a pack lets sand through. Quartz gravel is used because limestone would dissolve in acid treatment.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
cards.a: Uniformity coefficient = d60/d10 and effective size = d10 (Hazen), both read from the grain-size distribution (sieve analysis) curve of the aquifer sample.
cards.w: d10 means 10% of the sample is finer than that size. A low coefficient (near 1) means well-sorted, uniform sand.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
cards.a: The continuous-slot (wire-wound, Johnson type) screen, with V-shaped slots widening inward, gives the largest open area and resists clogging; louvre, bridge-slot and slotted-pipe screens have less open area.
cards.w: Any grain that passes the narrow outer edge of a V-slot falls freely inside, so grains do not wedge in the slot.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
cards.a: Well development removes drilling mud cake and fine particles around the screen to raise permeability and stabilise the formation, so the well gives sand-free water at maximum specific capacity.
cards.w: Drilling always damages and clogs the aquifer face. Development repairs that damage and grades the material around the screen.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
cards.a: Well development methods: overpumping, backwashing (rawhiding), mechanical surging with a surge block, compressed-air surging and air-lift pumping, high-velocity water jetting, and chemicals such as polyphosphates and acid.
cards.w: Good methods move water both in and out of the screen so that sand 'bridges' are broken. Simple overpumping moves water one way only, so it is the least effective.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
cards.a: In development, polyphosphates (such as sodium hexametaphosphate) disperse clay and drilling mud; acid treatment opens up limestone and dolomite aquifers; dry ice (solid CO2) gives a surging blast.
cards.w: Dispersed clay stays in suspension and can be pumped out. Acid dissolves carbonate rock and widens the fractures feeding the well.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
cards.a: Hydrofracturing improves the yield of poor hard-rock bore wells by injecting water at high pressure into a section sealed by packers, to clean, widen and connect fractures.
cards.w: A bore well's yield depends wholly on the fractures it meets. Forcing them open links the well to more of the fracture network.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
cards.a: Incrustation is the clogging of screen slots and gravel pack by deposits of calcium and magnesium carbonates, iron and manganese hydroxides, and slime from iron bacteria.
cards.w: Pressure drops near a pumping well, CO2 escapes, and carbonates precipitate there. Hard, alkaline water is incrusting; yield and specific capacity fall.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
cards.a: Incrustation is treated with acid (hydrochloric or sulphamic) for carbonate scale, chlorine for iron bacteria and slime, and polyphosphates for iron oxide and clay deposits, each followed by surging.
cards.w: Each chemical dissolves or loosens one type of deposit; surging then pushes it through the screen so it can be pumped out.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
cards.a: Corrosion of casing and screen is caused by acidic water (low pH), dissolved oxygen, carbon dioxide, hydrogen sulphide and high chloride or TDS; it enlarges slots and the well starts pumping sand.
cards.w: Corrosion removes metal; incrustation adds deposits. Corrosion-resistant screens (stainless steel, PVC, fibreglass) are the remedy.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
cards.a: The Langelier saturation index tells whether water will form scale or corrode: a positive value means carbonate scale-forming (incrusting), a negative value means corrosive.
cards.w: It is the measured pH minus the pH at which the water would be just saturated with calcium carbonate. The Ryznar stability index is used the same way.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
cards.a: A centrifugal pump at the surface can lift water by suction only about 6 to 7 m in practice (theoretical limit about 10.3 m); deeper water levels need submersible, vertical turbine or jet pumps.
cards.w: Suction works by atmospheric pressure, which can support only a 10.3 m column of water. Deep-well pumps sit below the water level and push the water up.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
cards.a: A completed well is tested for plumbness (verticality) and alignment, then disinfected with a chlorine solution such as bleaching powder before use.
cards.w: A crooked well damages vertical turbine pump shafts. Drilling tools and gravel carry bacteria into the well, so it must be sterilised.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - physical and chemical properties of water
cards.a: The major ions of groundwater are the cations Ca, Mg, Na and K and the anions HCO3, SO4 and Cl; together they make up over 90% of the dissolved solids.
cards.w: Carbonate, nitrate, fluoride, iron and silica are minor constituents. Major-ion ratios are what all the water-type diagrams plot.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - physical and chemical properties of water
cards.a: Physical properties of water tested for quality are colour, odour, taste, turbidity (in NTU), temperature and electrical conductivity.
cards.w: These can be sensed or measured on the spot. Temperature, pH and EC change after sampling, so they are measured in the field.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - physical and chemical properties of water
cards.a: Total dissolved solids (TDS) is the weight of residue left on evaporating a filtered sample, in mg/L; fresh water has TDS below 1000 mg/L, sea water about 35,000 mg/L.
cards.w: TDS is the single best overall index of salinity. Water between fresh and sea water is called brackish; water saltier than sea water is brine.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - physical and chemical properties of water
cards.a: Electrical conductivity (EC) is reported in microsiemens per cm at 25 degrees C; TDS (mg/L) is roughly 0.64 x EC, the factor ranging from 0.55 to 0.75.
cards.w: Dissolved ions carry current, so more salts mean higher EC. EC is quick to measure in the field and gives an instant estimate of TDS.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - physical and chemical properties of water
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
cards.a: Hardness is caused mainly by calcium and magnesium ions and is expressed as mg/L of CaCO3: total hardness = 2.5 x Ca + 4.1 x Mg (Ca and Mg in mg/L).
cards.w: Hard water does not lather with soap and forms scale in boilers. The factors 2.5 and 4.1 convert Ca and Mg into the equivalent weight of CaCO3.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - physical and chemical properties of water
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
cards.a: Temporary (carbonate) hardness is due to bicarbonates of Ca and Mg and is removed by boiling; permanent (non-carbonate) hardness is due to their sulphates and chlorides and is not removed by boiling.
cards.w: Boiling drives off CO2 and the calcium falls out as CaCO3 scale. Sulphates and chlorides stay dissolved and need chemical softening or ion exchange.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - physical and chemical properties of water
cards.a: Sawyer and McCarty hardness classes (mg/L as CaCO3): soft below 75, moderately hard 75 to 150, hard 150 to 300, very hard above 300.
cards.w: This is the classification used in Todd and most Indian groundwater reports. Remember that each class boundary doubles: 75, 150, 300.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - physical and chemical properties of water
cards.a: Concentration in meq/L = mg/L divided by equivalent weight (ionic weight / valence); equivalent weights are about Ca 20, Mg 12, Na 23, K 39, HCO3 61, SO4 48, Cl 35.5.
cards.w: Ions combine by charge, not by weight, so chemists compare them in milliequivalents. SAR, RSC, percent sodium and Piper plots all need meq/L.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - physical and chemical properties of water
cards.a: In a correct water analysis, total cations equal total anions in meq/L; an ion-balance error within about 5% is accepted.
cards.w: Water is electrically neutral. A large imbalance means an analytical mistake or an important ion left unmeasured.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - physical and chemical properties of water
cards.a: Alkalinity is the capacity of water to neutralise acid; in groundwater it is due mainly to bicarbonate and carbonate, and it is expressed as mg/L of CaCO3.
cards.w: Carbonate ions appear only above pH about 8.3; below that, alkalinity is practically all bicarbonate.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - physical and chemical properties of water
cards.a: Chebotarev sequence: along its flow path and with depth and age, groundwater evolves from bicarbonate type through sulphate type to chloride type, with rising TDS.
cards.w: Young shallow water has dissolved mostly CO2 and carbonates. Old deep water has had time to pick up the more soluble sulphate and chloride salts.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - physical and chemical properties of water
cards.a: Base (cation) exchange: clay minerals take up Ca and Mg from water and release Na, softening the water naturally and producing Na-HCO3 type water.
cards.w: Clays hold loosely bound ions on their surfaces and can swap them. Schoeller's chloro-alkaline indices are used to detect this exchange.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - physical and chemical properties of water
cards.a: The stable isotopes of oxygen (18O) and hydrogen (deuterium) in rain plot on the global meteoric water line, delta D = 8 x delta 18O + 10 (Craig, 1961).
cards.w: Groundwater that plots on this line came from rain. Shifts off the line show evaporation or rock-water exchange, so the isotopes trace the origin of water.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - physical and chemical properties of water
cards.a: Groundwater is dated with radioisotopes: tritium (half-life about 12.3 years) for young water recharged in recent decades, and carbon-14 (half-life 5730 years) for water up to about 40,000 years old.
cards.w: Tritium from 1950s-60s nuclear bomb tests labelled modern rain. Water with no tritium was recharged before about 1952.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: The Indian drinking water standard is IS 10500:2012 (BIS, second revision); it gives an 'acceptable limit' and a higher 'permissible limit in the absence of an alternate source' for each parameter.
cards.w: Above the acceptable limit water is not ideal but may be tolerated if nothing else is available. Above the permissible limit the source must be rejected.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: IS 10500:2012 limits (acceptable / permissible): pH 6.5 to 8.5 (no relaxation); TDS 500 / 2000 mg/L; total hardness as CaCO3 200 / 600 mg/L.
cards.w: Remember hardness and TDS as '200-600' and '500-2000'. High TDS gives a salty taste and may upset the stomach.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: IS 10500:2012 limits (acceptable / permissible): chloride 250 / 1000 mg/L; sulphate 200 / 400 mg/L; calcium 75 / 200 mg/L; magnesium 30 / 100 mg/L; total alkalinity 200 / 600 mg/L.
cards.w: Chloride gives a salty taste; sulphate with magnesium acts as a laxative. These are taste and comfort limits rather than poison limits.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: IS 10500:2012 fluoride: acceptable limit 1.0 mg/L, permissible limit 1.5 mg/L; the WHO guideline value is 1.5 mg/L.
cards.w: A little fluoride (about 0.5 to 1 mg/L) protects teeth from decay; more than 1.5 mg/L causes fluorosis.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: IS 10500:2012 nitrate (as NO3): 45 mg/L with no relaxation; the WHO guideline value is 50 mg/L.
cards.w: High nitrate causes methaemoglobinaemia (blue baby syndrome) in bottle-fed infants: the blood cannot carry enough oxygen.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: IS 10500:2012 arsenic: acceptable 0.01 mg/L (same as WHO); permissible 0.05 mg/L only if no alternate source (BIS has considered removing this relaxation). Toxic: a Table 3 parameter.
cards.w: Arsenic causes cancer, so the limit is very low. Remember 10 ppb (acceptable) and 50 ppb (old relaxation).

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: IS 10500:2012 iron: 0.3 mg/L, no relaxation (older IS 10500:1991 allowed 1.0 mg/L, the value CGWB still uses to flag iron-affected areas).
cards.w: Iron is not a health hazard at these levels. It gives a metallic taste, turns water brown on standing, and stains clothes, rice and vessels.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: IS 10500:2012 toxic metals, all with no relaxation: lead 0.01, cadmium 0.003, mercury 0.001, total chromium 0.05 mg/L; turbidity is 1 / 5 NTU and manganese 0.1 / 0.3 mg/L.
cards.w: Toxic metals build up in the body, so no higher fallback limit is given. Cadmium causes itai-itai disease and mercury causes Minamata disease.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: WHO Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality (4th edition; latest addenda 2022) give health-based guideline values: arsenic 0.01, lead 0.01, uranium 0.03, fluoride 1.5, nitrate 50 mg/L; none is set for TDS, hardness, chloride or iron.
cards.w: WHO sets values only where health is at risk. TDS, hardness, chloride and iron affect taste and acceptability, not health, at normal levels.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Bacteriological standard (IS 10500:2012 and WHO): E. coli or thermotolerant coliform bacteria must not be detectable in any 100 mL sample of drinking water.
cards.w: E. coli lives in the gut, so finding it shows faecal pollution and a risk of cholera, typhoid and diarrhoea. It is the indicator organism.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2016 Hydrogeology
cards.a: Sodium adsorption ratio: SAR = Na / square root of [(Ca + Mg) / 2], with all concentrations in meq/L; it measures the sodium (alkali) hazard of irrigation water.
cards.w: Sodium replaces calcium on soil clay and makes it disperse, so the soil turns hard and nearly impermeable. Calcium and magnesium counter this effect.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: USSL sodium hazard classes by SAR: S1 below 10 (low), S2 10 to 18 (medium), S3 18 to 26 (high), S4 above 26 (very high).
cards.w: The cut-offs go up in steps of 8 after 10. Low-SAR water can be used on almost all soils.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: USSL salinity hazard classes by EC (microsiemens/cm): C1 below 250 (low), C2 250 to 750 (medium), C3 750 to 2250 (high), C4 above 2250 (very high).
cards.w: Salty water makes it harder for roots to take up water (osmotic effect). Each boundary is three times the previous one.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: The US Salinity Laboratory (USSL; Richards, 1954) diagram plots SAR against EC on a log scale and divides irrigation water into 16 classes, from C1S1 (best) to C4S4 (worst).
cards.w: It judges the two main irrigation hazards together: salinity (EC) on the horizontal axis and sodium (SAR) on the vertical axis.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
cards.a: Percent sodium = (Na + K) x 100 / (Ca + Mg + Na + K), in meq/L. Wilcox classes: below 20 excellent, 20-40 good, 40-60 permissible, 60-80 doubtful, above 80 unsuitable.
cards.w: Like SAR, it shows the risk of sodium damaging soil structure. The Wilcox diagram plots percent sodium against EC.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Residual sodium carbonate: RSC = (CO3 + HCO3) - (Ca + Mg), in meq/L (Eaton, 1950); below 1.25 is safe, 1.25 to 2.5 marginal, above 2.5 unsuitable for irrigation.
cards.w: Excess bicarbonate precipitates calcium and magnesium as carbonates in the soil, leaving sodium behind. This raises the sodium hazard.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Other irrigation indices: Kelley's ratio Na/(Ca + Mg) should be below 1; magnesium hazard Mg x 100/(Ca + Mg) should be below 50%; Doneen's permeability index is also used.
cards.w: All are in meq/L and all test whether the water will harm soil structure or crop yield.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Boron is essential to plants in traces but is toxic to sensitive crops (such as citrus) above about 1 mg/L in irrigation water.
cards.w: The gap between 'needed' and 'toxic' is very narrow for boron. It is the main trace element checked in irrigation water.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Industrial criteria vary by use: boiler feed water must be very low in hardness and silica to avoid scale, while livestock can tolerate much higher TDS than humans.
cards.w: Scale on boiler tubes wastes fuel and can cause explosions. There is no single 'good' water; quality is judged against the intended use.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Graphical presentation of water quality data
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2016 Hydrogeology
cards.a: The Piper (1944) trilinear diagram has two lower triangles, cations on the left and anions on the right, and a central diamond onto which both points are projected; data are plotted as percent of meq/L.
cards.w: One point in the diamond shows the overall chemical character of a sample. Hundreds of samples can be compared on a single sheet.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Graphical presentation of water quality data
cards.a: On a Piper diagram, a mixture of two waters plots on the straight line joining them; its weakness is that it shows only ionic proportions, not actual concentrations.
cards.w: Because it uses percentages, a dilute and a salty water with the same ion ratios plot at the same point. TDS is sometimes shown by the size of a circle.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Graphical presentation of water quality data
cards.a: Hydrochemical facies (Back, 1961) are water types named after the dominant cation and anion, read from the Piper diagram: for example Ca-HCO3, Na-HCO3, Ca-Mg-Cl-SO4 and Na-Cl types.
cards.w: Ca-HCO3 marks fresh recharge water, Na-Cl marks saline or sea water, and Na-HCO3 marks water changed by ion exchange.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Graphical presentation of water quality data
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
cards.a: The Stiff (1951) pattern diagram plots cations to the left and anions to the right of a vertical zero axis in meq/L, and joins the points to form a polygon.
cards.w: Each water type gives a distinctive shape, and the width shows total salinity. Stiff patterns are placed on maps to show how quality changes across an area.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Graphical presentation of water quality data
cards.a: The Schoeller diagram is a semi-logarithmic plot: ion concentrations in meq/L on a vertical log scale, with points for each sample joined by a line.
cards.w: It shows actual concentrations, unlike Piper. Parallel lines for two samples mean the same ion ratios, so one is just a diluted form of the other.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Graphical presentation of water quality data
cards.a: The Collins (1923) bar diagram shows each analysis as a vertical bar in two halves, cations on the left and anions on the right, in meq/L; bar height is the total concentration.
cards.w: The two halves are equal in height because cations balance anions. It is the oldest and simplest method.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Graphical presentation of water quality data
cards.a: The Durov (1948) diagram projects points from a cation triangle and an anion triangle onto a central square; its extended forms add pH and TDS scales.
cards.w: It does the same job as Piper but with a square instead of a diamond. It can show total salinity alongside ion ratios.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Graphical presentation of water quality data
cards.a: The Gibbs (1970) diagram plots TDS against Na/(Na + Ca) or Cl/(Cl + HCO3) and shows which process controls water chemistry: precipitation, rock weathering, or evaporation-crystallisation.
cards.w: Low TDS with a high Na ratio means rain dominance, medium TDS means rock dominance, and very high TDS means evaporation dominance.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Graphical presentation of water quality data
cards.a: In circular (pie) diagrams the sectors show the share of each ion in meq/L and the radius is proportional to total concentration; isocone maps join points of equal concentration.
cards.w: Pie and Stiff symbols are handy on maps. Isocone lines are 'contours' of a quality parameter such as chloride or EC.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Graphical presentation of water quality data
cards.a: The Chadha (1999) diagram is a rectangular modification of the Piper diagram: it plots (Ca + Mg) - (Na + K) against (CO3 + HCO3) - (Cl + SO4) in percent meq/L.
cards.w: It can be drawn in any spreadsheet without special software, and its four quadrants give the water type. It was devised by an Indian (CGWB) hydrogeologist.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
cards.a: Groundwater quality problems by province of India: arsenic in the Ganga-Brahmaputra alluvium, fluoride in hard-rock and arid areas, inland salinity in the arid north-west, and sea-water salinity along the coasts.
cards.w: Most of India's groundwater is fresh Ca-Mg-HCO3 water. The problems are mostly geogenic (from the rocks themselves), not man-made.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2016 Hydrogeology
cards.a: Fluoride in groundwater is geogenic: it comes from fluorite (CaF2), fluorapatite, and the micas and amphiboles (biotite, hornblende) of granites and gneisses.
cards.w: In micas and amphiboles the fluoride ion sits in place of hydroxyl (OH) because the two are similar in size and charge. Weathering releases it to water.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
cards.a: High fluoride is typical of alkaline, Na-HCO3 type groundwater that is low in calcium, in arid and semi-arid climates with long residence time.
cards.w: Calcium locks fluoride up as insoluble fluorite. Where calcium is low and pH is high, fluoride stays dissolved; evaporation concentrates it further.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2016 Hydrogeology
cards.a: The states worst affected by fluoride are Rajasthan, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana (Nalgonda district); endemic fluorosis in India was first reported from Nellore district, Andhra Pradesh, in 1937.
cards.w: These are dry states with granite-gneiss terrain. Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Punjab, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh and many other states also have affected pockets.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
cards.a: Fluoride and health: below about 0.5 mg/L favours dental caries (tooth decay); above 1.5 mg/L causes dental fluorosis (mottled teeth); long use of much higher levels causes skeletal fluorosis.
cards.w: Fluoride replaces hydroxyl in the apatite of teeth and bones. A little hardens enamel; too much makes teeth brittle and stained and stiffens joints.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
cards.a: The Nalgonda technique of defluoridation, developed by NEERI (Nagpur), adds alum (aluminium sulphate), lime and bleaching powder to water, followed by flocculation, settling and filtration.
cards.w: Alum forms aluminium hydroxide flocs that carry fluoride down. Lime keeps the pH right and bleaching powder disinfects. It is named after Nalgonda district.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
cards.a: Other defluoridation methods are adsorption on activated alumina or bone char, ion exchange, and reverse osmosis.
cards.w: Activated alumina filters are common at hand pumps in India. Reverse osmosis is costly but removes nearly all dissolved salts along with fluoride.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
cards.a: India's main arsenic belt is the Bengal Delta Plain: shallow Holocene alluvial aquifers of the Ganga-Brahmaputra-Meghna system in West Bengal and Bangladesh; arsenic poisoning in West Bengal was first reported in 1983.
cards.w: Young, grey, organic-rich delta sediments release arsenic. Millions of shallow hand-pump tube wells tap exactly these beds.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
cards.a: Arsenic-affected states include West Bengal, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand, Assam and Manipur (alluvium of the Ganga-Brahmaputra plains); in Chhattisgarh (Rajnandgaon district) it occurs in hard rock.
cards.w: The alluvial cases follow the rivers draining the Himalaya. The Chhattisgarh case is different: arsenic there comes from sulphide minerals in volcanic and granitic rocks.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
cards.a: The accepted mechanism in the Bengal basin is reductive dissolution: in reducing, organic-rich sediments, iron oxyhydroxide coatings on grains dissolve and release the arsenic adsorbed on them.
cards.w: Bacteria feeding on buried organic matter use up oxygen and then reduce ferric iron. The older idea, oxidation of arsenic-bearing pyrite due to pumping, is now largely rejected.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
cards.a: Arsenic in groundwater occurs as arsenite, As(III), and arsenate, As(V); arsenite dominates in reducing groundwater and is the more toxic and more mobile form.
cards.w: Arsenite is an uncharged molecule at normal pH, so it does not stick to mineral surfaces and is harder to remove. Oxidising it to arsenate helps treatment.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
cards.a: In the Bengal basin arsenic is highest in shallow aquifers (roughly 20 to 100 m deep); deeper, older (Pleistocene) aquifers are mostly arsenic-safe.
cards.w: The older sediments are brown and oxidised, and their iron oxides still hold arsenic firmly. Tapping deep aquifers is one mitigation measure.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
cards.a: Long-term drinking of arsenic-rich water causes arsenicosis: dark spots on the skin (melanosis), hard patches on palms and soles (keratosis), and cancers of skin and internal organs.
cards.w: Arsenic builds up slowly in skin, hair and nails, so symptoms appear only after years. 'Blackfoot disease' of Taiwan is another arsenic effect.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
cards.a: Arsenic is removed by oxidation followed by coagulation and co-precipitation with iron salts or alum, by adsorption on activated alumina or granular ferric hydroxide, or by reverse osmosis.
cards.w: Arsenate sticks strongly to fresh iron hydroxide flocs. This is the same affinity that holds arsenic on iron-coated grains in the aquifer.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
cards.a: Nitrate in groundwater is mainly anthropogenic: nitrogen fertilisers, sewage, septic tanks and animal waste; it is highest in shallow aquifers of intensively farmed states such as Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan.
cards.w: Nitrate is very soluble and is not held by soil, so it leaches straight down with recharge. It is the commonest man-made groundwater pollutant.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
cards.a: Inland groundwater salinity is widespread in the arid and semi-arid north-west: Rajasthan, Haryana, Punjab and Gujarat.
cards.w: Low rainfall and high evaporation concentrate salts; canal irrigation has also raised water tables and caused waterlogging and soil salinity.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
cards.a: High iron in groundwater is common in the north-eastern states (Assam), West Bengal, Odisha and Kerala; it occurs as soluble ferrous iron in reducing or acidic water.
cards.w: Clear water drawn from the well turns reddish-brown on standing, because air oxidises ferrous iron to insoluble ferric hydroxide.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
cards.a: In Kerala, fluoride above the limit is known mainly from Palakkad district (Muthalamada area, in hornblende-biotite gneiss terrain) and from the deep Tertiary aquifers of Alappuzha district.
cards.w: Eastern Palakkad lies in the dry Palghat Gap, with rocks rich in fluoride-bearing minerals. Alappuzha town's water supply taps the deep confined Tertiary aquifers.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
cards.a: Groundwater in Kerala's laterite and coastal dug wells is typically low in TDS but slightly acidic (low pH), often high in iron, and frequently contaminated by coliform bacteria.
cards.w: Heavy rain leaches salts away and leaves acidic, iron-rich laterite. Closely spaced open wells and septic tanks cause bacterial pollution.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
cards.a: 2024 Kerala report to NGT, citing CGWB: fluoride above limit in pockets of Palakkad, Alappuzha and Malappuram; CGWB did not detect arsenic (one Kollam well reported high by KSPCB).
cards.w: Kerala lacks the young Himalayan-derived reducing alluvium of the Ganga plains, so arsenic is rare, though isolated cases can occur.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Saline water intrusion in coastal and other aquifers and its prevention
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2016 Hydrogeology
UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
cards.a: Ghyben-Herzberg relation: in a coastal unconfined aquifer the depth of the fresh-salt water interface below sea level is z = [df / (ds - df)] x h, which is about 40 h, where h is the water table height above sea level.
cards.w: Fresh water (density 1.000) floats on sea water (1.025) like an iceberg. A 1 m head of fresh water above sea level balances a 40 m column below it.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Saline water intrusion in coastal and other aquifers and its prevention
cards.a: By the Ghyben-Herzberg relation, every 1 m fall of the water table near the coast makes the salt-water interface rise by about 40 m.
cards.w: The balance works both ways. This is why even modest over-pumping near the coast can bring up salt water quickly.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Saline water intrusion in coastal and other aquifers and its prevention
cards.a: The relation is named after Badon Ghyben (1888-89, Netherlands) and Herzberg (1901, Germany), who found it independently.
cards.w: Both were studying wells on the sandy North Sea coast and islands, where fresh water was found far below sea level.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Saline water intrusion in coastal and other aquifers and its prevention
cards.a: Ghyben-Herzberg assumes hydrostatic balance and a sharp interface; in reality fresh water flows to the sea, the interface is a transition (diffusion) zone, and near the shore it lies deeper than predicted.
cards.w: Tides and pumping keep mixing the two waters, giving a brackish zone. Hubbert (1940) and Glover (1959) corrected the relation for flowing fresh water.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Saline water intrusion in coastal and other aquifers and its prevention
cards.a: On small oceanic islands such as the coral islands of Lakshadweep, fresh groundwater occurs as a thin lens floating on sea water; it is tapped by shallow skimming wells or infiltration galleries.
cards.w: Rain builds a lens-shaped body following Ghyben-Herzberg. Deep or heavy pumping would pull salt water up, so water is skimmed from the top.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Saline water intrusion in coastal and other aquifers and its prevention
cards.a: Upconing is the local cone-shaped rise of salt water beneath a pumping well; the cone stays stable only if its rise is under about one-third to one-half of the distance from well bottom to the original interface.
cards.w: Drawdown at the well reduces fresh-water head, so the interface below it bulges upward. Beyond the critical rise, salt water enters the well.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Saline water intrusion in coastal and other aquifers and its prevention
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
cards.a: Sea-water intrusion is caused mainly by over-pumping of coastal aquifers, which lowers the water table and reverses the natural seaward hydraulic gradient.
cards.w: Normally fresh water flows out to sea and holds the salt water back. Other routes are tidal rivers, creeks, canals and leaky well casings.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Saline water intrusion in coastal and other aquifers and its prevention
cards.a: Sea-water intrusion is recognised by rising chloride and EC and by a rising Cl / (CO3 + HCO3) ratio (Revelle's or Simpson's ratio); sea water has about 19,000 mg/L chloride.
cards.w: Chloride dominates sea water while bicarbonate dominates fresh groundwater. A low Ca/Mg ratio also points to sea water, which has far more Mg than Ca.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Saline water intrusion in coastal and other aquifers and its prevention
cards.a: Todd's five control methods for sea-water intrusion: modifying the pumping pattern, artificial recharge, an extraction barrier (pumping trough), an injection barrier (pressure ridge), and a subsurface physical barrier.
cards.w: All of them aim to keep fresh-water head near the coast higher than the sea, or to physically block the salt-water wedge.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Saline water intrusion in coastal and other aquifers and its prevention
cards.a: An injection barrier is a line of recharge wells along the coast that builds a fresh-water pressure ridge; an extraction barrier is a line of pumping wells that forms a trough and intercepts the incoming sea water.
cards.w: The ridge pushes sea water back. The trough pulls in both sea water and some fresh water, and the brackish water pumped out is wasted.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Saline water intrusion in coastal and other aquifers and its prevention
cards.a: Indian examples of sea-water intrusion: the Minjur aquifer north of Chennai (Tamil Nadu) and the Saurashtra and Kachchh coasts of Gujarat, where tidal regulators, bandharas and check dams are used for control.
cards.w: Heavy pumping for city supply and irrigation lowered heads below sea level in these areas, and the interface moved several kilometres inland.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Saline water intrusion in coastal and other aquifers and its prevention
cards.a: In Kerala, salinity reaches coastal aquifers mostly through tidal rivers and backwaters in summer; salt-water barriers such as the Thanneermukkom bund across Vembanad Lake and regulator-cum-bridges are used to check it.
cards.w: Kerala's rivers are short, and in the dry season tides push salt water far upstream. The Thanneermukkom bund protects the low-lying Kuttanad paddy fields.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Saline water intrusion in coastal and other aquifers and its prevention
cards.a: Saline water in inland aquifers comes from connate water in marine sediments, solution of evaporite beds, concentration by evaporation in arid areas, and upconing of deep saline water under heavy pumping.
cards.w: Salt water is not only a coastal problem. Any fresh aquifer lying over saline water can be spoiled by pumping too hard.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater exploration - resistivity and well logging
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
cards.a: The electrical resistivity method passes current through two current electrodes and measures potential between two potential electrodes. In the Wenner array all four are equally spaced: apparent resistivity = 2 pi a (V/I).
cards.w: Dry or massive rock resists current; water-filled pores and clay conduct it. 'a' is the electrode spacing; apparent resistivity is the value for an equivalent uniform ground.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater exploration - resistivity and well logging
cards.a: In the Schlumberger array the two potential electrodes are kept close together at the centre and only the current electrodes are moved outward; it is the most used array for vertical electrical sounding.
cards.w: Moving only two electrodes makes field work faster, and it is less affected by near-surface lateral changes than the Wenner array.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater exploration - resistivity and well logging
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2016 Hydrogeology
cards.a: Vertical electrical sounding (VES) widens the electrode spacing about a fixed centre to study changes with depth; resistivity profiling moves a fixed-spacing array along a line to find lateral changes such as dykes and fracture zones.
cards.w: Wider spacing sends current deeper. Sounding is 'electrical drilling', profiling is 'electrical trenching'.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater exploration - resistivity and well logging
cards.a: Three-layer VES curve types: H (r1 > r2 < r3), K (r1 < r2 > r3), A (r1 < r2 < r3) and Q (r1 > r2 > r3); the H-type is typical of hard-rock terrain.
cards.w: In hard rock a conductive, saturated weathered zone lies between dry top soil and highly resistive fresh rock, giving a bowl-shaped H curve.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater exploration - resistivity and well logging
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
cards.a: Typical resistivities: clay and saline-water sand are very low (under about 10 ohm-m), fresh-water sand and weathered rock are moderate (tens to a few hundred), massive crystalline rock is very high (thousands).
cards.w: Current is carried by the pore water, so more water, saltier water or more clay means lower resistivity. Archie's law links rock resistivity to porosity and water resistivity.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater exploration - resistivity and well logging
cards.a: The seismic refraction method is used in groundwater work to find the depth to bedrock and to the water table, because seismic velocity rises sharply in saturated sediments (about 1500 m/s) and in hard rock.
cards.w: It works only where velocity increases with depth. Loose dry soil has a velocity of only a few hundred metres per second.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater exploration - resistivity and well logging
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2016 Hydrogeology
cards.a: Electric logs: the spontaneous potential (SP) log marks permeable beds and helps estimate formation-water quality; resistivity logs (short normal 16 inch, long normal 64 inch) separate sand from clay and fresh from saline water.
cards.w: Electric logs need an uncased hole filled with drilling fluid, since steel casing would short-circuit the current. They guide where to place the well screens.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater exploration - resistivity and well logging
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
cards.a: Nuclear logs: the natural gamma log reads high against clay and shale; the neutron log responds to hydrogen and so shows water-filled porosity; the gamma-gamma log gives bulk density. They also work in cased holes.
cards.w: Clays hold radioactive potassium, uranium and thorium. Neutrons are slowed mostly by hydrogen, which in rocks means water.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater exploration - resistivity and well logging
cards.a: The caliper log records borehole diameter and so picks out caved zones and fractures; temperature and fluid-conductivity logs locate zones where water enters or leaves the hole.
cards.w: In hard-rock bore wells, a sudden widening of the hole often marks a water-bearing fracture.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater exploration - resistivity and well logging
cards.a: In hard-rock terrain, bore-well sites are chosen on lineaments (fractures, faults, joints seen as straight features on satellite images and aerial photos), especially at lineament intersections, and then checked by resistivity survey.
cards.w: Fresh crystalline rock has almost no pores; water is found only in the weathered zone and in fractures. Dykes may act as barriers or as conduits.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Aquifer storage and recovery (ASR) uses the same well to inject surplus water into an aquifer in the wet season and to pump it back in the dry season.
cards.w: The aquifer acts as an underground reservoir with no evaporation loss and no land needed.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.a: Recharge pits and recharge shafts are dug through a shallow clay or other poorly permeable layer so that surface water can reach the unconfined aquifer below.
cards.w: Spreading methods fail when an impermeable layer lies near the surface. A pit or shaft simply by-passes it; shafts are narrower and deeper than pits.

cards.a: Earthquake magnitude measures the energy released at the source (one value per earthquake), while intensity measures the shaking and damage felt at a place and varies from place to place.
cards.w: Magnitude comes from instruments (seismographs). Intensity comes from what people felt and what broke. One earthquake has one magnitude but many intensities.

cards.a: The Richter scale (1935) is logarithmic: each whole-number step means a 10-fold rise in recorded wave amplitude and roughly a 32-fold rise in energy released.
cards.w: So a magnitude 7 is not 'a bit bigger' than a 6. Its waves are 10 times taller and it releases about 32 times more energy.

cards.a: The Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) scale has 12 grades, written in Roman numerals from I (not felt) to XII (total destruction).
cards.w: Roman numerals show it is a description of effects, not a measurement. The MSK-64 intensity scale also has 12 grades.

cards.a: Moment magnitude (Mw) is calculated from seismic moment (rock rigidity x fault rupture area x average slip) and does not saturate for very large earthquakes.
cards.w: The Richter scale 'saturates' (stops rising) for giant earthquakes. Mw keeps growing with fault size, so it is the standard scale today.

cards.a: Under IS 1893 (Part 1): 2016, India has four seismic zones - II, III, IV and V - with Zone V the most hazardous. A 2025 revision adding Zone VI was withdrawn in March 2026.
cards.w: The old Zone I was merged into Zone II in 2002. BIS cancelled the 2025 code after objections, so the four-zone map is the one in force (checked 2026).

cards.a: Seismic Zone V of India covers north-east India, the Kashmir valley, parts of Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, north Bihar, the Rann of Kutch and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
cards.w: These lie on or near the Himalayan collision belt, the Kutch rift and the Andaman subduction zone - the places where the Indian plate is most stressed.

cards.a: The whole of Kerala lies in Seismic Zone III (moderate hazard) of the Indian seismic zoning map.
cards.w: Kerala is on the stable peninsular shield, far from the plate boundary, but it still has small tremors along old faults and lineaments.

cards.a: Earthquakes cannot be reliably predicted, so mitigation relies on seismic zoning and microzonation, earthquake-resistant building codes, retrofitting of weak buildings and preparedness drills.
cards.w: Earthquakes do not kill people; collapsing buildings do. Microzonation means mapping a city block by block for how strongly the ground will shake.

cards.a: Liquefaction is the loss of strength of loose, water-saturated sandy soil during earthquake shaking, when rising pore-water pressure makes the soil behave like a liquid.
cards.w: Shaking tries to pack the grains closer, but the water cannot escape quickly. The water takes the load, grains lose contact and buildings sink or tilt.

cards.a: The 1967 Koyna earthquake in Maharashtra is the classic Indian example of reservoir-induced seismicity (earthquakes triggered by filling a large reservoir).
cards.w: The weight of stored water and higher pore pressure in faults below the reservoir help the faults to slip.

cards.a: The Indian Ocean tsunami of 26 December 2004 was generated by a megathrust earthquake (Mw 9.1-9.3) off Sumatra; in Kerala the worst-hit area was Alappad in Kollam district.
cards.w: A megathrust is the huge fault where one plate dives under another. Its sudden slip lifted the sea floor and pushed up the whole water column.

cards.a: Nodal agencies in India: Geological Survey of India for landslides, Central Water Commission for flood forecasting, National Centre for Seismology for earthquake monitoring, and INCOIS (Hyderabad) for tsunami warnings.
cards.w: INCOIS hosts the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre, set up after the 2004 tsunami. Cyclone warnings come from the India Meteorological Department.

cards.a: Main flood types are riverine (fluvial) floods, flash floods, urban (pluvial) floods, coastal floods from storm surges, and outburst floods from glacial lakes or dam failure.
cards.w: Flash floods rise within a few hours of intense rain in steep, small catchments. Urban floods come from blocked or undersized drains and paved ground.

cards.a: Structural flood-control measures include storage reservoirs (dams), embankments or levees, channel improvement, diversion channels and detention basins.
cards.w: Structural means 'build something' to keep water away from people. These works either store the flood, confine it or lead it away.

cards.a: Non-structural flood measures include flood-plain zoning, flood forecasting and warning, flood proofing of buildings, flood insurance and evacuation planning.
cards.w: Non-structural means keeping people away from water instead of water away from people. Flood-plain zoning limits building in areas that flood often.

cards.a: A flood's return period T is the average interval between floods of that size or larger; its probability in any one year is 1/T, so a 100-year flood has a 1% yearly chance.
cards.w: A '100-year flood' can come two years in a row. The name gives the long-term average, not a timetable.

cards.a: The August 2018 Kerala floods were the state's worst since 1924 (the 'flood of 99'); gates of 35 dams were opened and all 14 districts were put on red alert.
cards.w: '99' is the Malayalam Era year 1099, which is 1924 CE. Over 480 people died in 2018 and the Centre declared a 'calamity of severe nature'.

cards.a: Varnes' (1978) classification of slope movements is based on two things: the type of movement and the type of material involved.
cards.w: Name = material + movement, for example 'rock fall', 'debris flow', 'earth slide'. This is the classification used worldwide and by GSI.

cards.a: Varnes' movement types are fall, topple, slide (rotational or translational), lateral spread, flow and complex; materials are rock, debris (coarse soil) and earth (fine soil).
cards.w: Fall = drops through air. Topple = tips forward. Slide = moves on a surface. Spread = stretches sideways. Flow = moves like a thick liquid. Complex = a mix.

cards.a: A rotational slide (slump) moves on a curved, concave-upward (spoon-shaped) surface, common in uniform soils; a translational slide moves on a planar surface such as bedding, joints or the soil-rock contact.
cards.w: Slumps leave a tilted-back block and a curved scarp. Translational slides are common where layers or joints dip out of the slope.

cards.a: The factor of safety of a slope is the ratio of resisting forces (shear strength) to driving forces (shear stress); the slope fails when it falls below 1.
cards.w: Above 1 the slope holds, at 1 it is on the edge, below 1 it moves. Engineers usually design for 1.5 or more.

cards.a: Water is the commonest landslide trigger: infiltrating rain raises pore-water pressure, which lowers effective stress and shear strength, and also adds weight to the slope.
cards.w: Pore pressure pushes grains apart, so friction between them drops. That is why most Indian landslides happen during the monsoon.

cards.a: Human causes of landslides include cutting the toe of a slope for roads and buildings, loading its top, quarrying and blasting, deforestation and blocking natural drainage.
cards.w: Removing the toe takes away the support at the bottom. Loading the top adds push from above. Both lower the factor of safety.

cards.a: Landslide mitigation measures include surface and subsurface drainage, flattening or benching the slope, retaining walls, rock bolts and anchors, soil nailing, shotcrete and vegetation (bioengineering).
cards.w: Drainage is usually the cheapest and most effective fix, because water is the main trigger. Rock bolts pin loose blocks to sound rock.

cards.a: Most Kerala landslides are rain-triggered debris flows in the Western Ghats, locally called 'urul pottal'; all districts except coastal Alappuzha are landslide-prone.
cards.w: Steep slopes, thick weathered soil over hard rock and very heavy monsoon rain combine. The soil cover turns to slurry and rushes down stream channels.

cards.a: Soil piping (tunnel erosion) is subsurface erosion that carves pipe-like cavities in soil; it affects the lateritic highlands of Kerala and was linked to the 2019 Puthumala landslide.
cards.w: Water washes out fine clay below the ground and leaves hidden tunnels. The roof later collapses, causing land subsidence or slope failure.

cards.a: On 30 July 2024 a massive debris flow starting near Punchirimattam devastated Mundakkai and Chooralmala in Meppadi panchayat, Wayanad, killing well over 250 people - Kerala's deadliest landslide.
cards.w: Extreme rain (over 570 mm in 48 hours) soaked the slope. The debris rushed down the Punnappuzha, a tributary of the Chaliyar.

cards.a: On 8 August 2019 two major landslides struck Kerala: Kavalappara in Malappuram district (59 deaths) and Puthumala in Wayanad district (17 deaths).
cards.w: Both came in the same spell of extreme rain. Hook: Kavalappara - Malappuram (Nilambur side), Puthumala - Wayanad (Meppadi side).

cards.a: The Pettimudi landslide of 6 August 2020 in Idukki district, near Eravikulam National Park, buried tea-plantation workers' quarters and took about 70 lives.
cards.w: Pettimudi is in the Munnar hills. The workers were asleep in their line houses (rows of estate quarters) when the debris came down at night.

cards.t: Natural hazards - river and coastal erosion
cards.a: River-bank erosion is strongest on the outer (concave) bank of a meander and is controlled by stone revetment or riprap, spurs (groynes), gabions, guide bunds and bank vegetation.
cards.w: Water flows fastest on the outside of a bend, so it cuts there. Spurs push the fast current away from the bank.

cards.t: Natural hazards - river and coastal erosion
cards.a: Excessive in-stream sand mining lowers the river bed, undermines bridge piers and banks, and lowers the water table in adjoining wells; it can also let salt water move further upstream.
cards.w: The river is 'hungry' after its sand is taken, so it cuts down. Groundwater then drains toward the deeper channel. This is a major problem in Kerala rivers.

cards.t: Natural hazards - river and coastal erosion
cards.a: A seawall is a hard structure built parallel to the shore to stop waves reaching the land; it reflects wave energy, which often scours and removes the beach in front of it.
cards.w: The wall protects what is behind it, not the beach itself. Most of Kerala's eroding coast is lined with rubble-mound seawalls.

cards.t: Natural hazards - river and coastal erosion
cards.a: A groyne is built roughly perpendicular to the shore to trap sand moving along the coast; sand builds up on its updrift side while the downdrift side is starved and erodes.
cards.w: It works like a comb catching longshore drift (sand moved along the beach by slanting waves). It only shifts erosion to the neighbour unless built as a field.

cards.t: Natural hazards - river and coastal erosion
cards.a: A breakwater is an offshore or shore-connected barrier that breaks wave energy to create calm water behind it, protecting harbours and causing sand to deposit in its shelter.
cards.w: Calm water cannot carry sand, so sand settles behind it. A detached breakwater may grow a sand bulge (salient) or a tombolo joining it to the shore.

cards.t: Natural hazards - river and coastal erosion
cards.a: Soft coastal protection includes beach nourishment, dune stabilisation and bioshields such as mangroves, whose dense roots damp wave energy and trap sediment.
cards.w: Soft measures work with nature and do not pass erosion on to the next beach. Mangrove areas are protected as CRZ-I under the CRZ rules.

cards.t: Natural hazards - river and coastal erosion
cards.a: Kerala's coast is about 590 km long and erodes most severely during the south-west monsoon, when high steep waves carry beach sand offshore; beaches partly rebuild in the fair season.
cards.w: Monsoon waves are short and steep and pull sand out to sea. Gentle swell after the monsoon pushes it back. Hard structures and sand mining upset this balance.

cards.t: Natural hazards - river and coastal erosion
cards.a: Mudbanks ('chakara') are calm nearshore patches of sea loaded with fluid mud that appear along the Kerala coast, notably near Alappuzha, during the south-west monsoon and damp the waves.
cards.w: The thick mud soaks up wave energy, so the sea is calm while it is rough elsewhere. The shore behind is protected and fish and prawns gather there.

cards.a: Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) is a study that predicts the environmental effects of a proposed project before a decision is taken; it was first made law by the USA's National Environmental Policy Act (1969).
cards.w: The idea is 'look before you leap'. An EIA report also proposes an Environmental Management Plan to reduce the harm.

cards.a: In India EIA became mandatory through the EIA Notification of 27 January 1994 under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; it was replaced by the EIA Notification of 14 September 2006.
cards.w: The 2006 notification is still the basic rule (with many amendments). A 2020 draft to replace it was widely criticised and has not replaced it.

cards.a: Environmental clearance under the EIA Notification 2006 has four stages in order: screening, scoping, public consultation and appraisal.
cards.w: Screening = is a full EIA needed? Scoping = what must be studied (terms of reference). Public consultation = hearing people. Appraisal = expert scrutiny.

cards.a: Under EIA Notification 2006, Category A projects are cleared by the central Environment Ministry on advice of an Expert Appraisal Committee; Category B projects by the State authority (SEIAA) on advice of the SEAC.
cards.w: Bigger or more risky projects go to Delhi, smaller ones to the State. Category B is split into B1 (EIA report needed) and B2 (not needed).

cards.a: Urbanisation covers the ground with impervious surfaces, which reduces infiltration and groundwater recharge and makes storm hydrographs peak higher and sooner (shorter lag time).
cards.w: Rain cannot soak into concrete, so it runs off fast through drains. Result: more urban flooding and less recharge. Sewage and landfill leachate also pollute shallow groundwater.

cards.t: Anthropogenic activities - open cast mining and quarrying
p: UPSC Civil Services Mains 2024 (Geology Paper II)
cards.a: Opencast mining and quarrying remove vegetation, topsoil and overburden, causing land degradation, dust, noise and blasting vibration, silting of streams and lowering of the water table by pit dewatering.
cards.w: The pit acts like a giant well: pumping it dry forms a cone of depression, so nearby wells and springs can dry up.

cards.t: Anthropogenic activities - open cast mining and quarrying
p: UPSC Civil Services Mains 2013 (Geology Paper II)
cards.a: Acid mine drainage forms when pyrite (FeS2) and other sulphides exposed by mining oxidise in air and water, producing sulphuric acid and dissolved iron; the acid water then leaches heavy metals.
cards.w: Pyrite + oxygen + water = sulphuric acid. Bacteria such as Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans speed it up. Streams turn orange from iron hydroxide ('yellow boy').

cards.t: Anthropogenic activities - open cast mining and quarrying
p: UPSC Civil Services Mains 2013 (Geology Paper II)
cards.a: Acid mine drainage is controlled by keeping sulphide waste away from air and water (sealing or flooding it) and treated by neutralising with limestone or lime, or by constructed wetlands.
cards.w: Limestone raises the pH, so dissolved metals drop out as solids. Prevention is cheaper than treatment, because the acid can keep forming for centuries.

cards.t: Anthropogenic activities - open cast mining and quarrying
cards.a: Mined land is reclaimed by backfilling pits with overburden, re-spreading the stored topsoil and re-vegetating it; Indian mining rules require progressive and final mine closure plans.
cards.w: Topsoil is the living layer, so it is stripped first and kept aside. 'Progressive' closure means restoring worked-out parts while mining continues.

cards.t: Anthropogenic activities - dumping of ores, mine waste and fly-ash
p: UPSC Civil Services Mains 2024 (Geology Paper II)
cards.a: Tailings are the fine waste slurry left after ore is crushed and the valuable mineral is separated; they are stored behind tailings dams and can release heavy metals, cyanide, acid or radioactivity.
cards.w: Fine grain size means a large surface area for chemical reaction. Dam failure or seepage carries the pollutants to rivers and groundwater.

cards.t: Anthropogenic activities - dumping of ores, mine waste and fly-ash
cards.a: Fly ash is the fine residue of pulverised coal burnt in thermal power stations, caught from flue gas by electrostatic precipitators; it consists mainly of silica, alumina, iron oxide and lime.
cards.w: The coarser ash that drops to the furnace floor is bottom ash. Indian coal has high ash content, so the country produces huge amounts of fly ash.

cards.t: Anthropogenic activities - dumping of ores, mine waste and fly-ash
cards.a: Fly ash is pozzolanic (its silica and alumina react with lime and water to form cement-like compounds), so it is used in Portland Pozzolana Cement, bricks, road embankments and mine filling.
cards.w: Using ash as a resource saves land and clay. Unused ash in ponds can leach arsenic, selenium, chromium and boron into groundwater and causes dust.

cards.t: Anthropogenic activities - dumping of ores, mine waste and fly-ash
cards.a: Fly ash is classed as Class F (low lime, from bituminous coal and anthracite, purely pozzolanic) or Class C (high lime, from lignite and sub-bituminous coal, partly self-cementing).
cards.w: C for 'calcium-rich'. Class C can harden with water alone. Class F needs added lime or cement to set.

cards.t: Anthropogenic activities - disposal of industrial and radioactive waste
cards.a: Radioactive waste is grouped as low-level, intermediate-level and high-level; high-level waste from spent fuel reprocessing is small in volume but holds most of the radioactivity and gives off heat.
