cards.w: Low-level waste (gloves, tools, filters) goes to engineered near-surface disposal. High-level waste needs cooling, solidifying and deep disposal.

cards.t: Anthropogenic activities - disposal of industrial and radioactive waste
cards.a: Vitrification immobilises high-level radioactive waste by melting it into borosilicate glass, which is then sealed in steel canisters; India has such plants at Trombay, Tarapur and Kalpakkam.
cards.w: 'Vitri' means glass. Glass is very durable and dissolves extremely slowly in water, so the radioactive atoms stay locked in.

cards.t: Anthropogenic activities - disposal of industrial and radioactive waste
cards.a: A deep geological repository places high-level waste several hundred metres deep in stable, dry, low-permeability rock such as granite, rock salt or clay, using multiple natural and engineered barriers.
cards.w: Barriers: glass, metal canister, bentonite clay packing, then the host rock. Finland's Onkalo, in crystalline bedrock, is the first such repository built for spent fuel.

cards.t: Anthropogenic activities - disposal of industrial and radioactive waste
cards.a: Hazardous industrial waste is placed in secure (engineered) landfills with a compacted clay and plastic (HDPE) liner, a leachate collection system and a cap; leachate is the polluted liquid draining from waste.
cards.w: Rain soaking through waste picks up chemicals, like water through tea leaves. The liner and drains stop this liquid from reaching groundwater.

cards.t: Anthropogenic activities - excess withdrawal of groundwater
cards.a: Excess groundwater withdrawal causes falling water levels, drying of wells and springs, reduced base flow to rivers, higher pumping cost, poorer water quality, sea-water intrusion on coasts and land subsidence.
cards.w: It is like spending more than the income of a bank account. Over-exploited means yearly extraction is more than yearly recharge.

cards.t: Anthropogenic activities - excess withdrawal of groundwater
cards.a: Land subsidence from over-pumping is caused mainly by compaction of compressible clay layers (aquitards) as pore-water pressure falls and effective stress rises; this compaction is largely permanent.
cards.w: Effective stress = total stress minus pore pressure (Terzaghi). Water was helping to carry the load. Once the clay is squeezed, refilling the aquifer does not lift the land back.

cards.t: Anthropogenic activities - excess withdrawal of groundwater
cards.a: Classic examples of land subsidence due to groundwater pumping are Mexico City, the San Joaquin Valley of California, Venice, Bangkok and Jakarta.
cards.w: All sit on thick, soft clay-rich sediments. Mexico City, built on an old lake bed, has sunk by several metres.

cards.t: Anthropogenic activities - excess withdrawal of groundwater
cards.a: At Plachimada in Palakkad district, Kerala, a soft-drink bottling plant was blamed for depleting and polluting local groundwater; after a long public agitation it stopped working in 2004.
cards.w: It became India's best-known case of a community asserting its right over groundwater against an industry.

cards.a: Nitrate from nitrogen fertilisers is highly soluble and is not held by soil, so it leaches easily to groundwater; IS 10500:2012 allows at most 45 mg/L nitrate (as NO3) in drinking water.
cards.w: Nitrate is a negative ion and soil clays are also negatively charged, so they repel it. The WHO guideline is 50 mg/L. Sewage and animal waste are other sources.

cards.a: High nitrate in drinking water causes methaemoglobinaemia ('blue baby syndrome') in infants: nitrate is reduced to nitrite, which changes haemoglobin to methaemoglobin that cannot carry oxygen.
cards.w: Without enough oxygen the baby's skin looks bluish. Bottle-fed infants under about six months are most at risk.

cards.a: Eutrophication is the enrichment of a water body with nutrients, mainly nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilisers and sewage, causing algal blooms whose decay uses up dissolved oxygen and kills fish.
cards.w: Phosphorus is usually the limiting nutrient in fresh water, so a little extra causes a big bloom. Dead algae feed bacteria that consume the oxygen.

cards.a: Organochlorine pesticides such as DDT and endosulfan are persistent and build up in the food chain; aerial spraying of endosulfan on cashew estates in Kasaragod, Kerala, caused severe health damage.
cards.w: They dissolve in fat, not water, so each step up the food chain concentrates them (biomagnification). The Supreme Court banned endosulfan in India in 2011.

cards.t: Organic and inorganic contamination of groundwater
cards.a: Groundwater pollution sources are point sources (a single spot such as a landfill, septic tank, leaking fuel tank or effluent pond) or non-point (diffuse) sources such as farm fertilisers and pesticides.
cards.w: Point sources give a distinct plume that can be traced and cleaned. Diffuse sources pollute large areas at low levels and are much harder to control.

cards.t: Organic and inorganic contamination of groundwater
cards.a: Light non-aqueous phase liquids (LNAPLs) such as petrol and diesel float on the water table, while dense ones (DNAPLs) such as trichloroethylene, PCE and creosote sink to the aquifer base.
cards.w: NAPL = liquid that does not mix with water, like oil. DNAPLs pool in low spots on clay layers and are the hardest contaminants to clean up.

cards.t: Organic and inorganic contamination of groundwater
cards.a: Minamata disease is methylmercury poisoning, first identified in 1956 at Minamata Bay, Japan, where people ate fish and shellfish contaminated by mercury in factory effluent.
cards.w: Bacteria turn mercury into methylmercury, which builds up in fish. It attacks the nervous system: numbness, loss of balance, damaged sight and speech.

cards.t: Organic and inorganic contamination of groundwater
cards.a: Itai-itai disease is cadmium poisoning that occurred along the Jinzu River in Toyama Prefecture, Japan, from zinc-mine waste; it softens bones and damages kidneys.
cards.w: 'Itai-itai' means 'it hurts, it hurts' in Japanese - a memory hook for painful bones. Cadmium entered rice through polluted irrigation water.

cards.t: Organic and inorganic contamination of groundwater
cards.a: Hexavalent chromium, Cr(VI), is the toxic, mobile and cancer-causing form of chromium; in India it is linked with tannery belts such as Kanpur and Ranipet and chromite mining at Sukinda, Odisha.
cards.w: Cr(III) is far less soluble and less harmful. Clean-up therefore aims to convert Cr(VI) to Cr(III).

cards.t: Organic and inorganic contamination of groundwater
cards.a: Coliform bacteria, especially E. coli, are the indicators of faecal contamination of water; shallow open wells close to septic tanks and pit latrines, as in much of Kerala, are most at risk.
cards.w: E. coli lives in the gut, so finding it means sewage has reached the water. Drinking water should have none in a 100 mL sample.

cards.a: In pump-and-treat remediation, contaminated groundwater is pumped out through wells and treated at the surface; it also controls the plume but is slow and works poorly for DNAPLs.
cards.w: Contaminants stuck on grains and in clays bleed out slowly, so concentrations 'tail' and often rebound when pumping stops.

cards.a: A permeable reactive barrier is an underground wall of reactive material, most often zero-valent iron, placed across a plume's path so that groundwater flowing through it is cleaned passively.
cards.w: No pumping is needed: natural flow carries the pollutant through the wall. Iron filings break down chlorinated solvents and convert Cr(VI) to harmless Cr(III).

cards.a: Bioremediation uses microorganisms to break down organic contaminants such as petroleum hydrocarbons; biostimulation adds nutrients or oxygen for native microbes, while bioaugmentation adds selected microbes.
cards.w: The microbes use the pollutant as food. It is cheap and works in place, but not for metals, which cannot be destroyed.

cards.a: Phytoremediation uses plants to remove or lock up contaminants; hyperaccumulators include Indian mustard (Brassica juncea) for lead and cadmium and the brake fern Pteris vittata for arsenic.
cards.w: 'Phyto' means plant. The plants take metals into their shoots, which are then harvested. It is slow and reaches only as deep as the roots.

cards.a: Volatile organic contaminants are removed by soil vapour extraction (vacuum wells in the unsaturated zone), often combined with air sparging (injecting air below the water table).
cards.w: Sparged air bubbles strip the volatile chemicals out of the groundwater. The vapours rise and are sucked out and treated at the surface.

cards.a: Soil erosion by water progresses from splash erosion to sheet erosion, then rill erosion and finally gully erosion; the Chambal ravines are India's best-known gully-eroded badlands.
cards.w: Raindrops loosen soil (splash). Thin flow removes a uniform layer (sheet). Flow gathers into finger-size channels (rills), which deepen into gullies too big to plough across.

cards.a: Soil erosion is controlled by contour ploughing and contour bunds, terracing, strip cropping, cover crops and mulching, check dams in gullies, afforestation, and shelterbelts against wind.
cards.w: All of these slow down water or wind and keep the soil covered. Contour means working across the slope, not up and down it.

cards.a: The Universal Soil Loss Equation is A = R x K x LS x C x P: rainfall erosivity, soil erodibility, slope length-steepness, cover management and conservation practice factors.
cards.w: It estimates average yearly soil loss from sheet and rill erosion. R is about the rain's power, K about how easily the soil detaches.

cards.a: Saline soils have electrical conductivity above 4 dS/m, exchangeable sodium percentage below 15 and pH below 8.5; they show a white salt crust and are reclaimed by leaching with good water and drainage.
cards.w: Called 'white alkali' or reh, kallar, usar. The salts are soluble, so flushing them down below the roots works if drainage is provided.

cards.a: Sodic (alkali) soils have exchangeable sodium percentage above 15 and pH above 8.5; they are reclaimed with gypsum, whose calcium replaces sodium on the clay, followed by leaching.
cards.w: Sodium makes clay disperse, so the soil becomes hard and nearly watertight ('black alkali'). Gypsum is CaSO4.2H2O. Pyrite is an alternative amendment.

cards.a: Canal irrigation without drainage raises the water table, causing waterlogging and secondary salinisation as capillary rise and evaporation leave salts at the surface.
cards.w: Seen in the canal commands of Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan. Remedies: drainage, canal lining, and pumping groundwater along with canal use (conjunctive use).

cards.a: Acid soils are corrected by liming; Kerala's laterite soils are acidic, and the 'kari' soils of Kuttanad are acid sulphate soils that turn extremely acidic when drained and oxidised.
cards.w: Lime (calcium carbonate) neutralises acidity. Kari soils contain pyrite, which makes sulphuric acid on exposure to air - the same chemistry as acid mine drainage.

cards.a: Desertification is land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas caused by climatic variation and human activities; it is addressed by the UN Convention to Combat Desertification (1994).
cards.w: It does not mean deserts marching forward. It means dryland losing its productivity through overgrazing, deforestation, over-cultivation and poor irrigation.

cards.t: Environment protection - legislative measures in India
cards.a: Article 48A (Directive Principle: the State shall protect and improve the environment, forests and wildlife) and Article 51A(g) (citizen's Fundamental Duty to do so) were added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
cards.w: 48A speaks to the State, 51A(g) to the citizen. Courts also read the right to a clean environment into Article 21 (right to life).

cards.t: Environment protection - legislative measures in India
cards.a: The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 protects wild animals and plants and provides for national parks and sanctuaries; its 2022 amendment cut the number of schedules from six to four.
cards.w: It is the oldest of the main environmental Acts. The 2022 amendment also brought in the CITES rules on international trade in endangered species.

cards.t: Environment protection - legislative measures in India
cards.a: The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 was India's first major pollution-control law and created the Central and State Pollution Control Boards.
cards.w: The boards set effluent standards and give 'consent to establish' and 'consent to operate' to industries. The same boards later took on air pollution.

cards.t: Environment protection - legislative measures in India
cards.a: The Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 requires prior approval of the Central Government before any forest land is diverted for non-forest purposes such as mining, dams or industry.
cards.w: Before 1980 States could release forest land on their own, and forests were shrinking fast. The Act put a central check on this.

cards.t: Environment protection - legislative measures in India
cards.a: By the Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act, 2023, in force from 1 December 2023, the 1980 Act was renamed Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980.
cards.w: The name means Forest (Conservation and Augmentation) Act. The amendment also exempted some land, such as strategic projects near the borders.

cards.t: Environment protection - legislative measures in India
cards.a: The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 controls air pollution through the Pollution Control Boards; a 1987 amendment brought noise within the definition of air pollutant.
cards.w: Order of the pollution Acts: Water 1974, then Air 1981, then the umbrella Environment (Protection) Act 1986.

cards.t: Environment protection - legislative measures in India
cards.a: The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, passed after the Bhopal gas tragedy of December 1984, is India's umbrella environmental law; EIA, CRZ and hazardous-waste rules are all issued under it.
cards.w: 'Umbrella' because it lets the Central Government regulate any environmental matter. It was enacted under Article 253 to give effect to the 1972 Stockholm Conference.

cards.t: Environment protection - legislative measures in India
cards.a: Hazardous waste in India was first regulated by rules of 1989, replaced in 2008 and now by the Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016.
cards.w: All were made under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. 'Transboundary movement' (import and export of waste) follows the Basel Convention.

cards.t: Environment protection - legislative measures in India
cards.a: Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) notifications were issued under the Environment (Protection) Act in 1991, 2011 and 2019; they regulate activities on land up to 500 m from the High Tide Line.
cards.w: They also cover a strip along tidal creeks and backwaters, which matters a lot in Kerala. Each new notification replaced the earlier one.

cards.t: Environment protection - legislative measures in India
cards.a: CRZ classes: CRZ-I ecologically sensitive areas (mangroves, corals, intertidal zone), CRZ-II developed urban areas, CRZ-III rural and undeveloped areas, CRZ-IV water area out to 12 nautical miles.
cards.w: In the 2019 notification the No Development Zone is 50 m from the High Tide Line in densely populated rural areas (CRZ-III A) and 200 m in the rest (CRZ-III B).

cards.t: Environment protection - legislative measures in India
cards.a: The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 implements the Convention on Biological Diversity through a three-tier system: National Biodiversity Authority (Chennai), State Biodiversity Boards and local Biodiversity Management Committees.
cards.w: The three levels match Centre, State and local body. The Act also aims at fair sharing of benefits from the use of biological resources.

cards.t: Environment protection - legislative measures in India
cards.a: The Disaster Management Act, 2005 set up the National Disaster Management Authority chaired by the Prime Minister, State authorities chaired by Chief Ministers and District authorities chaired by Collectors.
cards.w: It also created the National Disaster Response Force and the National Institute of Disaster Management. The Act was amended in 2025.

cards.t: Environment protection - legislative measures in India
cards.a: The National Green Tribunal, set up in October 2010 under the NGT Act, 2010, has its principal bench at New Delhi and zonal benches at Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata and Chennai.
cards.w: It is a special fast-track court for environmental cases. It is guided by natural justice, not the Civil Procedure Code, and tries to decide cases within six months.

cards.t: Environment protection - legislative measures in India
cards.a: The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 is the central law for mining; under its Section 15, State Governments make the rules for minor minerals such as building stone, gravel and ordinary sand.
cards.w: Major minerals follow central rules, minor minerals follow State rules. That is why every State has its own Minor Mineral Concession Rules.

cards.t: Environment protection - legislative measures in India
cards.a: The 2015 amendment of the MMDR Act brought in auction of mineral concessions, 50-year mining leases, District Mineral Foundations and the National Mineral Exploration Trust.
cards.w: District Mineral Foundations use money from miners for the welfare of mining-affected people. The 2021 amendment later removed end-use limits on captive mines.

cards.t: Environment protection - legislative measures in India
cards.a: The MMDR Amendment Act, 2023 introduced exploration licences and removed six minerals - lithium, beryllium, niobium, tantalum, titanium and zirconium - from the atomic minerals list, opening them to private miners.
cards.w: These are 'critical minerals' needed for batteries and electronics. The Centre can now auction concessions for critical and strategic minerals.

cards.t: Environment protection - legislative measures in India
cards.a: The Central Ground Water Authority was constituted in 1997 under Section 3(3) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, on the Supreme Court's direction, to regulate and control groundwater development.
cards.w: It issues No Objection Certificates for groundwater extraction by industries and projects. Do not confuse it with CGWB, the scientific survey body.

cards.a: The Kerala Ground Water (Control and Regulation) Act, 2002 set up the State Ground Water Authority; in 'notified areas' a permit is needed to dig a well and existing wells must be registered.
cards.w: A notified area is one where the Government finds that groundwater needs control. The Director of the Ground Water Department is the Authority's secretary.

cards.a: Under the Kerala Ground Water Act, 2002, no one may dig a well within 30 m of a public drinking-water source from which water is pumped, without the Authority's permission.
cards.w: This guards public supply wells from interference by private pumping close by.

cards.a: The Kerala Conservation of Paddy Land and Wetland Act, 2008, in force from 12 August 2008, prohibits conversion or reclamation of paddy land and wetland, monitored by Local Level Monitoring Committees.
cards.w: Paddy fields and wetlands store floodwater and recharge groundwater. The committees keep a 'data bank' listing the paddy land and wetland in each local body.

cards.a: Kerala Protection of River Banks and Regulation of Removal of Sand Act, 2001 regulates river sand mining through Kadavu Committees (chaired by the panchayat president/municipal chairperson) and District Expert Committees (chaired by the District Collector).
cards.w: A 'kadavu' is a sand-removal ghat on the river bank. Sand cannot be taken within 500 m of a bridge or 10 m of the bank.

cards.a: Quarrying of minor minerals in Kerala (granite building stone, laterite, ordinary sand, clay) is governed by the Kerala Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 2015, which replaced the 1967 Rules.
cards.w: The State made these rules under Section 15 of the central MMDR Act, 1957. Permits and leases come from the Department of Mining and Geology.

cards.a: The Western Ghats Ecology Expert Panel under Madhav Gadgil (report of August 2011) proposed treating the entire Western Ghats as ecologically sensitive, graded into three zones (ESZ 1, 2 and 3).
cards.w: It also proposed a Western Ghats Ecology Authority and strict limits on mining and quarrying in the most sensitive zones. States found it too restrictive.

cards.a: The Kasturirangan High Level Working Group (2013) recommended that about 37% of the Western Ghats (about 60,000 sq km) be declared Ecologically Sensitive Area, including 123 villages in Kerala.
cards.w: It was set up to review the Gadgil report and was less strict. It sought a ban on mining, quarrying and sand mining in the sensitive area.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - physical and chemical properties of water
cards.q: Dissolved oxygen is typically lowest in which of these waters?
o: A fast mountain stream over rapids
cards.e: Decay of algae and organic matter in still, nutrient-rich water uses up oxygen. Fast streams are tempting but they re-aerate constantly.

cards.t: Behaviour of minerals and rocks under deformation conditions
cards.q: Which change would make a rock weaker under deformation?
cards.e: Higher temperature makes minerals more ductile and lowers strength. Confining pressure does the opposite because it closes microcracks.

cards.t: Physical, chemical and crystallographic characteristics of common rock forming silicate mineral groups
cards.q: Which property is the main control on whether one ion can replace another in a mineral?
o: Same melting point of the metal
cards.e: A replacing ion must fit the site, so its radius should be close to that of the ion it replaces. Atomic mass has no bearing on fit.

cards.q: Which combustible gas is the main by-product of coalification that stays trapped in coal seams?
cards.e: Methane forms continuously as coal matures and is the gas of coal-bed methane. Carbon monoxide is not a normal coalification product.

cards.q: How is most methane stored in an unmined coal seam?
o: By adsorption on the organic surface of coal
As free gas in large open caves
cards.e: Coal has a huge internal surface where gas molecules adhere. That is why dewatering to drop the pressure is needed to produce coal-bed methane.

cards.q: Which oxide chiefly gives fire clay its refractoriness?
cards.e: High Al2O3 raises the fusion point of the clay. Iron oxide, lime and alkalis act as fluxes and make it melt sooner.

cards.q: Which tungsten mineral is easily spotted in the field with an ultraviolet lamp?
cards.e: Scheelite fluoresces blue-white. Wolframite, the other tungsten ore, does not fluoresce.

cards.q: Which guest molecule stabilises structure II gas hydrate?
cards.e: Propane and isobutane are too large for structure I cages and make structure II. Ethane, carbon dioxide and hydrogen sulphide fit structure I.

cards.q: Taconite is best described as:
o: A banded iron formation of magnetite and chert
cards.e: Taconite is cherty banded iron formation that needs beneficiation. It is low grade, not a high-grade lump ore.

cards.t: Classification and genesis of mineral deposits
cards.q: Which process removes light grains and concentrates heavy minerals in beach placers?
cards.e: Water sorting carries lighter grains away and leaves a heavy-mineral concentrate. Evaporation makes salt deposits, not placers.

cards.q: Polymetallic nodules on the deep sea floor consist mainly of:
o: Concentric layers of manganese and iron oxides
cards.e: Nodules are Mn-Fe oxide crusts that grow around a nucleus. Their value lies in the Ni, Cu and Co they hold.

cards.q: Which ore metal is NOT typically hosted by ultramafic rocks?
cards.e: Tin (cassiterite) is a granite-related metal. Chromite, nickel and PGE come from ultramafic and mafic magmas.

cards.t: Classification and genesis of mineral deposits
cards.q: Which feature of a pegmatite melt favours giant crystals and rare-metal enrichment?
o: Richness in volatiles and incompatible elements
Very low silica and high magnesium
cards.e: Water and fluorine lower viscosity and let rare elements concentrate in the last melt. Pegmatites cool slowly at depth, not quickly at the surface.

cards.t: Classification and genesis of mineral deposits
cards.q: Cyprus-type massive sulphide ore consists mainly of:
cards.e: Cyprus-type VMS is copper-rich, so pyrite plus chalcopyrite dominate. Galena-barite belongs more to lead-zinc types.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.q: In an undeformed succession the beds from top to bottom are sandstone, shale, limestone and conglomerate. Which is oldest?
cards.e: Superposition puts the oldest bed at the base. Folding or overturning would break this rule, but the succession is undeformed.

cards.q: On a map of scale 1:50,000, a distance of 2 cm represents how much on the ground?
cards.e: 2 cm x 50,000 = 100,000 cm = 1 km. Using 1 cm = 0.5 km gives the same result.

cards.q: Which of these volcanic rocks is generally LEAST permeable?
cards.e: Dense rhyolite lacks the open vesicles and rubble zones that make basalt aquifers. The basalt types listed all carry open voids.

cards.q: Which instrument measures soil moisture in the field by neutron scattering?
cards.e: The neutron probe counts neutrons slowed by hydrogen. A lysimeter measures evapotranspiration and an infiltrometer measures infiltration rate.

cards.q: About how much heat is absorbed when 1 g of water evaporates at ordinary temperature?
cards.e: The latent heat of vaporisation is about 590 cal/g near 15 C. The distractors are far off by factors of ten.

cards.t: Specific yield, specific retention, porosity, hydraulic conductivity, transmissivity, storage coefficient
cards.q: Which packing of equal spheres gives the lowest porosity?
cards.e: Rhombohedral packing is the tightest regular arrangement, about 26% voids. Simple cubic is the loosest at about 47.6%.

cards.t: Specific yield, specific retention, porosity, hydraulic conductivity, transmissivity, storage coefficient
cards.q: An aquifer whose hydraulic conductivity is equal in all directions is called:
cards.e: Direction-independence is isotropy. Heterogeneous refers to change from place to place, not direction.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: Which assumption is made in the Bernoulli equation?
o: Fluid density changes freely with pressure
cards.e: Bernoulli's equation treats the fluid as frictionless and incompressible. Viscous losses are exactly what it leaves out.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: In well hydraulics, a sand aquifer ending against thick clay behaves as:
cards.e: Water cannot enter clay at useful rates, so the contact stops flow like a wall. A recharge boundary would add water.

cards.q: How does permeability of crystalline rock generally change with depth?
o: Falls as fractures become fewer and tighter
Is greatest at the base of a deep hole
cards.e: Fractures open near the surface through unloading and weathering and close with depth. This is why shallow weathered and fractured zones give most hard-rock water.

cards.q: Which process after burial mainly reduces the primary porosity of limestone?
cards.e: Calcite cement fills pore spaces. The other three processes open or enlarge voids.

cards.t: Concepts of drainage basin and groundwater basin
cards.q: At a groundwater divide, groundwater:
cards.e: The divide is the high point of the water table, so flow goes down-gradient both ways. Convergence happens at a trough or discharge zone.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: In a steady-state groundwater system the mass of water stored:
cards.e: Steady state means inflow equals outflow, so storage does not change. Unsteady flow involves changing storage.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Types of wells and well construction
cards.q: Which tool is used to make a bored well in soft ground?
cards.e: Bored wells are dug by turning an auger. Percussion and down-the-hole hammers drill hard rock.

cards.q: The SPT N value is the number of hammer blows needed to drive the sampler by:
cards.e: After a 150 mm seating drive the blows for the next two 150 mm increments (300 mm) are added to give N.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: Which device picks up seismic waves in a refraction survey?
cards.e: Geophones convert ground motion to electrical signals. A magnetometer and gravimeter measure fields, not seismic waves.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: A high thermal-neutron capture cross-section in a pulsed-neutron log most likely indicates:
cards.e: Chlorine absorbs thermal neutrons strongly, so salty pore water raises the capture value. Fresh water, dry sand and gas do not.

cards.q: What mainly makes some sandstones poor aquifers?
cards.e: Cement and clay choke the pores and cut permeability. Good sorting, coarse grain and open joints all help yield.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: Electro-osmosis is mainly used to dewater:
cards.e: In very fine soils gravity pumping fails, so an electric field is used to move pore water. Coarse materials drain by ordinary pumping.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - criteria for different uses
cards.q: Which of these diseases is spread mainly through contaminated drinking water?
cards.e: Typhoid is water-borne. Malaria, dengue and filariasis are carried by mosquitoes.

cards.q: What role does aquifer material play when surface water is artificially recharged?
o: It acts as a natural filter
cards.e: Percolation through soil and sand strains out particles and many microbes. Clogging by those particles is the practical limit.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - physical and chemical properties of water
cards.q: In what form is the alkalinity of water usually expressed?
cards.e: Alkalinity is the acid-neutralising capacity and is expressed as equivalent CaCO3. NaCl relates to salinity.

cards.q: Which country extracts the most groundwater in the world?
cards.e: India's irrigation depends heavily on tube wells, putting it first in total abstraction. China and the USA follow.

cards.q: Which landform type does Munnar in Kerala represent?
cards.e: Munnar sits on the high-range plateau of the Western Ghats. Coastal plains and deltas lie near sea level.

cards.s: Stratigraphy: Principles, Dating and Precambrian of India
cards.q: The crystalline basement rocks of Kerala belong mainly to which time span?
cards.e: Charnockites, gneisses and khondalites are Precambrian. Only the thin coastal Tertiary and Quaternary beds are young.

p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Prelims 2021 (Geology Paper II)
cards.q: The nebular hypothesis for the origin of the solar system is associated with which pair of workers?
cards.e: Kant and Laplace proposed that the Sun and planets formed from one rotating cloud of gas and dust. Chamberlin and Moulton gave the planetesimal hypothesis, which needed a passing star.

cards.q: Which one of the following is NOT a terrestrial planet?
cards.e: Neptune is a Jovian (giant, low-density) planet. Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are the small, rocky terrestrial planets.

cards.q: The Widmanstatten pattern is a characteristic feature of:
cards.e: It is an intergrowth of two iron-nickel alloys seen on polished, etched iron meteorites. Chondrites are stony meteorites and show round chondrules instead.

cards.q: The mean density of the Earth as a whole is closest to:
cards.e: The whole Earth averages about 5.5 g/cm3. The value 2.7 g/cm3 is only for continental crust; the large difference points to a dense iron core.

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
cards.q: Which discontinuity marks the boundary between the crust and the mantle?
cards.e: At the Moho, P-wave velocity jumps to about 8 km/s as waves enter mantle peridotite. The Conrad discontinuity lies inside the continental crust, above the Moho.

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Prelims 2021 (Geology Paper II)
cards.q: The Conrad discontinuity separates:
o: Sial from sima within the crust
cards.e: The Conrad discontinuity divides the upper granitic crust (sial) from the lower basaltic crust (sima). The upper-lower mantle boundary is the Repetti discontinuity.

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
cards.q: The strongest seismic evidence that the Earth's outer core is liquid is that:
o: Surface waves are absent over the oceans
Earthquake foci are not found below 700 km
S waves do not pass through the outer core
P waves travel faster in the outer core than in the mantle
cards.e: S waves are shear waves and cannot travel through a liquid, so they stop at the core-mantle boundary. P waves actually slow down, not speed up, on entering the outer core.

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
cards.q: Which scientist is correctly matched with the discovery?
cards.e: Lehmann (1936) showed that a solid inner core exists inside the liquid outer core. Gutenberg is linked to the core-mantle boundary and Mohorovicic to the crust-mantle boundary, so those pairs are swapped.

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
cards.q: The P-wave shadow zone lies at an angular distance from the epicentre of approximately:
cards.e: The liquid outer core bends P waves so that none arrive directly between about 105 and 145 degrees. P waves do reach the far side of the Earth (near 180 degrees) after passing through the core.

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
cards.q: Which statement about seismic waves is correct?
o: S waves are the first to arrive at a seismic station
Love and Rayleigh waves are surface waves
Surface waves travel faster than body waves
cards.e: Love and Rayleigh waves travel along the surface and are the slowest but most damaging. P waves are compressional and arrive first; S waves are the shear waves.

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
cards.q: The seismic low velocity zone (LVZ) of the upper mantle corresponds to the:
cards.e: The LVZ marks the weak, partly molten top of the asthenosphere on which plates move. The outer core also slows P waves but lies far deeper, below 2,900 km.

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
cards.q: Who gave the first seismological evidence for the existence of the Earth's core, in 1906?
cards.e: Oldham, of the Geological Survey of India, showed from delayed waves that a central core exists. Gutenberg came later and fixed the depth of the core boundary at about 2,900 km.

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Mains 2020 (Geology Paper II)
cards.q: The 410 km seismic discontinuity in the mantle is explained by:
o: A change from basaltic to granitic composition
The top of the iron-nickel core
A change from solid rock to liquid
A phase change of olivine to a denser spinel-type structure
cards.e: Rising pressure repacks olivine into a denser crystal structure with the same chemistry, which raises wave speed. The mantle stays solid at this depth; the only liquid layer is the outer core.

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
cards.q: Which is the correct order of abundance (by weight, highest first) of elements in the Earth's crust?
cards.e: The crust is about 46% oxygen, 28% silicon, 8% aluminium and 5% iron. The order iron, oxygen, silicon, magnesium is for the whole Earth, because of the iron core.

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
cards.q: The surface temperature is 20 degrees C and the geothermal gradient is 25 degrees C per km. What is the temperature at a depth of 4 km?
cards.e: Temperature = surface value + gradient x depth = 20 + (25 x 4) = 120 degrees C. The answer 100 forgets to add the surface temperature.

cards.t: Planetary evolution of the earth and its internal structure
cards.q: What is the lithostatic pressure at 10 km depth in crust of density 2,700 kg/m3? (Take g = 10 m/s2.)
cards.e: Pressure = density x g x depth = 2,700 x 10 x 10,000 = 2.7 x 10^8 Pa = 270 MPa. A handy rule is about 27 MPa for every km of crust.

cards.q: Compared with continental crust, oceanic crust is:
cards.e: Oceanic crust is only about 7 km thick, basaltic (about 3.0 g/cm3) and nowhere older than about 180 million years. Continental crust is thicker, lighter and can be billions of years old.

cards.q: The oldest oceanic crust still present in the ocean basins is of about which age?
cards.e: Ocean floor is continually destroyed by subduction, so none older than Jurassic survives. Rocks as old as 3,800 million years are found only on continents.

p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Mains 2020 (Geology Paper II)
cards.q: Which is the correct sequence of an ophiolite suite from bottom to top?
o: Gabbro - peridotite - pillow lava - sheeted dykes - chert
Pillow lava - gabbro - peridotite - sheeted dykes - chert
Peridotite - sheeted dykes - gabbro - deep-sea sediments - pillow lava
Peridotite - gabbro - sheeted dykes - pillow lava - deep-sea sediments
cards.e: An ophiolite is oceanic lithosphere on land: mantle peridotite at the base, then gabbro, then feeder dykes, then pillow lava erupted on the sea floor, capped by sediments. Dykes must lie between the gabbro chamber and the lavas they feed.

cards.t: Major tectonic features of the Oceanic and Continental crust
cards.q: A guyot is best described as a:
o: Rift valley at a ridge crest
Ring-shaped coral reef around a lagoon
Deep linear trough at a subduction zone
cards.e: A guyot is a seamount whose top was planed flat by waves before it sank. A ring-shaped reef is an atoll, which may grow on top of such a sinking volcano.

cards.t: Major tectonic features of the Oceanic and Continental crust
cards.q: Which of the following is a passive (Atlantic-type) continental margin?
cards.e: The east coast of India lies inside the Indian plate, with no trench or volcanoes. The other three face subduction zones and are active margins.

cards.t: Major tectonic features of the Oceanic and Continental crust
cards.q: The Afar region of north-east Africa is a classic example of a:
cards.e: Three spreading arms meet at Afar: the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden and the East African Rift. It is a zone of pulling apart, not collision.

cards.t: Continental drift - geological and geophysical evidence, mechanics, objections, present status
cards.q: In Wegener's theory, the single ocean that surrounded Pangaea was called:
cards.e: Panthalassa ('all sea') was the world ocean around Pangaea. Tethys was the smaller sea that lay between Laurasia and Gondwanaland.

cards.t: Continental drift - geological and geophysical evidence, mechanics, objections, present status
p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Mains 2020 (Geology Paper II)
cards.q: Which fossil plant, found in India, Africa, South America, Australia and Antarctica, is key evidence for Gondwanaland?
cards.e: Glossopteris, a seed fern with tongue-shaped leaves, occurs on all the southern continents. Lepidodendron, Calamites and Sigillaria are typical of the northern coal-swamp flora.

cards.t: Continental drift - geological and geophysical evidence, mechanics, objections, present status
cards.q: In the continental drift debate, the Talchir boulder bed of India is cited as evidence of:
cards.e: The Talchir boulder bed is a glacial deposit (tillite) of Permo-Carboniferous age, matching tillites in the other southern continents. Cretaceous flood basalts in India are the Deccan Traps.

cards.t: Continental drift - geological and geophysical evidence, mechanics, objections, present status
cards.q: Which forces did Wegener himself propose as the cause of continental drift?
cards.e: Wegener used a pole-fleeing force from Earth's rotation and the tidal pull of the Sun and Moon. Jeffreys showed these were far too weak; convection currents were Holmes's later idea.

cards.t: Continental drift - geological and geophysical evidence, mechanics, objections, present status
cards.q: Who first suggested that convection currents in the mantle could move the continents?
cards.e: Holmes proposed mantle convection around 1930 as the engine of drift. Jeffreys was the leading critic of drift, and du Toit supported it with field evidence but not this mechanism.

cards.t: Gravity and magnetic anomalies at Mid-ocean ridges, deep sea trenches, continental shield areas and mountain chains
cards.q: The Bouguer gravity anomaly over a high mountain range such as the Himalaya is typically:
o: Alternately positive and negative in stripes
cards.e: The mountain has a deep root of light crustal rock that replaces dense mantle, giving a mass deficit and a negative Bouguer anomaly. Striped anomalies are magnetic, and are seen on the ocean floor.

cards.t: Gravity and magnetic anomalies at Mid-ocean ridges, deep sea trenches, continental shield areas and mountain chains
p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Mains 2020 (Geology Paper II)
cards.q: Belts of very large negative gravity anomaly, first mapped by Vening Meinesz from a submarine, are found over:
cards.e: Trenches are held down by the sinking plate and are out of isostatic balance, giving the largest negative anomalies. Ridge crests are nearly compensated, so their free-air anomaly is close to zero.

cards.t: Gravity and magnetic anomalies at Mid-ocean ridges, deep sea trenches, continental shield areas and mountain chains
p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Mains 2020 (Geology Paper II)
cards.q: The symmetric, striped magnetic anomalies on either side of mid-ocean ridges were explained in 1963 by:
cards.e: Vine and Matthews linked the stripes to sea-floor spreading plus reversals of the magnetic field. Bullard and Everett are known for the computer fit of the continents.

cards.q: The Curie temperature of magnetite is about:
cards.e: Magnetite loses its permanent magnetism above about 580 degrees C. Basalt lava erupts near 1,100 degrees C, so it becomes magnetised only after it has cooled well below its eruption temperature.

cards.q: A lava flow has a palaeomagnetic inclination I such that tan I = 2. Using tan I = 2 tan (latitude), the palaeolatitude at which it formed is:
cards.e: tan (latitude) = tan I / 2 = 1, so the latitude is 45 degrees. The value 63 degrees is the inclination itself, not the latitude.

cards.q: The present-day interval of normal magnetic polarity is called the:
cards.e: We live in the Brunhes normal chron, which began about 0.78 million years ago. The Matuyama chron just before it had reversed polarity.

cards.q: Apparent polar wander paths drawn from rocks of two continents do not coincide. The accepted explanation is that:
o: The Curie point differs between continents
The continents have moved relative to each other
The Earth had two north magnetic poles at the same time
The rocks were remagnetised by lightning
cards.e: There is only one pole at any time, so different paths mean the continents have shifted. When the continents are put back together the paths merge into one.

cards.q: The sea-floor spreading hypothesis, set out in the 1962 paper 'History of Ocean Basins', was proposed by:
cards.e: Hess proposed that new ocean floor forms at ridges and is consumed at trenches. Wilson is credited with transform faults and hotspots, not this paper.

cards.q: The concept of the transform fault was introduced by:
cards.e: Wilson defined transform faults in 1965 as faults that link offset ridge segments or trenches. Dietz is remembered for coining the term 'sea-floor spreading'.

p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Mains 2020 (Geology Paper II)
cards.q: Which of the following is a conservative (transform) plate boundary?
cards.e: Along the San Andreas Fault the Pacific and North American plates slide past each other, and crust is neither made nor destroyed. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is constructive and the Mariana Trench is destructive.

cards.q: Which feature is the result of ocean-ocean plate convergence?
cards.e: The Marianas form where the Pacific plate sinks beneath another oceanic plate. The Andes are ocean-continent, and the Himalaya continent-continent, convergence.

cards.q: Which force is considered the most important in driving plate motion?
cards.e: The cold dense slab sinking at a trench pulls the plate behind it; plates with long subducting edges move fastest. Ridge push helps but is much weaker.

cards.q: In the Wilson cycle, the Red Sea represents which stage?
o: Mature stage (wide ocean with passive margins)
cards.e: The Red Sea is a narrow new ocean with a young spreading centre. The embryonic stage, before any ocean floor forms, is shown by the East African Rift.

p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Prelims 2021 (Geology Paper II)
cards.q: 'Black smokers' found along mid-ocean ridges are:
o: Hydrothermal vents discharging hot, metal sulphide-rich water
Mud volcanoes on the accretionary prism
Plumes of methane gas from decaying sediments
cards.e: Hot water that has circulated through new crust carries dissolved metals; sulphides fall out as black particles when it meets cold sea water. They are hot-water vents, not ash eruptions.

cards.t: Island arcs, Oceanic islands and volcanic arcs
cards.q: The Wadati-Benioff zone is characteristic of which tectonic setting?
cards.e: It is the sloping band of earthquake foci that traces a sinking slab down to about 700 km. Ridges and rifts have only shallow earthquakes.

cards.t: Island arcs, Oceanic islands and volcanic arcs
cards.q: Which volcanic rock is most typical of volcanic arcs above subduction zones?
cards.e: Arc magmas are typically andesitic (calc-alkaline); the rock is named after the Andes. Kimberlite and carbonatite belong to stable continental interiors and rifts.

cards.t: Island arcs, Oceanic islands and volcanic arcs
cards.q: Going from the open ocean towards the overriding plate, the correct order of features in an arc-trench system is:
o: Trench - accretionary prism - fore-arc basin - volcanic arc - back-arc basin
Back-arc basin - trench - volcanic arc - fore-arc basin - accretionary prism
Accretionary prism - trench - back-arc basin - volcanic arc - fore-arc basin
Trench - volcanic arc - accretionary prism - back-arc basin - fore-arc basin
cards.e: Sediment scraped off at the trench builds the prism; the fore-arc basin lies between the prism and the arc; the back-arc basin lies behind the arc. 'Fore' means in front of the arc, on the trench side.

cards.t: Island arcs, Oceanic islands and volcanic arcs
cards.q: In the Hawaiian island chain the volcanoes become older towards the northwest. This shows that:
o: The chain is an island arc above a subduction zone
The hotspot is moving northwest under a fixed plate
A spreading ridge runs along the chain
The Pacific plate is moving northwest over a nearly fixed hotspot
cards.e: The plume stays nearly fixed; the plate carries each old volcano away to the northwest while a new one forms over the plume. An island arc would lie beside a trench and would be active all along its length.

cards.t: Island arcs, Oceanic islands and volcanic arcs
cards.q: India's only active volcano is located at:
cards.e: Barren Island in the Andaman Sea has erupted in recent decades. Narcondam is a dormant volcano nearby, and Baratang has only mud volcanoes.

cards.q: The term 'isostasy' was coined by:
cards.e: Dutton introduced the word in 1889. Airy and Pratt had put forward their models earlier, in the 1850s, but did not use this name.

cards.q: Which statement correctly describes Airy's model of isostasy?
o: Blocks have different densities and a common base level
Blocks have the same density and different thickness, so mountains have roots
The crust is rigid and is not compensated at depth
Mountains are supported only by the strength of the lithosphere
cards.e: Airy pictured equal-density blocks floating at different depths, like icebergs, so higher mountains have deeper roots. Different densities with a common base level is Pratt's model.

cards.q: Which of the following best describes an epeirogenic movement?
o: Intense folding and thrusting in a narrow belt
Horizontal sliding of plates along a transform fault
Sudden slip on a fault during an earthquake
Broad, gentle uplift or subsidence of a large region without significant folding
cards.e: Epeirogeny is slow vertical movement of large areas that leaves beds almost flat. Intense folding and thrusting in a narrow belt is orogeny.

p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Prelims 2021 (Geology Paper II)
cards.q: Which orogeny is correctly matched with its time?
cards.e: The Caledonian orogeny belongs to the early Palaeozoic (Ordovician-Silurian, ending in the early Devonian). The Hercynian is late Palaeozoic and the Alpine-Himalayan is Cenozoic.

cards.q: About what share of the world's earthquake energy is released in the Circum-Pacific belt?
cards.e: The Pacific is ringed by subduction zones, which release roughly four-fifths of all seismic energy. The figure of about 15% belongs to the Alpine-Himalayan belt.

cards.q: Deep-focus earthquakes (focal depth more than 300 km) are confined to:
cards.e: Only a cold sinking slab stays brittle enough to break at such depths. Ridges, rifts and transform faults have shallow earthquakes only.

cards.q: The elastic rebound theory of the origin of earthquakes was proposed by:
cards.e: Reid developed it from ground movements along the San Andreas Fault after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake. Richter devised the magnitude scale and Mercalli an intensity scale.

cards.q: Roughly how many times more energy does a magnitude 7 earthquake release than a magnitude 5 earthquake?
cards.e: Each magnitude unit means about 32 times more energy, so two units give 32 x 32, about 1,000 times. The figure 100 times is the increase in wave amplitude, not energy.

p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Prelims 2021 (Geology Paper II)
cards.q: The largest earthquakes on Earth (magnitude 9 and above) occur on:
o: Normal faults at mid-ocean ridge crests
Megathrusts between subducting and overriding plates
cards.e: The plate contact at a subduction zone is a huge, gently dipping fault, and a larger rupture area gives a larger earthquake. Ridge and transform earthquakes are shallow and much smaller.

cards.q: The collision of the Indian plate with the Eurasian plate began about:
cards.e: India met Eurasia about 50 million years ago, closing the Tethys Sea. In the Jurassic, India was still part of Gondwanaland in the southern hemisphere.

p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Mains 2020 (Geology Paper II)
cards.q: The Deccan Traps and the Chagos-Laccadive Ridge are linked to which hotspot?
cards.e: India passed over the Reunion hotspot about 66 million years ago, producing the Deccan Traps and then the Chagos-Laccadive track. Kerguelen is linked to the Rajmahal Traps and the Ninetyeast Ridge.

cards.q: The Deccan Trap volcanism is dated close to:
cards.e: The main Deccan eruptions fall at the Cretaceous-Palaeogene boundary, about 66 million years ago. The date of about 117 million years is for the Rajmahal Traps.

p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Prelims 2021 (Geology Paper II)
cards.q: Which structure marks the suture between the Indian and Eurasian plates?
cards.e: The Indus-Tsangpo Suture Zone carries ophiolites, the remains of the Tethys ocean floor, along the line of collision. The Main Central and Main Boundary Thrusts lie south of it, inside the Indian plate.

cards.q: Which thrust separates the Siwalik rocks from the Lesser Himalaya?
cards.e: The Main Boundary Thrust carries Lesser Himalayan rocks southward over the Siwaliks. The Himalayan Frontal Thrust lies further south, between the Siwaliks and the plains.

cards.q: The western boundary of the Indian plate on land is marked by the:
cards.e: The Chaman Fault in Pakistan and Afghanistan is a left-lateral transform boundary between the Indian and Eurasian plates. The Sagaing Fault lies on the eastern side, in Myanmar.

cards.q: As of March 2026, how many seismic zones does the BIS code in force in India (IS 1893 Part 1: 2016) recognise?
cards.e: The 2016 code has Zones II, III, IV and V; Zone I was merged into Zone II in 2002. A 2025 revision with a new Zone VI was withdrawn by BIS on 3 March 2026.

cards.q: Under the seismic zoning map of IS 1893 (Part 1): 2016, the State of Kerala falls in:
cards.e: Kerala lies on the stable Peninsular shield and is placed in Zone III (moderate hazard). Zone V is kept for the Himalayan belt, the north-east, Kutch and the Andaman-Nicobar Islands.

cards.q: Which Indian earthquake is the classic example of reservoir-induced seismicity?
cards.e: The Koyna earthquake followed the filling of the Koyna dam reservoir in Maharashtra. Latur was also in Maharashtra and intraplate, but no large reservoir was involved.

cards.q: The 'Allah Bund', a ridge raised across the Rann of Kutch, was formed by the earthquake of:
cards.e: The 1819 Kutch earthquake lifted a long low ridge that dammed a branch of the Indus. The 2001 Bhuj earthquake struck the same region but did not create the Allah Bund.

cards.q: Three of these earthquakes occurred along the Himalayan plate boundary. Which one was an intraplate earthquake in the Peninsular shield?
cards.e: Latur (Killari), Maharashtra, lies deep inside the stable Indian shield. Kangra, Bihar-Nepal and Assam were all caused by the India-Eurasia collision along the Himalaya.

cards.q: The 2004 Sumatra-Andaman earthquake that caused the Indian Ocean tsunami occurred at a:
o: Divergent boundary on the Carlsberg Ridge
Transform boundary along the Chaman Fault
Subduction zone where the Indian plate goes beneath the Burma plate
cards.e: It was a megathrust earthquake (Mw 9.1-9.3) on the Sunda-Andaman subduction zone, which lifted the sea floor. Ridge and transform earthquakes are too small and move the sea floor too little to raise such a tsunami.

cards.q: The plumb-line deflection discrepancy that led Pratt to the idea of compensation beneath the Himalaya was found between which two survey stations of India?
cards.e: In Everest's survey the measured deflection between Kalianpur and Kaliana (near the Himalayan foothills) was 5.24 seconds, against 15.89 seconds calculated by Pratt. The other pairs are well-known survey towns but were not the stations in this problem.

cards.q: In Airy's model, crust has a density of 2.7 g/cm3 and mantle 3.3 g/cm3. A plateau standing 2 km above sea level needs a crustal root of about:
cards.e: Root = height x crust density / (mantle density - crust density) = 2 x 2.7 / 0.6 = 9 km. The value 4.5 is only the ratio (root per km of height), not the root itself.

cards.q: The Brunhes-Matuyama reversal (0.78 million years old) is recorded 15.6 km from a ridge axis on each side. The half-spreading rate of this ridge is:
cards.e: Rate = distance / time = 15.6 km / 0.78 million years = 20 km per million years = 2 cm/year. The value 4 cm/year is the full rate (both sides added), not the half rate.

cards.t: Island arcs, Oceanic islands and volcanic arcs
cards.q: An extinct volcano on a hotspot track is 5 million years old and lies 400 km from the active volcano over the hotspot. The average speed of the plate over the hotspot is:
cards.e: Speed = 400 km / 5 million years = 80 km per million years = 8 cm/year (1 km per million years = 0.1 cm/year). The value 80 cm/year forgets this unit conversion.

cards.q: Across an ocean basin, the highest heat flow is measured over:
o: Abyssal plains on old sea floor
cards.e: Hot mantle rises and new crust forms at the ridge crest, so heat flow is highest there and falls with age. Trenches have very low heat flow because a cold slab is sinking.

p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Prelims 2021 (Geology Paper II)
cards.q: 'Trench rollback' at a subduction zone means that:
o: The plate reverses its direction of motion
The subducted slab rises back to the surface at the ridge
The overriding plate is thrust over the volcanic arc
The trench and slab hinge retreat towards the subducting-plate side
cards.e: A heavy slab sinks steeply and its hinge migrates backwards, towards the ocean it is consuming. This stretches the upper plate and opens back-arc basins; the plate does not reverse direction.

cards.q: Which hypothesis of the origin of the solar system does NOT need a second star?
o: Planetesimal hypothesis of Chamberlin and Moulton
Nebular hypothesis of Kant and Laplace
Binary star hypothesis of Russell and Lyttleton
Tidal hypothesis of Jeans and Jeffreys
cards.e: The nebular hypothesis builds the Sun and planets from one rotating cloud. The planetesimal and tidal hypotheses need a passing star, and the binary star hypothesis needs a companion star of the Sun.

cards.q: The Earth's equatorial radius is longer than its polar radius by about:
cards.e: The equatorial radius is about 6,378 km and the polar radius about 6,357 km, a difference of about 21 km. The bulge is real but small, only about 1 part in 300.

cards.q: What is the minimum number of seismograph stations needed to fix an earthquake epicentre from S-P time intervals?
cards.e: Each station gives only its distance from the earthquake, which is a circle on the map. Two circles cross at two points; a third circle picks the correct one.

cards.q: P waves travel at 7 km/s and S waves at 4 km/s. If the S wave arrives 30 seconds after the P wave, how far is the station from the earthquake?
cards.e: Time gap = d/4 - d/7 = 3d/28 = 30 s, so d = 280 km (S takes 70 s, P takes 40 s). The value 210 km wrongly multiplies the P speed by the time gap.

cards.q: In November 2025 BIS notified IS 1893 (Part 1): 2025, with a new highest-hazard Zone VI along the Himalayan arc. What was the status of this revision in March 2026?
o: In force across India with six zones numbered I to VI
In force only in the Himalayan States
Replaced by one uniform zone for the whole country
Withdrawn; the 2016 code with Zones II to V applies again
cards.e: BIS withdrew the 2025 revision in March 2026 after objections on cost and consultation, and the 2016 code with four zones (II to V) applies again. Zone VI is therefore not in force; recheck the status before the exam.

cards.q: In IS 1893 (Part 1): 2016, the zone factor (Z) for Seismic Zone V is:
cards.e: The zone factors rise with hazard: 0.10 (Zone II), 0.16 (Zone III), 0.24 (Zone IV) and 0.36 (Zone V). Kerala, in Zone III, has 0.16.

cards.q: The eastern syntaxis (sharp bend) of the Himalaya is located at:
cards.e: The Himalaya bends sharply around Namcha Barwa in the east, where the Tsangpo turns south. Nanga Parbat marks the western syntaxis, so it is the tempting wrong choice.

cards.q: The South Tibetan Detachment (STD), a north-dipping normal fault, separates the:
o: Greater Himalayan crystalline rocks from the Tethys Himalayan sediments
Tethys Himalaya from the Ladakh batholith
cards.e: The STD lies at the top of the Greater Himalayan crystallines, below the Tethyan sedimentary rocks. The Lesser Himalaya-Siwalik contact is the Main Boundary Thrust, which is a thrust, not a normal fault.

cards.q: In Kober's geosynclinal theory, a 'Zwischengebirge' is a:
o: Chain of volcanoes along the edge of a continent
Rigid foreland block bordering the geosyncline
Deep trough in front of a rising mountain chain
Median mass (plateau) lying between two marginal mountain ranges
cards.e: Kober called the less-folded block between two marginal ranges the Zwischengebirge or median mass; the Tibetan Plateau is the usual example. His rigid foreland blocks are 'kratogen'.

cards.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the seven major lithospheric plates?
cards.e: The Nazca plate, off the west coast of South America, is a smaller plate. The seven major plates are the Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian and Antarctic.

cards.q: Which sequence lists the geomagnetic polarity chrons correctly from youngest to oldest?
cards.e: The present normal chron is Brunhes; before it came Matuyama (reversed), Gauss (normal) and Gilbert (reversed). The sequence starting with Gilbert is the same list but oldest first.

cards.t: Island arcs, Oceanic islands and volcanic arcs
cards.q: Iceland is unusual among oceanic islands because it:
o: Is a fragment of old continental crust
Is an island arc above a subduction zone
Is a coral atoll built on a sunken volcano
Lies on a mid-ocean ridge that is also above a hotspot
cards.e: Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge over a mantle plume, so extra lava has built the ridge above sea level. There is no trench or subduction near Iceland, so it is not an island arc.

cards.q: The 'central seismic gap' of the Himalaya lies between the rupture zones of which two great earthquakes?
cards.e: The stretch between the Kangra and Bihar-Nepal ruptures (Uttarakhand to western Nepal) has not broken in a great earthquake for centuries. Latur and Bhuj are not Himalayan earthquakes at all.

cards.t: Island arcs, Oceanic islands and volcanic arcs
cards.q: Magma beneath a volcanic arc is generated mainly because:
o: Friction melts the base of the overriding crust
Water released from the subducting slab lowers the melting point of the mantle wedge
Mantle rises and decompresses beneath a spreading centre
The slab melts completely when it reaches the core
cards.e: At about 100 to 150 km depth the slab gives off water, which makes the hot mantle above it melt (flux melting). Decompression melting is the cause at mid-ocean ridges, not at arcs.

cards.t: Major tectonic features of the Oceanic and Continental crust
cards.q: The three mid-ocean ridges of the Indian Ocean meet at the:
cards.e: The Central Indian, Southwest Indian and Southeast Indian Ridges join at the Rodrigues Triple Junction. Afar is on land in Africa; Bouvet and Azores are in the Atlantic.

cards.t: Gravity and magnetic anomalies at Mid-ocean ridges, deep sea trenches, continental shield areas and mountain chains
cards.q: Which statement about gravity anomalies is correct?
o: Deep-sea trenches show the largest positive free-air anomalies on Earth
Bouguer anomalies are strongly positive over high mountain ranges
Bouguer anomalies are strongly negative over deep ocean basins
Old stable shields are close to isostatic balance and show small isostatic anomalies
cards.e: Shields have had a very long time to reach floating balance, so their isostatic anomalies are near zero. Bouguer anomalies are negative over mountains and positive over oceans, and trenches show large negative free-air anomalies.

cards.q: The gently dipping plate-contact fault beneath the Himalaya, into which the frontal, boundary and central thrusts merge at depth and which ruptured in the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, is the:
cards.e: The Main Himalayan Thrust is the basal decollement (sliding surface) along which India goes under the Himalaya. The Karakoram Fault is a strike-slip fault and the Great Boundary Fault is in Rajasthan.

cards.q: The ocean floor becomes deeper away from a mid-ocean ridge mainly because:
o: The weight of sediment pushes the old crust down
The lithosphere cools, contracts and becomes denser with age
The spreading rate falls with distance from the ridge
Old basalt is slowly dissolved by sea water
cards.e: New lithosphere is hot and buoyant; as it ages it cools, thickens and sinks, so depth grows roughly with the square root of age. Sediment adds some load but is far too thin to explain 3 km of deepening.

cards.q: According to Goldich's stability series, which of these minerals breaks down first under chemical weathering at the Earth's surface?
cards.e: Olivine forms at the highest temperature, so it is the least stable at the surface. Quartz is the tempting wrong pick, but it is the most resistant mineral in the series.

cards.q: Large rounded exfoliation domes in granite are produced mainly by
o: growth of salt crystals in pores
pressure release as the overlying rock is removed
cards.e: Granite formed under load expands when the load is eroded away, and sheets split off parallel to the surface. Salt crystal growth breaks rock too, but it gives small pits and flakes, not domes.

cards.q: In a soil profile, clay and iron washed down from above collect mainly in the
cards.e: The B horizon is the zone of illuviation (washing in). The E horizon is the opposite: it is the leached zone that loses clay and iron.

cards.q: Which of the following is NOT one of Jenny's five soil-forming factors?
cards.e: The five factors are climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time. Soil texture is a property of the soil that results from these factors; it is not a factor itself.

cards.q: Francis Buchanan first used the name 'laterite' (1807) for material he saw at
cards.e: Buchanan described and named the brick-like rock at Angadipuram, where GSI now has a National Geological Monument. Varkala is famous for its cliff section, not for the naming of laterite.

cards.q: Which statement about laterite is correct?
o: It forms by evaporation of saline groundwater in arid climates
It is a wind-blown silt deposit of dry regions
It is a chemical precipitate laid down on shallow sea floors
It is a residual product left after strong leaching of silica and bases in a hot, seasonally wet climate
cards.e: Laterite is what remains in place when tropical rain leaches silica and bases and leaves iron and aluminium oxides. It is not linked to arid climates; evaporation in dry regions gives caliche and salt crusts instead.

cards.q: The deep shrinkage cracks of regur (black cotton soil) in the dry season are due to its high content of
cards.e: Montmorillonite takes water between its layers, so it swells when wet and shrinks strongly when dry. Kaolinite has a fixed structure and shows very little swelling.

cards.q: In the Indo-Gangetic plain the term 'bhangar' refers to
o: the marshy belt where buried streams re-emerge
the pebbly porous belt at the foot of the Himalaya
the newer alluvium of the present flood plains
the older alluvium above flood level, containing kankar
cards.e: Bhangar is old alluvium on higher ground with lime nodules (kankar). The newer flood-plain alluvium is khadar; the pebbly belt is bhabar and the marshy belt is terai.

cards.q: Under very strong leaching in a well-drained humid tropical site, the aluminium-rich mineral that finally remains is
cards.e: With extreme leaching even the silica of clay is removed, leaving aluminium hydroxide (gibbsite), the main mineral of bauxite. Montmorillonite forms at the other end, where drainage is poor and leaching is weak.

cards.q: Tilted electric poles, curved tree trunks and down-bent ends of steeply dipping beds on a hillside indicate
cards.e: Creep is too slow to see, so it is known from its long-term effects on fixed objects. A slump also tilts things, but it leaves a clear curved scarp and a displaced block.

cards.q: A slope failure in which the block rotates backward along a curved, spoon-shaped surface is a
cards.e: Rotation on a concave-up surface defines a slump. A translational slide moves on a flat plane such as a bedding surface and the block does not tilt back.

cards.q: Prolonged heavy rain most commonly triggers a landslide because it
o: increases the angle of internal friction
increases the pore-water pressure and so reduces shear strength
increases the cohesion of the soil
reduces the weight of the slope material
cards.e: Water filling the pores pushes grains apart, lowering effective stress and shear strength. Rain actually adds weight and lowers cohesion, so the other options are the reverse of what happens.

cards.q: Solifluction is most typical of which environment?
cards.e: The thawed top layer becomes soaked because water cannot drain into the frozen ground below, and it flows slowly downslope. Tropical slopes fail too, but mainly by debris flows and slides.

cards.q: Peltier's morphogenetic regions are defined on the basis of
o: mean annual temperature and mean annual rainfall
cards.e: Peltier (1950) plotted temperature against rainfall to mark nine regions, each with its own dominant processes. Rock type and structure matter for landforms, but they are not part of his climatic scheme.

cards.q: The same bed of limestone forms a bold cliff in one region and a low valley in another. The cliff is most likely in a region that is
cards.e: Limestone is destroyed mainly by solution, which needs plenty of water. In a dry climate it resists erosion better than other rocks, so it stands out as cliffs.

cards.q: 'Landscape is a function of structure, process and stage' is the central statement of
cards.e: This trio is the basis of Davis's geographical cycle (1899). Penck rejected 'stage' and stressed the ratio between uplift and erosion instead.

cards.q: Which pairing of a geomorphologist with the planation surface of his model is correct?
cards.e: Davis's cycle ends in a peneplain. The others are mixed up: King - pediplain, Crickmay - panplain, Wayland - etchplain.

cards.q: Which statement best represents Walther Penck's view of landform development?
o: Landscapes pass through youth, maturity and old age in fixed order
Landform shape depends on the ratio between the rate of uplift and the rate of erosion
Plains are formed chiefly by sideways cutting of rivers
Erosion begins only after rapid uplift is complete
cards.e: Penck said uplift and erosion work at the same time, and their ratio decides whether slopes are convex, straight or concave. The first two options are Davis's ideas, which Penck opposed.

cards.q: A landscape of wide rock-cut pediments joined into one plain, with scattered steep-sided inselbergs, is the end product of the cycle proposed by
cards.e: This is King's pediplain, made by parallel retreat of scarps in semi-arid lands. Davis's end product is a peneplain with monadnocks, formed by wearing down, not wearing back.

cards.q: Knickpoints, incised meanders and paired terraces along a river are evidence of
cards.e: Uplift or a fall in base level gives the river fresh energy to cut down into its old valley. Aggradation (building up of the bed) is the opposite process and buries such features.

cards.q: The idea that landforms keep a near-steady shape because erosional processes and rock resistance are balanced, regardless of 'stage', was put forward in 1960 by
cards.e: This is Hack's dynamic equilibrium concept, a time-independent model. Davis is the tempting wrong answer, but his model is exactly the stage-based one that Hack rejected.

cards.q: A point bar is deposited
o: on the outer concave bank of a meander
at the foot of a waterfall
on the inner convex bank of a meander
where a river enters the sea
cards.e: Flow is slowest on the inside of a bend, so sand is dropped there as a point bar. The outer bank has the fastest flow and is eroded into a cut bank.

cards.q: Which set of conditions most favours a braided river pattern?
o: Fine suspended load, steady discharge and cohesive clay banks
Very low sediment load and a gentle slope
A bedrock channel with almost no sediment
Abundant coarse bed load, highly variable discharge and easily eroded banks
cards.e: A river overloaded with coarse sediment drops bars and splits around them. Fine load with cohesive banks gives a single meandering channel instead.

cards.q: Low ridges of silt and fine sand that run along both banks of a river and slope gently away into backswamps are
cards.e: Flood water leaving the channel slows suddenly and drops its coarsest load right at the bank, building levees. Terraces are old valley floors left high by downcutting, not flood deposits on the bank.

cards.q: Which river has the classic bird-foot delta?
cards.e: The Mississippi builds long finger-like distributary channels into a quiet gulf. The Nile and Ganga-Brahmaputra deltas are arcuate and the Tiber delta is cuspate.

cards.q: Which of these rivers of Kerala does NOT flow east?
cards.e: Pamba flows west into Vembanad lake. Kerala's three east-flowing rivers are Kabani, Bhavani and Pambar; the similar name Pambar is the trap.

cards.q: The longest river of Kerala is the
cards.e: Periyar is 244 km long. Bharathapuzha (209 km) is second, which makes it the most tempting wrong choice.

cards.q: In the standard three-fold physiographic division of Kerala, the midland lies between elevations of
cards.e: Lowland is below 7.5 m, midland is 7.5 to 75 m, and highland is above 75 m. The midland is the belt of laterite hills and valleys.

cards.q: Which statement about a barchan is correct?
o: Its horns point upwind and are fixed by vegetation
Its horns point downwind and it forms where sand is limited and wind direction is steady
It forms where winds blow from many directions
It is a long straight ridge parallel to the wind
cards.e: A barchan is a crescent dune with horns pointing downwind. Horns pointing upwind and held by plants describe a parabolic dune, the usual confusion.

cards.q: A pebble with three flat, polished faces meeting at sharp edges (dreikanter) is shaped by
cards.e: Dreikanters are ventifacts, cut by wind-driven sand. Glacial stones are also faceted, but they carry scratches (striations) and are not wind-polished.

cards.q: Which one of the following is a depositional feature of wind?
cards.e: Loess is wind-laid silt. Yardangs and zeugen are carved by wind abrasion and a deflation hollow is scooped out by wind, so all three are erosional.

cards.q: A gently sloping surface cut across bedrock at the foot of a desert mountain, with only a thin cover of gravel, is a
cards.e: A pediment is an erosional rock surface. The bajada lies beyond it and looks similar, but it is built of thick merged alluvial fans, so it is depositional.

cards.q: A sand bar that ties an offshore island to the mainland is a
cards.e: A tombolo joins an island to the shore. A spit is joined to land at one end only and its other end lies free in the water.

cards.q: Which is the correct order of development of erosional features on a rocky headland?
cards.e: Waves first hollow a cave, the cave cuts through to make an arch, the arch roof falls to leave a stack, and the stack is worn down to a stump.

cards.q: A ria coast indicates
o: submergence of a coast cut by river valleys
emergence of a smooth sea floor
cards.e: Rias are river valleys drowned by a rise in sea level, so they show submergence. Drowned glacial troughs are fjords, which are deeper and steep-walled.

cards.q: The backwaters (kayals) of Kerala are best described as
o: lagoons and estuaries enclosed behind barrier beaches and spits
tectonic rift lakes along a coastal fault
oxbow lakes left by west-flowing rivers
cards.e: Longshore drift built sand barriers parallel to the coast and trapped lagoons behind them, giving a barrier-lagoon coast. They are not river cut-offs, although many rivers drain into them.

cards.q: The largest freshwater lake of Kerala is
cards.e: Sasthamkotta in Kollam district is the largest freshwater lake. Vembanad is the largest lake overall, but it is a brackish backwater.

cards.q: Which sequence arranges karst depressions from smallest to largest?
cards.e: A doline is a single sinkhole, dolines merge into an uvala, and a polje is a very large flat-floored closed basin. Hook: D-U-P.

cards.q: Which karst feature is a surface of small solution grooves and ridges on bare limestone, and not a closed depression?
cards.e: Lapies (karren) are fluted, grooved rock surfaces. Doline, uvala and polje are all closed hollows of increasing size.

cards.q: A calcite deposit that grows upward from the floor of a limestone cave is a
cards.e: Stalagmites rise from the ground (G for ground). Stalactites hang from the ceiling (C for ceiling) and are the usual mix-up.

cards.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a roche moutonnee from a drumlin?
o: Roche moutonnee is laid by meltwater; drumlin is carved by wind
Roche moutonnee is made of till; drumlin is made of bedrock
Roche moutonnee is eroded bedrock with its steep side down-ice; drumlin is deposited till with its steep side up-ice
Both have their steep side facing up-ice
cards.e: A roche moutonnee is erosional, with a plucked steep lee side. A drumlin is depositional, with its blunt steep end facing the oncoming ice, so the two are opposite in asymmetry.

cards.q: A pyramidal peak (horn) such as the Matterhorn forms when
o: a tributary glacier valley is left high above the main trough
a glacier overrides a resistant rock knob
three or more cirques cut back into the same mountain
two valley glaciers join below a spur
cards.e: Headward erosion of cirques from several sides leaves a sharp pointed peak. Two cirques back to back give only a knife-edged ridge, the arete.

cards.q: A long, winding ridge of layered sand and gravel deposited by a meltwater stream flowing in a tunnel under a glacier is
cards.e: Eskers are sorted, stratified stream deposits that follow the old tunnel path. A lateral moraine is also a ridge, but it is unsorted till along the valley side.

cards.q: Which one of the following is NOT a landform of glaciated regions?
cards.e: An uvala is a karst depression made by merging sinkholes. Cirque and hanging valley are glacial erosional forms and a drumlin is a glacial deposit.

cards.q: A trellis drainage pattern indicates
o: folded or tilted beds of alternating hard and soft rock
cards.e: Long streams follow the soft beds along strike and short tributaries join them at right angles from the hard ridges. Uniform horizontal beds give a dendritic pattern.

cards.q: Streams flowing inward from all sides toward a central depression form which drainage pattern?
cards.e: Centripetal means 'centre-seeking'. Radial is the reverse: streams flow outward from a high centre such as a volcano or dome.

cards.q: A river that keeps its original course across a rising mountain range by cutting a deep gorge is
cards.e: An antecedent river existed before the uplift and cut down as fast as the land rose, like the Sutlej and Indus. A superimposed river also ignores structure, but it was let down from a cover of younger rocks.

cards.q: By Strahler's method, two third-order streams join, and the combined stream is then joined by a second-order stream. The order of the stream below the second junction is
cards.e: Two equal orders (3 + 3) raise the order to 4. A lower-order stream (2) joining does not change it, so it stays 4.

cards.q: A basin has 64 first-order, 16 second-order, 4 third-order and 1 fourth-order streams. Its mean bifurcation ratio is
cards.e: Bifurcation ratio = number of streams of one order / number of the next higher order. 64/16 = 16/4 = 4/1 = 4.

cards.q: Bifurcation ratios of 8 to 10 between successive stream orders in a basin most likely point to
o: a basin close to the peneplain stage
very high permeability of the rocks
strong structural control on the drainage
cards.e: Values of 3 to 5 are normal where rocks are uniform. Much higher values mean folds, faults or dipping beds are distorting the stream network.

cards.q: A drainage basin of 40 sq km has a total stream length of 100 km. Its drainage density is
cards.e: Drainage density = total stream length / basin area = 100 / 40 = 2.5 km per sq km. Dividing the wrong way round gives 0.4.

cards.q: Horton's form factor of a drainage basin is
o: total stream length divided by basin area
