cards.q: Zeolites often fill the gas cavities of Deccan basalts. Which of these cavity minerals is NOT a zeolite?
cards.e: Apophyllite commonly occurs with zeolites in the same cavities, but it is a sheet silicate, not a framework zeolite. Natrolite, stilbite and heulandite are true zeolites.

cards.t: Common minerals of igneous and metamorphic rocks
cards.q: In a typical granite, which of these minerals is an accessory mineral rather than an essential one?
cards.e: Zircon occurs only as tiny scattered grains and does not affect the rock name. Quartz and the two feldspars are essential minerals: without them the rock would not be called granite.

cards.t: Minerals of the carbonate, phosphate, sulphide and halide groups
cards.q: A white carbonate mineral with curved, saddle-shaped rhombohedral faces fizzes in cold dilute HCl only after it is powdered. It is
cards.e: Dolomite reacts with cold dilute acid only when powdered, and its curved saddle-shaped crystals are typical. Calcite and aragonite fizz briskly as lumps. Gypsum is a sulphate and does not fizz.

cards.t: Minerals of the carbonate, phosphate, sulphide and halide groups
cards.q: Which carbonate mineral is correctly matched with its formula?
cards.e: Siderite is iron carbonate (sideros = iron). Magnesite is MgCO3, rhodochrosite is MnCO3 and smithsonite is ZnCO3. All four share the calcite structure.

cards.t: Minerals of the carbonate, phosphate, sulphide and halide groups
cards.q: Rock phosphate (phosphorite), such as that mined at Jhamarkotra in Rajasthan, consists mainly of a fine-grained variety of
cards.e: Phosphorite is made of very fine apatite (collophane), the calcium phosphate used for fertilisers. Monazite and xenotime are rare-earth phosphates and are mined for rare earths and thorium, not fertiliser.

cards.t: Minerals of the carbonate, phosphate, sulphide and halide groups
cards.q: Which heavy mineral of the Chavara beach sands of Kerala is a rare-earth phosphate and the chief ore of thorium?
cards.e: Monazite is (Ce,La,Nd,Th)PO4 and is radioactive because of thorium. Zircon is a zirconium silicate; ilmenite and rutile are titanium oxides from the same sands.

cards.t: Minerals of the carbonate, phosphate, sulphide and halide groups
cards.q: Pyrite and chalcopyrite are both brass-yellow and both give a greenish-black streak. Which simple test separates them best?
o: Fizzing in cold dilute hydrochloric acid
Hardness: a knife scratches chalcopyrite but not pyrite
Streak colour on an unglazed porcelain plate
cards.e: Pyrite has hardness 6-6.5 and resists a knife; chalcopyrite (3.5-4) is easily scratched. Streak does not help because both give the same greenish-black powder.

cards.t: Minerals of the carbonate, phosphate, sulphide and halide groups
cards.q: What is the chemical formula of chalcopyrite, the most important ore mineral of copper?
cards.e: Chalcopyrite is CuFeS2 with 34.6% copper. Cu5FeS4 is bornite (peacock ore), Cu2S is chalcocite and CuS is covellite. Those are richer in copper but much less abundant.

cards.t: Minerals of the carbonate, phosphate, sulphide and halide groups
cards.q: A lead-grey mineral with bright metallic lustre breaks into small cubes, is soft (hardness 2.5) and feels very heavy (specific gravity about 7.5). It is
cards.e: Perfect cubic cleavage with very high density identifies galena, PbS. Molybdenite and graphite are also grey and soft, but they are flaky and much lighter. Stibnite forms long blades.

cards.t: Minerals of the carbonate, phosphate, sulphide and halide groups
cards.q: Which sulphide has a resinous lustre, perfect cleavage in six directions and a streak paler than its body colour?
cards.e: Sphalerite (ZnS) has dodecahedral cleavage in six directions and a non-metallic, resinous lustre. Galena has only three cleavages (cubic) and a metallic lustre.

cards.t: Minerals of the carbonate, phosphate, sulphide and halide groups
cards.q: Three of these ore minerals are sulphides. Which is the odd one out?
cards.e: Cassiterite is tin oxide, SnO2. Sphalerite (ZnS), galena (PbS) and pyrite (FeS2) are all sulphides. Cassiterite's heavy, metallic look makes it easy to mistake for a sulphide.

cards.t: Minerals of the carbonate, phosphate, sulphide and halide groups
cards.q: Halite and sylvite are both colourless cubic minerals with perfect cubic cleavage. They are most easily told apart by
cards.e: Halite (NaCl) tastes simply salty, while sylvite (KCl) tastes bitter. Their cleavage, crystal system and lustre are the same, so those properties do not help.

cards.t: Minerals of the carbonate, phosphate, sulphide and halide groups
cards.q: Which halide mineral is used as a flux in the electrolytic smelting of aluminium?
cards.e: Cryolite Na3AlF6 dissolves alumina and lowers its melting temperature in the smelting cell. Fluorite is the tempting answer: it is also a flux, but it is used in steel making.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.q: Which part of the polarising microscope is inserted to observe interference figures?
cards.e: The Bertrand lens focuses the interference figure formed at the back of the objective when converging light is used. The quartz wedge and mica plate are accessory plates used on the figure afterwards, not to see it.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.q: Which of these properties is observed with the analyser removed (plane polarised light)?
cards.e: Pleochroism is a change of the mineral's own colour and needs only the polariser. Extinction, interference colours and feldspar twinning appear only when the analyser is also in (crossed polars).

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.q: In a Nicol prism, what happens at the Canada balsam layer?
o: The two rays recombine into unpolarised light
The extraordinary ray is totally reflected and the ordinary ray passes through
The ordinary ray is totally reflected and the extraordinary ray passes through
The two rays are absorbed equally by the balsam
cards.e: The ordinary ray in calcite has a higher index (1.658) than the balsam, so it meets the layer beyond the critical angle and is totally reflected. The extraordinary ray passes on as plane polarised light. Hook: O = Out.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.q: When the stage is lowered slightly (the distance between objective and thin section is increased), the Becke line moves:
o: into the material with the lower refractive index
into the material with the higher refractive index
cards.e: On lowering the stage the bright line moves towards the higher index. It does not always go into the grain - it goes into the balsam if the balsam has the higher index.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.q: The speed of light in vacuum is 3.0 × 10^8 m/s. What is its speed in a mineral of refractive index 1.5?
cards.e: Speed in mineral = speed in vacuum / n = 3.0 × 10^8 / 1.5 = 2.0 × 10^8 m/s. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 4.5 × 10^8, which is impossible because light is slower inside a mineral.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.q: Which of these minerals shows negative relief in a balsam mount (index lower than the balsam)?
cards.e: Fluorite has a very low index (1.434), well below the balsam (1.54). Garnet, olivine and zircon all have indices far above the balsam and show strong positive relief.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.q: A marked change of relief as the stage is rotated in plane polarised light ('twinkling') is characteristic of:
cards.e: Calcite has one index (1.658) well above the balsam and the other (1.486) below it, so its relief changes on rotation. Quartz and orthoclase have both indices close to the balsam; garnet has only one index.

cards.q: Three of these minerals stay dark under crossed polars in every section and every stage position. Which one does NOT?
cards.e: Garnet, spinel and fluorite are cubic and therefore isotropic. Beryl is hexagonal, so it is anisotropic (uniaxial) and shows interference colours in most sections.

cards.q: Minerals of which crystal system are optically uniaxial?
cards.e: Tetragonal, hexagonal and trigonal minerals are uniaxial. Orthorhombic and monoclinic minerals are biaxial, and cubic minerals are isotropic.

cards.q: Which of these minerals is uniaxial positive?
cards.e: In quartz ε (1.553) is greater than ω (1.544), so it is positive. Calcite, apatite and tourmaline are all uniaxial negative.

cards.q: A quartz grain in a thin section stays dark throughout rotation under crossed polars. The most likely reason is that the grain is:
o: cut parallel to its optic axis
thicker than the rest of the section
cut perpendicular to its optic axis
cards.e: Light travelling along the optic axis is not split, so a basal section behaves as if isotropic. A section parallel to the optic axis shows the highest colour, not darkness.

cards.q: For a uniaxial negative mineral:
o: beta is closer to gamma than to alpha
cards.e: Negative means the extraordinary index ε is smaller than the ordinary index ω, as in calcite. Beta, gamma and alpha are indices of biaxial minerals, not uniaxial ones.

cards.q: A biaxial mineral is optically positive when:
cards.e: If Z (the gamma direction) bisects the acute angle between the optic axes, the mineral is positive; if X does, it is negative. Y is the optic normal and is never a bisectrix.

cards.q: The two optic axes of a biaxial mineral lie in the plane that contains:
cards.e: The optic axial plane is the XZ plane, which holds the largest and smallest indices. Y is perpendicular to this plane and is called the optic normal.

cards.q: The indicatrix of a uniaxial negative mineral such as calcite is:
o: a prolate ellipsoid of revolution (stretched along the optic axis)
an oblate ellipsoid of revolution (flattened along the optic axis)
cards.e: In negative minerals ε, measured along the optic axis, is the smaller index, so the figure is flattened (oblate). The prolate shape belongs to positive minerals like quartz.

cards.t: Birefringence of minerals and their relation with mineral composition
cards.q: A mineral with birefringence 0.009 is cut parallel to its optic axis in a section 30 micrometres thick. The retardation is:
cards.e: Retardation = thickness × birefringence = 30,000 nm × 0.009 = 270 nm. Remember to convert 30 micrometres to 30,000 nm first. This is the first-order white of quartz.

cards.t: Birefringence of minerals and their relation with mineral composition
cards.q: A grain in a 0.03 mm thin section shows a retardation of 1080 nm. Its birefringence in that section is:
cards.e: Birefringence = retardation / thickness = 1080 nm / 30,000 nm = 0.036. This is near the top of the second order, typical of muscovite or olivine.

cards.t: Birefringence of minerals and their relation with mineral composition
cards.q: Quartz grains (maximum birefringence 0.009) show a maximum retardation of 450 nm in a slide. The thickness of the section is about:
cards.e: Thickness = retardation / birefringence = 450 / 0.009 = 50,000 nm = 50 micrometres. The slide is too thick: at the standard 30 micrometres quartz would reach only 270 nm (white), not yellow-orange.

cards.t: Birefringence of minerals and their relation with mineral composition
cards.q: In a section of standard thickness, the highest interference colour shown by quartz is:
cards.e: Quartz has low birefringence (0.009), giving about 270 nm at 0.03 mm, which is first-order white. High-order pearly white belongs to carbonates such as calcite.

cards.t: Birefringence of minerals and their relation with mineral composition
cards.q: Which of these minerals has the highest birefringence?
cards.e: Calcite has an extreme birefringence of 0.172. Olivine is high (about 0.04) but far below calcite; quartz and orthoclase are low (under 0.01).

cards.t: Birefringence of minerals and their relation with mineral composition
cards.q: Anomalous 'Berlin blue' interference colours are typical of:
cards.e: Chlorite has very low birefringence that changes with wavelength, so it gives odd inky blue or brown colours not found on the Michel-Lévy chart. Muscovite, a look-alike sheet mineral, shows normal bright second-order colours.

cards.t: Birefringence of minerals and their relation with mineral composition
cards.q: A grain showing first-order grey (retardation 150 nm) lies at 45° with its slow direction parallel to the slow direction of a gypsum plate (550 nm). The total retardation becomes:
cards.e: Slow on slow means addition: 550 + 150 = 700 nm, a second-order blue. 400 nm (first-order yellow) would be the result of subtraction, when slow lies over fast.

cards.q: Which statement about a centred uniaxial optic-axis interference figure is correct?
o: It is obtained from sections cut parallel to the optic axis
It is a single straight bar that sweeps across the field
It is a cross that splits into two hyperbolas on rotation
It is a black cross whose arms stay in place as the stage is rotated
cards.e: A uniaxial cross does not move or break up on rotation. A cross that splits into two curved isogyres is the biaxial acute-bisectrix figure.

cards.q: In an interference figure, the melatope is the point where:
o: the colour rings are widest apart
cards.e: The melatope marks the emergence of an optic axis: one in a uniaxial figure (centre of the cross) and two in a biaxial acute-bisectrix figure. The optic normal (Y) emerges in a different, flash-type figure.

cards.q: In a centred biaxial optic-axis figure the isogyre stays practically straight as the stage is rotated. The optic angle 2V of the mineral is close to:
cards.e: The isogyre is straight when 2V is 90° and becomes more curved as 2V gets smaller. At 2V near 0° the figure looks like a uniaxial cross.

cards.q: How many times does an anisotropic grain go extinct during one complete (360°) rotation of the stage under crossed polars?
cards.e: The grain is dark whenever one of its two vibration directions is parallel to the polariser. This happens every 90°, so four times in a full turn.

cards.q: Wavy (undulose) extinction in a quartz grain indicates that the grain:
o: is cut perpendicular to the optic axis
is twinned on the Brazil law
cards.e: Strain bends the lattice, so different parts of the grain go dark at slightly different positions. A grain cut perpendicular to the optic axis would stay dark all the time instead.

cards.q: A green-brown, strongly pleochroic mineral shows two cleavages at 56° and 124° in basal sections and a maximum extinction angle of about 18°. It is:
cards.e: Cleavages at 56° and 124° with a small extinction angle (about 12°-30°) mean amphibole, here hornblende. Augite has cleavages near 90°, weak pleochroism and a larger angle (about 35°-48°).

cards.q: Which pyroxene gives parallel (straight) extinction in prismatic sections?
cards.e: Enstatite is an orthopyroxene (orthorhombic), so its vibration directions are parallel to the crystal axes. Augite, diopside and pigeonite are monoclinic and show oblique extinction.

cards.q: The Michel-Lévy method, which uses extinction angles measured on albite twin lamellae, is used to find the:
cards.e: The maximum symmetrical extinction angle of albite twins changes with the anorthite content, so it gives the plagioclase composition. Section thickness is found from the interference colour of quartz, not from this method.

cards.q: For the Michel-Lévy method, a suitable plagioclase grain is one in which:
o: no twinning is visible in any position
the lamellae form a cross-hatched (tartan) pattern
the grain stays dark throughout rotation
sharp twin lamellae go extinct at nearly equal angles on either side of the cross-hair
cards.e: Equal angles to the left and right show that the section is cut perpendicular to (010), which the method needs. A tartan pattern belongs to microcline, not plagioclase.

cards.q: Which statement about pleochroism is correct?
o: It is observed under crossed polars as the stage is rotated
It is observed in plane polarised light and is caused by unequal absorption in different vibration directions
It depends only on the thickness of the section
It is shown by coloured cubic minerals such as garnet
cards.e: Pleochroism is a colour change seen with the polariser alone, due to direction-dependent absorption. Colours seen under crossed polars are interference colours, and cubic minerals cannot be pleochroic.

cards.q: A brown prismatic mineral is darkest when its long axis is perpendicular to the vibration direction of the polariser. It is most likely:
cards.e: Tourmaline absorbs the ordinary ray most strongly, and that ray vibrates across the length of the crystal. Biotite and hornblende are darkest when the cleavage or length is parallel to the polariser direction.

cards.q: The dark pleochroic haloes seen in biotite around tiny zircon inclusions are caused by:
o: alpha particles from uranium and thorium in the inclusion damaging the host
oxidation of iron around the inclusion
strain produced by growth of the inclusion
cards.e: Zircon, monazite and allanite carry uranium and thorium, and their alpha particles damage a small sphere of the host mica. Strain would give bent cleavage or wavy extinction, not a coloured halo.

cards.q: Pleochroism from pale pink to pale green, together with parallel extinction and first-order interference colours, is diagnostic of:
cards.e: Hypersthene is an iron-bearing orthopyroxene: pink-to-green pleochroism, straight extinction and low colours. Augite is nearly non-pleochroic with oblique extinction and second-order colours.

cards.q: Cross-hatched ('tartan') twinning under crossed polars is characteristic of:
cards.e: Microcline shows two sets of twins (albite and pericline laws) crossing nearly at right angles. Orthoclase and sanidine show only simple Carlsbad twins, and albite shows parallel stripes.

cards.q: The twin plane of the albite law is:
cards.e: Albite twins are repeated on (010). The plane (001) is the Manebach twin plane and (021) is the Baveno twin plane of orthoclase.

cards.q: Which mineral - twin pair is correctly matched?
cards.e: Gypsum forms swallow-tail contact twins. Brazil twins belong to quartz, Carlsbad twins to orthoclase, and the spinel law to cubic minerals such as spinel and magnetite.

cards.q: Which statement about quartz twinning is correct?
o: Japan twins are penetration twins with parallel c axes
Brazil twins are related by a 180° rotation about the c axis
Brazil twins join a right-handed and a left-handed crystal
Dauphiné twins join a right-handed and a left-handed crystal
cards.e: Brazil twins unite quartz of opposite hand and are called optical twins. The 180° rotation about c describes the Dauphiné law, which joins crystals of the same hand.

cards.q: Which of these is NOT a twin law of quartz?
cards.e: Baveno is a twin law of orthoclase feldspar with twin plane (021). Brazil, Dauphiné and Japan are the three well-known quartz twin laws.

cards.q: In the spinel law the twin plane is parallel to a face of the:
cards.e: Spinel-law twins are joined on the octahedral plane {111}, as in spinel, magnetite and diamond macles. The cube and dodecahedron planes are symmetry planes in these crystals and so cannot be twin planes.

cards.q: Cross-shaped penetration twins, with the two crystals at about 90° or about 60° to each other, are typical of:
cards.e: Staurolite forms cruciform twins: a right-angle cross and an oblique (about 60°) cross. The cross in chiastolite is made of dark carbon inclusions inside one crystal and is not a twin.

cards.q: Albite-law twinning is absent in monoclinic orthoclase because:
o: orthoclase has no cleavage parallel to (010)
(010) is already a plane of symmetry in monoclinic crystals
cards.e: A twin plane can never be a symmetry plane of the crystal, and (010) is the mirror plane of monoclinic feldspar. Monoclinic crystals do twin by other laws - orthoclase shows Carlsbad twins.

cards.q: Normal dispersion in a transparent mineral means that its refractive index is:
o: higher for red light than for violet light
higher for violet light than for red light
cards.e: Short wavelengths (violet) are slowed more, so their index is higher. Sodium yellow light is only the standard colour used for quoting indices; it is not where the index peaks.

cards.q: The dispersion formula 'r > v' given for a biaxial mineral means that:
o: the optic angle 2V is larger for red light than for violet light
red light is absorbed more strongly than violet light
the refractive index is larger for red light than for violet light
the retardation is larger for red light than for violet light
cards.e: r > v describes dispersion of the optic axes: 2V measured in red light is greater than in violet. It does not refer to the indices themselves, which are normally higher for violet.

cards.q: Inclined, horizontal and crossed dispersion are the three types found in minerals of which crystal system?
cards.e: In monoclinic crystals only the b axis is fixed, giving these three cases. Orthorhombic minerals show rhombic dispersion, triclinic show asymmetric dispersion, and tetragonal minerals are uniaxial with no optic-axis dispersion.

cards.t: Birefringence of minerals and their relation with mineral composition
cards.q: As the iron content of olivine increases from forsterite to fayalite:
o: refractive indices rise and the optic sign changes from negative to positive
refractive indices rise and the optic sign changes from positive to negative
refractive indices stay constant and only the colour changes
refractive indices fall and the mineral becomes isotropic
cards.e: Iron raises the indices and birefringence. Forsterite is biaxial positive and fayalite is biaxial negative, so the sign goes from positive to negative, not the other way.

cards.t: Birefringence of minerals and their relation with mineral composition
cards.q: Which plagioclase has all its refractive indices lower than that of Canada balsam (1.54)?
cards.e: Plagioclase indices rise with calcium, from about 1.53 in albite to about 1.58 in anorthite. Only the sodic end (albite) falls below the balsam; labradorite and the more calcic members are clearly above it.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.q: Slender needles in a high-grade pelitic gneiss (such as khondalite) show parallel extinction, positive elongation (length-slow) and a small positive 2V. The mineral is:
cards.e: Sillimanite is length-slow with straight extinction and a small positive 2V. Andalusite also has straight extinction but is length-fast and negative; kyanite has oblique extinction.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.q: A colourless mineral in a basalt shows high relief, curved irregular cracks, no cleavage, parallel extinction, bright second-order colours and green serpentine along the cracks. It is:
cards.e: High relief, cracks without cleavage, bright colours and serpentine alteration identify olivine. Augite has cleavage and oblique extinction; garnet would be black under crossed polars; quartz has low relief and grey colours.

cards.t: Birefringence of minerals and their relation with mineral composition
cards.q: Which accessory of the polarising microscope gives a fixed retardation of about a quarter of a wavelength (roughly 150 nm)?
cards.e: The mica plate is the quarter-wave plate. The gypsum plate gives a full wavelength (about 550 nm, first-order red), and the quartz wedge gives a variable retardation.

cards.q: In a basal section of hornblende the cross-hairs bisect the angles between the two cleavage traces when the grain is dark. This type of extinction is called:
cards.e: Symmetrical extinction means the extinction position halves the angle between two cleavages. Parallel extinction needs a single cleavage or the crystal length lying along a cross-hair.

cards.q: An orthoclase crystal in a granite shows a simple twin: two halves, one bright and one dark under crossed polars, with the c axis as twin axis. The twin law is:
cards.e: Carlsbad twins have the c axis as twin axis and are the common simple twins of orthoclase. Baveno and Manebach are defined by twin planes, (021) and (001), and the pericline law has b as twin axis.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.q: A pale pink mineral in a gneiss has very high relief, irregular fractures and no cleavage, and stays black under crossed polars in every position. It is:
cards.e: Garnet is cubic, so it is isotropic and stays dark. Staurolite, kyanite and cordierite are anisotropic and show interference colours; cordierite also has low relief.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.q: Light travelling inside a mineral of refractive index 2.0 meets its boundary with air (index 1.0). The critical angle for total internal reflection is:
cards.e: sin C = lower index / higher index = 1.0 / 2.0 = 0.5, so C = 30°. 60° is the angle whose cosine is 0.5, a common slip.

cards.q: A coloured mineral of which crystal system can show three different pleochroic colours (trichroism)?
cards.e: Orthorhombic minerals are biaxial with three principal vibration directions (X, Y, Z), so three colours are possible. Tetragonal and hexagonal minerals are uniaxial (two colours at most), and cubic minerals are not pleochroic.

cards.t: Birefringence of minerals and their relation with mineral composition
cards.q: Which statement about normally zoned plagioclase is correct?
o: The core is richer in calcium than the rim
The core is richer in sodium than the rim
The core is richer in potassium than the rim
The core and the rim go extinct at exactly the same position
cards.e: Calcium-rich plagioclase crystallises first at high temperature, so it forms the core, and later sodic layers form the rim. Because extinction angle depends on composition, the zones go dark at different positions.

cards.t: Birefringence of minerals and their relation with mineral composition
cards.q: To find the order of an interference colour, an accessory is pushed in slowly over the grain until the colour falls to black, and the red bands passed are counted. The accessory is the:
cards.e: Only the quartz wedge gives a steadily increasing retardation, so it can cancel (compensate) any retardation of the grain. The mica and gypsum plates each give one fixed value.

cards.q: A grain of a uniaxial mineral shows its maximum interference colour when the section is cut:
cards.e: A section parallel to the optic axis contains both ω and ε, so it shows the full birefringence. A section perpendicular to the optic axis shows none and stays dark.

cards.q: Which of these minerals has a spherical optical indicatrix?
cards.e: Spinel is cubic and has one refractive index in every direction, so its indicatrix is a sphere. Zircon and tourmaline are uniaxial (ellipsoid of revolution) and olivine is biaxial (triaxial ellipsoid).

cards.q: A brown mineral with one perfect cleavage is darkest when the cleavage is parallel to the polariser's vibration direction and shows mottled 'bird's-eye' extinction. It is:
cards.e: One perfect cleavage, strong absorption parallel to it and bird's-eye extinction identify biotite. Tourmaline has no good cleavage and is darkest when its length lies across the polariser direction; hornblende has two cleavages.

cards.q: A colourless, low-relief feldspar shows many parallel light and dark stripes under crossed polars. It is most likely:
cards.e: Parallel stripes are polysynthetic albite twins, the hallmark of plagioclase. Orthoclase and sanidine show simple two-part Carlsbad twins, and leucite is a feldspathoid, not a feldspar.

cards.t: Optical properties of common rock forming silicate minerals
cards.q: Light reflected from a glass surface is completely plane polarised when the reflected and refracted rays are at right angles. This is stated by:
cards.e: Brewster's law gives the polarising angle: tan i = n. Snell's law only relates the angles of incidence and refraction; it says nothing about polarisation.

cards.q: A centred uniaxial optic-axis figure is viewed with a gypsum plate whose slow direction runs NE-SW. The NE and SW quadrants turn blue and the NW and SE quadrants turn yellow. The mineral could be:
cards.e: Blue (addition) in the quadrants along the plate's slow direction means the extraordinary ray is the slow ray, so the mineral is uniaxial positive: quartz. Calcite, tourmaline and apatite are negative and would show yellow there.

cards.q: Which of these deposits is syngenetic, that is, formed at the same time as its host rock?
o: Scheelite skarn at a granite contact
Lead-zinc ore filling caves in limestone
cards.e: A banded iron formation was laid down as a sediment, so ore and host rock are the same age. Veins, skarns and cave fillings are epigenetic: they entered or replaced a rock that already existed.

cards.q: In Lindgren's classification, hydrothermal deposits formed at shallow depth and at about 50-200 °C are called
cards.e: Epithermal means shallow and cool. Hypothermal is the opposite end: deep and hot (300-500 °C). Mesothermal lies in between at 200-300 °C.

cards.q: Nickel-copper sulphide ore bodies at the base of mafic intrusions (Sudbury type) are best explained by
o: Separation of an immiscible sulphide liquid from the magma
cards.e: A sulphide liquid does not mix with silicate magma; being heavy it sinks and gathers Ni and Cu. Crystal settling explains chromite layers, not massive sulphide bodies.

cards.q: A garnet-diopside-wollastonite rock carrying scheelite, found at the contact of a granite with limestone, is a
cards.e: Skarn forms when fluids from an intrusion react with carbonate rock (contact metasomatism). Greisen is tempting because it also goes with granite, but it is altered granite itself (quartz-muscovite-topaz) with tin.

cards.q: Which description fits a porphyry copper deposit?
o: A small lens of massive sulphide on pillow lava
Thin high-grade layers in ultramafic rock
Large-tonnage, low-grade disseminated and stockwork ore in a felsic intrusion
Heavy mineral bands in beach sand
cards.e: Porphyry deposits are huge but lean, with copper spread through a network of tiny veins (stockwork) in a porphyritic intrusion. A massive sulphide lens on pillow lava describes a VMS deposit.

cards.q: Cyprus-type volcanogenic massive sulphide (VMS) deposits are typically hosted in
o: Platform limestones far from any volcano
Felsic volcanic rocks of island arcs
cards.e: Cyprus-type ores are copper-rich and sit in the basalt of old ocean floor (ophiolite). Felsic arc volcanics host the Kuroko type, and black shales host SEDEX deposits.

cards.q: Which mineral is LEAST likely to be concentrated in a placer deposit?
cards.e: A placer mineral must be heavy and must resist weathering. Chalcopyrite is a sulphide that oxidises and breaks down quickly at the surface, so it does not survive transport.

cards.q: What is the correct order of zones, from the surface downward, in a weathered sulphide ore body?
o: Primary sulphide zone, supergene enriched zone, oxidised zone, gossan
Gossan, supergene enriched zone, oxidised zone, primary sulphide zone
Oxidised zone, gossan, primary sulphide zone, supergene enriched zone
Gossan, oxidised zone, supergene enriched zone, primary sulphide zone
cards.e: The iron-rich gossan caps the body, the oxidised zone lies above the water table, and enrichment happens at and just below the water table. The untouched primary ore is deepest.

cards.q: Which copper mineral is most typical of the supergene sulphide enrichment zone?
cards.e: Chalcocite (Cu2S) forms below the water table when descending copper solutions replace primary sulphides. Malachite and azurite are carbonates of the oxidised zone above; chalcopyrite is the primary mineral.

cards.q: A gossan is useful to an exploration geologist mainly because it
o: Shows that sulphide ore may lie below the rusty cap
Marks the top of an oil-bearing anticline
Indicates a kimberlite pipe at depth
Proves that the area has a placer gold deposit
cards.e: Gossan is the limonite-goethite residue left when sulphides near the surface are oxidised and leached. So a gossan at the surface points to possible sulphide ore beneath it.

cards.q: Compared with Superior-type banded iron formations, Algoma-type formations are
o: Young oolitic ironstones of Jurassic age
Larger and laid down on wide continental shelves
Products of lateritic weathering of basalt
Smaller and closely linked with volcanic rocks of greenstone belts
cards.e: Algoma-type BIF are thin, lens-like and tied to submarine volcanism, mostly in Archaean greenstone belts. The large shelf deposits are the Superior type.

cards.q: When sea water evaporates in a closed basin, which of these minerals precipitates first?
cards.e: Salts come out in order of solubility, least soluble first: gypsum comes before halite. Sylvite and carnallite (potash salts) are the most soluble and come last.

cards.q: Saddle reefs, as at Bendigo in Australia, are ore bodies localised
o: In the roof zone of kimberlite pipes
At the water table in weathered sulphide ore
Along the beds of old river channels
At the crests of anticlines, in gaps between folded beds
cards.e: Folding opens saddle-shaped spaces between beds at the fold crest, and gold-quartz fills them. This is a textbook example of structural control by folds.

cards.q: The copper deposits of Mosabani and Rakha and the uranium deposit of Jaduguda are all localised along the
cards.e: These deposits lie in an arc-shaped belt of sheared rock in Jharkhand called the Singhbhum Shear Zone, which guided the ore fluids. The Great Boundary Fault is in Rajasthan and is not linked to them.

cards.q: In the classic metal zoning of Cornwall (England), which metal was deposited closest to the granite, in the hottest zone?
cards.e: The order outward from the granite is tin, then copper, then lead-zinc, as the fluids cooled. Tin (cassiterite) needs the highest temperature, so it lies nearest the heat source.

cards.q: A region marked by a characteristic group of mineral deposits, such as the tin belt of South-East Asia, is called a
cards.e: Province refers to area; epoch refers to time. A paragenetic sequence is the order in which minerals formed in one deposit, and an ore shoot is the rich part of one vein.

cards.q: Most of India's coal resources were formed during the
cards.e: Indian Gondwana coal is Permian (Barakar and Raniganj Formations). Carboniferous is the great coal age of Europe and North America, not of India. Eocene-Oligocene coal of the north-east is a very small share.

cards.q: Diamond-bearing kimberlite pipes are characteristically found in
o: Old, stable cratons with thick lithosphere
cards.e: Diamond is stable only at great depth under cold, thick lithosphere, which exists beneath ancient cratons. Indian examples lie in the Dharwar and Bundelkhand cratons.

cards.q: The gold lodes of Kolar and Hutti in Karnataka occur in
o: Gondwana sandstones of a rift valley
Archaean schist (greenstone) belts of the Dharwar craton
cards.e: Both are gold-quartz lodes along shear zones in Archaean schist belts (Kolar and Hutti-Maski). Greenstone belts are the main home of lode gold all over the world.

cards.q: Which statement about gold in India is correct?
o: Most Indian gold is panned from the Nilambur valley of Kerala
Hutti in Raichur district, Karnataka, is the main working gold mine
Kolar Gold Fields is at present India's largest gold producer
The gold of Kolar occurs in kimberlite pipes
cards.e: Hutti is the chief producing mine; Karnataka gave about 99% of India's primary gold in 2021-22 (IBM). Kolar closed in 2001, and Nilambur has only small placer occurrences.

cards.q: Which deposit-metal pair is WRONGLY matched?
cards.e: Malanjkhand (Balaghat, Madhya Pradesh) is a copper deposit in granitoid. Chromite belongs to Sukinda in Odisha. The other three pairs are correct.

cards.q: Rampura-Agucha in Bhilwara district, Rajasthan, is best described as a
cards.e: Rampura-Agucha is a world-class stratiform zinc-lead (with silver) sulphide body in metasediments, of sedimentary exhalative origin. It has no link with a porphyry intrusion.

cards.q: Smithsonite is the carbonate ore mineral of
cards.e: Smithsonite is ZnCO3, formed in the oxidised zone of zinc deposits. Lead carbonate is cerussite, copper carbonates are malachite and azurite, and iron carbonate is siderite.

cards.q: The large East Coast bauxite deposits of Koraput and Kalahandi (Odisha) were formed by weathering of
cards.e: East Coast bauxite caps hills of khondalite, an alumina-rich garnet-sillimanite gneiss of the Eastern Ghats. Deccan basalt is the parent rock for bauxite in central and western India, not here.

cards.q: Chalcopyrite contains about 34.6% copper. An ore that has 5% chalcopyrite by weight and no other copper mineral has a tenor of about
cards.e: Tenor = fraction of mineral x metal in mineral = 0.05 x 34.6% = 1.73% Cu. The 5% figure is the mineral content, not the metal content.

cards.q: Which iron mineral has the highest iron content when pure?
cards.e: Magnetite (Fe3O4) has 72.4% Fe. Hematite (Fe2O3) is close behind at about 70%, which is why it is the tempting wrong answer. Siderite has only 48.2%.

cards.q: Which mine-state pair is correctly matched?
cards.e: Bailadila is in Dantewada district of Chhattisgarh. Noamundi is in Jharkhand, Kudremukh in Karnataka and Sukinda (chromite) in Odisha.

cards.q: Gondite, a spessartite garnet-quartz rock, is associated with the manganese ores of the
o: Sausar Group of Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra
cards.e: Gondite is the metamorphosed manganese sediment of the Sausar Group (Balaghat, Nagpur, Bhandara). The Eastern Ghats manganese rock is called kodurite, a different rock.

cards.q: About 96% of India's chromite resources (IBM, Indian Minerals Yearbook 2022) lie in
cards.e: The Sukinda valley and Baula-Nuasahi ultramafic belts of Odisha hold nearly all of India's chromite. Karnataka (Nuggihalli) and Tamil Nadu (Sittampundi) have only small deposits.

cards.q: The iron ore of Kudremukh (Karnataka) and of Kozhikode district (Kerala) is mainly
cards.e: Both are low-grade banded magnetite quartzite in Precambrian rocks. High-grade hematite is typical of Bailadila and Noamundi, not of these two.

cards.q: As coal rank increases from lignite to anthracite, the coal shows
o: Lower fixed carbon and lower heating value
Higher fixed carbon and lower volatile matter
Lower vitrinite reflectance and higher moisture
Higher moisture and higher volatile matter
cards.e: Deeper burial drives off water and gases, so carbon content and heating value go up while moisture and volatile matter fall. Vitrinite reflectance also rises with rank.

cards.q: The main coal-bearing formation of the Gondwana basins of India is the
cards.e: The Lower Permian Barakar Formation carries the thickest and best coal seams. The Talchir Formation below it is glacial (boulder bed) and has no coal.

cards.q: Which coalfield is of Tertiary age, unlike the other three, which are Gondwana coalfields?
cards.e: Makum in Assam has Oligocene coal, high in sulphur. Jharia, Raniganj and Talcher are Permian Gondwana coalfields.

cards.q: A special hydrogeological problem in mining the Neyveli lignite (Tamil Nadu) is
o: Salt water entering from the sea through limestone caves
Very deep water table that makes dust control hard
A confined aquifer under high pressure below the lignite seam
Acid mine drainage from thick pyrite beds
cards.e: Sands below the lignite hold water under artesian pressure. It must be pumped all the time to lower the pressure, or water would burst through the mine floor.

cards.q: The main reservoir rock of the Mumbai High oil field is
cards.e: Mumbai High produces mainly from Miocene limestone. Eocene sandstone is the reservoir of the Cambay basin fields such as Ankleshwar, which is the usual confusion.

cards.q: India's oldest oil field, with a refinery working since 1901, is
cards.e: Oil was struck at Digboi in Upper Assam in 1889 and its refinery started in 1901. Ankleshwar (1960) and Mumbai High (1974) were found much later.

cards.q: The uranium deposit at Tummalapalle (Andhra Pradesh) is hosted in
o: Sheared schists of the Singhbhum Shear Zone
Cretaceous sandstone of the Mahadek Formation
cards.e: Tummalapalle ore is stratabound in the Vempalle dolostone of the Cuddapah Supergroup. Mahadek sandstone hosts the Meghalaya deposits and the Singhbhum Shear Zone hosts Jaduguda.

cards.q: China clay used for making porcelain consists mainly of
cards.e: China clay (kaolin) is kaolinite, formed by alteration of feldspar. Montmorillonite is the mineral of bentonite, a swelling clay used in drilling mud.

cards.q: In a ceramic body made of clay, feldspar and quartz, the main role of feldspar is to act as a
o: Flux that melts and binds the body
cards.e: Feldspar melts first on firing and forms the glass that binds the body. Clay gives plasticity and quartz is the filler that controls shrinkage.

cards.q: Gypsum is added to Portland cement clinker during grinding in order to
o: Give the cement a white colour
Lower the burning temperature in the kiln
Slow down the setting of the cement
cards.e: About 3-5% gypsum controls (retards) setting, so the cement stays workable. Without it the cement would set almost at once.

cards.q: Laterite was first named and described by Francis Buchanan in 1807 from
cards.e: Buchanan saw the soft rock being cut into bricks at Angadipuram in present Malappuram district and named it from the Latin word for brick. The other places also have laterite but are not the type area.

cards.q: Which of these is a basic refractory?
cards.e: Magnesite (and dolomite) are basic refractories that resist basic slag. Silica and fire clay are acid refractories; graphite is neutral.

cards.q: The magnesite veins of the Chalk Hills near Salem (Tamil Nadu) were formed by
o: Alteration of dunite and peridotite by carbonated waters
Settling of crystals in a granite magma
Evaporation of sea water in a lagoon
cards.e: Waters carrying CO2 attacked magnesium-rich ultramafic rock and deposited MgCO3 as a network of white veins. Magnesite that replaces dolomite is the Uttarakhand type, not the Salem type.

cards.q: The Jhamarkotra deposit near Udaipur (Rajasthan) is India's leading source of
cards.e: Jhamarkotra is a stromatolitic rock phosphate deposit in dolomite of the Aravalli Supergroup. Gypsum is also big in Rajasthan, but in the Bikaner-Nagaur area, not at Jhamarkotra.

cards.q: Which mineral is a source of potash for fertilizers?
cards.e: Sylvite is KCl. Apatite gives phosphorus, gypsum gives calcium and sulphur, and halite is common salt (NaCl) with no potassium.

cards.q: Emery, a natural abrasive, is a granular mixture mainly of
cards.e: Emery is fine-grained corundum mixed with magnetite (and some hematite or spinel). The corundum, hardness 9, does the cutting.

cards.q: Alexandrite and cat's eye (cymophane) are gem varieties of
cards.e: Both are chrysoberyl, BeAl2O4, which occurs in pegmatites and gravels of south Kerala. Beryl is tempting because of the similar name, but its gems are emerald and aquamarine.

cards.q: Ruby and sapphire are gem varieties of which mineral?
cards.e: Both are corundum, Al2O3. A trace of chromium gives red ruby; iron and titanium give blue sapphire. Red spinel looks like ruby but is a different mineral.

cards.q: Wajrakarur in Anantapur district, Andhra Pradesh, is known for
cards.e: Wajrakarur has a field of kimberlite pipes, some carrying diamond. Barytes is at Mangampet, chromite at Sukinda and copper at Malanjkhand or Khetri.

cards.q: Which of these minerals is NOT one of the heavy minerals recovered from the Chavara beach sands of Kerala?
cards.e: Chavara sands yield ilmenite, rutile, zircon, monazite, sillimanite and garnet. Cassiterite (tin ore) is a placer mineral elsewhere, but it is not found in Kerala beach sands.

cards.q: Which mineral in the beach sands of Kerala is the source of thorium?
cards.e: Monazite is a phosphate of rare earths that also holds thorium. Ilmenite and rutile give titanium, and zircon gives zirconium.

cards.q: The Nilambur valley in Malappuram district of Kerala is known for occurrences of
cards.e: Placer gold occurs in river gravels of the Chaliyar system around Nilambur, with primary gold-quartz veins in the Wayanad-Nilambur belt. China clay is at Kundara and bauxite at Nileshwaram.

cards.q: Which Kerala mineral-locality pair is correctly matched?
cards.e: Glass-grade silica sand occurs in the Cherthala-Alappuzha belt. China clay belongs to Kundara, ilmenite to Chavara, bauxite to Nileshwaram and gold to Nilambur.

cards.q: Mangampet in the Cuddapah basin of Andhra Pradesh has one of the world's largest single deposits of
cards.e: Mangampet has thick bedded barytes (BaSO4), used as weighting material in oil-well drilling mud. Asbestos of the Cuddapah basin is at Pulivendla, which makes it the tempting wrong choice.

cards.q: The muscovite mica of the Koderma-Giridih belt (Jharkhand-Bihar) is mined from
cards.e: Large books of muscovite grow in pegmatites, the coarse rocks formed from the last water-rich granite melt. They cut the mica schists of the belt.

cards.q: Which igneous body is a sheet-like intrusion lying parallel to the bedding of the country rock?
cards.e: A sill is tabular and concordant (parallel to the layers). A dyke is also tabular but cuts across the layers, so it is discordant.

cards.q: A lens-shaped concordant intrusion occupying the crest of an anticline or the trough of a syncline is called a
cards.e: Phacoliths sit in fold hinges, where bending opens space for magma. A laccolith also is concordant, but it makes its own dome by lifting the roof and is not tied to fold crests.

cards.q: The Bushveld Complex of South Africa, a huge saucer-shaped mafic intrusion, is the classic example of a
cards.e: A lopolith is a very large concordant body sagging in the middle like a saucer. A laccolith is the opposite shape: flat floor and domed roof.

cards.q: Three of these igneous forms are concordant. Which one is the odd one out?
cards.e: A dyke cuts across the bedding, so it is discordant. Sill, laccolith and lopolith all follow the bedding planes (concordant).

cards.q: Laccoliths, with a flat floor and an up-arched roof, are most commonly built by which kind of magma?
cards.e: Sticky acid magma cannot spread far sideways, so it piles up and lifts the roof into a dome. Fluid basic magma spreads out and makes thin sills instead.

cards.q: A discordant granite pluton of the same nature as a batholith, but with an exposed area of less than 100 square km, is called a
cards.e: The 100 square km limit separates a batholith (larger) from a stock (smaller). Sill, lopolith and phacolith are concordant bodies, not batholith-like plutons.

cards.q: Which statement about cone sheets and ring dykes is correct?
o: Cone sheets form when a central block sinks (cauldron subsidence)
Ring dykes are lens-shaped bodies found at fold crests
Ring dykes are flat sheets lying parallel to bedding
Cone sheets dip inward towards a common centre at depth
cards.e: Cone sheets dip inward like a funnel and form when magma pressure pushes the roof up. Ring dykes are near-vertical and form by cauldron subsidence, not cone sheets.

cards.q: In a dolerite thin section, large augite plates completely enclose many plagioclase laths. This texture is
cards.e: Ophitic texture is plagioclase laths wrapped inside big augite crystals, and it is typical of dolerite. Intersertal texture has glass, not big augite, between the laths.

cards.q: Graphic texture, common in granite pegmatites, is a regular intergrowth of
cards.e: Graphic texture is angular quartz rods in alkali feldspar that look like ancient writing. Worm-like quartz in plagioclase is myrmekite, and albite in K-feldspar is perthite.

p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Mains 2020 Geology Paper II
cards.q: Rapakivi texture in granite is best described as
o: Plagioclase crystals mantled by a rim of K-feldspar
Rounded K-feldspar crystals mantled by a rim of plagioclase
Olivine blades set in a glassy groundmass
cards.e: Rapakivi means large rounded K-feldspar with an oligoclase (plagioclase) rim, named from Finland. Plagioclase rimmed by K-feldspar is the reverse case, called anti-rapakivi.

cards.q: Spinifex texture, made of long skeletal blades of olivine, is diagnostic of which rock?
cards.e: Spinifex forms when very hot ultramafic lava (komatiite) is chilled quickly, so olivine grows as long blades. Kimberlite is also ultramafic but shows rounded olivine grains, not blades.

cards.q: A plagioclase host crystal containing exsolved (unmixed) blebs of K-feldspar is called
cards.e: Antiperthite has a plagioclase host with K-feldspar blebs. Perthite is the reverse: a K-feldspar host with albite lamellae.

cards.q: Worm-like blebs of quartz inside sodic plagioclase, usually seen next to K-feldspar in granite, are called
cards.e: Myrmekite is vermicular (worm-like) quartz in plagioclase. Graphic intergrowth also has quartz, but as angular rods in alkali feldspar, not in plagioclase.

cards.q: In a basalt, the angular gaps between plagioclase laths are filled by small granules of pyroxene, with no glass. The texture is
cards.e: Granules of pyroxene between the laths give intergranular texture. If glass fills the gaps instead, the texture is intersertal.

cards.q: Large phenocrysts set in a fine-grained groundmass (porphyritic texture) in a lava are best explained by
o: Filling of gas cavities by later minerals
Very fast chilling of the whole magma at once
Two stages of cooling: slow at depth, then fast near the surface
cards.e: Big crystals grow slowly at depth; the rest of the melt then freezes quickly on eruption. Fast chilling of the whole magma would give only fine grains or glass.

cards.q: Why does slow cooling of magma at depth give a coarse-grained rock?
o: Many nuclei form and each grows very little
Few nuclei form and each has time to grow large
No nuclei form, so the melt turns to glass
Gas bubbles push the crystals apart
cards.e: With slow cooling, few crystal seeds (nuclei) form but they grow for a long time, giving large grains. Many nuclei with little growth is what fast cooling gives: a fine-grained rock.

cards.q: Gas cavities in a Deccan basalt flow that were later filled with zeolite, calcite or agate give which structure?
cards.e: Filled gas cavities are amygdales, so the structure is amygdaloidal. Vesicular structure is the earlier stage, when the cavities are still empty.

cards.q: Pillow structure in basalt is taken as evidence that the lava
o: Cooled slowly deep in the crust
cards.e: Lava entering water chills at once into rounded, glassy-skinned pillows. Pillows are therefore common in ocean-floor basalts and greenstone belts.

cards.q: Which statement about columnar joints in basalt is correct?
o: They are produced by folding long after the lava has solidified
They form only when lava erupts under the sea
They form by contraction on cooling, and the columns stand at right angles to the cooling surface
They form by gas bubbles escaping from the lava
cards.e: Cooling lava shrinks and cracks into polygonal columns that grow perpendicular to the cooling surface. Gas bubbles make vesicles, not columns.

cards.q: Basaltic lava with a smooth, billowy or ropy surface is called
cards.e: Pahoehoe is fluid lava with a smooth, ropy skin. Aa lava is more viscous and has a rough, clinkery surface.

cards.q: A light-coloured, frothy silicic volcanic glass, so full of gas holes that it can float on water, is
cards.e: Pumice is pale, silica-rich and extremely vesicular, so it floats. Scoria is also vesicular but is dark, basaltic and heavier.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.q: Which is the correct order of crystallisation, from high to low temperature, in Bowen's discontinuous reaction series?
cards.e: Olivine forms first, then reacts with the melt to give pyroxene, then amphibole, then biotite. The reversed order is the order of melting, not of crystallisation.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.q: A granite pluton has a hybrid margin crowded with partly digested blocks of country rock (xenoliths). This is field evidence of
cards.e: Assimilation is magma taking in and digesting wall rock, which leaves half-eaten xenoliths. Gravity settling is a type of crystal fractionation and leaves layers of cumulate crystals instead.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.q: At 1 atmosphere, the diopside-anorthite system is the textbook example of
o: A system with two immiscible liquids
A binary eutectic system with no solid solution
cards.e: Diopside and anorthite do not mix in the solid state; both crystallise together at one eutectic point (about 1274 °C). Complete solid solution is shown by albite-anorthite.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Mains 2020 Geology Paper II
cards.q: In the albite-anorthite system, a melt of composition An50 starts to crystallise. The first plagioclase crystals are
o: Richer in anorthite (calcium) than the melt
Richer in albite (sodium) than the melt
Of exactly the same composition as the melt
cards.e: The high-temperature end member (anorthite) goes into the crystals first, so early crystals are more calcic than the melt. This is why zoned plagioclase has calcic cores and sodic rims.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Mains 2020 Geology Paper II
cards.q: In the forsterite-silica system at 1 atmosphere, enstatite on heating
o: Melts congruently to a liquid of its own composition
Breaks down to quartz plus liquid
Melts incongruently to forsterite plus a more silica-rich liquid
cards.e: Enstatite melts incongruently at the peritectic (about 1557 °C), giving forsterite and liquid. Congruent melting means solid and liquid have the same composition, which is not the case here.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.q: At the eutectic of the two-component diopside-anorthite system at fixed pressure, diopside, anorthite and liquid coexist. Using F = C - P + 1, the number of degrees of freedom is
cards.e: C = 2 and P = 3, so F = 2 - 3 + 1 = 0. The point is invariant: temperature stays fixed until the liquid is used up.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.q: An igneous rock with 48% SiO2 by weight is classed, on silica content, as
cards.e: Basic rocks have 45-52% silica. Ultrabasic rocks have less than 45%, so 48% is just above that limit.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.q: In the IUGS QAPF classification of igneous rocks, the letter F stands for
cards.e: Q = quartz, A = alkali feldspar, P = plagioclase, F = feldspathoids (foids such as nepheline and leucite). Ferromagnesian (mafic) minerals are left out; the diagram is used only when they are below 90%.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.q: The TAS diagram, used to name fine-grained or glassy volcanic rocks, plots
o: Alkalis, iron oxide and magnesia on a triangle
Quartz, alkali feldspar and plagioclase on a triangle
cards.e: TAS = Total Alkali versus Silica, a chemical plot for volcanic rocks. The alkalis-iron-magnesia triangle is the AFM diagram, used to separate tholeiitic from calc-alkaline series.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.q: Which pair of minerals cannot crystallise together in equilibrium from the same magma?
cards.e: Nepheline forms only when silica is short; with free silica it would react to form albite. So quartz and nepheline never occur together.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.q: The CIPW norm of an igneous rock is
o: The volume percentage of dark minerals
The ratio of alkalis to alumina
The mineral percentages counted under the microscope
A set of ideal anhydrous minerals calculated from the chemical analysis
cards.e: The norm is calculated from chemistry; it is not measured. The mineral content actually counted in thin section is the mode.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites
cards.q: Which granite type forms by melting of sedimentary source rocks, is peraluminous, and typically carries muscovite, garnet or cordierite?
cards.e: S = sedimentary source; clay-rich sediments give alumina-rich minerals like muscovite and cordierite. I-type granites come from igneous sources and carry hornblende instead.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites
cards.q: A-type granites are characteristic of which tectonic setting?
o: Anorogenic settings such as continental rifts and plate interiors
cards.e: A = anorogenic (not tied to mountain building); these alkali-rich granites form in rifts and plate interiors. Subduction batholiths are I-type and collision belts give S-type.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites
cards.q: The Closepet Granite, a long north-south belt of late Archaean (about 2.5 billion years old) potassic granite, lies in the
cards.e: The Closepet Granite runs through Karnataka in the Dharwar Craton; Closepet is the old name of Ramanagara. The Bundelkhand Craton has its own granite, the Bundelkhand Granite.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites
cards.q: Which statement about the Malani Igneous Suite is correct?
o: It is an Archaean layered anorthosite complex of Tamil Nadu
It is a Neoproterozoic, rhyolite-dominated felsic province of western Rajasthan
It is a Permian basaltic province of Kashmir
It is an Early Cretaceous flood basalt province of Jharkhand
cards.e: Malani (about 750 million years old) is India's largest felsic volcanic province, in western Rajasthan. The Early Cretaceous basalts of Jharkhand are the Rajmahal Traps, and the Permian ones of Kashmir are the Panjal Traps.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites
cards.q: The Ambalavayal and Kalpetta granites, two younger (Neoproterozoic) granite intrusions of Kerala, are in which district?
cards.e: Both plutons lie in Wayanad and cut the older gneiss and charnockite basement. Idukki has a different younger granite, the Munnar granite.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites
cards.q: Charnockite, the orthopyroxene (hypersthene)-bearing granitic rock named by T.H. Holland, has its type area at
cards.e: Holland described charnockite from the St Thomas Mount-Pallavaram area near Chennai. Kabbaldurga and Ponmudi are known for 'incipient' (patchy, arrested) charnockite, not as the type area.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of basalts
cards.q: Compared with ocean island basalt (OIB), normal mid-ocean ridge basalt (MORB) is
o: Tholeiitic and depleted in incompatible elements such as potassium and rubidium
Formed by melting of subducted sediments
Strongly alkaline and rich in nepheline
Rich in quartz and K-feldspar phenocrysts
cards.e: MORB comes from upper mantle that has already lost melt before, so it is poor in incompatible elements (those that prefer the melt). OIB comes from plume sources and is enriched in them.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of basalts
cards.q: The Deccan Traps, tholeiitic flood basalts erupted about 66 million years ago, are linked to which hotspot?
cards.e: India passed over the Réunion hotspot at the end of the Cretaceous, giving the Deccan Traps. The Kerguelen hotspot is linked to the older Rajmahal Traps.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of basalts
cards.q: The Rajmahal Traps of Jharkhand are best described as
o: Late Cretaceous basalts linked to the Réunion hotspot
Permian basalts linked to the opening of the Neo-Tethys
Neoproterozoic rhyolites of a rift setting
Early Cretaceous basalts linked to the Kerguelen hotspot
cards.e: The Rajmahal (and Sylhet) Traps are about 117 million years old, of Early Cretaceous age, and tied to the Kerguelen hotspot. Late Cretaceous plus Réunion describes the Deccan Traps.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of granites, basalts, andesites and alkaline rocks
cards.q: On an AFM diagram, a marked early iron enrichment (the Fenner trend) is the hallmark of which magma series?
cards.e: Dry tholeiitic magmas keep iron in the melt, so the trend swings towards the iron corner first. Calc-alkaline magmas crystallise magnetite early and show no iron enrichment.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of andesites
cards.q: Andesites of the calc-alkaline series are most typical of
cards.e: Andesite is the signature lava of island arcs and continental arcs such as the Andes. Mid-ocean ridges erupt tholeiitic basalt, not andesite.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of andesites
cards.q: What mainly triggers melting of the mantle wedge above a subducting slab?
o: Heat from decay of radioactive elements in the slab
Rapid decompression of mantle rising under a spreading ridge
Water released from the slab lowers the melting point of the mantle
Impact of the slab on the core-mantle boundary
cards.e: Water driven off the sinking slab lowers the melting point of the hot mantle above it (flux melting). Decompression melting is the mechanism at mid-ocean ridges and hotspots.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of alkaline rocks
cards.q: The volcanic equivalent of nepheline syenite is
cards.e: Phonolite is the fine-grained rock with alkali feldspar and nepheline. Trachyte is the equivalent of ordinary syenite, which has no nepheline.

cards.t: Petrology and geotectonic evolution of alkaline rocks
cards.q: Sivamalai in Tamil Nadu is best known in petrology for its
cards.e: T.H. Holland described the nepheline syenites and corundum syenites of Sivamalai as the 'Sivamalai series'. The layered anorthosite with chromitite in Tamil Nadu is Sittampundi.

cards.q: A gabbroic rock made essentially of calcic plagioclase and olivine, with very little pyroxene, is called
cards.e: Troctolite = plagioclase + olivine. Norite is plagioclase + orthopyroxene, so it is the closest wrong choice.

p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Mains 2020 Geology Paper II
cards.q: The Merensky Reef, the world's leading source of platinum-group elements, is a layer within the
cards.e: The Merensky Reef is in the Bushveld Complex of South Africa, the largest layered intrusion. The Stillwater Complex also has a platinum-palladium layer, but it is called the J-M Reef.

cards.q: Which layered intrusion is correctly matched with its location?
cards.e: Skaergaard is in East Greenland and is the classic case of fractional crystallisation with iron enrichment. Bushveld is in South Africa, Stillwater in Montana (USA), and the Great Dyke in Zimbabwe.

p: UPSC Combined Geo-Scientist Mains 2020 Geology Paper II
cards.q: Which statement about kimberlites is correct?
o: They form large batholiths poor in volatiles
They carry mantle xenoliths such as garnet peridotite and occur as pipes in old cratons
They are found mainly along mid-ocean ridges
cards.e: Kimberlite is a volatile-rich ultramafic magma from more than 150 km depth that brings up mantle fragments and diamond. It forms narrow pipes in old stable cratons, not batholiths or ridge lavas.

cards.q: The Wajrakarur kimberlite field, with pipes about 1100 million years old, is located in
cards.e: Wajrakarur is in Anantapur district, Andhra Pradesh, in the Eastern Dharwar Craton. Madhya Pradesh is tempting because of the Majhgawan pipe at Panna.

cards.q: The Majhgawan diamond-bearing pipe, mined by NMDC, is in which district?
cards.e: Majhgawan is near Panna in Madhya Pradesh and is India's main primary diamond source. Anantapur has the Wajrakarur kimberlite field.

cards.q: Besides kimberlite, which ultrapotassic rock is an important primary host of diamond, as at Argyle in Western Australia?
cards.e: Lamproite is a potassium- and magnesium-rich rock with phlogopite and leucite, and the Argyle pipe is olivine lamproite. Carbonatite is also a deep, rift-related magma, but it is mined for niobium and rare earths, not diamond.

cards.q: The Sittampundi Complex of Tamil Nadu is best described as
o: An Archaean layered anorthosite complex with chromitite layers
A carbonatite ring complex with fluorite
A field of Proterozoic kimberlite pipes
cards.e: Sittampundi (Namakkal district) is a layered Archaean anorthosite with very calcic plagioclase and chromite layers. The carbonatite complex known for fluorite is Amba Dongar in Gujarat.

p: Uttarakhand PSC Geology paper 2017 (exam name not shown)
cards.q: Massif-type anorthosites are mostly of which age, and with which plagioclase?
cards.e: Massif anorthosites are large Proterozoic bodies of andesine-labradorite, often with ilmenite-magnetite ores. Archaean anorthosites are layered and much more calcic (bytownite-anorthite).

cards.q: Anorthosite is a plutonic rock made up of more than 90% of which mineral?
cards.e: Anorthosite is almost all plagioclase, usually labradorite or more calcic. The name comes from 'anorthose', an old word for plagioclase, not from orthoclase.

cards.q: The Amba Dongar carbonatite complex, which hosts India's largest fluorite deposit, is in
cards.e: Amba Dongar is in Chhota Udepur district, Gujarat, and is of Deccan Trap age. The other three states also have carbonatites (Sevattur, Sung Valley, Newania), but not Amba Dongar.

cards.q: Ol Doinyo Lengai, the only active volcano erupting carbonatite lava (natrocarbonatite), is in
cards.e: Ol Doinyo Lengai is in northern Tanzania, in the East African Rift. Its sodium-rich carbonate lava is cool, very fluid, and turns white in air.

cards.q: Carbonatites are the world's chief source of which commodities?
cards.e: Carbonatites carry pyrochlore (niobium) and bastnäsite (rare earths), as at Araxá and Bayan Obo. Chromium and platinum come from layered mafic intrusions like Bushveld.

cards.q: The zone of alkali-metasomatised country rock around a carbonatite or alkaline intrusion is called
cards.e: Fenite forms when sodium- and potassium-rich fluids from the intrusion soak the wall rock (fenitisation). Skarn forms where granite magma meets limestone, and greisen is altered granite with quartz, mica and topaz.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.q: Which list gives Barrow's index minerals in pelitic rocks in the correct order of increasing metamorphic grade?
o: Chlorite, garnet, biotite, kyanite, staurolite, sillimanite
Biotite, chlorite, garnet, staurolite, sillimanite, kyanite
Chlorite, biotite, garnet, staurolite, kyanite, sillimanite
Chlorite, biotite, staurolite, garnet, sillimanite, kyanite
cards.e: Barrow's zones in the Scottish Highlands are chlorite, biotite, garnet, staurolite, kyanite, sillimanite. The tempting error is to put sillimanite before kyanite; sillimanite is the highest-temperature zone and comes last.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.q: Which mineral is NOT one of the index minerals of the classic Barrovian zones?
cards.e: Cordierite is a low-pressure mineral and belongs to Buchan-type zones and contact aureoles. Staurolite, kyanite and garnet are all Barrovian (medium-pressure) index minerals.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.q: A regionally metamorphosed pelitic sequence shows the zones biotite, cordierite, andalusite and sillimanite with rising grade. This sequence indicates
o: Shock metamorphism at an impact site
cards.e: Cordierite and andalusite are stable only at low pressure, so this is the Buchan type first described from north-east Scotland. A Barrovian sequence would show staurolite and kyanite instead.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.q: In metamorphic mapping, an isograd is a line that joins points of
o: Equal depth of burial of the rocks
First appearance of a particular index mineral
Equal thickness of the contact aureole
cards.e: An isograd marks where an index mineral first appears as grade rises, so it is a line of equal metamorphic grade. It is not an isotherm of present temperature; it records past conditions. Tilley introduced the term.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.q: The concept of metamorphic facies was introduced by
cards.e: Eskola (1915) defined facies from mineral assemblages that reached equilibrium under the same P-T conditions. Barrow gave the index-mineral zones, Tilley the term isograd, and Grubenmann the depth zones.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.q: Which mineral pair in a metamorphosed basalt points to high-pressure, low-temperature conditions?
cards.e: Glaucophane (blue sodic amphibole) with lawsonite defines the blueschist facies of subduction zones. Chlorite + actinolite is greenschist facies, which is low temperature but not high pressure.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.q: Which mineral is characteristically ABSENT from a true eclogite?
cards.e: Eclogite is omphacite + garnet, and plagioclase is unstable at such high pressure. Rutile is a common accessory mineral in eclogite, so it is not the answer.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.q: The first appearance of which mineral in metabasic and quartz-feldspar rocks marks the start of the granulite facies?
cards.e: Orthopyroxene (hypersthene) forms when hornblende and biotite break down under hot, dry conditions. Hornblende is typical of the amphibolite facies just below.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.q: In metabasic rocks, the change from greenschist facies to amphibolite facies is marked by
o: Actinolite changing to hornblende and albite to more calcic plagioclase
cards.e: Amphibolite facies means hornblende + plagioclase more calcic than albite. Hornblende breaking down to orthopyroxene is the next step up, into granulite facies.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.q: The sanidinite facies represents which conditions?
o: Very high temperature and very low pressure
Very high pressure and low temperature
cards.e: Sanidinite facies rocks are xenoliths baked by basic magma near the surface (pyrometamorphism). Very high pressure with low temperature describes blueschist, not sanidinite.

cards.q: The most widely quoted position of the Al2SiO5 (kyanite-andalusite-sillimanite) triple point is close to
cards.e: Holdaway (1971) placed it at about 500 °C and 3.8 kbar (0.38 GPa), and this is the standard textbook value. The other values are far outside any experimental estimate.

cards.q: Which aluminosilicate is stable at the lowest pressures and is therefore typical of contact aureoles?
cards.e: Andalusite is the least dense Al2SiO5 polymorph, so low pressure favours it. Kyanite is the high-pressure form and sillimanite the high-temperature form. Mullite is not an Al2SiO5 polymorph.

cards.q: Kyanite and sillimanite coexist in equilibrium in a rock of pure Al2SiO5 composition. Using F = C - P + 2, the number of degrees of freedom is
cards.e: C = 1 and P = 2, so F = 1 - 2 + 2 = 1 (univariant line). F = 0 applies only at the triple point, where all three polymorphs coexist.

cards.q: Goldschmidt's mineralogical phase rule states that, for a rock in equilibrium over a range of pressure and temperature,
o: The number of phases is always one
The number of phases equals the number of components plus two
The number of phases cannot exceed the number of components
The number of components cannot exceed the number of phases
cards.e: With F at least 2, Gibbs' rule F = C - P + 2 gives P ≤ C. 'Components plus two' is the maximum number of phases only at an invariant point (F = 0), not in ordinary rocks.

cards.q: On Eskola's ACF diagram, where does anorthite (CaAl2Si2O8) plot?
o: At the centre of the triangle
cards.e: Anorthite has one Al2O3 and one CaO and no FeO or MgO, so it plots halfway between the A and C corners. Calcite and wollastonite plot at the C corner.

cards.q: Thompson's AFM diagram for pelitic schists is a projection from which mineral?
cards.e: The AFM diagram is projected from muscovite, which is present in nearly all medium-grade pelites (K-feldspar is used above muscovite breakdown). Biotite, garnet and chlorite are minerals plotted on the diagram, not the projection point.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.q: The parallel arrangement of mica flakes in a schist gives which texture?
cards.e: Lepidoblastic refers to parallel platy (flaky) minerals. Nematoblastic is the same idea but for needle-like or prismatic minerals such as hornblende.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.q: Three of these rocks are typically granoblastic. Which one is NOT?
cards.e: Phyllite is strongly foliated with parallel fine mica (lepidoblastic). Quartzite, marble and hornfels are mosaics of equal-sized grains without preferred orientation.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.q: A large staurolite crystal in a schist is crowded with tiny quartz inclusions. This texture is called
cards.e: A porphyroblast full of inclusions is poikiloblastic (sieve texture). Blastophitic is a relict igneous ophitic texture, not a growth feature of the new crystal.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.q: The term 'blastoporphyritic' describes a metamorphic rock in which
o: Broken crystals lie in a sheared, streaky matrix
Mica flakes are arranged at random
Large new metamorphic crystals grew in a fine matrix
The porphyritic texture of the igneous parent is still recognisable
cards.e: The prefix 'blasto-' marks a relict (palimpsest) texture inherited from the parent rock. Large new crystals in a fine matrix is porphyroblastic, which is the common confusion.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.q: Mylonite is formed mainly by
o: Ductile shearing with grain-size reduction by dynamic recrystallisation
Static heating next to a granite pluton
Frictional melting on a fault plane
Brittle crushing at shallow depth without any foliation
cards.e: Mylonite is a foliated fault rock of ductile shear zones, with porphyroclasts in a fine recrystallised matrix. Frictional melting gives pseudotachylite, and brittle crushing gives breccia, gouge or cataclasite.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.q: Which sequence shows the progressive metamorphism of a shale with increasing grade?
cards.e: Grain size of mica increases steadily: slate (invisible flakes), phyllite (silky sheen), schist (visible flakes), gneiss (banded). Phyllite is always between slate and schist.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.q: Which metamorphic rock - parent rock pair is correctly matched?
cards.e: Amphibolite (hornblende + plagioclase) forms from basalt or dolerite. Marble comes from limestone, quartzite from sandstone, and khondalite from clay-rich (pelitic) sediment.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.q: A fine-grained, tough, non-foliated rock with andalusite and cordierite is found next to a granite pluton. It is most likely a
cards.e: Hornfels is the typical non-foliated product of contact metamorphism, and andalusite + cordierite are low-pressure aureole minerals. Phyllite and mylonite are both foliated.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.q: Chiastolite, with its dark cross of carbonaceous inclusions, is a variety of
cards.e: Chiastolite is andalusite from contact-metamorphosed carbon-rich slates. Staurolite also shows crosses, but those are cross-shaped twins, not an inclusion pattern.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.q: Skarns typically form
o: Inside ductile shear zones cutting granite
At contacts between granitic intrusions and carbonate rocks
In subduction melanges at very high pressure
By tropical weathering of ultramafic rocks
cards.e: Skarn is a calc-silicate rock (garnet, pyroxene, wollastonite) made when magmatic fluids react with limestone or dolomite. It is a contact metasomatic rock, not a high-pressure or weathering product.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.q: In a siliceous limestone heated strongly in a contact aureole, calcite and quartz react to give
cards.e: CaCO3 + SiO2 = CaSiO3 (wollastonite) + CO2 is the classic decarbonation reaction. Periclase forms from dolomite, not from calcite + quartz, and diopside needs magnesium.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.q: During progressive metamorphism of a siliceous dolomite, which of these minerals appears at the LOWEST grade?
cards.e: Talc (then tremolite) forms first, at low temperature. Wollastonite and periclase need high temperatures, and larnite only forms at the extreme top of the series.

cards.q: Fenitisation is a type of alkali metasomatism found around
cards.e: Fenite forms when sodium- and potassium-rich fluids from carbonatite or alkaline magma soak the country rock. Tin granites are linked with greisen, and serpentinites with rodingite.

cards.q: The idea that granite can form from pre-existing solid rocks by metasomatism, without passing through a magma stage, is called
cards.e: Granitization is solid-state change to granite by added and removed material. Anatexis and palingenesis both involve melting, so they are magmatic routes.

cards.q: Who coined the term 'migmatite'?
cards.e: Sederholm introduced the term in 1907 for mixed gneisses of Finland. Mehnert later classified migmatite structures and parts, and Read is linked with the granite series.

cards.q: In migmatite terminology, the neosome consists of
cards.e: Neosome is the newly formed part: light leucosome plus dark melanosome. Palaeosome is the old parent rock and is, by definition, not part of the neosome.

cards.q: A migmatite that looks like a breccia, with angular blocks of older rock set in granitic material, is called
cards.e: Agmatite means 'fragment rock'. Nebulite is the opposite extreme, where the old rock survives only as faint ghost-like patches.

cards.q: Anatexis means
o: Crushing of rocks along a fault
Change in rock composition by fluids without melting
Change of high-grade minerals to low-grade minerals on cooling
Partial melting of crustal rocks during high-grade metamorphism
cards.e: Anatexis is partial melting that gives granitic melt and migmatites. Composition change by fluids without melting is metasomatism, a different process.

cards.q: The concept of paired metamorphic belts was put forward by
cards.e: Miyashiro (1961) described paired belts from Japan and linked them to island-arc settings. Eskola gave facies, Barrow gave zones and Winkler gave the grade scheme.

cards.q: In the classic paired metamorphic belts of south-west Japan, which is the high-pressure, low-temperature belt?
