cards.e: The Sanbagawa belt has glaucophane schists and lies on the Pacific side. The Ryoke belt is its low-pressure, high-temperature partner with granites, so it is the tempting wrong choice.

cards.q: Which statement about paired metamorphic belts is correct?
o: The high-pressure belt lies on the trench side and the high-temperature belt on the arc side
The high-pressure belt is the one crowded with granite batholiths
The two belts form on either flank of a mid-ocean ridge
The two belts normally differ in age by over a billion years
cards.e: The blueschist belt forms in the cold subduction complex near the trench, and the hot belt forms under the volcanic arc. Granites belong to the high-temperature belt, not the high-pressure one.

cards.q: Which facies sequence records the progressive metamorphism of oceanic crust carried down a subduction zone?
o: Albite-epidote hornfels, hornblende hornfels, pyroxene hornfels
cards.e: A cold slab follows the high-pressure, low-temperature path ending in eclogite. Greenschist-amphibolite-granulite is the medium-pressure path of collision belts.

cards.q: Barrovian-type (medium-pressure) regional metamorphism is most typical of
cards.e: Crustal thickening during collision gives the kyanite-sillimanite facies series. Accretionary wedges at trenches show the high-pressure blueschist series instead.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.q: In Miyashiro's facies series, the Barrovian zones belong to the
cards.e: Barrovian rocks pass from kyanite to sillimanite, so they define the medium-pressure type. The andalusite-sillimanite type is the Buchan or Abukuma type at lower pressure.

cards.q: Coesite-bearing ultra-high-pressure eclogites, showing deep subduction of Indian continental crust, are reported from
cards.e: The Tso Morari complex in the Himalaya of Ladakh has coesite-bearing eclogite. Ponmudi is known for incipient charnockite, a high-temperature feature, not ultra-high pressure.

cards.q: Which pair of minerals is taken as proof of shock (impact) metamorphism?
cards.e: Coesite and stishovite are very high-pressure forms of silica made by impact shock waves. Glaucophane and lawsonite also mean high pressure, but of the slow subduction kind.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.q: Which of these changes is an example of retrograde metamorphism?
o: Muscovite + quartz changing to K-feldspar + sillimanite
cards.e: Garnet to chlorite is a high-grade mineral going to a low-grade, water-bearing one. The other three are prograde changes that happen with rising temperature.

cards.q: In Harker's old grouping, which of these is an 'anti-stress' mineral, unlike the other three?
cards.e: Harker listed cordierite and andalusite as anti-stress minerals of thermal metamorphism. Kyanite, staurolite and chloritoid were his stress minerals of regional metamorphism.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.q: At the highest grade in pelitic rocks, muscovite + quartz break down to form
cards.e: This dehydration reaction marks the second sillimanite (sillimanite-K-feldspar) isograd. Chlorite and biotite are low-grade minerals and cannot be products of a high-grade breakdown.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.q: The rock name 'charnockite' was given by
cards.e: Holland named it after Job Charnock, whose tombstone is made of the rock. Fermor named gondite and kodurite, and Walker named khondalite.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.q: The stone of Job Charnock's tomb at Kolkata, which gave charnockite its name, came from
cards.e: The St. Thomas Mount - Pallavaram area near Chennai is the type area of charnockite. Ponmudi and Kabbaldurga are famous for incipient charnockite, which was described much later.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.q: Which mineral is essential for calling a quartz-feldspar rock a charnockite?
cards.e: Charnockite is a hypersthene (orthopyroxene)-bearing granite of the granulite facies. Muscovite and staurolite are lower-grade minerals that do not survive granulite conditions.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.q: Khondalite is best described as a
o: Rock made of omphacite and garnet
Spessartine-quartz rock derived from manganese-rich sediment
Garnet-sillimanite-graphite gneiss derived from pelitic sediment
cards.e: Khondalite is a granulite-facies metapelite with quartz, garnet, sillimanite and graphite, named after the Khonds of Odisha. The spessartine-quartz rock is gondite, a common mix-up.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.q: Gondite of the Sausar Group consists mainly of
cards.e: Gondite is a metamorphosed manganese-rich sediment of spessartine and quartz. K-feldspar + manganese garnet + apatite is kodurite of Andhra Pradesh.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.q: Kodurite, a manganese-bearing rock named by Fermor, takes its name from a locality in
cards.e: Kodur lies in the Eastern Ghats of north coastal Andhra Pradesh. Madhya Pradesh is the home of gondite, the other manganese rock named by Fermor.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.q: Patches of 'incipient charnockite' in gneiss quarries of south Kerala, such as Ponmudi, are commonly explained by
o: Addition of water-rich fluids during cooling
Influx of CO2-rich fluids that lowered water activity
cards.e: CO2-rich fluids moving along fractures dried the gneiss locally, so biotite or hornblende changed to orthopyroxene. Adding water would do the opposite and cause retrograde change.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.q: In the Kerala Khondalite Belt, the light-coloured garnet-bearing quartz-feldspar rock that is poor in dark minerals is called
cards.e: Leptynite is a garnetiferous quartz-feldspar granulite found with khondalite. Enderbite is an orthopyroxene-bearing tonalite of the charnockite series.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.q: The Kerala Khondalite Belt (Trivandrum Block) lies immediately south of which shear zone?
cards.e: The Achankovil Shear Zone separates the Madurai Block to the north from the Trivandrum Block (Kerala Khondalite Belt) to the south. The Palghat-Cauvery zone lies much farther north.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.q: As a shale is metamorphosed progressively to a sillimanite gneiss, the amount of water held in its minerals
o: Rises sharply at the garnet isograd and then stays high
cards.e: Prograde reactions are mostly dehydration reactions, so clay and chlorite give way to water-free minerals such as garnet and sillimanite. Water is added only during retrograde change.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.q: Which order of first appearance of minerals fits one standard textbook scheme for the progressive metamorphism of a siliceous dolomite?
cards.e: Water-bearing talc and tremolite come first, then diopside and forsterite, and wollastonite at high temperature. The reversed list is the retrograde order, the common trap.

cards.q: Coesite, the high-pressure polymorph of silica, is stable in which metamorphic facies?
cards.e: Coesite needs about 2.7 GPa, reached only in the (ultra-high-pressure) eclogite facies. Granulite facies is hot but its pressure is far too low for coesite.

cards.t: Textures and structures of metamorphic rocks
cards.q: Maculose (spotted) structure is typical of
o: Argillaceous rocks in the outer part of a contact aureole
cards.e: Spots are early clots of cordierite, andalusite or carbon in baked shales and slates. Mylonites are streaky and foliated, not spotted.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.q: The zeolite and prehnite-pumpellyite facies were established mainly from the work of
o: D. S. Coombs in New Zealand
cards.e: Coombs described these very low-grade facies from buried volcanic sediments of New Zealand. Barrow gave index-mineral zones and Miyashiro gave facies series and paired belts.

cards.q: Taking average rock density as 2800 kg/m3 and g as 10 m/s2, the lithostatic pressure at 30 km depth is about
cards.e: P = density x g x depth = 2800 x 10 x 30000 = 8.4 x 10^8 Pa = 0.84 GPa. The usual slip is a factor of ten in changing km to m or Pa to GPa.

cards.q: A metabasite recrystallised at 35 km depth at only 350 °C. The average geothermal gradient (about 10 °C/km) points to which setting?
o: A contact aureole around a granite
cards.e: 350 °C over 35 km is 10 °C per km, a very low gradient found only where a cold slab goes down; the rock would be a blueschist. Arcs, ridges and aureoles all have high gradients.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.q: Barrow's kyanite zone falls within which metamorphic facies?
cards.e: The staurolite, kyanite and sillimanite zones all lie in the amphibolite facies. The chlorite and biotite zones are the ones in greenschist facies.

p: UPSC Geologist Mains 2020 Geology Paper II (descriptive)
cards.q: The relation dP/dT = ΔS/ΔV, which gives the slope of a metamorphic reaction curve on a P-T diagram, is the
cards.e: Clausius-Clapeyron links slope to entropy and volume change of the reaction. The phase rules only count phases, components and degrees of freedom.

cards.q: Experiments showing that natural granites cluster near the minimum-melting composition of the quartz-albite-orthoclase-water system were published by
cards.e: Tuttle and Bowen (1958) gave this key evidence that granites form from melts. Read and Reynolds were leading supporters of granitization, the opposite view.

cards.q: Three of these terms name parts of a migmatite. Which one does NOT?
cards.e: A porphyroclast is a large surviving grain in a mylonite. Leucosome (light part), melanosome (dark part) and palaeosome (old parent rock) are all migmatite terms.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.q: In Holland's charnockite series, the basic member is essentially a
cards.e: The basic member is hypersthene + plagioclase rock, that is, norite. All members of the series carry hypersthene, which rules out syenite and trondhjemite.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.q: The East Coast bauxite deposits of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh formed by weathering mainly of
cards.e: Alumina-rich khondalite of the Eastern Ghats weathered to laterite and bauxite. Deccan basalt is the parent of bauxite in western and central India, not on the East Coast.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.q: Granulite-facies metamorphism of the Kerala Khondalite Belt took place at about
cards.e: The Trivandrum Block was metamorphosed in the Pan-African event, like Sri Lanka and Madagascar. The 2500 million year age belongs to granulites of the northern part of the Southern Granulite Terrain.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.q: Which assemblage is the best-known indicator of ultra-high-temperature (UHT) metamorphism?
cards.e: Sapphirine + quartz is stable only above about 900 °C. Glaucophane + lawsonite is the opposite extreme, high pressure at low temperature.

cards.q: At the high pressures of the blueschist and eclogite facies, albite breaks down to
cards.e: Albite = jadeite + quartz is the classic high-pressure reaction. Anorthite and sanidine are feldspars of low-pressure rocks, so they cannot be high-pressure products.

cards.q: Skarn developed by replacement of the margin of the igneous intrusion itself is called
cards.e: Endo = inside the intrusion. Exoskarn, the tempting choice, replaces the carbonate country rock outside the intrusion.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.q: Which facies - diagnostic mineral pair is correctly matched?
cards.e: Laumontite is a zeolite of the lowest-grade facies. Glaucophane belongs to blueschist, orthopyroxene to granulite, and plagioclase is absent from eclogite.

cards.t: Regional and contact metamorphism of pelitic and impure calcareous rocks
cards.q: Which statement about contact metamorphism is correct?
o: Grade rises towards the intrusion and the rocks are mostly non-foliated
It affects whole orogenic belts thousands of km long
Kyanite is its typical aluminosilicate mineral
Directed stress is its main agent
cards.e: Heat from the intrusion is the main agent, so the hottest (highest-grade) rocks are at the contact and no foliation forms. Andalusite, not kyanite, is the usual aluminosilicate because pressure is low.

cards.q: The Median Tectonic Line of south-west Japan separates which pair of metamorphic belts?
cards.e: The Sanbagawa (high-pressure) belt lies on the Pacific side and the Ryoke (high-temperature) belt on the inner side of the line. Kamuikotan-Hidaka is also a Japanese pair, but in Hokkaido.

cards.t: Characteristics of different grades and facies of metamorphism
cards.q: A metabasite contains hornblende + albite + epidote. It belongs to the
cards.e: Hornblende with albite and epidote is the transitional epidote-amphibolite facies. In true greenschist facies the amphibole is actinolite, not hornblende.

cards.q: Which field observation was used as evidence FOR granitization rather than for magmatic intrusion?
o: Angular, rotated xenoliths near the roof
Relict bedding traceable through the granite (ghost stratigraphy)
Sharp contacts cutting across the country-rock structure
Chilled fine-grained margins of the granite
cards.e: Old layering passing undisturbed through granite suggests the rock changed in place. Chilled margins, sharp cross-cutting contacts and rotated xenoliths all show a mobile magma.

cards.q: In India, blueschist-facies rocks marking an old subduction zone are found in the
cards.e: Blueschists occur with ophiolites in the Indus Suture Zone (and in the Nagaland-Manipur ophiolite belt). The Kerala Khondalite Belt is a high-temperature granulite terrain, the opposite kind of metamorphism.

cards.q: Thermal models of crust thickened in a continental collision predict that a buried rock reaches its peak temperature
o: Long before its peak pressure, during early burial
After its peak pressure, during uplift
Only after it is exposed at the surface
cards.e: Rock heats slowly, so temperature keeps rising after burial stops and uplift has begun. This gives the clockwise P-T-t path of collision belts.

cards.q: The ZTR index used in heavy mineral studies is based on which three minerals?
cards.e: ZTR stands for zircon, tourmaline and rutile, the three most stable transparent heavy minerals. Topaz, zoisite and titanite are heavy minerals too, but they are less stable and are not part of the index.

cards.q: A sandstone has a very high ZTR index. What does this most likely tell us?
o: It is a mineralogically mature sediment that has survived long weathering or recycling
Its source was a high-grade metamorphic terrain
It was deposited directly by a glacier
It is first-cycle sediment dumped close to a granite source
cards.e: Only the toughest heavy minerals (zircon, tourmaline, rutile) survive long weathering, transport and recycling, so a high ZTR index means a mature sediment. First-cycle or glacial sediment keeps unstable minerals such as hornblende and pyroxene, giving a low index.

cards.q: Which of these changes is NOT a diagenetic process?
o: Growth of quartz overgrowths in pore spaces
Growth of garnet porphyroblasts in a schist
Squeezing out of pore water during burial
cards.e: Garnet porphyroblasts grow during metamorphism, at much higher temperature and pressure than diagenesis. Cementation by quartz overgrowths, dolomitisation and compaction are all standard diagenetic changes.

cards.q: When calcite is replaced mole-for-mole by dolomite, the volume of solid mineral:
o: Increases by about 12-13%, which destroys porosity
Decreases by about 12-13%, which can create porosity
cards.e: Dolomite is denser than calcite, so the same number of moles takes up about 12-13% less space. This shrinkage is why many dolomites are good oil reservoirs. The volume does not increase.

cards.q: Glauconite grains in a sandstone (greensand) are a good indicator of:
o: A marine shelf with slow sedimentation
cards.e: Glauconite is an authigenic (formed in place) green iron-potassium mineral that grows only on the sea floor where sediment builds up slowly. It does not form in rivers, lakes or deserts.

cards.q: Sanidine grains and glass shards in a sandstone suggest that the source area had:
cards.e: Sanidine is the high-temperature potash feldspar of rhyolite and trachyte, and glass shards come from explosive eruptions. Gneisses would give microcline or orthoclase and metamorphic heavy minerals instead.

cards.q: Roundness of a sand grain describes:
o: The sharpness of its corners and edges
The ratio of its longest axis to its shortest axis
How close its overall shape is to a sphere
How polished or frosted its surface is
cards.e: Roundness is about corners and edges only. Closeness of the whole shape to a sphere is sphericity, which is a separate property; a grain can be rod-shaped yet well rounded.

cards.q: According to Folk, a sandstone with almost no clay, good sorting but angular grains is texturally:
cards.e: Folk's stages remove clay first (submature), then improve sorting (mature), then round the grains (supermature). Well sorted but not yet rounded is the mature stage; supermature needs rounded grains too.

cards.q: A dune sand is very well sorted and well rounded but contains 30% feldspar. It is best described as:
cards.e: Good sorting and rounding mean high textural maturity. Abundant feldspar, an unstable mineral, means low mineralogical maturity. The two kinds of maturity are judged separately.

cards.q: Which sandstone is the most mineralogically mature?
cards.e: Quartz arenite is over 95% quartz, the most stable common mineral, so it is the end product of long weathering and reworking. Arkose and greywacke still hold unstable feldspar and rock fragments.

cards.t: Framework, matrix and cement of terrigenous sediments
cards.q: Which statement correctly separates matrix from cement in a sandstone?
o: Matrix and cement are two names for the same pore-filling material
Matrix is fine detrital material deposited with the grains; cement is precipitated chemically in the pores later
Matrix is the sand-size fraction; cement is the gravel-size fraction
Matrix is precipitated chemically in the pores; cement is fine detrital mud
cards.e: Matrix is mechanical: fine silt and clay washed in with the sand. Cement is chemical: minerals such as quartz or calcite that grow in the pores after deposition. Mixing up the two is the common mistake.

cards.t: Framework, matrix and cement of terrigenous sediments
cards.q: Tillite, in which scattered clasts float in abundant fine matrix, is an example of:
cards.e: Paraconglomerates are matrix-supported, with more than 15% matrix; tillite and pebbly mudstone are the classic examples. Orthoconglomerates are grain-supported with little matrix, like river gravels.

cards.t: Framework, matrix and cement of terrigenous sediments
cards.q: What distinguishes shale from mudstone?
o: Shale is fissile and splits into thin sheets
cards.e: Shale and mudstone have the same grain size and clay content. The difference is fissility: in shale the platy clay flakes lie parallel, so it splits into thin sheets.

cards.t: Definition, measurement and interpretation of grain size
cards.q: In the Udden-Wentworth scale, the boundary between sand and silt lies at:
cards.e: Sand runs from 2 mm down to 1/16 mm (0.0625 mm, or 4 phi). 2 mm is the sand-gravel boundary, and the silt-clay boundary is at 1/256 mm (about 0.004 mm).

cards.t: Definition, measurement and interpretation of grain size
cards.q: What is the phi value of a grain 0.25 mm in diameter?
cards.e: Phi = -log2(d in mm). 0.25 = 2 to the power -2, so log2 is -2 and phi is +2. A negative phi would mean a grain coarser than 1 mm.

cards.t: Definition, measurement and interpretation of grain size
cards.q: A clast has a size of -3 phi. Its diameter and size class are:
cards.e: Diameter = 2 to the power of minus phi = 2 cubed = 8 mm, which falls in the pebble class (4-64 mm). 1/8 mm would be +3 phi; forgetting the minus sign is the usual error.

cards.t: Definition, measurement and interpretation of grain size
cards.q: Phi values read from a cumulative curve are phi16 = 1.0, phi50 = 2.0 and phi84 = 3.3. The Folk and Ward graphic mean is:
cards.e: Graphic mean = (phi16 + phi50 + phi84) / 3 = (1.0 + 2.0 + 3.3) / 3 = 2.1 phi. The value 2.0 phi is only the median (phi50), not the mean.

cards.t: Definition, measurement and interpretation of grain size
cards.q: For a sand, phi5 = 1.50, phi16 = 1.80, phi84 = 2.40 and phi95 = 2.49. The Folk and Ward sorting value and class are:
cards.e: Sorting = (phi84 - phi16)/4 + (phi95 - phi5)/6.6 = 0.60/4 + 0.99/6.6 = 0.15 + 0.15 = 0.30 phi. Values below 0.35 phi are very well sorted. Using only the first term's numerator (0.60) is the tempting slip.

cards.t: Definition, measurement and interpretation of grain size
cards.q: A positively skewed (fine-skewed) grain size distribution has:
o: A tail of excess coarse grains
A tail of excess fine grains
cards.e: Fine grains have high phi values, so a tail on the high-phi side gives positive skewness. A coarse tail gives negative skewness, which is common in beach sands.

cards.t: Definition, measurement and interpretation of grain size
cards.q: The pipette method of size analysis for silt and clay is based on:
cards.e: Fine particles are sized by how fast they settle in water, and Stokes' law links settling speed to diameter. Darcy's law is about groundwater flow through a porous medium, not settling.

cards.t: Definition, measurement and interpretation of grain size
cards.q: According to Stokes' law, if the diameter of a settling silt grain is doubled, its settling velocity becomes:
cards.e: Stokes' settling velocity is proportional to the square of the diameter. Doubling the diameter gives 2 squared = 4 times the speed.

cards.t: Definition, measurement and interpretation of grain size
cards.q: A beach sand has a median size of 1.5 phi. In the Wentworth scale it is:
cards.e: Medium sand is 1 to 2 phi (0.5-0.25 mm). Coarse sand is 0 to 1 phi and fine sand is 2 to 3 phi. Remember that a larger phi means a finer grain.

cards.q: On the base of a turbidite sandstone, a flute cast shows the current direction because the flow moved:
o: At right angles to its long axis
From the bulbous, deep nose toward the flared, shallow end
From the flared, shallow end toward the bulbous nose
cards.e: The eddy scours deepest where it first hits the mud, making the bulbous nose at the upcurrent end; the mark then widens and fades downcurrent. Reading it backwards is the common error.

cards.q: Which structure gives only the line (trend) of the palaeocurrent, not which way it flowed?
cards.e: A groove cast is a straight scratch made by a dragged object, so it looks the same from both ends. Flute casts, cross-beds and current ripples are asymmetrical and show the true flow sense.

cards.q: In river gravel, imbricated flat pebbles dip:
o: At right angles to the flow
cards.e: Flat pebbles overlap like roof tiles and lean against the current, so their flat faces dip upstream. Cross-bed foresets, in contrast, dip downstream.

cards.q: Herringbone cross-bedding is characteristic of:
cards.e: Adjacent sets dip in opposite directions because flood and ebb tides flow opposite ways. Rivers flow one way only, so their cross-beds dip in one general direction.

cards.q: Hummocky cross-stratification is formed by:
o: Turbidity currents on the abyssal plain
Storm waves on the shelf below fair-weather wave base
cards.e: Hummocky cross-stratification is the signature of storm beds (tempestites) on the shelf, between fair-weather and storm wave base. Turbidity currents give graded Bouma sequences instead.

cards.q: In a complete Bouma sequence, which division is made of ripple cross-laminated or convolute fine sand?
cards.e: From base to top: Ta massive graded sand, Tb parallel-laminated sand, Tc rippled or convolute sand, Td laminated silt, Te mud. Tb is parallel laminated, not rippled.

cards.q: Which of these is NOT a reliable top-and-bottom (way-up) indicator?
cards.e: Parting lineation is a faint streaking on bedding planes that shows the flow trend but looks the same either way up. Graded beds, mud cracks and truncated cross-beds all have a clear top and bottom.

cards.q: How do load casts differ from flute casts?
o: Load casts form by sand sinking into soft mud and give no current direction
Load casts form only in wind-blown sand
Load casts are made by burrowing animals
Load casts are found only on the top surface of beds
cards.e: Load casts are irregular bulges made when dense sand sags into weak mud; no current is needed, so they give no direction. Flute casts are current scours with a clear upcurrent nose. Both occur on the base of sandstone beds.

cards.q: A mud-dominated bed containing isolated lenses of rippled sand is called:
cards.e: Lenticular bedding is mostly mud with sand lenses. Flaser bedding is the reverse: mostly rippled sand with thin mud streaks. Both are typical of tidal flats.

p: UPSC Geologist Mains 2019 Geology Paper II
cards.q: A palaeocurrent rose diagram shows two modes about 180 degrees apart (bimodal-bipolar). The most likely environment is:
cards.e: Two opposite modes record flood and ebb tidal currents. Rivers, alluvial fans and submarine fans all flow down a slope and give a single (unimodal) direction.

cards.q: Antidunes are bedforms of the:
o: Upper flow regime, in fast supercritical flow
Deep sea floor below storm wave base
Lower flow regime, in very slow flow
cards.e: Antidunes form under fast, shallow, supercritical flow (Froude number above 1) and are in phase with surface waves. Ripples and dunes are the lower flow regime bedforms.

cards.q: Which statement about cross-bedding is correct?
o: Foresets dip upcurrent and are truncated at the base of the set
Cross-bedding forms only under water, never in wind
Foresets meet the top of the set tangentially and are cut off at the base
Foresets dip downcurrent and are truncated at the top of the set
cards.e: Sand avalanches down the lee face of a moving dune, so foresets dip downcurrent. They curve gently into the base and are cut off sharply at the top, which also makes cross-bedding a way-up indicator. Wind dunes form cross-bedding too.

cards.q: A sandstone bed shows grain size decreasing steadily from coarse at the base to fine at the top. This structure and its usual cause are:
o: Graded bedding, from a waning turbidity current
cards.e: Normal graded bedding forms when a slowing current drops coarse grains first and fine grains last; turbidity currents are the classic cause. Cross-bedding is inclined layering, not an upward size change.

cards.q: Stylolites in limestone are produced by:
o: Drying and shrinking of lime mud
cards.e: Stylolites are tooth-like seams where rock has dissolved under pressure, leaving a dark film of insoluble clay. Drying gives mud cracks, not sutured seams.

cards.q: Stromatolites are laminated structures built mainly by:
cards.e: Sticky mats of cyanobacteria trap and bind fine sediment layer by layer. Corals and bryozoans build skeletal reefs, not laminated mats, and appeared long after the first Precambrian stromatolites.

cards.q: Which pairing of ichnofacies and environment is correct?
cards.e: Seilacher's order from shore to deep sea is Skolithos, Cruziana, Zoophycos, Nereites. Nereites grazing trails mark deep-sea turbidite basins; Skolithos vertical burrows mark sandy shores and Cruziana marks the shelf.

cards.q: A concretion with internal radiating and polygonal cracks filled by calcite is called a:
cards.e: Septarian nodules have shrinkage cracks (septa) filled by calcite veins. A geode is a hollow cavity lined with inward-pointing crystals, without the crack network.

p: UPSC Geologist Mains 2019 Geology Paper II
cards.q: Which of these is a chemical (diagenetic) sedimentary structure rather than a biogenic one?
cards.e: A concretion grows by chemical precipitation around a nucleus inside the sediment. Burrows, stromatolites and trackways are all made by living organisms, so they are biogenic.

cards.q: Walther's law of facies states that:
o: Facies found in a conformable vertical sequence were once deposited side by side
Sediments are always laid down in horizontal layers
Fossils succeed one another in a definite order
Older beds always lie below younger beds
cards.e: As environments shift sideways through time, neighbouring facies end up stacked on top of each other. Older-below-younger is the law of superposition, a different principle.

cards.q: A point bar of a meandering river produces which vertical sequence?
o: Uniform sand with no vertical change
Fining-upward, from channel lag gravel to floodplain mud
cards.e: Flow is fastest in the deep channel and slowest on the upper bar, so as the bar migrates sideways it stacks fine over coarse. Coarsening-upward is the pattern of a prograding delta or shoreline.

cards.q: In a prograding delta, the sequence from bottom to top is:
o: Prodelta mud, delta-plain coal, delta-front sand
Prodelta mud, delta-front sand, delta-plain deposits
Delta-front sand, prodelta mud, delta-plain deposits
Delta-plain coal, delta-front sand, prodelta mud
cards.e: As a delta builds seaward, shallower and coarser deposits cover deeper and finer ones, giving a coarsening-upward sequence: prodelta mud, delta-front sand, then delta-plain channel sand, mud and coal.

cards.q: Which feature would you NOT expect in an ancient desert dune sandstone?
o: Abundant clay matrix and mica flakes
cards.e: Wind blows away clay and light mica flakes, so dune sands are clean. Giant cross-beds, frosted rounded grains and excellent sorting are the typical aeolian features.

cards.q: Varves are:
o: Storm beds deposited on the shelf
Annual pairs of laminae deposited in glacial lakes
cards.e: Each varve is a light summer silt layer plus a dark winter clay layer, together recording one year in a glacial lake. Counting varves gives time in years.

cards.q: The bird's-foot delta of the Mississippi is the type example of a:
cards.e: Where river input is strong and waves and tides are weak, distributary channels build far out as long fingers, like a bird's foot. Wave-dominated deltas (Nile) have smooth arcuate fronts; the Ganga-Brahmaputra is tide-dominated.

cards.q: When seawater evaporates, the salts precipitate in which order?
cards.e: The least soluble salt comes out first: calcium carbonate, then gypsum, then halite, and last the very soluble potassium-magnesium salts. Halite never comes before gypsum.

cards.q: On the deep ocean floor below the carbonate compensation depth (CCD), the typical sediment is:
cards.e: Below the CCD all calcium carbonate dissolves, so only red clay (and siliceous ooze) can collect. Calcareous ooze survives only above the CCD; coral and oolitic sands are shallow-water sediments.

cards.q: A sabkha is best described as:
o: A supratidal salt flat on an arid coast where evaporites grow within the sediment
A freshwater swamp behind a river levee
A deep-sea trench filled with turbidites
cards.e: In a sabkha, salty groundwater rises by capillary action and evaporates, so gypsum, anhydrite and halite grow inside the sediment. The Persian Gulf coast is the type area.

cards.q: The Talchir Boulder Bed at the base of the Gondwana sequence is interpreted as:
cards.e: It is unsorted, with faceted and striated boulders, and records the Permo-Carboniferous glaciation of Gondwanaland. Dune deposits would be well sorted sand without boulders.

cards.q: In Dott's sandstone classification, arenites and wackes are separated at a matrix content of:
cards.e: Under 15% matrix is an arenite (clean sandstone); 15-75% matrix is a wacke (dirty sandstone). 75% is the upper limit of wacke, above which the rock is a mudstone.

cards.q: A sandstone with more than 25% feldspar, derived from granite or gneiss, is called:
cards.e: Arkose is the feldspar-rich sandstone, usually pink and coarse, shed from nearby granite or gneiss. Greywacke is defined by its muddy matrix, and lithic arenite by rock fragments.

cards.q: Greywacke is most typical of which deposit?
o: Beach sands on a stable craton
cards.e: Greywacke is a dark, poorly sorted, matrix-rich sandstone dumped quickly by turbidity currents in deep basins beside rising mountain belts. Beach and dune sands are clean quartz arenites.

cards.q: A sandstone has 50% quartz, 30% feldspar, 8% rock fragments and 12% matrix. In Dott's scheme it is:
cards.e: Matrix is under 15%, so it is an arenite, not a wacke. Feldspar exceeds rock fragments and is well above 25% of the grains, so it is arkosic arenite (arkose).

cards.q: How does Folk's sandstone classification differ from Dott's?
o: Folk ignores the matrix and names the rock from quartz, feldspar and rock fragments alone
Folk uses cement type as one pole of the triangle
Folk's scheme applies only to carbonate rocks
Folk uses grain size instead of composition
cards.e: Folk recalculates quartz, feldspar and rock fragments to 100% and plots them on a QFR triangle, leaving matrix out of the name. Dott adds matrix percentage to split arenites from wackes.

cards.q: A limestone made of ooids cemented by clear sparry calcite is named, in Folk's scheme:
cards.e: Folk joins the allochem prefix (oo- for ooids) to the material between grains (-sparite for clear calcite cement). Oomicrite would have lime mud between the ooids.

cards.q: A lime-mud-supported limestone contains about 30% scattered shell fragments. In Dunham's scheme it is a:
cards.e: Mud-supported with more than 10% grains is wackestone. Dunham's mudstone has under 10% grains, and packstone is grain-supported, with grains touching one another.

cards.q: Dunham's limestone classification is based mainly on:
o: Depositional texture (mud support versus grain support)
cards.e: Dunham asks whether the rock is held up by mud or by grains, and whether mud is present. Folk's scheme, in contrast, is based on the type of allochem and on micrite versus sparite.

cards.q: Which Dunham rock type is grain-supported and contains no lime mud?
cards.e: Grainstone is clean, mud-free and grain-supported, and forms in high-energy water. Packstone is also grain-supported but still has mud between the grains.

cards.q: Folk's biolithite is equivalent to which Dunham term?
cards.e: Both names describe reef rock whose components were bound together by organisms as it grew. Grainstone is loose-grain sediment later cemented, not organically bound.

cards.q: In a limestone, abundant micrite (lime mud) between the grains indicates:
cards.e: Lime mud settles and stays only where the water is calm. In agitated water the mud is washed away and the pores are later filled by clear sparry calcite cement.

cards.q: Which of these is NOT a Category I (commercially producing) basin in the DGH three-category scheme (2017 onward)?
cards.e: The seven Category I basins are Cambay, Mumbai Offshore, Rajasthan, Krishna-Godavari, Cauvery, Assam Shelf and Assam-Arakan Fold Belt. Kutch has discoveries but no commercial production, so it is Category II.

cards.q: In the DGH three-category scheme (2017 onward), the Kerala-Konkan Basin is placed in:
o: Category II - discoveries awaiting commercial production
No category, as it is not counted as a sedimentary basin
cards.e: Kerala-Konkan has no commercial discovery yet, so it is one of the 14 Category III basins. Category II basins (Kutch, Saurashtra, Vindhyan, Mahanadi, Andaman) already have discoveries.

cards.q: The Cambay Basin is best described as:
o: A foreland basin in front of the Himalaya
A narrow north-south intracratonic rift graben
cards.e: Cambay is a Tertiary rift graben in Gujarat, floored by Deccan Traps and bounded by faults. The foreland basin of India is the Siwalik-Ganga belt, and Cambay is far younger than Proterozoic.

cards.q: The main producing reservoir of the Mumbai High field is:
cards.e: Mumbai (Bombay) High produces mainly from Miocene shelf limestone. The tempting wrong idea is a sandstone reservoir, which is true of Cambay and Assam but not of Mumbai High.

cards.q: India's first commercial oil well was drilled in 1889 at:
cards.e: Digboi in Upper Assam is India's oldest oil field. Ankleshwar (Cambay Basin) was found in 1960 and Mumbai High in 1974.

cards.q: Which pairing of oil or gas field and basin is correct?
cards.e: Ankleshwar is the best-known field of the Cambay Basin. Ravva belongs to the Krishna-Godavari Basin, Narimanam to the Cauvery Basin and Naharkatiya to Upper Assam.

p: UPSC Geologist Mains 2019 Geology Paper II
cards.q: The Gondwana coal basins of peninsular India are:
cards.e: Gondwana sediments are preserved in fault-bounded troughs along the Damodar, Son-Mahanadi and Pranhita-Godavari valleys, inside the craton. They are not linked to a mountain front or a continental margin.

cards.q: In the Tertiary sequence of coastal Kerala, the fossil-bearing marine limestone of Miocene age belongs to the:
cards.e: The Quilon limestone is the marine Miocene unit, seen near Padappakkara. The Warkalli Formation above it is sandstone, clay and lignite, and the Vaikom beds below are mainly sandstone and gravel.

cards.q: The Mangala oil field (discovered in 2004) lies in the:
cards.e: Mangala is the largest onshore oil find in India in recent decades and lies in the Barmer-Sanchor sub-basin of the Rajasthan Basin. The Barmer rift is the northern continuation of the Cambay rift, which makes Cambay the tempting wrong choice.

cards.q: As listed by the Directorate General of Hydrocarbons (2017 reassessment), India has how many sedimentary basins?
cards.e: DGH lists 26 basins covering about 3.36 million sq km. Seven is only the number of Category I basins and 14 the number of Category III basins.

cards.q: Which Indian basin is a forearc (island-arc) basin at a convergent plate margin?
cards.e: The Andaman-Nicobar Basin lies where the Indian plate is subducting below the Burma plate. Cauvery is a passive-margin rift basin, Cambay an intracratonic rift and Vindhyan a Proterozoic intracratonic basin.

cards.t: Origin of water: meteoric, juvenile, magmatic and sea waters
cards.q: Water that was trapped in the pores of a sedimentary rock at the time the sediment was deposited is called:
cards.e: Connate means 'born with' the rock; it is usually old, salty water. Juvenile water is new water from the deep Earth and was never inside a sediment at deposition.

cards.t: Origin of water: meteoric, juvenile, magmatic and sea waters
cards.q: Water coming from the Earth's deep interior that joins the hydrologic cycle for the very first time is termed:
cards.e: Juvenile means new: this water has never been at the surface before. Meteoric water is the opposite case, because it has already passed through the atmosphere as rain or snow.

cards.t: Origin of water: meteoric, juvenile, magmatic and sea waters
cards.q: Almost all the groundwater pumped from wells for drinking and irrigation is of which origin?
cards.e: Usable groundwater is rain or snow water that has soaked into the ground, so it is meteoric. Juvenile and magmatic waters are tiny in amount, and connate water is usually too salty to use.

cards.t: Origin of water: meteoric, juvenile, magmatic and sea waters
cards.q: Which statement about the origin of subsurface water is correct?
o: Juvenile water has already passed through the hydrologic cycle many times.
Connate water is normally fresher than present-day rain water.
Magmatic water released from magma at shallow depth is called volcanic water.
Meteoric water is water brought to the Earth by meteorites.
cards.e: Magmatic water is called volcanic water when it separates at shallow depth and plutonic water when it separates at great depth. 'Meteoric' refers to the atmosphere (weather), not to meteorites.

cards.q: If ice caps and glaciers are left out, the largest store of fresh water on Earth is:
cards.e: Groundwater is only about 0.6% of all water on Earth, but that is far more than all rivers and lakes together. Lakes look big, yet they hold only a small fraction of the groundwater volume.

cards.q: A closed basin receives 1500 mm of rain in a year. Runoff out of the basin is 600 mm and evapotranspiration is 700 mm. With no other gains or losses, the change in storage is:
cards.e: Water balance: change in storage = inflow - outflow = 1500 - (600 + 700) = +200 mm. The +800 and +900 values come from subtracting only one of the two outflows.

cards.q: Which of the following is a non-recording rain gauge, long used as the standard gauge in India?
cards.e: The Symons gauge only collects rain; an observer measures it once a day. The tipping-bucket, weighing-bucket and siphon gauges are all recording gauges that trace rainfall against time.

cards.q: In which method of finding mean rainfall over a basin is each rain gauge weighted by an area bounded by the perpendicular bisectors of the lines joining neighbouring gauges?
cards.e: Perpendicular bisectors build a polygon around each gauge, and the polygon area is the weight. The isohyetal method uses areas between lines of equal rainfall, not polygons.

cards.q: For a hilly basin with strong orographic (mountain-caused) rainfall, the most accurate method of estimating mean areal rainfall is the:
cards.e: Isohyets (lines of equal rainfall) can be drawn to follow the hills, so the method takes relief into account. Thiessen polygons depend only on gauge positions and ignore topography.

cards.q: Three rain gauges have Thiessen polygon areas of 20, 30 and 50 km2 and record 10, 20 and 30 mm of rain respectively. The Thiessen mean rainfall is:
cards.e: Mean = (20x10 + 30x20 + 50x30) / 100 = 2300 / 100 = 23 mm. The value 20 mm is the simple arithmetic mean, which ignores the areas.

cards.q: Which tool is used to check whether the long-term record of a rain gauge station is consistent, for example after the gauge was shifted?
cards.e: In a double-mass curve, cumulative rain at the station is plotted against the cumulative average of nearby stations; a break in slope shows inconsistency. A hyetograph only shows rainfall intensity against time for one storm.

cards.q: According to Horton's equation, the infiltration capacity of a soil during a long, steady storm:
o: Decreases exponentially to a constant value
cards.e: Horton: f = fc + (f0 - fc)e^(-kt). The rate starts high on dry soil and decays to a steady final rate fc. It does not fall to zero, because saturated soil still lets water pass.

cards.q: In a double-ring infiltrometer, the purpose of the water-filled outer ring is to:
o: Increase the head of water on the soil
Collect surface runoff from the plot
Stop water from the inner ring spreading sideways
cards.e: The outer ring acts as a buffer, so flow below the inner ring is vertical and the reading is reliable. A single ring over-reads because water also spreads sideways.

cards.q: A storm of uniform intensity gives 10 cm of rain in 8 hours and produces 6 cm of direct runoff. The phi-index of the storm is:
cards.e: Phi-index = (rainfall - runoff) / duration = (10 - 6) / 8 = 0.5 cm/h. The value 1.25 cm/h is the rainfall intensity itself, not the loss rate.

cards.q: A lysimeter is an instrument used to measure:
cards.e: A lysimeter is a tank of soil with plants in which every water input and output is measured, so the water used by evapotranspiration can be worked out. Infiltration is measured with an infiltrometer.

cards.q: A Class A evaporation pan beside a reservoir loses 8 mm of water in a day. Taking a pan coefficient of 0.7, the evaporation from the reservoir is about:
cards.e: Lake evaporation = pan evaporation x pan coefficient = 8 x 0.7 = 5.6 mm. A small metal pan heats up more than a lake, so the pan value must be reduced, not increased (11.4 mm comes from dividing).

cards.q: A stream hydrograph is a plot of:
cards.e: A hydrograph shows how stream discharge (or stage) changes with time. Rainfall intensity against time is a hyetograph, a commonly confused term.

cards.q: The base flow that keeps a perennial river flowing through the dry season is supplied by:
cards.e: Base flow is groundwater seeping into the channel, so it continues long after rain stops. Interflow is shallow and quick; it ends within days of a storm.

cards.q: Which part of a storm hydrograph is controlled by the release of water from basin storage and is almost independent of the storm that caused it?
cards.e: After the rain stops, the stream is fed only by water draining out of storage, so the recession limb reflects the basin alone. The rising limb and peak depend on storm intensity and duration as well.

cards.q: A unit hydrograph of a basin is the direct runoff hydrograph produced by:
o: 1 cm of total rainfall falling at any one rain gauge
Any storm that lasts exactly one hour
A steady discharge of 1 cubic metre per second at the outlet
1 cm of effective rainfall falling uniformly over the basin in a specified duration
cards.e: The 'unit' is one unit depth (1 cm) of effective rainfall, that is, rain that actually becomes direct runoff. It is not total rainfall, because part of the rain is lost to infiltration.

cards.q: The peak of a 2-hour unit hydrograph is 40 m3/s. A 2-hour storm gives 3 cm of effective rainfall, and the base flow is 10 m3/s. The peak of the flood hydrograph is:
cards.e: Unit hydrograph ordinates scale with rainfall excess: 3 x 40 = 120 m3/s of direct runoff. Add the base flow of 10 m3/s to get 130 m3/s. Stopping at 120 forgets the base flow.

cards.q: In the straight-line method of base flow separation, the number of days N from the peak to the end of direct runoff (N = 0.83 A^0.2) is estimated from the:
cards.e: A is the drainage area in km2: bigger basins keep delivering direct runoff for longer. The empirical formula does not use the peak discharge or the rainfall depth.

cards.q: A stream whose bed lies below the water table, so that groundwater flows into it, is called:
cards.e: Effluent (gaining) stream: groundwater flows out into the channel. An influent (losing) stream is the reverse; its water seeps down to a water table lying below the bed.

cards.t: Subsurface movement and vertical distribution of groundwater
cards.q: The correct order of subsurface water zones from the ground surface downward is:
o: Soil-water zone, capillary fringe, intermediate zone, zone of saturation
Intermediate zone, soil-water zone, capillary fringe, zone of saturation
Capillary fringe, soil-water zone, intermediate zone, zone of saturation
Soil-water zone, intermediate zone, capillary fringe, zone of saturation
cards.e: The soil-water zone is at the top (root zone), and the capillary fringe sits directly on the water table. The intermediate zone lies between them.

cards.t: Subsurface movement and vertical distribution of groundwater
cards.q: The capillary fringe above the water table would be thickest in which material?
cards.e: Capillary rise increases as pores get smaller, so fine silt lifts water much higher (about a metre) than sand or gravel (a few centimetres). Coarse materials have wide pores and almost no fringe.

cards.t: Subsurface movement and vertical distribution of groundwater
cards.q: At the water table, the pressure of the pore water is:
o: Equal to the weight of the overlying rock
cards.e: The water table is defined as the surface where water pressure equals atmospheric pressure. Above it (including the capillary fringe) the pressure is less than atmospheric; below it, greater.

cards.t: Subsurface movement and vertical distribution of groundwater
cards.q: Which statement about the water table is correct?
o: It is the upper surface of a confined aquifer.
It is a subdued copy of the land surface, higher under hills than under valleys.
It is always a flat, horizontal surface.
It marks the top of the capillary fringe.
cards.e: The water table rises under hills and falls toward valleys, but with gentler relief than the ground. The capillary fringe lies above the water table, and confined aquifers have a piezometric surface instead.

cards.t: Subsurface movement and vertical distribution of groundwater
cards.q: The imaginary surface joining the levels to which water rises in tightly cased wells that tap a confined aquifer is the:
cards.e: Confined water is under pressure, so it rises above the top of the aquifer to the piezometric surface. The water table is a real surface of saturation and belongs to unconfined aquifers.

cards.t: Subsurface movement and vertical distribution of groundwater
cards.q: The ground surface at a non-flowing observation well is 85 m above mean sea level, and the depth to water in the well is 12 m. The hydraulic head at the well is:
cards.e: Hydraulic head = elevation of the measuring point - depth to water = 85 - 12 = 73 m above mean sea level. Adding the two numbers (97 m) is the usual slip.

cards.q: A spring formed simply because the land surface dips down and cuts the water table is a:
cards.e: In a depression spring the ground falls below the water level, so water flows out. A contact spring needs a permeable bed resting on a less permeable bed.

cards.q: On a hill slope, water seeps out along the line where a permeable sandstone rests on an impermeable shale. This is a:
cards.e: Water moving down through the sandstone cannot enter the shale, so it moves sideways and comes out along the contact. A tubular spring issues from solution channels or lava tubes.

cards.q: A hot spring that throws out water and steam at intervals, driven by superheated water at depth, is a:
cards.e: In a geyser, deep water becomes superheated, flashes to steam and ejects the water column from time to time. A fumarole gives out only steam and gases, with no water eruption.

cards.q: In Bryan's classification of springs (as given in Todd), which one of the following results from non-gravitational forces?
cards.e: Volcanic and fissure springs are the non-gravitational group; they are usually thermal. Depression, contact and artesian springs are all gravity springs, driven by ordinary hydraulic head.

cards.q: A saturated clay bed that holds a lot of water but cannot transmit it at a useful rate is best called an:
cards.e: An aquiclude stores water but does not yield it; clay is the classic example. An aquifuge neither stores nor transmits water, so it is wrong for a porous, water-filled clay.

cards.q: Massive, unfractured granite that neither contains nor transmits water is an example of an:
cards.e: An aquifuge has no connected openings, so it neither holds nor passes water. An aquiclude (such as clay) does hold water but will not release it.

cards.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
cards.e: Sandy clay lets water leak through slowly, which is what an aquitard does. Gravel and coarse sand are good aquifers, and massive granite is an aquifuge.

cards.q: An aquifer that gains or loses water through a semi-pervious confining layer above or below it is called a:
cards.e: When the confining layer is an aquitard, water leaks vertically through it, so the aquifer is leaky. A fully confined aquifer has impermeable layers with no such leakage.

cards.q: A small body of groundwater held above the main water table by a local clay lens is a:
cards.e: The clay lens acts like a saucer and holds a perched water body within the zone of aeration. It is not confined, because its upper surface is a free (perched) water table.

cards.q: A well tapping a confined aquifer will flow at the surface without pumping when:
o: The storage coefficient of the aquifer exceeds 0.1
The piezometric surface lies above the ground surface
The well is drilled to below mean sea level
The water table lies above the top of the aquifer
cards.e: Water in the well rises to the piezometric surface; if that is higher than the ground, the well overflows (flowing artesian well). Depth of the well or sea level has nothing to do with it.

cards.q: When a confined aquifer is pumped and remains fully saturated, the water released from storage comes mainly from:
o: Compression of the aquifer and expansion of the water
cards.e: Lower pressure lets the water expand slightly and the aquifer skeleton compress, and this squeezes out a little water. Gravity drainage of pores happens only in unconfined aquifers.

cards.t: Concepts of drainage basin and groundwater basin
cards.q: The boundary of a surface drainage basin (watershed) is the:
cards.e: Rain falling inside the ridge line (topographic divide) drains to one outlet. A groundwater divide is a ridge in the water table and bounds groundwater flow, not surface flow.

cards.t: Concepts of drainage basin and groundwater basin
cards.q: Which statement about a groundwater basin is correct?
o: Its boundary need not coincide with the surface drainage divide.
It always has exactly the same boundary as the river basin above it.
It can contain only one unconfined aquifer.
It is defined only by the topographic ridges around it.
cards.e: A groundwater basin is bounded by geology (faults, rock contacts) and groundwater divides, which may differ from surface ridges. It may hold one aquifer or several connected aquifers.

cards.t: Concepts of drainage basin and groundwater basin
cards.q: A ridge (crest) in the water table from which groundwater flows away in opposite directions is called a:
cards.e: No groundwater crosses a groundwater divide; flow diverges from it on both sides. A cone of depression is the opposite shape, a hollow in the water table around a pumped well.

cards.q: A sand has a porosity of 20% (n = 0.20). Its void ratio is:
cards.e: Void ratio e = n / (1 - n) = 0.20 / 0.80 = 0.25. The value 0.17 comes from wrongly using n / (1 + n), which is the formula for getting n from e.

cards.q: Which of the following materials normally has the highest total porosity?
cards.e: Clay has a porosity of about 45-55%, more than gravel (25-40%). Gravel is the better aquifer only because its pores are large and connected; porosity and permeability are different things.

cards.q: Equal-sized spheres in the tightest (rhombohedral) packing have a porosity of about:
cards.e: Rhombohedral packing gives the minimum porosity, about 26%. About 48% (47.6%) is the value for the loosest, cubic packing.

cards.t: Hydrological properties of rocks - specific yield, specific retention
cards.q: An aquifer material has a porosity of 35% and a specific retention of 12%. Its specific yield is:
cards.e: Porosity = specific yield + specific retention, so Sy = 35 - 12 = 23%. Adding the two (47%) is wrong, because retention is the part of the pore water that does not drain.

cards.t: Hydrological properties of rocks - specific yield, specific retention
cards.q: The water table in an unconfined aquifer of area 10 km2 falls by 2 m. If the specific yield is 0.15, the volume of water drained is:
cards.e: Volume = area x fall x Sy = 10,000,000 m2 x 2 m x 0.15 = 3,000,000 m3. The 20 million m3 figure is the full rock volume dewatered, without applying specific yield.

cards.t: Hydrological properties of rocks - hydraulic conductivity
cards.q: Intrinsic permeability, the property measured in darcys, has the dimensions of:
cards.e: Intrinsic permeability depends only on the pore geometry of the rock, and 1 darcy is about 10^-12 m2. Velocity (L/T) is the dimension of hydraulic conductivity, the usual confusion.

cards.t: Hydrological properties of rocks - hydraulic conductivity
cards.q: Hydraulic conductivity differs from intrinsic permeability because it also depends on:
o: The saturated thickness of the aquifer
The density and viscosity of the fluid
cards.e: K = k x density x g / viscosity, so the same rock has a different K for water, oil or warm water. Saturated thickness enters only when K is multiplied by it to give transmissivity.

cards.q: A confined sand aquifer is 25 m thick and has a hydraulic conductivity of 12 m/day. Its transmissivity is:
cards.e: T = K x b = 12 x 25 = 300 m2/day. Adding the numbers (37) or dividing them (0.48) are the common slips.

cards.q: The SI-based unit commonly used for transmissivity is:
cards.e: Transmissivity = hydraulic conductivity (m/day) x thickness (m) = m2/day. The unit m/day belongs to hydraulic conductivity, and 1/m to specific storage.

cards.t: Hydrological properties of rocks - storage coefficient
cards.q: A pumping test gives a storage coefficient of 0.0002. The aquifer tested is most likely:
cards.e: Confined aquifers have very small storativity (about 0.00005 to 0.005) because water comes only from compression. Unconfined, perched and water-table aquifers drain their pores, giving values of about 0.01 to 0.30.

cards.t: Hydrological properties of rocks - storage coefficient
cards.q: Which of the following aquifer properties is dimensionless?
cards.e: Storage coefficient is a volume of water per unit area per unit head change, so the units cancel. Specific storage is per unit volume per unit head and has the unit 1/m.

cards.t: Hydrological properties of rocks - hydraulic conductivity
cards.q: An aquifer in which the hydraulic conductivity at a point is the same in every direction is described as:
cards.e: Isotropy is about direction: K is equal in all directions at a point. Homogeneity is about place: K is the same at every point. An aquifer can be homogeneous and still anisotropic.

cards.t: Hydrological properties of rocks - hydraulic conductivity
cards.q: Two horizontal beds, each 5 m thick, have hydraulic conductivities of 10 m/day and 30 m/day. The equivalent hydraulic conductivity for flow parallel to the beds is:
cards.e: Parallel to layers: K = (10x5 + 30x5) / 10 = 20 m/day (thickness-weighted arithmetic mean). The value 15 m/day is the harmonic mean, which applies to flow across the beds.

cards.q: When atmospheric pressure rises, the water level in a well tapping a confined aquifer:
o: Rises in summer and falls in winter
cards.e: The extra air pressure acts fully on the water in the open well, but the aquifer skeleton carries part of the load, so the well level is pushed down. In unconfined aquifers there is almost no response.

cards.q: The barometric efficiency of a confined coastal aquifer is 0.65. Its tidal efficiency is:
cards.e: For a confined aquifer, barometric efficiency + tidal efficiency = 1, so tidal efficiency = 1 - 0.65 = 0.35. The value 1.54 comes from wrongly taking the reciprocal.

cards.q: A shallow water table under dense vegetation falls during the day and recovers at night. The cause of this daily cycle is:
cards.e: Plants with roots near the water table (phreatophytes) draw water in daylight; at night the draft stops and the level recovers. Barometric effects appear mainly in confined aquifers, not at a shallow water table.

cards.q: After the monsoon the water table in an unconfined hard-rock aquifer rises by 4 m. If the specific yield is 0.03, the recharge by the water table fluctuation method is:
cards.e: Recharge depth = specific yield x rise = 0.03 x 4 m = 0.12 m = 120 mm. Dividing the rise by the yield (133) is the usual mistake.

cards.q: In most of India, the deepest groundwater levels of the year are recorded in:
cards.e: Levels fall through the dry season and reach their lowest just before the south-west monsoon. August and November are during or after the rains, when levels are shallow.

cards.q: The Tertiary sedimentary formations of the Kerala coast, arranged from oldest to youngest, are:
cards.e: Alleppey beds are at the bottom and Warkalli beds at the top. Memory hook: A-V-Q-W is alphabetical order from the base upward.

cards.q: Which Tertiary aquifer of Kerala is the most extensively developed (most heavily tapped by wells)?
cards.e: Warkalli sands are the shallowest Tertiary aquifer, so they are the easiest to tap and the most used. The Vaikom aquifer is regarded as the most potential, but it lies deeper.

cards.q: Among the Tertiary formations of coastal Kerala, which is regarded by CGWB as the most potential aquifer, with thick coarse sands and gravels?
cards.e: The Vaikom beds contain thick, coarse sand and gravel layers that give high yields. Quilon beds are mainly limestone and clay and form a poor aquifer.

cards.q: In the crystalline rock areas of Kerala, deep bore wells draw their water mainly from:
o: Primary pores between mineral grains of the fresh rock
Fractures and joints in the hard rock
cards.e: Fresh charnockite, khondalite and gneiss have almost no primary porosity, so deep water is found only in fractures. Solution caverns belong to limestone, and vesicles to basalt.

cards.q: In the 2024 dynamic groundwater resource assessment of Kerala, which of these blocks was placed in the 'critical' category?
cards.e: In 2024 Kerala had three critical blocks: Kasaragod, and Chittur and Malampuzha in Palakkad district. No block in the state was over-exploited.

cards.q: Under the GEC-2015 methodology, an assessment unit with a stage of groundwater extraction of 95% is categorised as:
cards.e: Critical = above 90% and up to 100%. Over-exploited applies only above 100%, when extraction is more than the annual extractable resource.

cards.q: A block has an annual extractable groundwater resource of 60 million m3 and an annual extraction of 45 million m3. Its stage of extraction and GEC-2015 category are:
cards.e: Stage = (45 / 60) x 100 = 75%. Semi-critical covers above 70% and up to 90%; safe is only up to 70%. Dividing the wrong way round gives 133%.

cards.q: The dynamic groundwater resources of India are at present (2025 assessment) estimated using which methodology?
cards.e: GEC-2015 (Groundwater Estimation Committee, 2015) replaced GEC-1997 and is used by CGWB and the States together. NAQUIM is the aquifer mapping programme, not a resource estimation method.

cards.q: The headquarters of the Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) is at:
cards.e: CGWB, under the Ministry of Jal Shakti, has its headquarters at Faridabad in Haryana. Roorkee has the National Institute of Hydrology, Hyderabad the NGRI and Kolkata the GSI headquarters.

cards.q: According to the national Dynamic Ground Water Resources assessment of 2025, the stage of groundwater extraction for India as a whole was about:
cards.e: The 2025 figure is 60.63%: about 247 BCM extracted out of about 408 BCM extractable. The national average is in the safe range, though about 11% of units are over-exploited.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: The measuring point of an observation well is at 86.0 m above mean sea level and the depth to water below it is 11.5 m. What is the hydraulic head at the well?
cards.e: Head = elevation of measuring point minus depth to water = 86.0 - 11.5 = 74.5 m. Adding the two (97.5 m) is the common slip; water stands below the measuring point, so depth is subtracted.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: Two piezometers 600 m apart along the flow direction show heads of 52 m and 49 m. The hydraulic gradient is:
cards.e: i = head loss / distance = 3 / 600 = 0.005. Gradient has no units, so '3 m' is only the head loss, and 200 is the ratio turned upside down.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: What is the minimum number of wells, not in a straight line, needed to fix the direction of groundwater flow in an area?
cards.e: Three head values define the plane of the water table, like a three-point problem for strike and dip. Two wells give only the apparent gradient along the line joining them.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: Groundwater always moves from a point of:
o: higher hydraulic head to lower hydraulic head
cards.e: Hydraulic head (elevation head plus pressure head) is the driving potential. Water can move toward higher pressure (downward in recharge areas) or uphill toward higher elevation (in discharge areas), as long as total head falls.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: Which of these is one of the Dupuit assumptions for flow in an unconfined aquifer?
o: The aquifer is confined above and below by impermeable beds
Flow is vertical everywhere in the saturated zone
The hydraulic gradient equals the slope of the water table and does not change with depth
Flow is turbulent near the water table
cards.e: Dupuit assumed horizontal flow (vertical equipotentials) with gradient equal to the water table slope. The theory is for unconfined aquifers and laminar flow, so the other options contradict it.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: When flow lines pass from a low-conductivity layer into a high-conductivity layer, they:
o: bend away from the normal and run more nearly parallel to the boundary
bend toward the normal to the boundary
continue without any change in direction
cards.e: By the tangent law, K1/K2 = tan(a1)/tan(a2), the angle from the normal is larger in the more permeable layer. So water travels a long way along permeable beds and crosses tight beds by the shortest path.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: The Laplace equation describes groundwater flow that is:
o: steady, in a homogeneous and isotropic medium
cards.e: Combining Darcy's law with continuity for steady flow in a homogeneous isotropic medium gives the Laplace equation. Unsteady flow needs an extra storage term (S/T x dh/dt).

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
cards.q: An aquifer has hydraulic conductivity 10 m/day, hydraulic gradient 0.01 and cross-sectional area 500 square metres. The discharge through it by Darcy's law is:
cards.e: Q = K i A = 10 x 0.01 x 500 = 50 cubic metres per day. The other values come from misplacing the decimal point of the gradient.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: A sand has K = 20 m/day and effective porosity 0.25. Under a hydraulic gradient of 0.005, the seepage (actual) velocity of groundwater is:
cards.e: Darcy velocity = K i = 20 x 0.005 = 0.1 m/day. Seepage velocity = 0.1 / 0.25 = 0.4 m/day. 0.1 m/day is the Darcy velocity, and 0.025 comes from multiplying by porosity instead of dividing.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: A pollutant enters an aquifer with K = 50 m/day, hydraulic gradient 0.002 and effective porosity 0.2. About how long will it take to reach a well 100 m down-gradient, moving at the speed of the water?
cards.e: Seepage velocity = K i / ne = 50 x 0.002 / 0.2 = 0.5 m/day, so 100 m takes 200 days. Using the Darcy velocity (0.1 m/day) wrongly gives 1000 days.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: Darcy's law is valid only when groundwater flow is:
o: transitional, with Reynolds number between 100 and 1000
unsaturated, with air filling most pores
laminar, with Reynolds number below about 1 (up to about 10)
cards.e: The law needs head loss to be proportional to velocity, which is true only for laminar flow at very low Reynolds numbers. The figure 2000 is the laminar limit for pipes, not for porous media.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: Which statement about Darcy velocity and seepage velocity is correct?
o: The two are equal in every well-sorted sand
Seepage velocity is always smaller than Darcy velocity
Darcy velocity is an apparent velocity; seepage velocity is larger and equals Darcy velocity divided by effective porosity
Seepage velocity equals Darcy velocity multiplied by porosity
cards.e: Darcy velocity spreads the discharge over the whole area, grains included. Real flow uses only the pores, so actual velocity = Darcy velocity / effective porosity, which is always larger since porosity is less than 1.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: A falling-head permeameter is preferred over a constant-head permeameter for measuring the hydraulic conductivity of:
cards.e: Fine-grained samples pass too little water to measure a steady discharge, so the slow fall of head in a thin standpipe is timed instead. Coarse sand and gravel are tested with the constant-head type.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: An aquifer 2 km wide has transmissivity 500 square metres per day and a hydraulic gradient of 0.004. The groundwater flow through it is:
cards.e: Q = T i W = 500 x 0.004 x 2000 = 4000 cubic metres per day. Remember to convert 2 km to 2000 m; using 2 gives only 4.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: Darcy's law is LEAST likely to hold in which of the following?
o: Fine sand of an alluvial aquifer
Medium sand far from any pumping well
Large solution conduits in karst limestone
cards.e: Wide karst conduits carry fast, turbulent flow, so head loss is no longer proportional to velocity. Flow through sand and silt under natural gradients is slow and laminar.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.q: The Thiem equation is used to analyse pumping-test data for:
o: steady radial flow, using drawdowns in two observation wells
unsteady radial flow in a confined aquifer
flow to a well in a leaky aquifer with storage in the aquitard
recovery of water level after pumping stops
cards.e: Thiem (1906) is the equilibrium (steady-state) equation and needs two observation wells. Unsteady flow is handled by Theis and recovery by the Theis recovery method.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.q: A well in a confined aquifer is pumped at 1500 cubic metres per day until steady state. Drawdowns are 3 m and 1 m in observation wells 10 m and 100 m away. Transmissivity by the Thiem equation is about:
cards.e: T = Q ln(r2/r1) / [2 pi (s1 - s2)] = 1500 x 2.303 / (2 x 3.1416 x 2) = about 275. Using log10 (which is 1) instead of the natural log (2.303) gives the wrong value of about 120.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
cards.q: In a constant-rate test at 500 cubic metres per day, the Cooper-Jacob time-drawdown line for an observation well shows a drawdown of 0.5 m per log cycle of time. Transmissivity is about:
cards.e: T = 2.303 Q / (4 pi ds) = 2.303 x 500 / (4 x 3.1416 x 0.5) = about 183. The value 366 comes from using 2 pi, which belongs to the distance-drawdown method.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.q: In a Cooper-Jacob analysis, T = 100 square metres per day, the straight line cuts the zero-drawdown axis at t0 = 0.001 day, and the observation well is 15 m from the pumped well. The storativity is:
cards.e: S = 2.25 T t0 / r^2 = 2.25 x 100 x 0.001 / 225 = 0.001. Forgetting to square the distance gives 0.015. A value of 0.001 is typical of a confined aquifer.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.q: The Cooper-Jacob straight-line method is a valid simplification of the Theis equation when:
o: the pumping rate varies with time
cards.e: For small u (long time or small distance) the higher terms of the well function become negligible and drawdown varies with log time. Large u means early time, when the data still curve.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.q: Which of the following is NOT an assumption of the Theis non-equilibrium equation?
o: The aquifer is of infinite areal extent
The aquifer receives leakage through its confining bed
The well fully penetrates the aquifer
Discharge is constant throughout the test
cards.e: Theis assumed a perfectly confined aquifer with no leakage or recharge; all water comes from storage. Leaky aquifers need the Hantush-Jacob method.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.q: In the Theis recovery method, transmissivity is obtained from a plot of:
o: discharge against drawdown on log-log paper
drawdown against distance on arithmetic scales
residual drawdown against the logarithm of t/t' (time since pumping began / time since it stopped)
cards.e: Residual drawdown plotted against log(t/t') is a straight line whose slope gives T = 2.303 Q / (4 pi ds'). Specific capacity against discharge belongs to the step-drawdown test.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.q: During a pumping test near an impermeable dyke, the Jacob semi-log time-drawdown line will, after some time:
o: reverse and show rising water levels
cards.e: A barrier boundary acts like an image pumping well, so the rate of drawdown doubles. The line turns horizontal near a recharge boundary such as a river, not a barrier.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.q: In the method of images, a fully penetrating river near a pumping well is replaced by:
o: an imaginary discharging well at the same distance on the other side of the river
a real observation well on the river bank
an imaginary recharging well at the same distance on the other side of the river
an impermeable wall along the river
cards.e: A recharging image well cancels drawdown along the river line, giving the constant-head condition. A discharging image well is used for an impermeable barrier.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.q: Which pair of 'aquifer condition - method of pumping-test analysis' is correctly matched?
o: Steady flow in confined aquifer - Neuman method
Unconfined aquifer with delayed yield - Thiem method
Large-diameter dug well - Cooper-Jacob distance-drawdown method
cards.e: Hantush and Jacob (1955) solved flow to a well in a leaky aquifer. Delayed yield is handled by Boulton and Neuman, steady confined flow by Thiem, and large-diameter wells by Papadopulos-Cooper.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.q: Which statement about a slug test is correct?
o: It is unsuitable for low-permeability formations
It gives hydraulic conductivity of only a small volume of aquifer around the tested well
It requires pumping at constant discharge for 24 hours or more
It needs at least two observation wells
cards.e: A slug test changes the water level suddenly in one well and times its recovery, so it samples only the material close to that well. It needs no pump or observation wells and suits tight formations.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.q: At a point between two pumping wells, well A alone would cause 1.2 m of drawdown and well B alone 0.8 m. With both pumping in a confined aquifer, the drawdown at that point is:
cards.e: By the principle of superposition, drawdowns add: 1.2 + 0.8 = 2.0 m. This is well interference; it is why closely spaced wells each yield less.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Theory of groundwater flow - well hydraulics and pumping tests
cards.q: Compared with a well in a highly transmissive aquifer pumped at the same rate, a well in a low-transmissivity aquifer has a cone of depression that is:
cards.e: A poor aquifer needs a steep gradient to move the same quantity of water, so the cone is deep and steep but limited in spread. High transmissivity gives a shallow, wide cone.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: The specific capacity of a well is defined as:
o: volume of water released per unit decline in head per unit area
discharge per unit thickness of aquifer
cards.e: Specific capacity = Q/s, the yield for each metre of drawdown. Drawdown per unit discharge is its inverse (specific drawdown); the option about volume released per unit head decline per unit area defines storativity.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: A well pumped at 600 litres per minute shows a stabilised drawdown of 12 m. Its specific capacity is:
cards.e: Specific capacity = Q/s = 600 / 12 = 50 litres per minute per metre of drawdown. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 7200.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: In Jacob's equation for drawdown in a pumping well, sw = BQ + CQ^2, the term CQ^2 stands for:
o: formation loss due to laminar flow in the aquifer
drawdown due to a barrier boundary
well loss due to turbulent flow through the screen and inside the well
loss of head due to partial penetration only
cards.e: CQ^2 is the well loss: it rises with the square of discharge because flow through the gravel pack, screen and casing is turbulent. BQ is the formation loss, which is proportional to Q.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: A step-drawdown test shows that at the design discharge the formation loss is 8 m and the well loss is 2 m. The well efficiency is:
cards.e: Efficiency = formation loss / total drawdown = 8 / (8 + 2) = 80%. The value 20% is the share of well loss, and 25% wrongly divides well loss by formation loss.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: For a well with well-loss constant C = 0.00002 day^2/m^5, the well loss at a discharge of 500 cubic metres per day is:
cards.e: Well loss = C Q^2 = 0.00002 x 500 x 500 = 5 m. Forgetting to square the discharge gives 0.01 m.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: In a step-drawdown test, specific drawdown (s/Q) is plotted against discharge (Q). The intercept of the straight line on the s/Q axis gives:
cards.e: Dividing sw = BQ + CQ^2 by Q gives s/Q = B + CQ: intercept B, slope C. Storativity cannot be found from the pumped well alone.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: As the pumping rate of a well is increased, its specific capacity generally:
o: increases, because more water enters the well
decreases, because well loss grows as the square of discharge
cards.e: Drawdown rises faster than discharge because of the CQ^2 term, so Q/s falls. Specific capacity also falls with pumping time, so the rate and duration must always be stated.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: A well with a central caisson and horizontal screened pipes pushed out radially into river-bed sand is called a:
cards.e: The radial collector or Ranney well draws river water through sand by induced infiltration and gives very large yields. A cavity well is a vertical tube well with no screen.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: Filter-point wells are best suited to which hydrogeological setting in Kerala?
o: Hard laterite capping on hill tops
Shallow sandy coastal alluvium with a high water table
