cards.e: A filter-point well is a shallow, small-diameter pipe with a short screen jetted or bored into loose saturated sand. It cannot be sunk in hard rock or hard laterite, and deep Tertiary aquifers need proper tube wells.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: 'Surangams', the traditional horizontal tunnel wells cut into laterite hills, are typical of which district of Kerala?
cards.e: Surangams of Kasaragod tap the water table inside laterite hills and deliver water by gravity, like the qanats of Iran. Alappuzha is a flat coastal district of filter-point and tube wells.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: Which statement about a cavity tube well is correct?
o: It is a large-diameter open well in hard rock
It has a long screen surrounded by gravel pack
It has horizontal laterals radiating from a caisson
It has no screen and draws water from a hollow formed in sand below a strong clay roof
cards.e: A cavity well ends just below a stiff clay layer; sand is pumped out until a stable cavity forms, and water enters by spherical flow. Screens and gravel packs belong to strainer-type tube wells.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: Which statement about a typical bore well in hard crystalline rock is correct?
o: It draws water mainly from intergranular pores of fresh rock
It is 3 to 6 m in diameter and lined with masonry
It is cased only through the loose overburden, and the rest is left as an open hole
It is screened and gravel-packed over its whole depth
cards.e: Hard rock stands without support, so casing is needed only in the weathered top. Water comes from fractures, not pores; full screens and gravel packs are for tube wells in loose sediments.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: Which drilling method is fastest and most widely used for bore wells in hard rocks such as the charnockites and gneisses of Kerala?
cards.e: The DTH air hammer strikes the bit at the hole bottom and compressed air blows out the cuttings, giving fast progress in hard rock. Reverse rotary, augers and jetting work only in soft, unconsolidated material.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: In reverse-circulation rotary drilling, the drilling fluid moves:
o: as compressed air down the annulus
down the drill pipe and up the annulus
down the annulus and up through the drill pipe
cards.e: The fluid and cuttings are sucked up through the wide drill pipe at high velocity, and clean water flows back down the annulus. Down the pipe and up the annulus is direct rotary.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: In cable-tool (percussion) drilling, the cuttings are removed from the hole by:
cards.e: The crushed rock forms a slurry with water in the hole, and a bailer (a pipe with a bottom valve) lifts it out. Mud circulation, compressed air and suction belong to rotary and DTH methods.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of drilling mud in direct rotary drilling?
o: Increasing the permeability of the aquifer around the hole
Supporting the borehole wall with a mud cake
cards.e: Mud actually reduces permeability near the hole by plastering the wall and invading the formation. That is why the well must be developed afterwards.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: Shallow wells in soft clay and sand, made with a rotary bucket-type tool that cuts and lifts the soil, are called:
cards.e: Augers bore the hole and bring up the soil in the bucket or on the screw. Driven wells are hammered in, and jetted wells are washed in by a water stream.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
cards.q: To limit head loss, sand entry and incrustation, the entrance velocity of water through a well screen should not exceed about:
cards.e: The standard design figure is 0.03 m/s (3 cm/s, or 0.1 foot per second). The screen length, diameter and open area are chosen so that the design discharge enters at or below this speed.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
cards.q: In a thick, homogeneous unconfined aquifer, the well screen is best placed in:
o: the bottom one-third to one-half of the aquifer
the top one-third of the aquifer
the entire thickness including the unsaturated zone
cards.e: Drawdown dewaters the upper part of an unconfined aquifer, so screen there would stand dry. Screening the lower third to half leaves room for drawdown while keeping the screen submerged.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
cards.q: The uniformity coefficient used in well-screen and gravel-pack design is the ratio:
cards.e: Uniformity coefficient = d60/d10 from the grain-size curve; d10 alone is the effective size. A value near 1 means very uniform sand.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
cards.q: An artificial gravel pack around the screen is most needed when the aquifer is:
cards.e: Fine uniform sand would need extremely narrow slots and would still enter the well. A coarser pack holds the sand back and allows wider slots. Coarse graded material develops its own natural pack; hard rocks need no screen.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
cards.q: Which of the following is NOT a method of well development?
o: Cement grouting of the annular space
cards.e: Grouting seals the space outside the casing against pollution; it does nothing to clean the aquifer face. Surging, jetting and backwashing all loosen and remove fines and mud cake.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
cards.q: The main purpose of well development is to:
o: remove mud cake and fine particles so the well yields sand-free water at maximum specific capacity
increase the depth of the well
test the verticality of the casing
cards.e: Development repairs the clogging caused by drilling and grades the material around the screen. Sealing saline zones is done with blank casing and grout, not by development.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
cards.q: A tube well screen is choked by calcium carbonate scale. The usual chemical treatment is:
cards.e: Acid dissolves carbonate incrustation. Polyphosphates are for dispersing clay and iron oxide, and chlorine (bleaching powder) is for iron bacteria and slime.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
cards.q: Which chemical character of groundwater is most likely to cause CORROSION, rather than incrustation, of a steel well screen?
o: High bicarbonate alkalinity with dissolved iron above 2 mg/L
Low pH with dissolved carbon dioxide, oxygen or hydrogen sulphide
High carbonate hardness and high pH
cards.e: Acidic water with dissolved gases attacks metal. Hard, alkaline water and a positive Langelier index point to scale formation (incrustation), and iron-rich water deposits iron hydroxide.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
cards.q: Hydrofracturing is a technique used mainly to:
o: improve the yield of low-yielding bore wells in hard rock
measure the storage coefficient of confined aquifers
cards.e: Water injected at high pressure between packers cleans and opens fractures and links them to the bore well. It is a yield-improvement method for hard-rock bore wells, not a drilling or testing method.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Construction, design, development and maintenance of wells
cards.q: The pumping water level in a tube well is 30 m below ground. A centrifugal pump placed at ground level cannot be used mainly because:
o: its discharge is always too small
suction lift is limited by atmospheric pressure to about 10 m in theory and 6 to 7 m in practice
cards.e: A surface pump relies on atmospheric pressure to push water up the suction pipe, which sets a limit of about 10.3 m (less in practice). Deeper levels need a submersible or vertical turbine pump placed in the well.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - physical and chemical properties of water
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
cards.q: A water sample has 40 mg/L calcium and 12 mg/L magnesium. Its total hardness, as CaCO3, is about:
cards.e: Total hardness = 2.5 x Ca + 4.1 x Mg = 100 + 49 = about 150 mg/L as CaCO3. Simply adding Ca and Mg (52) ignores the conversion to CaCO3 equivalents.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - physical and chemical properties of water
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
cards.q: Temporary hardness of water, which can be removed by boiling, is caused by:
cards.e: Boiling breaks down bicarbonates and calcium carbonate settles out. Sulphates and chlorides of Ca and Mg cause permanent hardness; sodium and potassium salts do not cause hardness at all.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - physical and chemical properties of water
cards.q: A water analysis reports calcium as 100 mg/L. Expressed in milliequivalents per litre, this is about:
cards.e: meq/L = mg/L / equivalent weight. Calcium has atomic weight 40 and valence 2, so its equivalent weight is 20 and 100/20 = 5 meq/L. Dividing by the atomic weight (40) gives the wrong 2.5.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - physical and chemical properties of water
cards.q: A groundwater sample has an electrical conductivity of 1000 microsiemens/cm at 25 degrees C. Its TDS is most likely about:
cards.e: TDS in mg/L is roughly 0.64 x EC (range 0.55 to 0.75), so about 640 mg/L. TDS in mg/L is always numerically less than EC in microsiemens/cm for natural waters.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - physical and chemical properties of water
cards.q: According to the Chebotarev sequence, the dominant anion of groundwater changes along the flow path and with depth in the order:
cards.e: Young, shallow recharge water is bicarbonate type; with age and depth it gains sulphate and finally chloride, the most soluble, and TDS rises. The reverse order would mean water getting fresher with age.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - physical and chemical properties of water
cards.q: Alkalinity and hardness of water are both conventionally reported as mg/L of:
cards.e: Both are expressed as the equivalent amount of calcium carbonate so they can be compared directly. This lets carbonate and non-carbonate hardness be separated by simple subtraction.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - physical and chemical properties of water
cards.q: Which isotope is most suitable for identifying 'young' groundwater recharged within the last few decades?
cards.e: Tritium has a half-life of only about 12.3 years and was added to rain by nuclear tests after 1952, so its presence proves recent recharge. Carbon-14 (5730 years) dates water thousands of years old.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality - physical and chemical properties of water
cards.q: Sodium-bicarbonate type groundwater with very low calcium and magnesium is commonly produced by:
cards.e: Clays take Ca and Mg out of the water and give Na in return, softening it naturally. Sea water would give Na-Cl water, gypsum Ca-SO4 water, and pyrite oxidation acidic sulphate water.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: As per IS 10500:2012, the acceptable limit and the permissible limit (in the absence of an alternate source) for fluoride in drinking water are:
cards.e: BIS gives 1.0 mg/L as acceptable and 1.5 mg/L as the upper permissible limit; WHO's guideline value is 1.5 mg/L. Above 1.5 mg/L dental fluorosis begins.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: As per IS 10500:2012, the limit for nitrate (as NO3) in drinking water, with no relaxation, is:
cards.e: The BIS limit is 45 mg/L as NO3 (WHO: 50 mg/L). 10 mg/L is the same limit expressed as nitrate-nitrogen in US practice, and 250 mg/L is the BIS acceptable limit for chloride.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: As per IS 10500:2012, the acceptable and permissible limits for total dissolved solids in drinking water are:
cards.e: TDS: 500 mg/L acceptable, 2000 mg/L permissible. The pair 200/600 is for total hardness and 250/1000 is for chloride, which is why they are tempting.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: The WHO guideline value for arsenic in drinking water, which is also the BIS acceptable limit, is:
cards.e: The limit is 0.01 mg/L, that is 10 micrograms per litre (10 ppb). Arsenic causes cancer on long exposure, so the limit is among the lowest for any common constituent.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: Which pair of 'water constituent in excess - health effect' is correctly matched?
cards.e: Excess fluoride causes dental fluorosis (mottled enamel). Nitrate causes blue baby syndrome, arsenic causes skin lesions and cancer, and Minamata disease is from mercury (cadmium causes itai-itai).

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2016 Hydrogeology
cards.q: Irrigation water has Na = 10, Ca = 4 and Mg = 4, all in meq/L. Its sodium adsorption ratio (SAR) is:
cards.e: SAR = Na / sqrt[(Ca + Mg)/2] = 10 / sqrt(4) = 10 / 2 = 5. Forgetting to halve the sum gives 10 / sqrt(8) = 3.5. An SAR of 5 falls in class S1 (low sodium hazard).

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: A water sample has CO3 = 0.5, HCO3 = 6.0, Ca = 2.0 and Mg = 1.5 (all meq/L). Its residual sodium carbonate (RSC) and irrigation class are:
cards.e: RSC = (CO3 + HCO3) - (Ca + Mg) = 6.5 - 3.5 = 3.0 meq/L. Water with RSC above 2.5 is unsuitable; below 1.25 is safe.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: The US Salinity Laboratory (USSL) diagram for classifying irrigation water plots:
o: sodium adsorption ratio against electrical conductivity
TDS against the ratio Na/(Na + Ca)
cards.e: USSL plots SAR (sodium hazard) against EC (salinity hazard), giving classes C1S1 to C4S4. The Wilcox diagram uses percent sodium against EC, and TDS against Na/(Na + Ca) is the Gibbs diagram.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: A water sample has (Na + K) = 3 meq/L and (Ca + Mg) = 7 meq/L. Its percent sodium and Wilcox quality class are:
cards.e: Percent sodium = 3 x 100 / (3 + 7) = 30%, which lies in the 20-40% 'good' class. The value 43% comes from dividing by (Ca + Mg) alone instead of by total cations.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: In the USSL classification, irrigation water of class C3 (high salinity hazard) has an electrical conductivity of:
cards.e: C1 is below 250, C2 250-750, C3 750-2250 and C4 above 2250 microsiemens/cm. C3 water needs good drainage and salt-tolerant crops.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: Water with a high sodium adsorption ratio harms irrigated land mainly because sodium:
o: precipitates as insoluble sodium carbonate in pores
disperses soil clay and reduces soil permeability
is directly poisonous to all crops at any level
cards.e: Sodium replaces calcium on clay particles; the clay disperses and seals the soil, which becomes hard and poorly drained. Sodic soils are alkaline, not acidic, and sodium carbonate is very soluble.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Graphical presentation of water quality data
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2016 Hydrogeology
cards.q: In a Piper trilinear diagram, the central field onto which points from the cation and anion triangles are projected has the shape of a:
cards.e: Piper's diagram has two triangles and a diamond between them. The Durov diagram projects onto a square, which is the tempting wrong choice.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Graphical presentation of water quality data
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
cards.q: Which pair of 'diagram - main feature' is correctly matched?
o: Schoeller diagram - two triangles and a diamond
Gibbs diagram - vertical bars of cations and anions
Collins diagram - TDS against Na/(Na + Ca)
Stiff diagram - polygon with cations on the left and anions on the right of a vertical axis
cards.e: Stiff patterns are polygons drawn about a central vertical axis in meq/L. Two triangles and a diamond is Piper, vertical bars is Collins, and TDS against Na/(Na + Ca) is Gibbs.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Graphical presentation of water quality data
cards.q: Which diagram shows ion concentrations in meq/L on a logarithmic vertical scale, with the points of each sample joined by a line?
cards.e: The Schoeller semi-logarithmic diagram shows actual concentrations, and samples with parallel lines have the same ion ratios. Piper and Durov show only percentages; Wilcox is for irrigation suitability.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Graphical presentation of water quality data
cards.q: The Gibbs diagram is used to find out:
o: whether precipitation, rock weathering or evaporation controls the water chemistry
the suitability of water for irrigation
cards.e: Gibbs (1970) plotted TDS against Na/(Na + Ca) or Cl/(Cl + HCO3) and marked fields of precipitation, rock and evaporation dominance. Irrigation suitability is read from USSL and Wilcox diagrams.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Graphical presentation of water quality data
cards.q: Which of the following is NOT a method of presenting water-chemistry data?
cards.e: The Hjulstrom diagram relates stream velocity to erosion, transport and deposition of sediment grains. Piper, Stiff and Schoeller diagrams all display major-ion chemistry of water.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Graphical presentation of water quality data
cards.q: Two water samples plot at exactly the same point in the diamond field of a Piper diagram. This shows that they have:
o: the same relative proportions of major ions
cards.e: Piper diagrams use percentages of meq/L, so they show ion ratios only. A dilute and a very saline water can plot at the same point, which is the main limitation of the diagram.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Graphical presentation of water quality data
cards.q: Fresh, recently recharged groundwater in a humid hard-rock area would most likely belong to which hydrochemical facies?
cards.e: Recharge water rich in CO2 dissolves silicates and carbonates to give dilute Ca-HCO3 (or Ca-Mg-HCO3) water. Na-Cl facies indicates sea water, connate water or very old, evolved groundwater.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
cards.q: The Nalgonda technique of defluoridation uses which set of chemicals?
cards.e: Alum forms flocs that remove fluoride, lime corrects the pH and bleaching powder disinfects. The method was developed by NEERI and named after fluoride-hit Nalgonda district.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
cards.q: Which mineral is the odd one out as a geological source of fluoride in groundwater?
cards.e: Arsenopyrite (FeAsS) is a source of arsenic, not fluoride. Fluorite and fluorapatite contain fluorine as a main element, and biotite carries it in place of hydroxyl.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
cards.q: High fluoride concentrations are most typical of groundwater that is:
o: alkaline, sodium-bicarbonate type and poor in calcium
very young and of low TDS in a high-rainfall area
of Ca-SO4 type from gypsum beds
cards.e: Calcium removes fluoride by forming insoluble fluorite, so only low-calcium, alkaline Na-HCO3 water can hold much fluoride. Calcium-rich water therefore usually has little fluoride.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
cards.q: Endemic fluorosis in India was first reported, in 1937, from:
cards.e: Shortt and co-workers described it from Nellore district (then in Madras Presidency) in 1937. Nalgonda is famous as a badly affected district and for the Nalgonda technique, but it was not the first report.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
cards.q: The widely accepted cause of high arsenic in the shallow aquifers of the Bengal basin is:
o: reductive dissolution of arsenic-bearing iron oxyhydroxides in organic-rich Holocene sediments
intrusion of sea water into the delta
cards.e: The arsenic is geogenic. Under reducing conditions created by decaying organic matter, iron oxyhydroxide coatings dissolve and release their adsorbed arsenic. It is not an industrial or agricultural pollutant.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
cards.q: In which of these states does arsenic contamination of groundwater occur in hard-rock terrain rather than in river alluvium?
cards.e: In Rajnandgaon district of Chhattisgarh arsenic comes from sulphide-bearing volcanic and granitic rocks. In Bihar, Assam and Uttar Pradesh it occurs in young alluvium of the Ganga and Brahmaputra plains.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
cards.q: Which district of Kerala is best known for fluoride above the permissible limit in groundwater from crystalline rocks?
cards.e: The Muthalamada area of eastern Palakkad, in the dry Palghat Gap with hornblende-biotite gneiss, has well-known high fluoride. Alappuzha is the other known area, but there it comes from deep sedimentary aquifers.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
cards.q: Water from a dug well in the laterite midlands of Kerala is clear when drawn but turns reddish-brown on standing. The most likely cause is:
cards.e: Dissolved ferrous iron is oxidised by air to insoluble reddish-brown ferric hydroxide. Laterite is iron-rich and its water slightly acidic, so iron is a common problem; fluoride and nitrate give no colour.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater quality in different provinces of India - problems of arsenic and fluoride
cards.q: High nitrate in shallow groundwater most commonly comes from:
o: nitrogen fertilisers, sewage and animal waste
cards.e: Unlike fluoride and arsenic, nitrate is mainly man-made. It is very soluble and leaches easily from farm land and septic tanks to the water table.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Saline water intrusion in coastal and other aquifers and its prevention
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2016 Hydrogeology
cards.q: In a coastal unconfined aquifer the water table stands 2 m above mean sea level. By the Ghyben-Herzberg relation, the depth of the fresh-salt water interface below sea level is about:
cards.e: z = 40 h = 40 x 2 = 80 m below sea level. The factor 40 comes from 1.000 / (1.025 - 1.000).

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Saline water intrusion in coastal and other aquifers and its prevention
cards.q: Over-pumping lowers the water table near a coast by 0.5 m. By the Ghyben-Herzberg relation, the salt-water interface will finally rise by about:
cards.e: The interface moves 40 times the change in water table: 40 x 0.5 = 20 m. This large multiplier is why small declines in coastal water levels are dangerous.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Saline water intrusion in coastal and other aquifers and its prevention
cards.q: If saline groundwater has a density of 1.020 g/cm3 and fresh water 1.000 g/cm3, the depth to the interface below sea level where the water table is 1.5 m above sea level is:
cards.e: z = [df / (ds - df)] x h = (1.000 / 0.020) x 1.5 = 50 x 1.5 = 75 m. The usual factor of 40 (giving 60 m) applies only when the salt-water density is 1.025.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Saline water intrusion in coastal and other aquifers and its prevention
cards.q: 'Upconing' in a coastal aquifer means:
o: the upward leakage of water through an aquitard
the seaward flow of fresh water over the salt-water wedge
the local cone-shaped rise of the salt-water interface beneath a pumping well
the rise of the water table after monsoon recharge
cards.e: Drawdown under the well lowers fresh-water head, so the denser salt water below bulges up as an inverted cone. If pumping is too heavy the cone reaches the well and the water turns salty.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Saline water intrusion in coastal and other aquifers and its prevention
cards.q: A line of recharge wells along the coast that creates a fresh-water 'pressure ridge' to hold back sea water is called:
cards.e: Injected fresh water raises the head near the coast above sea level and stops the wedge. An extraction barrier does the opposite: it pumps a trough to capture the incoming sea water.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Saline water intrusion in coastal and other aquifers and its prevention
cards.q: Which of the following would NOT help to control sea-water intrusion into a coastal aquifer?
o: Building a subsurface impermeable barrier parallel to the coast
Artificial recharge of the coastal aquifer
Deepening the coastal wells and increasing their pumping rate
cards.e: Heavier and deeper pumping lowers fresh-water head and draws the interface inland and upward. The other three raise the head near the coast or physically block the salt water.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Saline water intrusion in coastal and other aquifers and its prevention
cards.q: Which chemical ratio is commonly used to detect sea-water contamination of coastal groundwater?
cards.e: Chloride dominates sea water and bicarbonate dominates fresh groundwater, so a rising Cl/(CO3 + HCO3) ratio (Revelle's ratio) signals intrusion. Chloride is also conservative: it is not removed by reactions in the aquifer.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Saline water intrusion in coastal and other aquifers and its prevention
cards.q: The Thanneermukkom bund in Kerala was built mainly to:
o: prevent tidal salt water from entering the Kuttanad region through Vembanad Lake
store drinking water for Kochi city
recharge the laterite aquifers of the midlands
cards.e: It is a salt-water barrier across Vembanad Lake, closed in the dry season to protect the below-sea-level paddy fields of Kuttanad. It is not a storage dam or a power project.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Saline water intrusion in coastal and other aquifers and its prevention
cards.q: On a small coral island with a thin fresh-water lens floating on sea water, groundwater is best extracted by:
o: DTH bore wells drilled to 100 m
shallow skimming wells or infiltration galleries with low drawdown
reverse-circulation wells screened at the base of the lens
cards.e: Skimming a little water from the top of the lens over a wide area keeps drawdown small and avoids upconing of salt water. Deep or heavily pumped wells would quickly turn saline.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Saline water intrusion in coastal and other aquifers and its prevention
cards.q: Compared with the depth predicted by the simple Ghyben-Herzberg relation, the real fresh-salt water interface near the shoreline is:
o: shallower, because fresh water is static
deeper, because fresh water is flowing seaward and needs an outflow face
cards.e: Ghyben-Herzberg assumes no flow, which would give zero fresh-water thickness at the shore. Since fresh water does discharge to the sea, the interface lies somewhat deeper and is a mixing zone, not a sharp line.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater exploration - resistivity and well logging
p: UPSC Geo-Scientist and Geologist Exam 2019 Hydrogeology
cards.q: In a Wenner resistivity survey with electrode spacing 10 m, a current of 100 mA gives a potential difference of 50 mV. The apparent resistivity is about:
cards.e: Apparent resistivity = 2 pi a (V/I) = 2 x 3.14 x 10 x (50/100) = 31.4 ohm-m. Using pi instead of 2 pi gives 15.7.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater exploration - resistivity and well logging
cards.q: Vertical electrical sounding (VES) differs from resistivity profiling in that VES:
o: increases the electrode spacing about a fixed centre to study variation with depth
keeps the electrode spacing fixed and moves the whole array along a line
cards.e: Wider spacing makes current go deeper, so sounding gives a resistivity-depth picture at one spot. Moving a fixed-spacing array along a line is profiling, used to locate lateral changes such as dykes.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater exploration - resistivity and well logging
cards.q: A VES curve from granite-gneiss terrain shows top soil of moderate resistivity, a low-resistivity saturated weathered zone, and very high-resistivity fresh rock below. This three-layer curve is of:
cards.e: H-type has a low-resistivity middle layer (r1 > r2 < r3), giving a bowl-shaped curve, typical of hard-rock areas. K-type is the opposite, with a resistive middle layer.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater exploration - resistivity and well logging
cards.q: Which of these subsurface materials would show the LOWEST electrical resistivity?
cards.e: Salt water is rich in ions and conducts current very well, so resistivity can fall below 1 to 5 ohm-m. Dry sand and massive granite are very resistive, and fresh-water sand is moderate.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater exploration - resistivity and well logging
cards.q: On a natural gamma-ray log of a borehole in alluvium, the highest counts are normally recorded against:
cards.e: Clays and shales hold radioactive potassium-40, uranium and thorium, so they read high. Clean sand and gravel aquifers read low; this contrast is used to place well screens.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.t: Groundwater exploration - resistivity and well logging
cards.q: Which borehole log can still be run usefully after steel casing has been installed in the well?
cards.e: Gamma rays pass through steel casing, so nuclear logs work in cased holes. SP and normal resistivity logs need direct electrical contact between the fluid-filled open hole and the formation.

cards.s: Hydrogeology: Flow, Wells and Water Quality
cards.q: A recharge shaft is the preferred artificial recharge structure where:
o: the water table is at ground level
only saline water is available for recharge
a poorly permeable clay layer lies between the land surface and the unconfined aquifer
the aquifer is exposed at the surface as permeable sand
cards.e: A shaft pierces the clay layer and lets water pass directly to the aquifer. Where permeable sand is at the surface, simple spreading basins are cheaper and work well.

cards.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes earthquake magnitude from intensity?
o: Magnitude is written in Roman numerals; intensity is written in decimals
Magnitude falls with distance from the epicentre; intensity stays the same everywhere
Magnitude is a single value for an earthquake; intensity changes from place to place
Magnitude is found from damage surveys; intensity is read from seismograms
cards.e: Magnitude measures energy released at the source, so each earthquake has one value. Intensity describes shaking and damage at a place, so it varies with distance and ground type. The other options swap the two ideas.

cards.q: On the Richter scale, the maximum wave amplitude recorded for a magnitude 6 earthquake is how many times that for a magnitude 4 earthquake at the same distance?
cards.e: The scale is logarithmic: each unit means 10 times the amplitude. Two units mean 10 x 10 = 100 times. About 1000 times is the ratio of energy, not amplitude.

cards.q: According to the seismic code in force in India in 2026 (IS 1893 Part 1: 2016), the country is divided into how many seismic zones?
cards.e: There are four zones, II to V. Five zones (I to V) was the older scheme before Zone I was merged into Zone II in 2002. The 2025 revision that added a Zone VI was withdrawn by BIS in March 2026.

cards.q: In which seismic zone of India does the whole of Kerala lie?
cards.e: All of Kerala is in Zone III, the moderate hazard zone. Zone II is tempting because Kerala is on the stable peninsula, but the State was placed in Zone III.

cards.q: Which of these cities does NOT lie in Seismic Zone V, the highest hazard zone of India?
cards.e: Chennai is in Zone III. Guwahati (north-east India), Srinagar (Kashmir valley) and Bhuj (Kutch) are all in Zone V.

cards.q: Earthquake-induced liquefaction is most likely in which ground condition?
o: Loose, water-saturated fine sand and silt
cards.e: Loose saturated sand tries to compact when shaken, pore-water pressure shoots up and the grains lose contact. Dry or dense soils and clays with cohesion do not liquefy easily.

cards.q: The 1967 Koyna earthquake in Maharashtra is most often cited as an example of:
o: An earthquake caused by mine collapse
cards.e: It followed the filling of the Koyna (Shivajisagar) reservoir, whose water load and pore pressure triggered slip on faults below. Koyna is inside the plate, far from any plate boundary.

cards.q: The Indian Ocean tsunami of 26 December 2004 was generated by:
o: A submarine landslide off the Makran coast
A submarine volcanic eruption at Krakatoa
A strike-slip earthquake on the Chaman fault
A megathrust earthquake at the subduction zone off Sumatra
cards.e: A giant thrust rupture (Mw 9.1-9.3) where the Indian plate dives under the Burma plate lifted the sea floor. Krakatoa caused a tsunami in 1883, not 2004. Strike-slip faults move sideways and rarely make big tsunamis.

cards.q: Which of the following is a NON-structural flood-management measure?
cards.e: Flood-plain zoning controls land use so that people and property stay out of the flood's way. The other three are engineering structures or works, so they are structural measures.

cards.q: A flood with a return period of 50 years has what probability of being equalled or exceeded in any single year?
cards.e: Annual probability = 1/T = 1/50 = 0.02, which is 2%. A 5% chance would be a 20-year flood.

cards.q: What is the approximate probability that a 100-year flood occurs at least once in a period of 100 years?
cards.e: Risk = 1 - (1 - 1/T)^n = 1 - (0.99)^100, which is about 0.63. It is not 100%, because a return period is only a long-term average.

cards.q: How does urbanisation of a catchment typically change the storm hydrograph of its stream?
o: Higher peak discharge and shorter lag time
Lower peak discharge and shorter lag time
Higher peak discharge and longer lag time
Lower peak discharge and longer lag time
cards.e: Paved surfaces and drains stop infiltration and deliver run-off quickly. So the peak is higher and comes sooner. Forested catchments show the opposite: a low, delayed peak.

cards.q: The Kerala floods of August 2018 are described as the worst in the State since the 'flood of 99'. In which year did that earlier flood occur?
cards.e: '99' refers to the Malayalam Era year 1099, which is 1924 CE. 1899 and 1999 are tempting only because they end in 99.

cards.q: Varnes' classification of slope movements is based on:
o: Type of movement and type of material
Volume of material and area affected
cards.e: Varnes named each landslide by its material (rock, debris, earth) and its movement (fall, topple, slide, spread, flow). Rainfall, volume and damage are not part of the scheme.

cards.q: A slump (rotational slide) characteristically moves along:
o: No surface at all - it falls freely through the air
A planar bedding or joint surface
cards.e: In a rotational slide the mass rotates on a spoon-shaped surface, leaving a curved scarp and a back-tilted block. Movement on a flat plane is a translational slide.

cards.q: For a slope, the forces resisting sliding total 450 kN and the forces driving sliding total 500 kN. The factor of safety and the condition of the slope are:
cards.e: Factor of safety = resisting / driving = 450 / 500 = 0.90. Below 1 the driving forces win, so the slope fails. 1.11 comes from dividing the wrong way round.

cards.q: Prolonged heavy rain triggers landslides mainly because it:
o: Raises pore-water pressure, lowering effective stress and shear strength
Increases the cohesion of clay in the slope
Raises the angle of internal friction
Reduces the weight of the slope material
cards.e: Water in the pores pushes grains apart, so friction and strength fall. Rain also adds weight; it does not reduce it. Cohesion and friction angle do not increase on wetting.

cards.q: Which action would REDUCE the stability of a slope instead of improving it?
o: Building a retaining wall at the toe
Dumping fill on the crest of the slope
cards.e: Extra load at the top adds to the driving force. Drains lower pore pressure, a toe wall adds support and rock bolts tie blocks together, so those three improve stability.

cards.q: The Mundakkai-Chooralmala landslide disaster in Wayanad district, Kerala, occurred on:
cards.e: It struck in the early hours of 30 July 2024. The other dates are real Kerala events: Kavalappara and Puthumala (8 August 2019), Pettimudi (6 August 2020) and Kokkayar-Koottickal (16 October 2021).

cards.q: Which landslide-district pair from Kerala is correctly matched?
cards.e: Pettimudi is near Munnar in Idukki. Kavalappara is in Malappuram and Puthumala in Wayanad (the two are swapped here), and Amboori is in Thiruvananthapuram.

cards.q: 'Soil piping', reported from the lateritic highlands of Kerala, refers to:
o: Subsurface erosion that forms tunnels or cavities within the soil
Cementing of soil pores by iron oxides
Laying of perforated pipes to drain a slope
Swelling of clay soil on wetting
cards.e: Flowing subsurface water washes out fine particles and leaves pipe-like tunnels, which may collapse and cause subsidence or landslides. It is a natural erosion process, not a drainage work.

cards.t: Natural hazards - river and coastal erosion
cards.q: A groyne built on an eroding beach is a structure that:
o: Is a sand ridge planted with grass
Lies offshore, parallel to the coast, to create calm water
Runs along the shore on land to reflect waves
Runs roughly perpendicular to the shore and traps sand moving along the coast
cards.e: A groyne sticks out across the beach and catches longshore drift on its updrift side. A shore-parallel wall on land is a seawall, and an offshore barrier is a breakwater.

cards.t: Natural hazards - river and coastal erosion
cards.q: Which of the following is a 'soft' coastal protection method?
cards.e: Beach nourishment adds sand to rebuild the beach and works with natural processes. Seawalls, tetrapods and groynes are hard engineering structures.

cards.t: Natural hazards - river and coastal erosion
cards.q: The mudbanks ('chakara') of the Kerala coast are best described as:
o: Calm nearshore patches of muddy sea that appear in the south-west monsoon and damp the waves
Mangrove-covered tidal flats present all through the year
Sand bars that close river mouths in the dry season
Coral reef flats exposed at low tide in summer
cards.e: Thick fluid mud in suspension absorbs wave energy, giving calm water and rich fishing during the rough monsoon. Sand bars closing river mouths ('pozhi') are a different, dry-season feature.

cards.t: Natural hazards - river and coastal erosion
cards.q: Indiscriminate sand mining from a river bed most directly leads to:
o: Raising of the river bed and more frequent overbank floods
More sediment supply to the coast
Rapid growth of the river delta
Lowering of the river bed and of the water table in nearby wells
cards.e: Taking out more sand than the river brings makes the channel cut down. Groundwater then drains to the deeper channel and wells go dry. The coast gets less sediment, not more.

cards.q: 'Kadavu Committees' for regulating sand removal are provided for under which Kerala law?
o: Kerala Ground Water (Control and Regulation) Act, 2002
Kerala Protection of River Banks and Regulation of Removal of Sand Act, 2001
Kerala Conservation of Paddy Land and Wetland Act, 2008
cards.e: A kadavu is a river-bank ghat where sand is removed; the 2001 Act sets up a committee for each. The Minor Mineral Rules deal with quarries and ordinary sand elsewhere, not with river kadavus.

cards.q: What is the correct sequence of the four stages of environmental clearance under the EIA Notification, 2006?
cards.e: First decide if an EIA is needed (screening), then what it must cover (scoping), then hear the public, and finally the expert committee appraises. Appraisal comes last because it uses the EIA report and the public's views.

cards.q: Under the EIA Notification, 2006, Category 'A' projects are appraised at the central level by the:
o: Expert Appraisal Committee of the Environment Ministry
cards.e: Category A projects go to the Union Environment Ministry, advised by an Expert Appraisal Committee. The State committee (SEAC) handles Category B. The NGT is a court that hears challenges; it does not appraise projects.

cards.t: Anthropogenic activities - open cast mining and quarrying
p: UPSC Civil Services Mains 2013 (Geology Paper II)
cards.q: Acid mine drainage is produced mainly by the oxidation of which mineral?
cards.e: Pyrite (FeS2) reacts with oxygen and water to give sulphuric acid and dissolved iron. Calcite actually neutralises acid. Hematite and gypsum are already oxidised minerals.

cards.t: Anthropogenic activities - open cast mining and quarrying
p: UPSC Civil Services Mains 2013 (Geology Paper II)
cards.q: Which of the following is a standard passive treatment for acid mine drainage?
o: Recirculating the water through the old mine workings
Adding sulphuric acid to precipitate the metals
Aerating the water over pyrite-rich waste rock
Passing the water through limestone drains to neutralise the acid
cards.e: Limestone (calcium carbonate) raises the pH, and dissolved metals then settle out as solids. Adding acid or more pyrite would make the problem worse.

cards.t: Anthropogenic activities - dumping of ores, mine waste and fly-ash
cards.q: Fly ash can partly replace cement in concrete because it is:
o: Rich in gypsum that sets on drying
A swelling clay that fills the voids
Pozzolanic - its silica and alumina react with lime and water to form cementing compounds
Mostly unburnt carbon that binds the aggregate
cards.e: A pozzolan has no binding power alone but reacts with the lime freed by cement to form extra binder. This is the basis of Portland Pozzolana Cement. Fly ash is glassy silica-alumina, not gypsum, carbon or clay.

cards.t: Anthropogenic activities - disposal of industrial and radioactive waste
cards.q: In vitrification, high-level radioactive waste is immobilised in:
cards.e: The waste is melted with glass-forming material into borosilicate glass, which is very durable. Cement and bitumen are used for low- and intermediate-level waste. Bentonite is a clay buffer packed around canisters.

cards.t: Anthropogenic activities - disposal of industrial and radioactive waste
cards.q: The internationally preferred option for final disposal of high-level radioactive waste is:
o: Burial in a shallow sanitary landfill
A deep geological repository in stable rock with multiple barriers
cards.e: Deep stable rock isolates the waste for the very long time it stays dangerous. Sea dumping of radioactive waste is banned internationally, and shallow burial is only for low-level waste.

cards.t: Anthropogenic activities - excess withdrawal of groundwater
cards.q: Land subsidence caused by heavy groundwater pumping results mainly from:
o: Compaction of compressible clay layers as pore pressure falls
cards.e: When water pressure drops, the load shifts to the grain skeleton and soft clay layers are squeezed for good. Quartz does not dissolve measurably, and salt-water movement does not lower the land.

cards.t: Anthropogenic activities - excess withdrawal of groundwater
cards.q: Which of the following is NOT a likely result of long-term over-pumping of a coastal aquifer?
o: Increase in base flow to streams
cards.e: Base flow is groundwater seeping into streams; it falls when the water table drops. The other three are well-known effects of over-pumping.

cards.q: 'Blue baby syndrome' (infant methaemoglobinaemia) is linked with drinking water that is high in:
cards.e: Nitrate is changed to nitrite in the infant's gut, and nitrite stops haemoglobin from carrying oxygen. Fluoride causes fluorosis and arsenic causes skin lesions, not blueness.

cards.q: Under IS 10500:2012, the maximum nitrate (as NO3) allowed in drinking water is:
cards.e: The nitrate limit is 45 mg/L, with no relaxation. The other figures are the familiar limits for arsenic (0.01 mg/L), fluoride (1.5 mg/L) and chloride (250 mg/L).

cards.q: Eutrophication of lakes downstream of farmland is driven mainly by run-off carrying:
cards.e: Nitrogen and phosphorus feed algal blooms; when the algae die, their decay uses up dissolved oxygen. Salts and heavy metals pollute water but do not cause blooms.

cards.q: The pesticide whose aerial spraying on cashew plantations in Kasaragod district, Kerala, caused a major health disaster is:
cards.e: Endosulfan, a persistent organochlorine, was sprayed from helicopters for over two decades. The Supreme Court banned it in India in 2011. DDT is also an organochlorine but is not the Kasaragod case.

cards.t: Organic and inorganic contamination of groundwater
cards.q: Which disease-contaminant pair is correctly matched?
cards.e: Minamata disease is methylmercury poisoning from eating contaminated fish. Itai-itai is due to cadmium, blue baby syndrome to nitrate and blackfoot disease to arsenic.

cards.t: Organic and inorganic contamination of groundwater
cards.q: Which of these is a DNAPL - a liquid that sinks through groundwater to the base of an aquifer?
cards.e: TCE, a chlorinated solvent, is denser than water and does not mix with it, so it sinks. Petrol, benzene and diesel are lighter than water (LNAPLs) and float on the water table.

cards.t: Organic and inorganic contamination of groundwater
cards.q: Itai-itai disease in the Jinzu river basin of Japan was caused by:
o: Mercury discharged by a chemical factory
Cadmium from zinc-mine waste entering irrigation water and rice
cards.e: Cadmium from upstream zinc mining polluted the river, the paddy fields and the rice. It weakened bones and kidneys. Mercury from a factory is the Minamata story.

cards.q: The reactive filling most widely used in permeable reactive barriers to treat chlorinated solvents and hexavalent chromium is:
cards.e: Iron metal gives up electrons, which break down chlorinated solvents and reduce Cr(VI) to insoluble Cr(III). Bentonite is used for impermeable cut-off walls, the opposite of a permeable barrier.

cards.q: Which remediation method extracts contaminated groundwater through wells and cleans it in a plant at the surface?
cards.e: Pump-and-treat brings the water up for treatment. A reactive barrier treats water in the ground as it flows through, and natural attenuation relies on natural processes with monitoring only.

cards.q: Supplying oxygen and nutrients to a petrol-contaminated aquifer so that native bacteria break down the hydrocarbons faster is called:
cards.e: Biostimulation is bioremediation that feeds the microbes already present. Vitrification is turning waste into glass, and incineration is burning it, neither of which uses microbes.

cards.q: Growing Indian mustard or the brake fern (Pteris vittata) to take up heavy metals or arsenic from polluted soil and shallow groundwater is an example of:
cards.e: Phytoremediation uses plants ('phyto') to extract or hold contaminants. Bioaugmentation adds microbes, while biosparging and bioventing pump air into the ground for microbes.

cards.q: Sodic (alkali) soils are commonly reclaimed by applying:
cards.e: Calcium from gypsum replaces sodium on the clay, and the sodium is then leached away. Lime is the remedy for acid soils, the opposite problem.

cards.q: A soil has an electrical conductivity of 8 dS/m, an exchangeable sodium percentage of 8 and a pH of 7.9. It is classified as:
cards.e: EC above 4 dS/m with ESP below 15 and pH below 8.5 defines a saline soil. A sodic soil needs ESP above 15; a saline-sodic soil has high EC and high ESP together.

cards.q: What is the correct order of water-erosion stages as run-off becomes more concentrated?
cards.e: Raindrop splash loosens the soil, thin sheet flow carries it, the flow gathers into small rills and rills deepen into gullies. Rills come before gullies because they are smaller.

cards.q: Which international agreement deals specifically with desertification and land degradation in drylands?
cards.e: The UNCCD (1994) is the dryland degradation treaty. Ramsar is on wetlands, Montreal on ozone-depleting substances and Basel on hazardous waste movement.

cards.t: Environment protection - legislative measures in India
cards.q: Articles 48A and 51A(g), which deal with protection of the environment, were added to the Constitution of India by the:
cards.e: The 42nd Amendment added Article 48A (a Directive Principle for the State) and Article 51A(g) (a Fundamental Duty of citizens). The 73rd Amendment is on Panchayati Raj.

cards.t: Environment protection - legislative measures in India
cards.q: Arrange these Acts in order of enactment, earliest first: (1) Environment (Protection) Act, (2) Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, (3) Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, (4) Wild Life (Protection) Act.
cards.e: Wildlife 1972, Water 1974, Air 1981, Environment 1986. Hook: animals first, then water, then air, then the umbrella over everything.

cards.t: Environment protection - legislative measures in India
cards.q: Which Act, passed in the wake of the Bhopal gas tragedy, is called India's 'umbrella' environmental legislation?
o: Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981
Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
cards.e: The 1986 Act lets the Central Government act on any environmental matter, so it covers the gaps left by earlier Acts. The Public Liability Insurance Act also followed Bhopal, but it only covers relief to accident victims.

cards.t: Environment protection - legislative measures in India
cards.q: After the 2023 amendment (in force from 1 December 2023), the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 is officially named:
cards.e: The new name means Forest (Conservation and Augmentation) Act; the year 1980 was kept. Van Adhikar Adhiniyam, 2006 is the separate Forest Rights Act.

cards.t: Environment protection - legislative measures in India
cards.q: Which statement about the National Green Tribunal is correct?
o: It must follow the procedure of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
It was set up in 2010 under the NGT Act with its principal bench at New Delhi
It was created under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 with its principal bench at Bhopal
It tries criminal offences under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972
cards.e: The NGT has its own Act of 2010 and sits mainly at New Delhi; Bhopal is only a zonal bench. It is guided by natural justice, not the Civil Procedure Code, and it has no criminal jurisdiction.

cards.t: Environment protection - legislative measures in India
cards.q: Who is the ex officio Chairperson of the National Disaster Management Authority?
cards.e: The Disaster Management Act, 2005 makes the Prime Minister the chairperson. The Home Ministry is the nodal ministry, which makes the Home Minister a tempting wrong choice.

cards.t: Environment protection - legislative measures in India
cards.q: The Central Ground Water Authority was constituted in 1997 under which Act?
o: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
cards.e: It was notified under Section 3(3) of the Environment (Protection) Act on the Supreme Court's direction. The Water Act deals with pollution boards, not with regulating groundwater extraction.

cards.t: Environment protection - legislative measures in India
cards.q: Coastal Regulation Zone notifications regulate land on the landward side generally up to what distance from the High Tide Line?
cards.e: The CRZ covers land up to 500 m from the High Tide Line. 50 m and 200 m are the No Development Zone widths for rural areas (CRZ-III A and III B) in the 2019 notification.

cards.t: Environment protection - legislative measures in India
cards.q: Under Section 15 of the MMDR Act, 1957, rules for granting concessions for minor minerals such as building stone and ordinary sand are made by:
cards.e: Minor minerals are left to the States, which is why Kerala has its own Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 2015. The Centre makes the rules for major minerals.

cards.t: Environment protection - legislative measures in India
cards.q: The MMDR Amendment Act, 2023 removed six minerals from the list of atomic minerals. Which of these was NOT one of the six?
cards.e: The six were lithium, beryllium, niobium, tantalum, titanium and zirconium. Uranium and thorium remain atomic minerals reserved for the Government.

cards.q: The recommendation that about 37% of the Western Ghats be notified as Ecologically Sensitive Area came from:
o: The High Level Working Group headed by K. Kasturirangan
The Western Ghats Ecology Expert Panel headed by Madhav Gadgil
The M. S. Swaminathan committee on coastal regulation
The Kerala State expert committee headed by Oommen V. Oommen
cards.e: The Kasturirangan group (2013) marked about 37% (about 60,000 sq km) as sensitive. The earlier Gadgil panel (2011) wanted the entire Western Ghats treated as sensitive in three graded zones.

cards.q: Under the Kerala Ground Water (Control and Regulation) Act, 2002, a permit from the State Ground Water Authority is needed to dig a well in:
o: Any holding larger than one hectare
Any panchayat with more than 10,000 people
cards.e: The Government declares 'notified areas' where groundwater needs regulation; there a permit is needed for a new well and existing wells must be registered. The Act has no population or land-size test.

cards.q: The Kerala law that prohibits conversion and reclamation of paddy fields and wetlands came into force in:
cards.e: The Kerala Conservation of Paddy Land and Wetland Act came into force on 12 August 2008. 2001 is the river sand Act, 2002 the Ground Water Act and 2015 the Minor Mineral Concession Rules.

cards.t: Anthropogenic activities - excess withdrawal of groundwater
cards.q: Plachimada in Palakkad district, Kerala, is known in environmental history for:
o: A public agitation against groundwater depletion and pollution by a soft-drink bottling plant
A hydro-electric project dropped to save a rainforest
Coastal erosion blamed on black-sand mining
Health damage from aerial spraying of endosulfan
cards.e: Villagers blamed the bottling plant for dry and polluted wells, and it stopped working in 2004. Endosulfan is the Kasaragod case and the dropped hydel project is Silent Valley.
